### [1] [PhysLDM: Latent Diffusion for High-Fidelity Deformable Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07609)
*Yu Zhang,Xudong Xu,Xingang Pan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhysLDM is a unified latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation, using a spatiotemporal VAE to achieve ~2.48mm reconstruction precision at 78x token compression, and demonstrating that diffusion models outperform deterministic regression for chaotic deformable dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is challenging due to error accumulation in autoregressive methods and computational prohibitive direct multi-frame prediction. There's a need for compact spatiotemporal latent representation for mesh-based volumetric physics, and it's unclear whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is better for prediction.

Method: 1) A holistic spatiotemporal VAE that avoids "staircase" artifacts of standard temporal compression; 2) Systematic comparison between regression and diffusion methods in the learned latent space; 3) Latent diffusion model trained on Objaverse-scale dataset for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation.

Result: Achieves ~2.48 mm reconstruction precision on meter-scale scenes at up to 78x token compression. Diffusion better models chaotic deformable dynamics while deterministic regression produces non-physical averages. A single PhysLDM generalizes zero-shot to unseen OOD datasets (GSO and Toys4K). Enables efficient solution of inverse problems and higher-order design optimization.

Conclusion: PhysLDM is the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation. The key insight is that diffusion models are superior for modeling chaotic deformable dynamics compared to deterministic regression.

Abstract: Neural simulation of high-fidelity deformable bodies is a foundational challenge in computer graphics and physical AI. Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is hard: autoregressive methods are susceptible to error accumulation, while direct multi-frame prediction at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. This motivates a compact spatiotemporal latent representation, which is largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is the more appropriate predictive paradigm. To address these coupled challenges, we introduce PhysLDM, a unified latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation. Its core is a holistic spatiotemporal VAE that avoids the "staircase" artifacts of standard temporal compression (as in common video VAEs), achieving ~2.48 mm reconstruction precision on meter-scale scenes at up to 78x token compression. Based on this reliable latent space, we systematically compare regression and diffusion methods. Our experiments uncover a key modeling insight: complex deformable dynamics are often chaotic, and in this regime deterministic regression tends to produce non-physical averages, whereas diffusion better models their distribution. Accordingly, we employ a latent diffusion model that effectively learns from the chaotic data to generate physically plausible trajectories. Trained purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale dataset, a single PhysLDM generalizes zero-shot to unseen OOD datasets (GSO and Toys4K). Its differentiability further enables efficient solution of inverse problems and higher-order design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM is the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation.

</details>


### [2] [Medical Image Alignment Assessment as a Test of Generalist Visual Reasoning in Frontier Multimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06896)
*Ross Callaghan,Niannu Gao,Hojjat Azadbakht,Hui Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on medical image alignment assessment tasks, testing whether they can perform novel visual judgments without task-specific optimization. GPT-6 achieved over 85% accuracy across most scenarios, while older models performed barely above chance. Fine-tuned local models matched frontier performance on trained tasks but transferred poorly to new settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether frontier MLLMs can perform novel visual judgments that humans make reliably, without task-specific parameter optimization. Medical image alignment assessment was chosen as the test case since human visual assessment remains the gold standard but is impractical to scale.

Method: Evaluated recent generations of MLLMs on two medical image alignment tasks, varying prompting strategies and image-presentation methods. Compared against a locally fine-tuned MLLM and a task-specific CNN. Tested generalization to unseen settings.

Result: GPT-6 achieved over 85% accuracy across almost all scenarios tested. Models released only a few months ago generalized poorly and performed barely above chance in some settings. Fine-tuned local models could match or exceed frontier-model performance on trained tasks but transferred substantially less effectively to unseen settings.

Conclusion: Medical image alignment is a useful test bed for generalist visual reasoning. Frontier multimodal models are beginning to acquire capabilities that could support a common quality-control mechanism across heterogeneous medical-imaging pipelines, representing an inflection point in MLLM visual assessment capabilities.

Abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly positioned as general purpose visual reasoners as part of the quest for artificial general intelligence. A key test of this generality is whether they can perform novel visual judgments that humans can make reliably from visual evidence and task instructions, without task-specific parameter optimisation. We investigate this question through the task of medical image alignment assessment, where the goal is to establish whether there is anatomical correspondence between two images. Human visual assessment of image alignment is still the gold standard and most common approach; however, it requires trained operators and is impractical to scale for large datasets. We evaluate recent generations of MLLMs on two exemplar medical image alignment tasks, varying both prompting strategies and image-presentation methods. We compare against a locally fine-tuned MLLM and a task-specific CNN to examine the trade-off between frontier general purpose models and smaller models that require specific task optimisation but can be used locally. We show that are reaching an inflection point, where frontier MLLMs can now perform effective visual assessment of medical image alignment. Models released only a few months ago generalise poorly and, in some settings, perform barely above chance, whereas GPT-6 achieves over 85% across almost all scenarios tested. Fine-tuned local models can match or exceed frontier-model performance on the tasks on which they are trained, but transfer substantially less effectively to unseen settings. These findings identify medical image alignment as a useful test bed for generalist visual reasoning and suggest that frontier multimodal models are beginning to acquire capabilities that could support a common quality-control mechanism across heterogeneous medical-imaging pipelines.

</details>


### [3] [View Matters: Keyframe-Guided Text-Driven 3D Gaussian Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08179)
*Kaizhe Zhang,Yijie Zhou,Weizhan Zhang,Xuanyu Wang,Feng Lei,Sha Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: View Matters is a view-importance-aware framework for text-driven 3D Gaussian editing that identifies reliable keyframes and propagates their editing signals asymmetrically to non-keyframes, achieving superior CLIP text-image similarity and directional similarity while maintaining cross-view coherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-driven 3D Gaussian editing typically treats all views equally, ignoring that different viewpoints provide supervision of substantially different quality. Less informative views can weaken the editing results when they are given the same weight as reliable views that clearly show the scene and match the edit instruction.

Method: The framework consists of three components: (1) Keyframe Importance Estimation (KIE) - identifies reliable views using geometric visibility, semantic distinctiveness, and edit relevance; (2) Keyframe-Guided Editing (KGE) - propagates editing signals asymmetrically from keyframes to non-keyframes without noisy reverse influence; (3) Importance-Aware Optimization (IAO) - preserves reliability preference during 3DGS optimization.

Result: Across 23 scene-prompt pairs, View Matters achieves the highest average CLIP text-image similarity of 0.2822 and directional similarity of 0.2564 among evaluated methods, with a four-minute editing time. Adjacent-view analysis shows the fidelity-oriented editing process maintains cross-view coherence.

Conclusion: View Matters successfully addresses the view-equality problem in text-driven 3D Gaussian editing by introducing view-importance awareness, achieving state-of-the-art editing quality while maintaining cross-view coherence and efficient editing time.

Abstract: Text-driven 3D Gaussian editing commonly does not distinguish the editing reliability of rendered views, although different viewpoints provide supervision of substantially different quality. Views that clearly show the scene and match the edit instruction provide reliable guidance, while less informative views may weaken the edit when all views are treated equally. We present View Matters, a view-importance-aware framework that conducts editing around reliable keyframes. Keyframe Importance Estimation (KIE) identifies reliable views using geometric visibility, semantic distinctiveness, and edit relevance. Keyframe-Guided Editing (KGE) then propagates their editing signals asymmetrically to non-keyframes without noisy reverse influence, while Importance-Aware Optimization (IAO) preserves this reliability preference during 3DGS optimization. Across 23 scene-prompt pairs, View Matters achieves the highest average CLIP text-image similarity of 0.2822 and directional similarity of 0.2564 among the evaluated methods, with a four-minute editing time. Additional adjacent-view analysis indicates that the fidelity-oriented editing process maintains cross-view coherence.

</details>


### [4] [RADC: Risk-Aware Dual Caching for Vision-Language Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06932)
*Siyu Huang,Yueyong Chen,Xuejiao Li,Jun Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RADC is a cache-based test-time adaptation method for vision-language models that addresses background bias through a Semantic Foreground Cache and improves cache admission reliability using Gaussian Risk Admission, achieving state-of-the-art performance on cross-domain and OOD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cache-based test-time adaptation for vision-language models suffers from two key limitations: (1) background bias in global representations that interferes with category learning, and (2) unreliable entropy-based cache admission when representations vary under distribution shift.

Method: RADC introduces two novel components: (1) Semantic Foreground Cache that aggregates category-consistent spatial evidence from CLIP representations to create foreground prototypes that complement the global cache while mitigating background interference; (2) Gaussian Risk Admission that models multi-view representations as diagonal Gaussian distributions and jointly considers class separation and feature uncertainty to prioritize reliable cache candidates. The method integrates zero-shot logits with complementary global- and foreground-cache predictions for robust inference.

Result: Extensive experiments on cross-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate consistent state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: RADC successfully addresses background bias and unreliable cache admission through dual caching mechanisms, significantly improving robustness of vision-language models under distribution shift.

Abstract: Cache-based test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models is often hindered by background bias in global representations and unreliable entropy-based cache admission under representation variations. To address these limitations, we propose RADC, which enhances prototype learning through reliable dual caching. RADC introduces a Semantic Foreground Cache that aggregates category-consistent spatial evidence from CLIP representations, yielding foreground prototypes that complement the global cache while mitigating background interference. To reliably manage both caches, Gaussian Risk Admission models multi-view representations as diagonal Gaussian distributions and jointly considers class separation and feature uncertainty to prioritize reliable cache candidates. RADC integrates zero-shot logits with complementary global- and foreground-cache predictions for robust inference. Extensive experiments on cross-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate consistent state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [5] [PDB: Point-Based Deformation Blending for Facial Animation Retargeting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08672)
*Sihun Cha,Hyeonseung Shin,Suah Yu,Junyong Noh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PDB (Point-Based Deformation Blending) is a mesh-agnostic facial animation retargeting method that predicts deformed control points from source expressions and blending weights from target meshes, enabling cross-identity expression transfer without surface artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing facial animation retargeting methods struggle to preserve facial motion while avoiding surface artifacts when transferring expressions across meshes with different structures.

Method: PDB predicts compact deformed control points from source neutral-expression pairs and blending weights from target neutral meshes. ReLU enforces non-negative weights with exact zeros, followed by row-wise normalization. The target mesh is reconstructed by multiplying weights and control points without predefined cages, precomputed coordinates, learned per-element deformation decoders, or global reconstruction solves. Training uses only self-retargeting reconstruction supervision.

Result: Experiments demonstrate accurate retargeting with fast inference and localized support in learned weights. Joint evaluation shows reduced surface artifacts relative to dense displacement methods while retaining intended motion. Perceptual evaluations confirm expression fidelity and visual quality in both self- and cross-retargeting.

Conclusion: PDB successfully enables mesh-agnostic facial animation retargeting with cross-identity support, achieving better surface preservation and expression fidelity compared to evaluated methods while supporting fast inference.

Abstract: Mesh-agnostic facial animation retargeting transfers expressions across meshes with different structures, but preserving facial motion without surface artifacts remains challenging. To address this, we present PDB, Point-Based Deformation Blending for facial animation retargeting. PDB predicts a compact set of deformed control points from a source neutral-expression pair and blending weights from the target neutral mesh. The weights are computed once per target and reused across frames, while the control points vary with each source expression. ReLU enforces non-negative weights and permits exact zeros, followed by row-wise normalization. The target mesh is reconstructed directly by multiplying the weights and control points, without a predefined cage, precomputed coordinates, a learned per-element deformation decoder, or a global reconstruction solve. Trained only with self-retargeting reconstruction supervision, PDB supports cross-identity transfer without paired cross-identity training expressions. Experiments demonstrate accurate retargeting, fast inference, and localized support in the learned weights. Joint evaluation of expression accuracy and local surface preservation shows reduced surface artifacts relative to the evaluated dense displacement method while retaining the intended motion. Perceptual evaluations further support expression fidelity and visual quality in both self- and cross-retargeting.

</details>


### [6] [UniPro: Unified Multi-Mode Medical Image Segmentation from 2D Images to 3D Volumes via Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06938)
*Bangwei Guo,Yunhe Gao,Meng Ye,Yang Zhou,Difei Gu,Guoning Zhang,Leon Axel,Dimitris Metaxas*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniPro is a unified medical image segmentation model that bridges different segmentation paradigms (semantic, in-context, interactive) and data dimensionality (2D/3D) using a slice-based framework with propagation mechanisms to extend 2D segmentation to 3D volumes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image segmentation is fragmented across segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality. Clinical workflows require various segmentation approaches, and 2D edits must propagate coherently to 3D volumes. Existing methods are specialized for either specific paradigms or specific dimensions, creating a gap in unified solutions.

Method: The key insight is that volumetric propagation and in-context segmentation share the same reference-conditioned prediction mechanism, differing only in whether reference image-mask pairs come from other cases (in-context) or from previously segmented neighboring slices (propagation). UniPro uses a slice-based framework with class priors, reference exemplars, user clicks, and neighboring-slice predictions as conditioning inputs. Bidirectional and 3D supervision are incorporated to improve propagation reliability.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse modalities and anatomies show UniPro achieves strong performance across all segmentation settings, enabling annotation-efficient 3D segmentation from sparse 2D initialization and reducing slice-by-slice correction effort.

Conclusion: UniPro successfully unifies multiple segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality within a single framework, demonstrating practical clinical utility through reduced annotation effort and efficient 3D segmentation from minimal 2D inputs.

Abstract: Medical image segmentation remains fragmented along two axes: segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality. Existing methods are typically developed separately for semantic, in-context, and interactive segmentation, and are further specialized to either native 2D images or 3D volumetric data. In clinical practice, however, segmentation workflows take many forms: a case may be initialized by semantic prediction, reference-guided segmentation, or user interaction. Regardless of how it begins, fine-grained refinement is naturally performed on 2D views; for volumetric scans, such 2D edits must propagate coherently to the rest of the volume. We present UniPro, a unified model that bridges segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality, using propagation to extend 2D segmentation to 3D volumes. Our key insight is that volumetric propagation and in-context segmentation share the same reference-conditioned prediction mechanism, differing only in whether the reference image-mask pairs come from other cases or from previously segmented neighboring slices. Building on this view, UniPro supports semantic, in-context, interactive, and propagation-based segmentation within a single slice-based framework, using class priors, reference exemplars, user clicks, and neighboring-slice predictions as mode-specific conditioning inputs. To improve propagation reliability, UniPro further incorporates bidirectional and 3D supervision to regularize slice-wise propagation beyond per-slice losses. Extensive experiments across diverse modalities and anatomies show that UniPro achieves strong performance across all segmentation settings, enabling annotation-efficient 3D segmentation from sparse 2D initialization and reducing slice-by-slice correction effort.

</details>


### [7] [4D-HOF: Hand-Object Flow Matching for Feed-Forward 4D Interaction Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08782)
*Shiqi Li,Sean Cho,Yijie Li,Fengzhi Guo,Bowen Wen,Cheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 4D-HOF is a feed-forward framework that reconstructs 4D hand-object interactions from coarse estimates produced by vision foundation models, using conditional flow matching to correct errors in translation, rotation, and alignment while enabling test-time guidance via physical constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 4D hand-object reconstruction methods rely on costly per-sequence optimization, while generative approaches that synthesize interactions from random noise often lead to unstable interaction predictions. There is a need for a method that can efficiently and robustly reconstruct 4D hand-object interactions without these limitations.

Method: 4D-HOF uses a conditional flow matching model that transports foundation-model-derived hand-object states toward an interaction manifold. This allows correction of errors in translation, rotation, and alignment in a feed-forward manner. The method incorporates test-time guidance by directly steering evolving generative states using physical interaction constraints and observed 2D evidence, enabling refinement as part of the generative process itself.

Result: Experiments on out-of-domain benchmarks show that 4D-HOF achieves state-of-the-art performance, producing more stable and accurate 4D hand-object reconstructions. The method generalizes robustly to challenging in-the-wild scenarios due to training on diverse datasets.

Conclusion: 4D-HOF successfully addresses the limitations of existing methods by providing a feed-forward solution that combines the advantages of generative models with physical constraints. The approach demonstrates superior performance in stability and accuracy for 4D hand-object reconstruction across diverse scenarios.

Abstract: Existing methods for 4D hand-object reconstruction often rely on costly per-sequence optimization, while generative approaches typically synthesize interactions from random noise, which can lead to unstable interaction prediction. We introduce 4D-HOF, a feed-forward framework that reconstructs 4D hand-object interactions from coarse but informative estimates produced by vision foundation models. Concretely, we learn a conditional flow matching model that transports foundation-model-derived hand-object states toward an interaction manifold, allowing the model to correct errors in translation, rotation, and alignment in a feed-forward manner. A key advantage of our generative formulation is that it naturally enables test-time guidance within the transport process. Rather than applying a separate post-hoc optimization after reconstruction, we directly steer the evolving generative states using physical interaction constraints and observed 2D evidence, allowing the reconstruction to be refined as part of the generative process itself. By training the generative model on diverse datasets, 4D-HOF generalizes robustly to challenging in-the-wild scenarios. Experiments on out-of-domain benchmarks show that 4D-HOF achieves state-of-the-art performance, producing more stable and accurate 4D hand-object reconstructions.

</details>


### [8] [Beyond the Linear Representation Hypothesis: Non-Linear Activation Steering in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06945)
*Muhammad Atif Butt,Paweł Skierś,Joost Van De Weijer,Kamil Deja*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper challenges the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) in mechanistic interpretability by showing that natural visual concepts often require nonlinear transitions between endpoints. It proposes KANSteer, which uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to model concept traversal as a curve through intermediate states rather than a straight line, providing smoother and more accurate representation of gradual concept changes in text-to-image diffusion transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Linear Representation Hypothesis assumes concepts are encoded as linear directions in activation space. However, natural visual concepts (e.g., weather states from sunny to stormy, metamorphosis from caterpillar to butterfly) involve intermediate states that are not simply weaker versions of endpoints. Current text-to-image models rarely produce activations along straight lines when prompted for intermediate attributes, suggesting true intermediate states are represented nonlinearly.

Method: The paper proposes KANSteer, which models concept traversal as a curve passing through intermediate states. KANs provide a one-dimensional coordinate with learned functions that define the trajectory, allowing the steering direction to vary along the concept while maintaining interpretability. The method was tested across several concepts and text-to-image diffusion transformers.

Result: The activation trajectories in tested models substantially deviate from straight lines. KANSteer provides a closer fit to these nonlinear trajectories and enables smoother traversal of intermediate attributes compared to linear steering methods.

Conclusion: The Linear Representation Hypothesis is insufficient for representing natural visual concepts that require nonlinear transitions. KANSteer successfully captures the nonlinear nature of concept traversal in activation space, offering a more accurate and interpretable approach for steering text-to-image models through intermediate concept states.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), which assumes that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in activation space. Yet a natural visual concept does not necessarily require a linear visual transition: between sunny and stormy lies an intermediate weather state such as a sky with a few white clouds, not simply a weaker storm; between a caterpillar and a butterfly, the progression is not a caterpillar with continuously growing wings. This raises the question of whether such true intermediate states are also represented nonlinearly by the model. Indeed, when we prompt text-to-image models directly for intermediate attributes, their activations rarely fall along the straight direction connecting the endpoints. Therefore, we propose KANSteer, which models concept traversal as a curve passing through its intermediate states. Seeking a representation that is both simple and interpretable, we propose to use Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs), which provide a one-dimensional coordinate whose learned functions define the trajectory. This allows the steering direction to vary along the concept while preserving an interpretable representation. Across several concepts and text-to-image diffusion transformers, we find that their activation trajectories substantially deviate from straight lines, and that KANSteer provide a closer fit and smoother traversal of intermediate attributes than linear steering.

</details>


### [9] [DistScene: Object-to-Scene Distillation for 3D Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06960)
*Kunming Luo,Hongyu Yan,Ken Deng,Chengcheng Zhou,Tianyu Liu,Haipeng Li,Haibin Huang,Xuelong Li,Ping Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DistScene is a framework for single-image compositional 3D scene generation that jointly models environment and individual objects by introducing Scene-Frame Generation, Object-Centric Refinement, and Object-to-Scene Distillation, achieving improved scene-level spatial coherence over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods represent scenes primarily as collections of objects without adequate geometric context from the environment. This limits spatial coherence between objects and their surrounding environment. There is a need to model the environment as an explicit scene component to provide geometric context for object placement.

Method: Three key components: (1) Scene-Frame Generation jointly generates separate environment and object components in a shared coordinate frame, allowing geometry and relative placement to be learned together; (2) Object-Centric Refinement refines each object in a local frame with scene context; (3) Object-to-Scene Distillation transfers pretrained object-generation priors to scene generation through automatically composed and rendered synthetic scenes.

Result: Evaluations on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate improved scene-level spatial coherence over evaluated baselines.

Conclusion: The framework successfully improves scene-level spatial coherence by explicitly modeling environment geometry and enabling transfer of object priors to scene generation, representing a meaningful advance in compositional 3D scene generation from single images.

Abstract: We present DistScene, a framework for single-image compositional 3D scene generation by jointly modeling the environment and individual objects. Unlike existing methods that represent scenes primarily as collections of objects, we model the environment as an explicit scene component to provide geometric context for object placement. Specifically, we introduce Scene-Frame Generation, which jointly generates separate environment and object components in a shared coordinate frame, allowing their geometry and relative placement to be learned together. Then we introduce Object-Centric Refinement to refine each object in a local frame with scene context. Finally, we develop Object-to-Scene Distillation to transfer pretrained object-generation priors to scene generation through automatically composed and rendered synthetic scenes. Evaluations on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate improved scene-level spatial coherence over the evaluated baselines. Project page: https://coolbeam.github.io/DistScene/

</details>


### [10] [BoT-Feedback: Grounding Multimodal Reasoning in Biomechanical Evidence for Explainable Human Action Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06972)
*Xu Dong,Wanqing Li,Anthony Adeyemi-Ejeye,Andrew Gilbert*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BoT-Feedback introduces a framework that grounds Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in structured biomechanical evidence for human action feedback generation, addressing limitations of generic advice and hallucinations in existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM methods for coaching feedback inference from visual observations produce generic advice with limited interpretability and physically implausible hallucinations, whereas expert human coaches use explicit biomechanical reasoning over joint kinematics, posture, and body dynamics.

Method: The framework proposes Biomechanics of Thought (BoT), a four-stage reasoning process that: (1) identifies the action, (2) localizes critical body regions, (3) analyzes quantitative biomechanical differences between expert and student performances, and (4) synthesizes interpretable coaching feedback. Supporting components include a plug-and-play Biomechanical Data Parser (BDP) for converting videos into structured biomechanical descriptors, and a temporal alignment strategy for matching expert and student motions.

Result: BoT-Feedback improves average expert evaluation score from 2.07 to 2.95 (+40%) across twelve open- and closed-source MLLMs, substantially reducing biomechanical hallucinations and improving feedback quality, interpretability, and robustness. Compact open-source MLLMs can approach the performance of substantially larger proprietary systems.

Conclusion: Grounding MLLM reasoning in biomechanical evidence is a promising direction for explainable action feedback generation, enabling smaller models to achieve competitive performance with larger proprietary systems.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in visual understanding and multimodal reasoning, yet they remain fundamentally limited in Human Action Feedback Generation. Existing methods infer coaching feedback directly from visual observations, producing generic advice, limited interpretability, and physically implausible hallucinations. In contrast, expert human coaches diagnose performance through explicit biomechanical reasoning over joint kinematics, posture, and body dynamics. We introduce BoT-Feedback, a framework that grounds MLLM reasoning in structured biomechanical evidence. Our key contribution is Biomechanics of Thought (BoT), a four-stage reasoning framework that progressively identifies the action, localises the critical body regions, analyses quantitative biomechanical differences between expert and student performances, and synthesises interpretable coaching feedback. To support this reasoning process, we develop a plug-and-play Biomechanical Data Parser (BDP) that converts videos into structured biomechanical descriptors and an alignment strategy that temporally matches expert and student motions. We further introduce BiomAF, a benchmark containing paired teacher-student videos, 3D skeletons, biomechanical attributes, and expert-coaching annotations. Experiments across twelve open- and closed-source MLLMs demonstrate that grounding reasoning in biomechanical evidence consistently improves feedback quality, interpretability, and robustness while substantially reducing biomechanical hallucinations. BoT-Feedback improves the average expert evaluation score from 2.07 to 2.95 (+40%), enabling compact open-source MLLMs to approach the performance of substantially larger proprietary systems for explainable action feedback generation.

</details>


### [11] [Event Cameras for Melt-Pool Monitoring in Additive Manufacturing: A Benchmark and a Cross-Machine Transfer Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06973)
*Mohamad Yazan Sadoun,Sarah Sharif,Yingtao Liu,Zahed Siddique,Yaser Mike Banad*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SynAM-E is the first public benchmark for event-camera-based metal additive manufacturing melt-pool monitoring, containing 85 physics-calibrated event shards from 15 sources across 8 institutions. The benchmark demonstrates that event-based monitoring can match dense-frame accuracy while requiring significantly less data and energy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution and low data rates, making them ideal for capturing melt-pool transients in metal additive manufacturing. However, no public benchmark existed for this domain, limiting research and development in this area.

Method: The researchers created a synthetic event-camera benchmark (SynAM-E) with physics-calibrated event shards from multiple institutions. They conducted experiments including: (1) comparing event-spatial monitoring with dense-frame accuracy, (2) testing fusion of absolute intensity with events, (3) evaluating a near-sensor event-rate counter on NIST AMMT build, and (4) testing a compact spiking neural network model. They also included a built-in trust test to detect camera identity shortcuts.

Result: Event-spatial monitoring achieved 0.874 macro-F1 versus 0.863 for dense frames. Fusion added only +0.006. The event-rate counter recovered a 528.7 Hz intensity oscillation at ~380 times less sensor readout. A 93k-parameter spiking model ran at 15x lower inference energy with 0.073 macro-F1 cost. The trust test revealed that process-type classification passes while material classification remains confounded by camera band.

Conclusion: Event cameras are viable for melt-pool monitoring, offering comparable accuracy to frame-based methods with significant advantages in data efficiency and energy consumption. The benchmark enables further research, while the trust test exposes a structural limitation regarding camera identity shortcuts in cross-source tasks.

Abstract: Melt-pool monitoring is central to qualifying metal additive manufacturing (AM), yet no public event-camera benchmark exists for this domain. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond timing instead of reading full frames, giving the temporal resolution AM transients demand at a fraction of the data rate. We present SynAM-E (Synthetic AM Events), the first public multi-source simulated event-camera benchmark for metal-AM melt-pool monitoring: 85 physics-calibrated event shards from 15 sources across 8 institutions, with public baselines and fixed cross-machine evaluation splits. On a single-machine case study, event-spatial monitoring matches dense-frame accuracy (0.874 versus 0.863 macro-F1), and the absolute intensity that events discard adds only +0.006 under fusion. On the NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed (AMMT) build, a near-sensor event-rate counter recovers a raw-frame-confirmed 528.7 Hz intensity oscillation at ~380 times less sensor readout than the frame stream requires. A compact 93 k-parameter spiking model runs at 15 times lower modeled inference energy for a 0.073 macro-F1 cost. Every cross-source task includes a built-in trust test against camera identity shortcuts: process-type classification passes while material classification remains confounded by camera band, a corpus-structural limitation the release documents and the trust test exposes.

</details>


### [12] [Visual-Invariance-Augmented Feature Optimal Alignment for Transferable Adversarial Attacks against Closed-Source MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06977)
*Xiaojun Jia,Simeng Qin,Yiming Li,Jie Liao,Sensen Gao,Ke Ma,Yang Liu,Xiaochun Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IAU-FOA is a targeted transfer attack against multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that improves adversarial transferability from open-source surrogate models to closed-source MLLMs by aligning adversarial and target samples at both global and local levels using adaptive unbalanced transport and visual-invariance augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing targeted transfer attacks only use global image-level features (like encoder CLS embeddings) for alignment, which fails to exploit patch-level visual structures and limits transferability across heterogeneous closed-source MLLMs in black-box settings.

Method: The proposed method combines: (1) a cosine-based objective for global semantic gap narrowing, (2) optimal transport for patch-level local feature alignment with clustering, (3) confidence-adaptive unbalanced transport to reduce unreliable local alignment, and (4) visual-invariance augmentation using bidirectional pixel-intensity rescaling and per-channel white-balance to simulate exposure, contrast, illumination, and color-temperature variations.

Result: Extensive experiments on both open-source and closed-source MLLMs show that IAU-FOA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transferable attack methods.

Conclusion: The multi-level feature alignment (global + local) combined with visual-invariance augmentation effectively improves targeted transferability against closed-source MLLMs, demonstrating the importance of exploiting patch-level visual structures and input transformation invariance in transfer attacks.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain vulnerable to transferable adversarial examples, especially in black-box settings where only open-source surrogate models are accessible. Existing targeted transfer attacks mainly align adversarial and target samples using global image-level features, such as encoder [CLS] embeddings. However, such coarse alignment insufficiently exploits patch-level visual structures, limiting transferability across heterogeneous closed-source MLLMs. We propose IAU-FOA, a visual-invariance-augmented feature optimal alignment attack with adaptive unbalanced transport, to improve targeted transferability against closed-source MLLMs. IAU-FOA aligns adversarial and target samples at both global and local levels: a cosine-based objective narrows their global semantic gap, while patch tokens are clustered into compact local patterns and matched through optimal transport for fine-grained feature alignment. Balanced optimal transport enforces fixed marginal masses even for local clusters without reliable counterparts, potentially introducing misleading alignment gradients. We therefore introduce confidence-adaptive unbalanced transport to relax these constraints for weakly matched clusters, aiming to reduce unreliable local alignment and improve adversarial transferability. We further study the effect of input transformations and propose visual-invariance augmentation, which applies bidirectional pixel-intensity rescaling and per-channel white-balance adjustment to simulate exposure, contrast, illumination, and color-temperature variations. This strategy encourages adversarial perturbations to generalize across different visual encoders. Extensive experiments on open-source and closed-source MLLMs show that IAU-FOA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transferable attack methods. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaxiaojunQAQ/IAU-FOA.

</details>


### [13] [Hierarchy-GBP: Accelerating Factor Graph Inference via Abstraction and Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06978)
*Yuzhou Cheng,Tom Yates,Ignacio Alzugaray,Danyal Akarca,Pedro A. M. Mediano,Andrew J. Davison*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP), a two-stage framework that accelerates Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) by using graph abstraction to solve global errors quickly, then refining with standard GBP for local errors. It proves convergence and shows speedups on Pose Graph Optimization and Bundle Adjustment problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GBP is effective for local error correction but slow for global errors across distant graph regions. The authors aim to accelerate GBP by handling global errors through coarse graph approximations before refining locally.

Method: H-GBP uses a two-stage iterative approach: (1) abstraction - create a coarse graph approximation to solve global errors, (2) recovery - project results back to original graph, then (3) refine remaining local errors with standard GBP. Convergence is proven via spectral radius analysis of the combined matrix operator.

Result: H-GBP converges fundamentally faster than standard GBP on linear sparse graphs. For Pose Graph Optimization (PGO), it markedly accelerates large-scale problems. For Bundle Adjustment (BA), it achieves state-of-the-art runtime across all tested scales.

Conclusion: H-GBP successfully accelerates GBP inference while maintaining convergence guarantees, demonstrating practical effectiveness on important spatial inference problems like PGO and BA.

Abstract: Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) is a distributed inference algorithm that passes messages in graphical models, making it attractive for scalable spatial intelligence. However, we find GBP most effective locally: it rapidly smooths message errors that vary sharply between neighbor variables, but corrects global errors across distant graph regions incrementally through long-range message propagations. We propose Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP), an iterative, two-stage framework that accelerates GBP by first solving these global errors with a coarse graph approximation (abstraction) and projecting the results back to the original graph (recovery), then refining the remaining local errors with GBP. We prove H-GBP convergence to the optimum by deriving the combined matrix operator of our abstraction and recovery steps and analyzing its spectral radius. Experiments on linear sparse graphs show that H-GBP converges fundamentally faster than standard GBP. Moreover, we validate H-GBP on two important spatial problems: Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) and Bundle Adjustment (BA). H-GBP markedly accelerates large-scale PGO and achieves state-of-the-art runtime across all tested BA scales.

</details>


### [14] [State-Aware Interaction MIL for Rare Joint Molecular Phenotype Prediction in Colorectal Cancer and Lung Adenocarcinoma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06991)
*Dasari Naga Raju,Tripti Bameta*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes State-Aware Interaction MIL, a weakly supervised method for joint molecular phenotype prediction from histopathology images. It addresses the limitations of existing approaches by preserving biomarker-specific histological representations and modeling their interactions within a complete four-state molecular configuration framework. The method was evaluated on two cancer types (colorectal and lung adenocarcinoma) using two pathology foundation models (UNI2-h and CONCH), showing improved average precision for rare joint-positive phenotype detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint molecular phenotype prediction is challenging due to small joint-positive populations (rare events) and overlapping histological features. Existing methods either predict biomarkers independently (missing interactions) or use binary joint prediction (losing information by collapsing multiple negative states into one class).

Method: State-Aware Interaction MIL is a weakly supervised method that: (1) preserves biomarker-specific histological representations, (2) models their interaction, and (3) supervises the complete four-state molecular configuration (double-negative, single-positive x2, joint-positive). Evaluated using two pathology foundation models (UNI2-h and CONCH) for: (1) BRAF+/MSI+ in colorectal cancer, (2) EGFR+/TP53+ in lung adenocarcinoma.

Result: With UNI2-h: Average precision of 0.5566 (vs 0.5161 for NaiveMTL) in colorectal cancer (joint-positive prevalence 6.8%), and 0.2784 (vs 0.2525 for IndependentPair) in lung adenocarcinoma (joint-positive prevalence 8.6%). With CONCH: 0.4410 (vs 0.3932 for DirectJoint) in colorectal cancer, and 0.1659 (vs 0.1226 for DirectJoint) in lung adenocarcinoma.

Conclusion: Pathology foundation-model representations contain predictive information for rare joint molecular phenotypes. Preserving biomarker-specific representations within a structured molecular-state formulation improves prediction of these phenotypes from histopathology.

Abstract: Joint molecular phenotype prediction is complicated by small joint-positive populations and overlapping histological features across alternative molecular states. Existing computational pathology approaches typically predict biomarkers independently or formulate the joint-positive phenotype as a binary endpoint. Independent prediction does not model interactions between biomarker-specific histological representations, whereas binary joint prediction collapses the double-negative and two single-positive configurations into a single negative class. We propose State-Aware Interaction MIL, a weakly supervised method that preserves biomarker-specific histological representations, models their interaction, and supervises the complete four-state molecular configuration. We evaluate the proposed approach for joint BRAF+/MSI+ prediction in colorectal cancer and EGFR+/TP53+ prediction in lung adenocarcinoma using frozen UNI2-h and CONCH pathology foundation-model representations. With UNI2-h, State-Aware Interaction MIL achieved an average precision of 0.5566 in colorectal cancer (joint-positive prevalence 6.8%) compared with 0.5161 for NaiveMTL, and 0.2784 in lung adenocarcinoma (joint-positive prevalence 8.6%) compared with 0.2525 for IndependentPair. With CONCH, State-Aware achieved an average precision of 0.4410 compared with 0.3932 for DirectJoint in colorectal cancer and 0.1659 compared with 0.1226 for DirectJoint in lung adenocarcinoma. These results indicate that pathology foundation-model representations contain predictive information for rare joint molecular phenotypes and that preserving biomarker-specific representations within a structured molecular-state formulation can improve prediction of these phenotypes from histopathology.

</details>


### [15] [Learning to Curate What You Generate for Generalizable Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07008)
*Junhui Yin,Yuchen Yang,Yilin Yin,Shuai Na,Haoran Xi,Jianhua Yang,Muyi Sun,Man Zhang,Shengfeng He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses Generalizable FSCIL (G-FSCIL), a challenging setting where both base and incremental sessions contain limited data. The authors propose a framework that uses a frozen latent diffusion model to generate synthetic data, combined with a knowledge curation strategy to select semantically consistent and diverse samples. They also introduce boundary-stable incremental adaptation techniques including prototype initialization and bidirectional boundary calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing FSCIL methods assume a sufficiently large base session, which fails in realistic scenarios where both base and incremental data are scarce. This leads to weak initial representations, semantic drift, and unstable boundaries. The authors identify this as an underexplored but important problem called G-FSCIL.

Method: The proposed framework has three main components: 1) Class-specific synthetic candidate pool construction using a frozen latent diffusion model with class inversion at first observation; 2) Knowledge curation strategy that selects samples with semantic consistency and visual diversity, distilled into a transferable selection policy; 3) Boundary-stable incremental adaptation with synthetic-informed prototype initialization and bidirectional boundary calibration to mitigate old-new class conflicts.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the method consistently outperforms existing FSCIL baselines, with reduced forgetting and improved balance between old and new classes.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the G-FSCIL problem through curating trustworthy synthetic knowledge from latent diffusion models and implementing boundary-stable incremental adaptation strategies, achieving superior performance over baselines in the scarce-data scenario.

Abstract: Few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) aims to learn novel classes from limited annotations while preserving prior knowledge. Existing methods typically assume a sufficiently large base session, but this assumption fails when both base and incremental data are scarce, leading to weak initial representations, semantic drift, and unstable boundaries. We study this underexplored yet realistic setting, termed Generalizable FSCIL (G-FSCIL), where the base session itself contains only a few classes. Although synthetic data can alleviate supervision scarcity, naively mixing generated samples often introduces semantic noise and exacerbates old-new boundary conflicts. To address this, we propose a framework that curates trustworthy synthetic knowledge for stable G-FSCIL. Specifically, we first construct class-specific synthetic candidate pools using a frozen latent diffusion model, where class inversion is performed at the first observation and the resulting condition embeddings are reused for on-demand generation. Building on these candidates, we learn a knowledge curation strategy that selects samples with both semantic consistency and visual diversity, and distill this process into a transferable selection policy during the base session, which is then reused without further optimization. Leveraging the curated synthetic data, we further design a boundary-stable incremental adaptation scheme, including synthetic-informed prototype initialization and bidirectional boundary calibration to mitigate old-new conflicts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing FSCIL baselines, with reduced forgetting and improved balance between old and new classes. Code is available at https://github.com/NiHaoWoJiaoYYC/G-FSCIL.

</details>


### [16] [DTFormer: Text-Guided Semantic Alignment for RGB-D Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07014)
*Ziang Wei,Yinlong Liu,Yan Xia,Alois Knoll,Hu Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DTFormer is a tri-modal (RGB-D-Text) semantic segmentation framework that uses text priors to inject semantic discriminability into RGB-D segmentation models through a Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mainstream RGB-D semantic segmentation models learn features from pixel-level supervision without high-level semantic constraints. This work addresses the question of whether external knowledge (language priors) can enhance semantic discriminability in RGB-D segmentation models.

Method: DTFormer introduces TSAM that encodes textual cues into semantic prototypes and explicitly aligns multi-modal RGB-D features with these prototypes at multiple encoder and decoder layers, providing strong semantic regularization on representation learning.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show consistent performance gains while remaining simple and efficient.

Conclusion: Explicit semantic alignment via text priors offers an effective and practical route to improving RGB-D semantic segmentation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

Abstract: RGB-D semantic segmentation has made notable progress by fusing RGB and Depth, yet mainstream models still learn features almost exclusively from pixel-level supervision, lacking direct high-level semantic constraints. This raises a central question-can external knowledge such as language priors inject stronger semantic discriminability into mainstream RGB-D segmentation models. We present DTFormer, a novel tri-modal (RGB-D-Text) semantic segmentation framework. At its core is Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM) that first encodes textual cues into a set of semantic prototypes and then explicitly aligns multi-modal RGB-D features with these prototypes at multiple encoder and decoder layers. This design imposes strong semantic regularization on representation learning, guiding the network toward more discriminative features. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that DTFormer delivers consistent gains while remaining simple and efficient. Our results demonstrate that explicit semantic alignment offers an effective and practical route to improving RGB-D semantic segmentation. The code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [17] [Anchor and Adapt: Asymmetric Prompt Adaptation for Few-Shot Industrial Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07016)
*Mengyang Zhao,Teng Fu,Haiyang Yu,Ke Niu,Bin Li,Xiangyang Xue*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Anchor and Adapt, a two-stage prompt learning framework for few-shot industrial anomaly detection that separates anomaly semantics acquisition from target normal appearance adaptation, using transferable normal/abnormal anchors learned from auxiliary data and adapting to target domains without synthetic anomaly generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In few-shot industrial anomaly detection, the few normal target images provide no defect supervision, making anomaly prompts difficult to learn. Existing vision-language methods rely on manually specified descriptions which require product-specific effort and depend on prompt selection effectiveness.

Method: The proposed Anchor and Adapt framework has two stages: Stage I learns transferable normal and abnormal anchors from annotated auxiliary data. Stage II keeps these anchors fixed and adapts an additional normal branch using few target normal samples. The inherited and adapted normal branches jointly characterize target normality, with text-anchor regularization encouraging consistency with generic normal prior and separation from abnormal anchors.

Result: Cross-dataset experiments between MVTec-AD and VisA under 1-, 2-, and 4-shot settings demonstrate competitive detection and localization performance. Controlled ablations assess the roles of transferred anchors, asymmetric adaptation, dual-normal representations, and anchor regularization.

Conclusion: The method retains learned anomaly knowledge while reducing dependence on category-specific anomaly templates, without requiring synthetic anomaly generation.

Abstract: In few-shot industrial anomaly detection, the few normal target images provide no direct defect supervision, making anomaly prompts difficult to learn from these samples alone. Some vision-language methods therefore use manually specified descriptions to supply explicit anomaly semantics. However, constructing these descriptions requires product-specific effort, and their effectiveness depends on prompt selection. We propose Anchor and Adapt, a two-stage prompt learning framework that separates the acquisition of anomaly semantics from adaptation to target normal appearance. Stage I learns transferable normal and abnormal anchors from annotated auxiliary data. Stage II keeps these anchors fixed and adapts an additional normal branch using the few target normal samples. The inherited and adapted normal branches jointly characterize target normality, with text-anchor regularization encouraging consistency with the generic normal prior and separation from the abnormal anchors. This design retains learned anomaly knowledge while reducing dependence on category-specific anomaly templates, without requiring synthetic anomaly generation. Cross-dataset experiments between MVTec-AD and VisA under 1-, 2-, and 4-shot settings demonstrate competitive detection and localization performance. Controlled ablations assess the roles of transferred anchors, asymmetric adaptation, dual-normal representations, and anchor regularization.

</details>


### [18] [WiSPER: Pose-Supervised Predictive and Residual Flow Refinement For Multi-Person 3D Pose Estimation With WiFi CSI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07025)
*Gabriel Lee Jun Rong,Shanhong Liu,Pai Chet Ng,Konstantinos N. Plataniotis,Jamal Seyedmohammadi,S. Mohammad Sheikholeslami*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WiSPER is a two-stage framework for multi-person 3D pose estimation from WiFi CSI. It combines pose-aware masked embedding learning (PAMEL) for pretraining with conditional residual flow refinement (ReFT) for accurate pose reconstruction. The method achieves 63.72 mm MPJPE on PiW3D, representing a 40.0% improvement over WiFi-JEPA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-person 3D pose estimation using WiFi CSI is challenging because reflections from different people overlap without directly identifying individual joints. Existing methods like masked embedding objectives capture wireless relationships without explicit pose supervision, while structured decoders retain coordinate errors.

Method: WiSPER employs a two-stage architecture: (1) Pose-Aware Masked Embedding Learning (PAMEL) couples masked latent prediction with auxiliary pose-set supervision on the same CSI context, guiding the encoder toward joint localization from partial observations. (2) Residual Flow refinement with Transformer (ReFT) generates pose candidates for variable numbers of people and refines each candidate through conditional flow guided by coarse coordinates and per-joint decoder features. Both stages use paired CSI and pose annotations during training, while inference requires only CSI.

Result: WiSPER achieves an overall mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) of 63.72 mm, a 40.0% reduction relative to WiFi-JEPA. For two people, MPJPE is reduced by 42.1%; for three people, by 38.1%. Pose-supervised pretraining yields lower errors than CSI-only JEPA. Enabling the trained residual refiner reduces overall MPJPE by 13.8-15.6% across evaluated configurations.

Conclusion: The proposed WiSPER framework successfully addresses multi-person 3D pose estimation from WiFi CSI through a combination of pose-aware pretraining and residual flow refinement. The approach demonstrates significant improvements over prior methods, particularly for multi-person scenarios, with the residual refiner providing substantial error reduction.

Abstract: Multi-person 3D pose estimation with WiFi channel state information (CSI) is challenging because reflections from different people overlap without directly identifying individual joints. Existing masked embedding objectives capture wireless relationships without explicit pose supervision, while structured decoders can retain coordinate errors. We propose WiSPER, a two-stage framework combining pose-aware predictive pretraining with conditional residual flow refinement. Pose-Aware Masked Embedding Learning (PAMEL) couples masked latent prediction with auxiliary pose-set supervision on the same CSI context, guiding the encoder toward joint localization from partial observations. Residual Flow refinement with Transformer (ReFT) generates a set of pose candidates to accommodate a variable number of people and refines each candidate through a conditional flow guided by its coarse coordinates and per-joint decoder features. Both stages use paired CSI and pose annotations during training, while inference requires only CSI. Experiments on the PiW3D dataset show that WiSPER achieves an overall mean per-joint position error of 63.72 mm, a 40.0% reduction relative to WiFi-JEPA. For experiments with two and three people, WiSPER reduces MPJPE by 42.1% and 38.1%, respectively. Pose-supervised pretraining configurations obtain lower errors than CSI-only JEPA, and enabling the trained residual refiner reduces overall MPJPE by 13.8-15.6% across the evaluated configurations.

</details>


### [19] [Artemis: Geometry-Grounded Multi-Agent Driving World Models with Shared 3D State and Progressive Memory Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07031)
*Sitian Shen,Jiuming Liu,Mengmeng Liu,Yian Wang,Michael Ying Yang,Francesco Nex,Hao Cheng,Daniele De Martini,Ayush Tewari,Per Ola Kristensson*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Artemis, a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model that addresses limitations of existing approaches by reconstructing explicit 3D world maps from multi-agent observations, enabling high cross-view consistency and handling uncontrolled background dynamics through a novel GeoAdapter module.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent video world models suffer from: (1) implicit inter-agent communications lacking explicit geometry constraints, (2) poor multi-view consistency, (3) inability to recover out-of-sight agents, and (4) assumption of static backgrounds, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics.

Method: The proposed Artemis method includes: (1) reconstructing explicit 3D world maps from multi-agent observations to enforce unified 3D state across agents, (2) developing an action-guided geometric injection module that renders decomposed foreground-background control maps injected into a diffusion transformer via GeoAdapter block, (3) conditioning uncontrolled non-agent dynamics on multi-frame history positions, and (4) using keyframes from progressive video rollouts to update 3D world maps. A new dataset MA-CARLA was curated from CARLA simulator.

Result: Experiments demonstrate superiority in visual fidelity and cross-view consistency. Artemis supports simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, and scales to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera settings.

Conclusion: Artemis successfully addresses multi-agent world model limitations through geometry-grounded design, achieving improved cross-view consistency and handling dynamic backgrounds. The approach scales to multiple agents and cameras, representing a significant advance in multi-agent video world modeling.

Abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.

</details>


### [20] [Crop Yield Prediction for Punjab, Pakistan: A Tree-Ensemble and Leaf-Health Prototype, and What Random Validation Hides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07059)
*Amina Asif,Qurat ul ain Asif,Noor Bakhat Asif*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a crop-yield forecasting prototype for Punjab, Pakistan that initially showed high accuracy (R2=0.991) but subsequent audits revealed critical data quality issues: only 46 independent observations instead of 414 due to duplicated temperature records. When properly validated (holding out whole years), models failed dramatically. A simple linear trend outperformed all ML models on clean data. The leaf health classifier performed well but couldn't be integrated with yield data. The paper primarily reports negative findings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation was to build a practical crop-yield forecasting system combining multiple ML models and a leaf-health classifier for Punjab, Pakistan, to help planners and farmers with decisions on inputs, storage, and imports.

Method: The study combined Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and a Ridge-stacked ensemble with a MobileNetV2 leaf-health classifier, deployed as a web application with SHAP explanations. They conducted extensive data audits, tested various validation strategies (random splits, leave-one-year-out), and compared against simple linear trends.

Result: 1) Initial high R2=0.991 on flawed data (414 rows with only 46 independent observations)
2) XGBoost R2 dropped from 0.994 to -0.20 when holding out whole years
3) Simple per-crop linear trend (RMSE 0.29) beat all ML models (RMSE 0.84-1.06) on clean data
4) Pesticise and temperature don't explain yield variation
5) Leaf classifier reached 99.87% accuracy but couldn't be integrated with yield data

Conclusion: The study demonstrates the critical importance of data quality and proper validation in ML for agriculture. The apparent success of complex models was entirely due to data leakage. Simple linear trends outperform sophisticated ML on proper data. The leaf health classifier, despite high accuracy, adds no value without paired yield data. Spatial variation (district-level) explains most yield variation in Punjab.

Abstract: Yield forecasts help planners and farmers decide on inputs, storage and imports, but small agricultural tables can make reported accuracy fail on a new season. We built a crop-yield prototype for Punjab, Pakistan that combines Random Forest, XGBoost, support vector regression and a Ridge-stacked ensemble with a MobileNetV2 leaf-health classifier, and deployed it as a web application with SHAP explanations. A random 80/20 split of a merged Kaggle-derived table (414 rows) gives the ensemble an R2 of 0.991. An audit showed that the table contains only 46 independent observations: a join with nine temperature records per year copied every crop-year nine times. Holding out whole years takes XGBoost on the same rows from R2 = 0.994 to -0.20. On deduplicated data, and on a longer FAOSTAT table (1990-2024, 70 observations), a per-crop linear trend (leave-one-year-out RMSE 0.29 Ton/Ha) beats every model not given the year (0.84-1.06). Neither pesticide use nor national temperature change explains the trend residuals. An apparent pesticide gain in the Kaggle table disappears on FAOSTAT, where the pesticide series is mostly imputed and the two releases disagree. An independent district-level wheat panel (36 districts, 13 seasons) shows that most variation in Punjab is spatial and that a district mean with a common trend matches the learned models. The leaf classifier reaches 99.87% accuracy on held-out PlantVillage images and recalls 96.4% of 336 unseen diseased leaves after near-duplicates were removed. However, no leaf image is paired with a yield record, so the health score used in the yield models had to be constructed and adds nothing. We report these negative findings together with the prototype.

</details>


### [21] [Decomposition-Guided Curvelet Thresholding for Sharp-to-Soft CT Kernel Conversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07067)
*Mahmoud Nasr,Jan K. Argasinski,Krzysztof Brzostowski,Adam Piorkowski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A hybrid image denoising framework combining decomposition techniques (EMD, VMD, MEMD, BEMD) with curvelet transform thresholding, using both soft and hard thresholding. VMD achieves highest PSNR and SSIM, with soft thresholding preserving details and hard thresholding providing better noise reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve CT image quality by minimizing noise while preserving essential structural elements, addressing limitations of traditional denoising methods in medical imaging.

Method: Hybrid denoising approach combining multiple decomposition techniques (EMD, VMD, MEMD, BEMD) with curvelet transform thresholding. Each decomposition mode processed through both soft and hard thresholding, then combined to rebuild the final image.

Result: VMD consistently achieves highest PSNR and SSIM among all methods. Soft thresholding maintains intricate visual details while hard thresholding provides enhanced noise reduction. The method outperforms traditional techniques in both reference (PSNR, SSIM) and non-reference quality criteria.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid framework surpasses traditional denoising techniques and shows potential for broader application in medical imaging, with future work to incorporate adaptive thresholding algorithms.

Abstract: Image denoising is a crucial task in image processing, focused on improving image quality by minimizing noise while maintaining essential structural elements. This study presents a hybrid denoising framework that combines several decomposition techniques, including empirical mode decomposition (EMD), variational mode decomposition (VMD), multichannel EMD (MEMD), and bidimensional EMD (BEMD), with curvelet transform thresholding. Each decomposition mode undergoes processing through both soft and hard thresholding, and the denoised modes are combined to rebuild the final image. Comprehensive evaluations of standard CT image datasets reconstructed with various kernels (B50, B46, B41, B36) reveal substantial enhancements in denoising efficacy. VMD consistently achieves the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), signifying exceptional noise reduction and feature preservation. The study analyses the trade-offs between soft and hard thresholding: soft thresholding maintains intricate visual details, whilst harsh thresholding provides enhanced noise reduction. The suggested method surpasses traditional techniques in both reference and non-reference quality criteria, indicating its potential for broader application in medical imaging and future incorporation with adaptive thresholding algorithms.

</details>


### [22] [A BEMD-Based Quaternion Filtering Approach Sharp-to-Soft Kernel CT Image Conversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07071)
*Mahmoud Nasr,Jan K. Argasinski,Krzysztof Brzostowski,Adam Piorkowski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes BEMD-QBF, a novel CT image enhancement method that combines Bidimensional Empirical Mode Decomposition with Quaternion Bilateral Filtering to convert sharp-kernel CT images into soft-kernel-like representations while preserving anatomical structures. The method outperforms existing filtering techniques in SSIM and PSNR metrics across multiple reconstruction kernels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CT image quality is compromised by reconstruction kernel selection: sharp kernels enhance spatial resolution but increase noise, while soft kernels reduce noise but sacrifice edge clarity. There is a need for a method to combine the advantages of both kernel types.

Method: The study proposes an innovative enhancement framework using Bidimensional Empirical Mode Decomposition combined with Quaternion Bilateral Filtering (BEMD-QBF). This technique decomposes CT images into intrinsic mode functions via BEMD and processes them within a quaternion framework to achieve noise reduction while preserving structural integrity. The method was evaluated using multiple reconstruction kernels (B50, B46, B41, B36, B35, B31) and compared with other filtering methods including Non-Local Means, Anisotropic Diffusion, Bilateral Filtering, and Quaternion Bilateral Filtering.

Result: Quantitative evaluations using Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) demonstrate that BEMD-QBF consistently achieves superior structural fidelity and competitive noise reduction across all evaluated kernels.

Conclusion: BEMD-QBF represents an effective approach for enhancing post-reconstruction CT images, providing superior image quality without requiring access to raw projection data.

Abstract: The quality of computed tomography (CT) images is significantly affected by the selection of reconstruction kernels: sharp kernels improve spatial resolution but increase noise, whereas soft kernels diminish noise at the expense of edge clarity. This study presents an innovative enhancement framework utilising Bidimensional Empirical Mode Decomposition in conjunction with Quaternion Bilateral Filtering (BEMD--QBF) to convert sharp-kernel CT images into representations resembling soft-kernels, while maintaining critical anatomical structures. The technique disaggregates each image into intrinsic mode functions via BEMD and analyzes them inside a cohesive quaternion framework to attain efficient noise reduction and structural integrity. The proposed methodology is evaluated using several reconstruction kernels (B50, B46, B41, B36, B35, B31) and compared with recognised filtering strategies, including Non-Local Means, Anisotropic Diffusion, Bilateral Filtering, and Quaternion Bilateral Filtering. Quantitative evaluations of the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) indicate that BEMD-QBF consistently attains superior structural fidelity and competitive noise reduction across all evaluated kernels. The results underscore the efficacy of the proposed strategy as a viable approach to enhancing post-reconstruction CT images, yielding superior image quality without requiring access to raw projection data.

</details>


### [23] [Beyond Perturbation Magnitude: Direction-Dependent Responses in Multimodal Geometric Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08533)
*Yongsheng Luo,Wengan He,Yu Li,Rouying Wu,Wei Lv*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates how geometric alignment scores (based on Gram determinants) respond to multimodal degradation (video blur, audio noise). The key finding is that displacement magnitude alone cannot explain the response (only 15% variance explained). The authors propose Directional Geometric Response (DGR), which uses the projection of displacement onto the local volume gradient, achieving 83.8-96.9% variance explanation and high accuracy (86-96% ranking accuracy, 90-99% sign accuracy).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how geometric alignment scores behave under modality degradation is critical for multimodal learning. Prior work lacks analysis of how these scores respond to perturbations, which is essential for robust deployment.

Method: The authors used two datasets (MSR-VTT N=878, DiDeMo N=980) and applied controlled video blur and audio noise. They analyzed the relational geometry and developed a closed-form first-order expansion (DGR) based on the Gramian volume gradient.

Result: DGR explains 83.8-96.9% out-of-sample variance in the response, with matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963 and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989. Direction-free alternatives failed. A gain-normalization candidate also failed.

Conclusion: Geometric response depends on three factors: (1) the clean operating point, (2) displacement magnitude, and (3) displacement direction. DGR captures all three jointly, making it a powerful explanatory quantity for understanding multimodal geometric degradation.

Abstract: Geometric alignment scores based on Gram determinants provide a compact way to model higher-order consistency among modalities, yet how such scores respond to modality degradation is poorly understood. This paper asks whether the response of a multimodal geometric score is determined primarily by the magnitude of the perturbation-induced displacement. Using frozen cohorts from MSR-VTT (N=878) and DiDeMo (N=980), we apply controlled video blur and audio noise and analyze the response in the relational geometry on which the score is defined. Displacement magnitude explains at most 15% of the out-of-sample variance in the absolute response, and magnitude-matched pairs respond systematically differently, so scalar magnitude does not organize the response. The closed-form first-order expansion of the Gramian volume yields the Directional Geometric Response (DGR): the projection of the displacement onto the local volume gradient, which jointly captures the clean operating point, displacement magnitude, and displacement direction. The absolute first-order DGR term explains the observed response with out-of-sample R^2 of 0.838-0.969, matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963, and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989, whereas the tested direction-free alternatives remain weak or unstable under the corresponding evaluation protocols. A pre-specified gain-normalization candidate, V/(g_V+eps), fails its predictability and clean-order gates.
