DGR uses the observed degraded-state displacement and is therefore an explanatory quantity, not a deployment-time predictor: geometric response depends on where the representation operates, how far degradation moves the relational geometry, and in which direction it moves.

</details>


### [24] [On Color Alignment in VAE Latent Spaces and Its Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07072)
*Julian D. Santamaria,Kai Wang,Jesús Malo,Javier Vazquez-Corral,Alexandra Gómez-Villa*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates how color is represented in the latent spaces of VAEs used in text-to-image models. The authors discover a consistent color subspace aligned with brightness and opponent-color axes across multiple VAE architectures (SD1.5 to FLUX.2 and Z-Image). Based on this finding, they develop three applications: ColorTuning for precise numerical color generation, saturation control, and color transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite VAEs being known to disentangle factors of variation in data, with color being one of the most structured factors in natural images (decorrelating into luminance and two opponent-color axes), how color emerges in VAE latent spaces remains largely unexplored. This work aims to characterize and leverage this color representation.

Method: The authors used a linear approximation of the encoder combined with targeted latent steering to identify the color subspace. They validated their approach across a broad range of VAEs from SD1.5 to FLUX.2 and Z-Image.

Result: The study confirms that VAEs of text-to-image models share a color subspace aligned with brightness and opponent-colors, consistent across different architectures. The proposed applications achieve: (1) State-of-the-art results in precise numerical color generation on GenColorBench (fine-grained CSS3/X11 system), (2) global chromatic intensity adjustment through saturation control, and (3) palette matching via color transfer.

Conclusion: Color emerges as a distinct factor in VAE latent spaces in a structured way aligned with perceptual color theory. This characterization enables practical color control applications with state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a key part of modern text-to-image models, which generate images within their latent space. VAEs are known to disentangle the main factors of variation in the data, and color is known to be one of the most structured of these in natural images: decorrelating it yields one luminance axis and two opponent-color axes. Color should therefore be expected to emerge as a distinct factor in the VAE latent space. Yet how these latent spaces represent color remains largely unexplored. In this work, we show that the VAEs of text-to-image models share a color subspace aligned with brightness and opponent-colors. Through a linear approximation of the encoder and targeted latent steering, we find this subspace consistently across a broad range of VAEs, from SD1.5 to FLUX.2 and Z-Image. Building on this characterization, we propose three applications: ColorTuning, which achieves state-of-the-art in precise numerical color generation on the fine-grained CSS3/X11 system of GenColorBench, saturation control, to adjust the global chromatic intensity, and color transfer, to change the palette to match a reference. The code and models are publicly available at https://julian075.github.io/Color_Subspace/

</details>


### [25] [Graph-Based Recognition of Simulated Train-Driver States From Facial and Upper-Body Keypoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07083)
*Olivia Nocentini,Marta Lagomarsino,Gokhan Solak,Younggeol Cho,Qiyi Tong,Sara Zeynalpour,Marta Lorenzini,Alessandro Ledda,Arash Ajoudani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a vision-based train driver fatigue monitoring system using a single RGB camera and graph neural network to classify driver states into alert, not-alert, and emergency behaviors. The combined facial and skeletal features achieved 81% accuracy for 3-class classification and 99% for 2-class (alert/not-alert) under light conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional driver fatigue systems like dead-man switches offer limited and basic alertness checks. There's a need for more sophisticated, passive, and non-contact monitoring systems to improve railway safety.

Method: The study uses a single front-facing RGB camera and a graph neural network (GNN). An ablation study compared three feature configurations: skeletal-only, facial-only, and a combined approach. The system was tested under three illumination conditions.

Result: Combining facial and skeletal features yielded the highest accuracy (81%) for the three-class model under light conditions, outperforming models using only facial or skeletal features. For alert/not-alert classification (2-class), the combination achieved 99% accuracy in light conditions.

Conclusion: The combination of facial and upper-body (skeletal) dynamics provides an effective approach for passive, non-contact train driver state recognition. The study also contributes a new controlled RGB video dataset containing alert, not-alert, and acted emergency-like behaviors under three illumination conditions.

Abstract: Driver fatigue poses a significant challenge to railway safety, with traditional systems like the dead-man switch offering limited and basic alertness checks. This study presents a vision-based monitoring system that relies solely on a single front-facing RGB camera and a graph neural network to classify simulated train-driver states into alert, not-alert, and an emergency class comprising acted emergency-like behaviours. To optimize input representations for the model, an ablation study was performed, comparing three feature configurations: skeletal-only, facial-only, and a combination of both. Experimental results show that combining facial and skeletal features yields the highest accuracy (81%) for the three-class model under the light condition, outperforming models that use only facial or skeletal features. Furthermore, the combination of facial and skeletal features achieves 99% accuracy in the alert/not alert classification in light condition. Additionally, we introduced a controlled RGB video dataset containing alert, not alert, and acted emergency-like behaviours recorded under three illumination conditions. These contributions represent a step toward passive and non-contact train-driver state recognition based on facial and upper-body dynamics.

</details>


### [26] [A Data-Centric Review of Plant Disease Datasets: Taxonomy, Critical Analysis, Environmental Variability, and Implications for Precision Agriculture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07087)
*Aamir Hilal,Shabir Ahmad Sofi,Neeraj Goel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This review paper analyzes visual and deep learning approaches for plant disease detection, focusing on the critical bottleneck of dataset limitations. It establishes a taxonomy for evaluating plant disease datasets based on acquisition settings, accessibility, plant/disease diversity, and class imbalance, while highlighting the gap between laboratory-generated and real-field datasets. The paper also examines multimodal approaches integrating environmental parameters with image data for improved field deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in AI, reliable real-world plant disease detection remains challenging due to poor generalization of models trained on laboratory datasets lacking environmental diversity and realistic conditions. Existing surveys have insufficiently examined dataset imbalance issues (intra-class, inter-crop, cross-dataset) and environmental variability impacts.

Method: Critical review and comparative analysis of visual and deep learning approaches for plant disease detection, with emphasis on plant disease datasets. Established a taxonomy based on acquisition setting, accessibility, plant diversity, disease composition, class structure, and imbalance severity. Compared laboratory vs. real-field datasets and analyzed multi-level dataset imbalance effects.

Result: The review identifies critical gaps between laboratory and real-field datasets that hinder disease detection. Key findings include: (1) laboratory datasets lack environmental diversity and realistic backgrounds; (2) class imbalance severely affects model performance; (3) multi-level imbalance (intra-class, inter-crop, cross-dataset) and limited environmental variability impact model robustness; (4) integrating environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, leaf wetness) with image data improves prediction under dynamic field conditions.

Conclusion: The review provides a foundation for developing next-generation multimodal frameworks for precision agriculture. Key challenges identified include dataset construction, environmental variability, structural imbalance, standardization, and multimodal disease monitoring. Future directions should focus on constructing diverse real-field datasets and developing multimodal frameworks that combine visual data with environmental parameters for improved real-world deployment.

Abstract: Despite rapid advances in artificial intelligence, reliable real-world plant disease detection remains a persistent challenge. Visual and deep learning approaches have shown promising results, but their deployment under field conditions remains limited. A key bottleneck is the reliance on laboratory-generated datasets that lack environmental diversity, realistic backgrounds, and balanced class distributions, resulting in poor generalization. In contrast, datasets collected directly from agricultural environments capture natural variability and better reflect challenges faced by farmers across regions. This review presents a critical analysis of visual and deep learning approaches for plant disease detection, with emphasis on plant disease datasets. It establishes a taxonomy based on acquisition setting, accessibility, plant diversity, disease composition, class structure, and imbalance severity, and examines their implications for model generalization and real-world deployment. A comparative analysis of laboratory and real-field datasets identifies critical gaps that hinder disease detection. The review further analyzes how multi-level dataset imbalance, including intra-class, inter-crop, and cross-dataset imbalance, and limited environmental variability affect model performance and robustness, an area insufficiently examined in existing surveys. Beyond image-based approaches, it highlights the importance of integrating environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, and leaf wetness with image data to improve prediction under dynamic field conditions. Finally, the review identifies key challenges, research gaps, and future directions concerning dataset construction, environmental variability, structural imbalance, standardization, and multimodal disease monitoring. It provides a foundation for developing next-generation multimodal frameworks for precision agriculture.

</details>


### [27] [MoonGS: High-quality Representation of the Lunar Surface via Gaussian Splatting Using Robust Depth Features from Image Pairs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07110)
*Yun Jiang,Bo Zheng,Yingying Zhang,Xueming Xiao,Tao Hu,Hutao Cui,Zhiguo Meng,Ke Gao,Yang Gao,Meibao Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoonGS is the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for high-quality lunar terrain reconstruction from only two sparse rover images, without per-scene optimization. It integrates vision foundation models, semantic priors, and an entropy-guided resampling strategy to achieve state-of-the-art results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous lunar exploration requires high-quality 3D terrain reconstruction, but existing methods struggle with insufficient viewpoint overlap, weak surface textures, and limited data volume from sparse rover images.

Method: MoonGS proposes three key innovations: (i) An adaptable backbone integrating advanced vision foundation models (e.g., VGGT) for robust depth features; (ii) Semantic priors via two mechanisms - merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and a semantic ranking loss for background depth regularization; (iii) An entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy that selects informative distant viewpoints to augment sparse observations.

Result: MoonGS outperforms state-of-the-art feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines by +4.9 dB PSNR, +0.29 SSIM, and 40% lower LPIPS while maintaining sub-second inference. It achieves the best visual quality on real Chang'e mission imagery, and effectively leverages modern backbones like VGGT for significant performance boost.

Conclusion: MoonGS demonstrates the first successful feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting approach for lunar terrain reconstruction, achieving superior quality-speed tradeoff. The framework shows broad applicability through integration with various vision foundation models and robust performance on real lunar data, making it promising for autonomous lunar exploration.

Abstract: High-quality 3D reconstruction of lunar terrain from sparse rover images is indispensable for autonomous lunar exploration, but remains challenging because viewpoint overlap is insufficient, surface textures are weak, and data volume is limited. We propose MoonGS, the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored to lunar scenes. Given only two input images, MoonGS predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass and renders photorealistic novel views without any per-scene optimization. MoonGS (i) adopts an adaptable backbone design that seamlessly integrates advanced vision foundation models to extract robust depth features; (ii) integrates semantic priors in two manners: merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and adopting a semantic ranking loss that regularizes background depth; and (iii) employs an entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy to augment sparse observations by selecting the most informative distant viewpoints with negligible overhead. Experiments on the LuSNAR benchmark and our synthetic weak-texture MoonBlender dataset show that MoonGS surpasses state-of-the-art feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines by +4.9 dB PSNR, +0.29 SSIM, and 40\% lower LPIPS while maintaining sub-second inference. Furthermore, we validate the broad applicability of our framework by demonstrating that it effectively leverages state-of-the-art backbones, including VGGT, to significantly boost performance. Qualitative evaluations on Chang'e mission imagery also show the best visual quality among compared methods, indicating robustness on real lunar data. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/InRobots/MoonBlender.

</details>


### [28] [R2RI: A Multi-View Event and RGB Dataset for Robot-to-Robot Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07117)
*Gabriele Magrini,Riccardo Catalini,Federico Becattini,Guido Borghi,Pietro Pala,Roberto Vezzani,Lorenzo Seidenari*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: R2RI is the first large-scale benchmark dataset specifically designed for Robot-Robot Interaction (RRI) research, featuring over 6.5M frames and ~5000 videos at 120fps with both Event and RGB modalities from multiple viewpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study of robot interactions is a compelling research direction but progress has been severely hampered by the absence of large-scale benchmarks. Understanding and modeling interactions between autonomous agents is fundamental for collaborative systems, social robotics, and human-robot coexistence.

Method: The R2RI dataset consists of different humanoid robots with realistic interactions modeled on real human social behaviors. It provides complementary viewpoints: egocentric (from robot onboard sensors) and exocentric (from external fixed cameras). The dataset includes Event and RGB domains captured at 120 fps.

Result: The dataset comprises more than 6.5M frames and approximately 5000 videos at 120 fps, including both Event and RGB domains. The paper investigates pros and cons of each domain and compares state-of-the-art approaches for key sensing and interaction-based tasks.

Conclusion: The dataset and its annotations for all tasks and modalities are publicly released, enabling future research in robot-robot interaction, spatial understanding, and interaction dynamics analysis.

Abstract: Understanding and modeling interactions between autonomous agents is a fundamental challenge in robotics, with broad implications for collaborative systems, social robotics, and human-robot coexistence. Although the study of robot interactions has emerged as a compelling research direction, progress has been severely hampered by the absence of large-scale benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce Robot-to-Robot Interaction (R2RI), the first dataset specifically designed to address the Robot-Robot Interaction (RRI) task. R2RI consists of different humanoid robots and realistic interactions modeled on real human social behaviors. Complementary viewpoints are available, \textit{i.e.}, an egocentric perspective from each robot's onboard sensors, and an exocentric perspective from external fixed cameras, thus enabling rich spatial and contextual understanding of the interaction dynamics. The dataset comprises more than $6.5$M frames and $\approx5000$ videos at $120$ fps, including Event and RGB domains. We investigate pros and cons of each domain, comparing state-of-the-art approaches for a number of key sensing and interaction based tasks. We publicly release the dataset and its annotations for all tasks and modalities at https://github.com/MagriniGabriele/R2RI.

</details>


### [29] [PlaySuite: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Interactive Visual Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07127)
*Dheeraj Varghese,Anna Vettoruzzo,Walter Simoncini,Michelle Lorena Acevedo Callejas,Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani,Kristof Meding,Joaquin Vanschoren,Cees G. M. Snoek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PlaySuite is a large-scale benchmark with 5K+ open-source video games for evaluating interactive visual intelligence in dynamic environments, addressing the gap between static perception benchmarks and real-world agentic behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal foundation models excel on static benchmarks but fail to act competently in dynamic environments over extended time horizons. Existing evaluations overlook this crucial aspect of intelligence.

Method: 1) Curated 5K+ open-source games from PyWeek and itch.io spanning multiple genres and engines (Pygame, HTML5, Godot, Unity). 2) Developed unified closed-loop interaction framework optimized for HPC clusters. 3) Created Video-LLM-as-a-judge protocol mapping gameplay milestones to standardized progress levels. 4) Evaluated 14 recent open models including vision-language models, computer-use agents, and vision-language-action models.

Result: Strong evidence of a perception-action gap: despite strong reasoning capabilities, current models struggle with sustained progress, spatial grounding, action execution, and self-correction in interactive game environments.

Conclusion: PlaySuite provides a reproducible, extensible testbed for measuring progress from visual perception to goal-directed interaction, serving as a foundation for developing models that can act, adapt, and generalize in dynamic visual environments.

Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models yield strong performance on static perception and reasoning benchmarks, yet such evaluations largely overlook a central aspect of intelligence: acting competently in dynamic environments over extended time horizons. We introduce PlaySuite, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating interactive visual intelligence across more than 5K open-source video games curated from PyWeek and itch.io. Spanning diverse genres and engines, including Pygame, HTML5, Godot, and Unity, these independent games are largely out-of-distribution for current models, reducing the likelihood that success can be achieved by retrieving memorized walkthroughs or web-scale training artifacts. To enable scalable evaluation across heterogeneous titles, we develop a unified closed-loop interaction framework optimized for HPC clusters alongside a Video-LLM-as-a-judge protocol that maps observable gameplay milestones to standardized progress levels. We evaluate fourteen recent open models spanning vision-language models, computer-use agents, and vision-language-action models. Our results yield strong evidence of a perception-action gap: despite strong reasoning capabilities, current models struggle to make sustained progress and exhibit recurring failures in spatial grounding, action execution, and self-correction. PlaySuite provides a reproducible and extensible testbed for measuring progress from visual perception to goal-directed interaction, and a foundation for developing models that can act, adapt, and generalize in dynamic visual environments.

</details>


### [30] [CALR: Continuous Anchored Latent Reasoning via Render-of-Thought Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07175)
*Zhaoyang Wei,Bowen Jiang,Yanchao Hao,Wenchao Ding,Zheng Wei,Shaocheng Wu,Zhenjun Han,Jianbin Jiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CALR addresses limitations in visual latent reasoning by connecting latent formation with answer use through functional anchoring, achieving 26.0 percentage points improvement over continuous methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual latent reasoning approaches (continuous and discrete) fail to meet two functional requirements: answers must rely on latent states, and those states must carry valid problem-specific reasoning. Continuous latents have collapsed reasoning content, while discrete latents retain recoverable reasoning that answer prediction bypasses.

Method: CALR uses functional anchoring combining: (1) information-balanced compression with reference latents, (2) latent-mediated answer supervision routing answer supervision through intermediate states, (3) derivation-level semantic anchoring grounding decoded content in problem-specific derivations, and (4) parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum developing sequential reasoning by conditioning subsequent latent blocks on generated prefixes.

Result: Substantial accuracy gains on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks across model families. Under matched budgets, CALR gains 26.0 percentage points over comparable continuous latent reasoning method. Latents support answer prediction and carry problem-specific intermediate reasoning.

Conclusion: CALR successfully addresses the core limitations of prior approaches by ensuring latent states are both used for answer prediction and contain valid reasoning content, representing a meaningful advance in visual latent reasoning for mathematical problem-solving.

Abstract: Visual latent reasoning compresses rendered derivations into compact intermediate states, reducing textual reasoning overhead. Existing approaches differ in how they represent these states: continuous methods avoid vocabulary constraints, whereas discrete methods improve accuracy through quantization into a finite codebook. Our analysis of representative continuous and discrete systems identifies two functional requirements: answers must rely on latent states, and those states must carry valid, problem-specific reasoning. Continuous latents influence answers despite collapsed reasoning content, whereas discrete latents retain recoverable intermediate reasoning that answer prediction largely bypasses. To address these challenges, we propose Continuous Anchored Latent Reasoning (CALR), which connects latent formation with answer use through functional anchoring. With reference latents from information-balanced compression, CALR couples latent-mediated answer supervision with derivation-level semantic anchoring: the former routes answer supervision through intermediate states, while the latter grounds their decoded content in problem-specific derivations. A parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum develops sequential reasoning by conditioning subsequent latent blocks on generated prefixes. Evaluations on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks across model families show substantial accuracy gains. Under matched budgets, CALR gains 26.0 percentage points over a comparable continuous latent reasoning method. Further analyses show that its latents support answer prediction and carry problem-specific intermediate reasoning.

</details>


### [31] [Deep Learning Based Illegal Bowling Action Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07223)
*Debopom Sutradhar,Niful Islam,Sudipto Mondal,Tasmima Hossain Jamim,Jubaer Muhammad Shufol,Swakkhar Shatabda*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A computer vision-based deep learning system to detect illegal bowling actions in live cricket matches by analyzing arm angle changes between shoulder and release frames. The system flags deliveries with angle differences exceeding 15 degrees as potentially illegal, achieving high true positive rate on 62 videos of 11 bowlers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting illegal bowling actions is crucial for fair play but challenging for umpires to monitor in real time. Existing sensor-based solutions have limitations in live match scenarios, making real-time assessment difficult.

Method: Computer vision-based deep learning solution using two key frames (shoulder frame and release frame) to analyze the change in bowling arm's angle. If the angle difference exceeds 15 degrees, the delivery is flagged as potentially illegal. Dataset: 62 videos of 11 male bowlers from multiple angles (front, back, side).

Result: The proposed system achieved a high true positive rate on the custom dataset, suggesting potential effectiveness in real-time match settings.

Conclusion: This is the first AI-based computer vision method for detecting illegal bowling actions in cricket. The system achieved high true positive rate on a custom dataset of 62 videos with 11 bowlers. Further validation across diverse conditions and larger datasets is needed for generalizability and robustness in real-world match scenarios.

Abstract: Cricket, often referred to as the "gentleman's game," adheres to a strict rule set for both batsmen and bowlers, where each delivery can significantly impact the match outcome. Detecting illegal bowling actions is crucial for maintaining fair play, yet it remains challenging for umpires to monitor in real time. Existing sensor-based solutions have limitations in live match scenarios, making real-time assessment difficult. This paper proposes a computer vision-based deep learning solution to detect illegal bowling actions in live cricket matches. To develop and evaluate our approach, we compiled a dataset of 62 videos featuring 11 male bowlers, capturing both legal and illegal bowling actions from multiple angles-front, back, and side. However, the dataset predominantly comprises right-handed bowlers with conventional actions. The proposed system identifies two key frames, the shoulder frame and the release frame from video footage of a bowler's delivery and analyzes the change in the bowling arm's angle between these frames. If the angle difference exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g., 15 degrees), the delivery is flagged as potentially illegal. We evaluated the system on a custom dataset and achieved a high true positive rate, suggesting the system's potential effectiveness in real-time match settings. However, further research is required to validate the system across diverse environmental conditions and larger datasets to ensure generalizability and robustness in various live match scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first AI-based computer vision method for detecting illegal bowling actions in cricket.

</details>


### [32] [Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network for Early Breast Cancer Detection in Low-Resource Clinical Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07243)
*Simon Hadush Nrea,Filimon Gidey Gebremichael,Gebrekirstos Hagos Gebrekirstos,Yaecob Girmay Gezahegn*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces HCMAN (Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network), a deep learning model that combines mammogram images with structured clinical data for breast cancer diagnosis in Sub-Saharan Africa. The model uses transformer-based cross-modal attention to address the unique challenges of limited radiology expertise and fragmented clinical data systems in African healthcare settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in Sub-Saharan Africa. Delayed diagnosis results from limited radiology expertise and fragmented clinical data systems. Existing deep learning models rely solely on imaging data and are trained on Western populations, making them unsuitable for African healthcare settings.

Method: The HCMAN integrates mammogram images with structured clinical data using transformer-based cross-modal attention mechanisms. The model was developed and validated using a locally collected dataset of 2,560 mammogram images from 1,024 patients across four Ethiopian referral hospitals, with biopsy-confirmed ground truth labels.

Result: The proposed framework achieves 97.8% accuracy, 97.2% sensitivity, 98.3% specificity, and an AUC of 0.987, significantly outperforming image-only baselines. The system demonstrates robustness to low-quality images typical of resource-limited settings, with only 3.2% performance degradation compared to 8.7% for image-only models. Cross-modal attention analysis reveals clinically appropriate behavior: higher reliance on clinical features for ambiguous cases such as dense breasts and young patients. The model's lightweight architecture enables deployment on standard hospital workstations (<2 seconds inference on CPU).

Conclusion: This work advances sustainable, context-aware AI solutions for equitable breast cancer diagnostics in Africa, demonstrating that incorporating clinical data alongside imaging improves diagnostic accuracy, especially in resource-limited settings.

Abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in Sub-Saharan Africa, where delayed diagnosis results from limited radiology expertise and fragmented clinical data systems. Although deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance in mammographic analysis, most rely solely on imaging data and are trained on Western populations, limiting their applicability in African healthcare settings. This paper presents a Hybrid Cross-Modal Attention Network (HCMAN) that integrates mammogram images with structured clinical data using transformer-based cross-modal attention mechanisms. The model was developed and validated using a locally collected dataset of 2,560 mammogram images from 1,024 patients across four Ethiopian referral hospitals, with biopsy-confirmed ground truth labels. The proposed framework achieves 97.8% accuracy, 97.2% sensitivity, 98.3% specificity, and an AUC of 0.987, significantly outperforming image-only baselines. The system demonstrates robustness to low-quality images typical of resource-limited settings, with only 3.2% performance degradation compared to 8.7% for image-only models. Cross-modal attention analysis reveals clinically appropriate behavior: higher reliance on clinical features for ambiguous cases such as dense breasts and young patients. The model's lightweight architecture enables deployment on standard hospital workstations (<2 seconds inference on CPU). This work advances sustainable, context-aware AI solutions for equitable breast cancer diagnostics in Africa.

</details>


### [33] [What Words Keep of a Place: Zero-Shot Language Reasoning for Cross-View Geo-Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07269)
*Ayesh Abu Lehyeh,Jay Hwasung Jung,Safwan Wshah*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether cross-view geo-localization (matching ground-level panoramic images to satellite tiles) can be solved through language alone using multimodal large language models (MLLMs), without any training. The approach uses MLLMs to generate structured text descriptions of both ground and satellite views, then compares these descriptions for localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cross-view geo-localization methods require large paired supervision and lack interpretability—they cannot explain what evidence supports a match. This paper explores whether language alone can solve this task and provide interpretable localization through explicit reasoning about description consistency.

Method: The authors prompt a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to describe ground panoramas and satellite tiles as structured text, then localize by comparing descriptions. No components are trained. They evaluate on 9,826 VIGOR pairs across four U.S. cities in three settings: (1) full pool ranking by description similarity, (2) narrowed pool of 10 neighboring tiles using an MLLM judge for structural consistency, and (3) MLLM judge placed on a trained visual retriever for reranking.

Result: Setting 1 (full pool): Description similarity achieves only 0.39% Recall@1—descriptions are faithful but not discriminative. Setting 2 (10-neighbor pool): The MLLM judge doubles random ranking and matches a strong lexical baseline, while also providing interpretable reasoning about which fields agree/conflict. Setting 3 (reranking): Reranking from images works better than from descriptions (23.5% vs 10.7% Recall@1). Scene structure survives language conversion, but fine appearance detail needed to separate nearby places does not.

Conclusion: Language alone can provide coarse localization and interpretability (identifying structural consistency), but lacks fine-grained visual detail needed for precise matching. The MLLM judge can explain its reasoning (which description fields agree/conflict), offering a step toward interpretable localization, but cannot replace visual embeddings for precise retrieval. Scene structure transfers to language, while distinguishing nearby locations requires visual detail that gets lost in text descriptions.

Abstract: Cross-view geo-localization is commonly solved as an image retrieval problem, matching a ground-level image against a database of satellite tiles through a jointly trained embedding. Such models are accurate, but they need large paired supervision and cannot show what evidence supports a match. In this paper, we study a different question: how much of this task can be solved through language alone? We prompt a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to describe each ground panorama and each satellite tile as structured text, and localize by comparing these descriptions. No component is trained. We evaluate on 9,826 VIGOR pairs from four U.S. cities, in three settings. First, the descriptions are faithful but not discriminative. They agree closely across the two views, yet ranking the full pool by description similarity almost never returns the correct tile (0.39% Recall@1). Second, we narrow the pool to ten neighboring tiles, as a coarse prior would do. The same descriptions now become useful: an MLLM judge that scores structural consistency doubles random ranking and matches a strong lexical baseline. It also states which fields of the two descriptions agree and which conflict, which an embedding distance cannot do, and which we see as a step toward interpretable localization. Third, we place the judge on a trained visual retriever. On the queries it ranks wrongly, reranking from images works, while reranking from our descriptions does not (23.5% against 10.7% Recall@1). Scene structure survives the conversion into language, while the fine appearance detail needed to separate nearby places does not. Code and prompts are publicly available at https://github.com/AyeshAbuLehyeh/GeoLingual.

</details>


### [34] [Localize Any Object in X-Ray Security Scans without Human Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07326)
*Yaqi Cai,Mingxuan Liu,Lorenzo Vaquero,Ning Wang,Nan Pu,Feng Xue,Elisa Ricci,Nicu Sebe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAO-X is a self-supervised framework for universal object localization in X-ray security scans that uses synthesized data and granularity-aware supervision to adapt SAM2 to X-ray images without human annotations, achieving 2-23% mAP improvements over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: X-ray security inspection lacks generalizable perception models due to: (1) distinct color patterns, ambiguous boundaries, and compositional structures different from RGB images; (2) scarce annotated X-ray data requiring expert labeling; (3) inability to directly transfer RGB foundation models to X-ray domain via zero-shot or fine-tuning approaches.

Method: LAO-X employs: (1) Saliency-guided X-ray object mining module to separate diverse object instances; (2) Physics-guided synthesis in the absorbance domain using the mined objects; (3) Occlusion-controlled curriculum strategy to fine-tune SAM2, progressively adapting to X-ray scans with increasing object counts and overlap levels.

Result: Experiments on six X-ray benchmarks show LAO-X substantially improves category-agnostic localization, achieving 2% to 23% mAP gains over SAM2 and X-ray-specific baselines in heavily cluttered scenarios, entirely without human-annotated labels.

Conclusion: LAO-X successfully bridges the gap between RGB foundation models and X-ray inspection by using self-supervised learning with synthesized data, enabling generalizable object localization without expensive human annotations. The framework demonstrates that data scaling principles can be extended to X-ray domain through intelligent synthesis and curriculum-based adaptation.

Abstract: Universal object localization in X-ray security inspection is critical for automated threat detection in safety-critical venues. However, unlike everyday RGB images that dominate web-scale visual data, X-ray scans exhibit distinct color patterns, ambiguous boundaries, and compositional structures caused by volumetric superposition. These gaps hinder the direct zero-shot transfer of dense perception foundation models trained on web-scale RGB data. Moreover, annotated X-ray data is scarce and requires expert labeling, limiting both the training of generalizable X-ray native models and the adaptation of RGB foundation models for X-ray data via fine-tuning. Given these challenges, the bright promise of highly generalizable perception models, enabled by data scaling laws in the RGB domain, remains largely out of reach for X-ray inspection. To this end, we introduce LAO-X, a self-supervised adaptation framework that Locates Any Object in X-ray scans using diverse synthesized image--annotation pairs with granularity-aware supervision. LAO-X first designs a saliency-guided X-ray object mining module to separate diverse object instances, which are then used for physics-guided synthesis in the absorbance domain. LAO-X further incorporates an occlusion-controlled curriculum strategy to fine-tune a Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) localizer, progressively adapting it to X-ray scans with increasing object counts and overlap levels. Experiments on six X-ray benchmarks show that LAO-X substantially improves category-agnostic localization, achieving 2\% to 23\% mAP gains over SAM2 and X-ray specific baselines in heavily cluttered scenarios, entirely without human-annotated labels.

</details>


### [35] [Compositional Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07337)
*Chen Dai,Ganyu Zou,Nathan Self,Kevin Piper,Ramachandra Rao Seethiraju,Karthik Shyamsunder,Chang-Tien Lu,Naren Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HGSS is a training-free framework for removing copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified concepts from deployed text-to-image diffusion models without modifying model weights or adding learned parameters. It addresses limitations of existing training-free methods that fail on compositional prompts where erase targets are invoked through related classes or have modifier migration issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to remove specific concepts (copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified) from deployed text-to-image diffusion models is practical. Existing weight-editing methods require retraining and modify model checkpoints, while training-free methods suffer from text-side routing failures on compositional prompts—where the erase target may be invoked through a related class rather than its lexical name, and modifiers may migrate onto preserved objects.

Method: HGSS introduces two key mechanisms: (1) Hierarchical span grounding that resolves erase-target spans through lexical, taxonomic, and semantic evidence while guarding against false positives from broad-hypernym and compound-head patterns; (2) Dynamic attribute binding that refines text conditioning during early denoising via a counterfactual reference and preserve-aware cross-attention objective to keep surviving attribute-noun bindings intact.

Result: On SEE dataset: hierarchical evasion reduced from 29.54 to 10.02, pairwise attribute leakage roughly halved, achieving best Neighbor E and AttrP scores among reported erasure methods. On UnlearnCanvas: slightly improved six-metric average over matched Semantic Surgery baseline, reaching state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: HGSS successfully provides a training-free solution for compositional concept erasure that selectively removes erase targets without updating model weights or adding learned parameters, achieving superior performance on multiple benchmarks compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Removing copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified concepts from a deployed text-to-image diffusion model is now a practical requirement. Weight-editing methods can suppress fixed targets, but they require per-target retraining and modify the model checkpoint. Training-free methods, on the other hand, are deployment-friendly, but they suffer from text-side routing failures on compositional prompts. In such prompts, the erase target may be invoked through a related class rather than its lexical name, and its modifiers may migrate onto preserved objects. This paper proposes Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery (HGSS), a training-free framework for compositional concept erasure. The framework lifts both the routing signal and the edit operator used by text-side erasure. First, hierarchical span grounding resolves erase-target spans through lexical, taxonomic, and semantic evidence, while guarding against broad-hypernym and compound-head false positives. Second, dynamic attribute binding refines the text conditioning during early denoising via a counterfactual reference and a preserve-aware cross-attention objective, keeping surviving attribute-noun bindings intact. HGSS selectively removes the erase target without updating model weights or adding learned parameters. On SEE, HGSS cuts hierarchical evasion from 29.54 to 10.02 and roughly halves pairwise attribute leakage, achieving the best Neighbor E and AttrP scores among the reported erasure methods. On UnlearnCanvas, HGSS slightly improves the six-metric average over the matched Semantic Surgery baseline, reaching state-of-the-art.

</details>


### [36] [A doctrine-grounded visual question answering dataset for Tactical Combat Casualty Care](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07339)
*Junseob Kim,Jade Chng,Ayman Ali,Victor Moas,Yichun Lee,Po-Chun Chin,Sunil Hwang,Rishikesan Kamaleswaran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TC3-VQA is a dataset of 581 items with 1,860 questions designed to train and evaluate vision-language models for Tactical Combat Casualty Care. It links visual observations of injuries and interventions to authoritative TC3 clinical guidance, covering intervention recognition, doctrine, clinical reasoning, procedural guidance, and cases where visual information is insufficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current vision-language models for TC3 lack supervision that connects visible evidence to traceable clinical doctrine. Developing such models requires dataset that bridges visual observations with established clinical guidance, enabling evaluation of recognition, doctrine recall, and appropriate abstention.

Method: Dataset constructed from public instructional/field TC3 videos and authoritative TC3 documents using: (1) visual annotation of equipment boxes, anatomical labels, temporal segments; (2) passage retrieval from authoritative documents; (3) entailment checks; (4) verification across model families; (5) quality assessment by 2 physicians and 2 medical students (88 retained items rated).

Result: 581 items spanning 11 concepts with 1,860 questions covering intervention recognition, doctrine, clinical reasoning, procedural guidance, and refusal scenarios. Doctrine-based answers preserve verbatim source passages and character offsets. Equipment boxes, anatomical labels, temporal segments, and source metadata are included.

Conclusion: TC3-VQA provides a resource for adapting vision-language models to TC3, studying the connection between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, and evaluating model capabilities in recognition, doctrine recall, and appropriate abstention when visual information is insufficient.

Abstract: Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TC3) requires responders to connect visual observations of injuries and interventions with established clinical guidance. Developing vision-language models to support this process requires supervision that links visible evidence to traceable doctrine. We present TC3-VQA, a dataset constructed from public instructional and field TC3 videos and authoritative TC3 documents. It contains 581 items spanning 11 concepts, with 1,860 questions covering intervention recognition, doctrine, clinical reasoning, procedural guidance, and refusal when visual information is insufficient. Doctrine-based answers preserve verbatim source passages and character offsets. Construction combines visual annotation, passage retrieval, entailment checks, and verification across model families. Equipment boxes, anatomical labels, temporal segments, and source metadata accompany the question-answer pairs. Automated audits and ratings by two physicians and two medical students characterize annotation quality, with human ratings available for 88 retained items. The dataset provides a resource for adapting vision-language models to TC3, studying the connection between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, and evaluating recognition, doctrine recall, and abstention.

</details>


### [37] [Tracking Is Not Permanence: What Video World Models Keep of a Hidden Object](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07355)
*Peng Xie,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether video world models (like V-JEPA 2, VideoMAE, and Cosmos) can track objects that are hidden from view (object permanence). The researchers found that while the encoder retains information about hidden objects, the predictor/decoder loses this information quickly - a moving object disappears within 0.3s, and objects in closed containers become unrecoverable after 0.5s. However, this deficit can be fixed with cheap training on synthetic containers, improving performance on IntPhys-2019 from 84.2% to 93.3%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers wanted to understand what video world models "keep" of objects they cannot see. While these models track visible objects well, it's unclear whether they maintain beliefs about occluded objects - a fundamental capability called object permanence that is essential for physical reasoning.

Method: The researchers hid objects from a frozen V-JEPA 2 predictor and compared its predictions for hidden regions with the encoder's representations. They tested: (1) stationary objects vs. moving objects, (2) objects in open vs. closed containers, (3) different masking strategies (tube mask vs. block mask), and (4) multiple architectures (V-JEPA 2, VideoMAE, Cosmos). They also trained the predictor on synthetic containers to install permanence as a prior.

Result: Key findings: (1) The predictor loses moving objects within 0.3s (0.5s with tube mask), while a baseline copying the last view retains them for 1.1s. (2) Stationary objects are partially kept, but objects in closed containers are completely lost. (3) The encoder retains full information (1.00) about object presence and keeps container contents decodable for 3.5s, but the predictor's output only contains the ball in 2% of scenes after 0.5s. (4) Training on synthetic containers for 3000 steps improved permanence from 0.05 to 1.00. (5) IntPhys-2019 improved from 84.2% to 93.3%, but a curriculum without containers also worked, raising questions about what the benchmark actually measures. (6) VideoMAE keeps almost nothing, while Cosmos keeps stationary hidden objects but not ones in moving containers.

Conclusion: Object permanence is not intrinsic to latent video prediction - it can be installed cheaply through training. The encoder retains hidden information but the predictor discards it. The IntPhys benchmark's scoring rules significantly affect which training habits it credits. Continued training with tube masks achieves 1.1-1.6s of moving-object carry-over, suggesting the deficit is fixable rather than fundamental.

Abstract: Video world models track objects they can see; we ask what they keep of objects they cannot. We hide an object from a frozen V-JEPA 2 predictor and compare its prediction for the hidden region with the encoder's representation of two worlds that differ only inside that region. The predictor's decision keeps a stationary object in part and one carried inside a container not at all, and loses a moving one within 0.3 s (0.5 s under V-JEPA's own tube mask; ViT-H keeps it to 1.1 s at pretraining's 90% masking ratio); in projection a trace remains, below the midpoint, at 14-60% of what a baseline copying the last view retains. The information is there: the encoder reads the object's presence at 1.00 and keeps a closed container's contents decodable for 3.5 s, while the predictor's output, read with the encoder's own probe, contains the ball in 2% of scenes once the box has been closed for half a second. On rendered scenes, permanence is missing on the predictor's side, and training installs it cheaply as a prior: three thousand predictor-only steps on synthetic containers take this belief from 0.05 to 1.00 against two matched controls. They also raise IntPhys-2019 from 84.2% to 93.3%, but so does a curriculum without containers, and which training habit the benchmark credits changes with its scoring rule. Continued training with tube masks produces 1.1-1.6 s of moving-object carry-over on manipulation and internet-style video, so the deficit is not intrinsic to latent prediction. VideoMAE keeps almost nothing, and Cosmos's next-token prediction keeps a stationary hidden object but not one carried inside a moving container.

</details>


### [38] [Identity-Conditioned Score Fusion for Open-Set Person Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07366)
*Manyi Yao,Jurijs Nazarovs,Eunji Chong,Abhishek Sharma,Rohan Sarkar,Yue Guo,Christian R. Shelton,Amit K. Roy-Chowdhury,Debashish Pal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces identity-conditioned score fusion for person re-identification, a training-free framework that adapts fusion weights to each gallery identity by analyzing intra-identity consistency vs. cross-identity impostors, achieving up to 8.8% reduction in false non-identification rate on clothes-changing benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current adaptive fusion methods for person re-identification focus on query quality but ignore that model strength varies across different identities. The authors aim to address this limitation by developing an identity-conditioned fusion approach that tailors weights to each gallery identity without requiring training.

Method: The proposed method extracts identity-specific profiles by contrasting intra-identity consistency against cross-identity impostors. These profiles couple with query-conditioned adaptation through a parameter-free rule, allowing the framework to work without training while widening the separation between true and false matches.

Result: Evaluations on three clothes-changing person re-identification benchmarks show consistent improvement over statistical, rank-based, and learned baselines. The method achieves up to an 8.8% absolute reduction in false non-identification rate while preserving score calibration.

Conclusion: Identity-conditioned fusion demonstrates significant value in open-set person re-identification by tailoring fusion weights to each gallery identity without training. The approach successfully separates true from false matches better than existing methods, particularly in challenging clothes-changing scenarios.

Abstract: Robust person re-identification often combines complementary cues such as face, gait, and body shape. While adaptive fusion typically targets query quality, model strength also varies across identities. We introduce identity-conditioned score fusion, a framework that tailors weights to each gallery identity without training. By contrasting intra-identity consistency against cross-identity impostors, it extracts identity-specific profiles that couple with query-conditioned adaptation via a parameter-free rule. This widens the separation between true and false matches while preserving score calibration. Evaluations on three clothes-changing person re-identification benchmarks show that our method consistently outperforms statistical, rank-based, and learned baselines, achieving up to an 8.8% absolute reduction in the false non-identification rate and demonstrating the value of identity-conditioned fusion in open-set person re-identification.

</details>


### [39] [SimCortex v2: Joint Cortical Surface Reconstruction with Near-Zero Collisions and Self-Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07378)
*Kaveh Moradkhani,Sylvain Bouix*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SimCortex v2 is a deep learning framework for simultaneous reconstruction of cortical white matter and pial surfaces from T1-weighted MRI. It uses a ribbon-conditioned U-Net to predict multi-scale stationary velocity fields for joint refinement of all four surfaces, achieving comparable accuracy to baselines while significantly reducing geometric artifacts (inter-surface collisions and self-intersections).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstructing cortical WM and pial surfaces from structural MRI is essential for surface-based neuroanatomical analysis but remains challenging due to the cortex being thin and tightly folded. Existing methods, including recent deep learning approaches, produce geometric artifacts such as mesh self-intersections and collisions between cortical surfaces.

Method: SimCortex v2 estimates topologically correct initial surfaces from volumetric segmentation and refines all four surfaces (left/right WM and pial) jointly using multi-scale stationary velocity fields predicted by a ribbon-conditioned, U-Net-like network.

Result: On 560 cases from 14 cohorts (13 unseen during training), SimCortex v2 matched the surface-distance accuracy of the strongest baseline (average symmetric surface distance 0.253 mm). It achieved no detected inter-surface collision in 92.14% of cases and the lowest self-intersection fraction (0.044%) among learning-based methods, while every baseline produced at least one collision in every case.

Conclusion: SimCortex v2 successfully reduces geometric artifacts in cortical surface reconstruction while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods, across diverse populations (ages 6-89, healthy and clinical) and scanners from three vendors.

Abstract: Reconstructing cortical WM and pial surfaces from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a prerequisite for surface-based neuroanatomical analysis, yet remains challenging because the cortex is thin and tightly folded. Reconstruction methods can produce geometric artifacts such as mesh self-intersections and collisions between cortical surfaces, and although recent deep learning methods have reduced reconstruction time from hours to minutes, these artifacts persist. We propose SimCortex v2, a deep learning framework for simultaneous reconstruction of the left and right WM and pial surfaces from T1-weighted MRI. SimCortex v2 estimates topologically correct initial surfaces from a volumetric segmentation and refines all four jointly using multi-scale stationary velocity fields predicted by a ribbon-conditioned, U-Net-like network. We evaluated SimCortex v2 on 560 cases from 14 cohorts, thirteen of them unseen during training, spanning ages 6-89, healthy and clinical populations, and scanners from three vendors. SimCortex v2 matched the surface-distance accuracy of the strongest baseline (average symmetric surface distance 0.253 mm) while showing no detected inter-surface collision in 92.14% of cases and the lowest self-intersection fraction (0.044%) among learning-based methods, whereas every baseline produced at least one collision in every case. Source code, configuration files, pretrained weights, preprocessed data, and the exact evaluation splits are publicly released.

</details>


### [40] [GeoWM: Efficient Direct World Modeling in Explicit Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07381)
*Mehrdad Noori,Guile Wu,Sam Hosseini,Dongfeng Bai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GeoWM is a geometry world model that directly forecasts future scene geometry at specified horizons without recursive rollout, using a geometry foundation model and flow-matching transformer, outperforming existing world models in depth, camera pose, and 3D geometry forecasting while reducing inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current world models for autonomous driving and robotics predict future images or latent representations but fail to explicitly model geometric structure. They rely on recursive rollouts to reach longer prediction horizons, causing error accumulation and increasing computational cost.

Method: 1) Use a geometry foundation model to transform observed RGB frames into geometric history. 2) Condition a flow-matching transformer to predict scene geometry at specified future horizons. 3) Employ a lightweight camera-motion predictor to estimate future viewpoint. 4) Project observed geometry into predicted viewpoint as geometric prior for forecasting.

Result: Outperforms evaluated world models in forecasting depth, camera pose, and 3D scene geometry. substantially reduces inference time at longer horizons on four datasets spanning urban driving, aerial flight, and dynamic manipulation.

Conclusion: GeoWM successfully addresses limitations of existing world models by directly forecasting future scene geometry without recursive rollout, achieving better performance while being computationally more efficient.

Abstract: Modeling 3D scene geometry and its evolution over time is essential for autonomous driving and robotics. A common paradigm is to use world models to predict future images or latent representations of the environment and subsequently recover geometry from these predictions. However, this paradigm does not explicitly model geometric structure and typically relies on recursive rollouts to reach longer prediction horizons, leading to error accumulation and increasing computational cost. To address these limitations, we present GeoWM, a geometry world model that directly forecasts future scene geometry at specified future horizons without recursive rollout. The key idea is to leverage a geometry foundation model to transform observed RGB frames into a geometric history, which conditions a flow-matching transformer to predict the scene geometry at a specified future horizon. We further show that a lightweight camera-motion predictor can accurately estimate the future viewpoint, and that projecting the observed geometry into the predicted viewpoint provides an effective geometric prior for future geometry forecasting. Extensive experiments on four datasets spanning urban driving, aerial flight, and dynamic manipulation demonstrate that GeoWM outperforms the evaluated world models in forecasting depth, camera pose, and 3D scene geometry, while substantially reducing inference time at longer horizons.

</details>


### [41] [WildMatch: Weakly Supervised Image Matcher Adaptation for Wildlife Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07384)
*Turhan Can Kargin,Piotr Kubaty,Ekaterina Rostovskaya,Izabela Wierzbowska,Bartosz Zieliński,Marcin Przewięźlikowski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a weakly supervised adaptation method for pretrained keypoint matchers to improve individual animal re-identification from camera-trap imagery. Using only identity labels (without keypoint or geometric correspondence annotations), the method contrastively fine-tunes matching networks to strengthen correspondences for same-identity pairs while suppressing them for different identities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current animal re-identification approaches either learn global embeddings (requiring many labeled images per individual, ignoring local evidence) or use off-the-shelf domain-agnostic image matchers (challenging to adapt due to small wildlife datasets lacking correspondence annotations). There was a need for a method that can adapt pretrained matchers to wildlife domains using only identity labels available in typical monitoring datasets.

Method: The method involves: 1) Mining informative image pairs using a pretrained matcher; 2) Deriving weak positive and negative supervision from identity agreement (same identity = positive, different identity = negative); 3) Contrastively fine-tuning the matching network to strengthen correspondences for same-identity pairs and suppress them for different identities. This is done without any keypoint-level or geometric correspondence ground truth.

Result: The approach improves accuracy over off-the-shelf matchers and a state-of-the-art local-global fusion method across open-source wildlife re-identification datasets. Under an open-world protocol with held-out individuals, it learns a transferable correspondence prior rather than memorizing training identities.

Conclusion: This is the first study of matcher-level, identity-supervised adaptation for animal re-identification. The method enables data-efficient specialization of image matching models to wildlife domains using identity annotations already available in typical monitoring datasets, without requiring expensive keypoint or correspondence annotations.

Abstract: Individual animal re-identification from camera-trap imagery is an instance retrieval problem central to non-invasive wildlife monitoring: a query image must retrieve the correct individual from a reference set of known animals. This requires computer vision models to recognize distinctive local patterns in fur, skin, or other visual markings. Current approaches either learn global embeddings as a classification problem, requiring many labeled images per individual while largely ignoring local evidence, or apply off-the-shelf, domain-agnostic image matchers. Although such matchers are pretrained on large and diverse image collections, adapting them to wildlife imagery is challenging because available datasets are small and lack correspondence-level annotations. We study weakly supervised adaptation of a pretrained keypoint matcher using only identity labels, without keypoint-level or geometric correspondence ground truth. We mine informative image pairs with the pretrained matcher, derive weak positive and negative supervision from identity agreement, and contrastively fine-tune the matching network to strengthen correspondences for same-identity pairs and suppress them for different identities. Across open-source wildlife re-identification datasets, our approach improves accuracy over off-the-shelf matchers and a state-of-the-art local--global fusion method. Under an open-world protocol with held-out individuals, it learns a transferable correspondence prior rather than memorizing training identities. To our knowledge, this is the first study of matcher-level, identity-supervised adaptation for animal re-identification. Our method enables data-efficient specialization of image matching models to wildlife domains using identity annotations already available in typical monitoring datasets.

</details>


### [42] [Semantic Capability Acquisition and Specialization During Vision-Language Model Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07385)
*Suguru Onda,Matthew Bailey,Ryan Farrell*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates the temporal dynamics of semantic capability acquisition in fine-tuned vision-language models (VLMs). The authors propose a trajectory-based framework to track how semantic capabilities (identity- and attribute-based) evolve over training, and introduce Structured Semantic Routing (SSR) to study how supervision representation shapes acquired capabilities. Across six pretrained backbones, they find that fine-tuning can acquire semantic capabilities beyond the pretrained state, but different capabilities peak at different training stages, and continued optimization can preserve target class retrieval while reducing previously acquired transferable semantic capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLM fine-tuning evaluation uses a single downstream checkpoint, which obscures whether a semantic capability was never acquired, emerged earlier and later declined, or peaked at a different stage. This limits understanding of the capability acquisition dynamics and transferability.

Method: The authors propose: (1) A trajectory-based framework separating capability acquisition, capability-specific optima, and later specialization; (2) Structured Semantic Routing (SSR) to study how representation of supervision shapes acquired capabilities. They conduct experiments across six pretrained backbones (DFN, MetaCLIP, OpenAI CLIP) tracking identity- and attribute-based capabilities over training.

Result: Key findings: (1) Fine-tuning can acquire semantic capability beyond the pretrained state, including gains on held-out evaluations; (2) Unstructured name-and-attribute supervision produces strong name-and-attribute retrieval but weak name-free attribute-profile retrieval; (3) SSR yields substantially stronger name-free attribute-profile retrieval, enhanced by stochastic name-branch dropout; (4) Different capabilities peak at different stages - checkpoint selected by target class-name retrieval need not coincide with transferable semantic optimum; (5) Late specialization is consistent with reduced cross-modal semantic accessibility while image-only class structure remains.

Conclusion: The study reveals that semantic capabilities follow non-monotonic trajectories during VLM fine-tuning. A single checkpoint evaluation is insufficient for understanding capability dynamics. The proposed SSR method and trajectory-based framework provide valuable tools for understanding and improving VLM fine-tuning. Practitioners should consider capability trajectories rather than single checkpoints when deploying fine-tuned VLMs.

Abstract: Fine-tuning vision-language models (VLMs) is typically evaluated at a single downstream checkpoint, obscuring whether a semantic capability was never acquired or emerged earlier and later declined during specialization. We ask how semantic capabilities are acquired, when they peak, how well they transfer, and what remains at deployment. We study these dynamics as a semantic capability trajectory, tracking identity- and attribute-based capabilities over training.
  We formulate a trajectory-based framework that separates capability acquisition, capability-specific optima, and later specialization, and introduce Structured Semantic Routing (SSR) to study how the representation of supervision shapes what is acquired. Across six pretrained backbones spanning DFN, MetaCLIP, and OpenAI CLIP, we show that fine-tuning can acquire semantic capability beyond the pretrained state, including gains observed on held-out evaluations. Unstructured name-and-attribute supervision produces strong name-and-attribute retrieval with comparatively weak name-free attribute-profile retrieval, whereas SSR yields substantially stronger name-free attribute-profile retrieval and is further strengthened by stochastic name-branch dropout. Different capabilities can peak at different stages, so a checkpoint selected by target class-name retrieval need not coincide with a transferable semantic optimum. Continued optimization can therefore preserve strong target class-name retrieval while reducing previously acquired transferable semantic capability. In a representative diagnostic study, this late specialization is consistent with reduced cross-modal semantic accessibility while substantial image-only class structure remains available.

</details>


### [43] [ElasticFit: Fit-Aware 3D Object Insertion via VLM Reasoning and Generative Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07460)
*Tzu-Hsin Hsieh,Ricardo Marroquim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ElasticFit is a VLM-guided framework for inserting objects into 3D scenes that ensures geometric fit, semantic intent, and physical plausibility. It infers structured fitting cues from language instructions and scene observations, converts them into 3D constraints, generates scene-conditioned object priors, and refines meshes through mode-specific fitting (rigid, uniform scaling, or elastic).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLMs and generative models lack sufficient 3D grounding and geometric control when inserting objects into constrained local spaces. Objects must fit local geometry while preserving semantic intent and physical plausibility—requiring more than just plausible location selection.

Method: ElasticFit uses a novel scene-grounded representation to infer structured fitting cues (grounding location, occupied volume, orientation, adaptation mode) from language instructions and rendered scene observations. These cues become explicit 3D constraints for object generation. The pipeline includes: scene-conditioned object prior generation, 3D reconstruction, and mode-specific fitting (rigid placement, uniform scaling, or elastic fitting) with collision avoidance, contact consistency, and physical grounding enforcement.

Result: ElasticFit improves spatial relation success from 50.8% to 69.7% and support success from 48.3% to 91.7% over the strongest baseline, while enabling novel generative "make-it-fit" insertions in complex scenarios.

Conclusion: ElasticFit demonstrates that VLM-guided reasoning combined with explicit 3D constraints and mode-specific fitting can significantly improve object insertion quality in 3D scenes, achieving substantial gains in spatial and support relationships while enabling new elastic fitting capabilities.

Abstract: Inserting objects into existing 3D scenes requires more than selecting a plausible location:
  the inserted object must also fit local geometry while preserving semantic intent and physical plausibility.
  Although recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and generative models enable semantic reasoning and visual content creation, they offer limited 3D grounding and geometric control when an inserted object must fit into constrained local spaces.
  We introduce \textbf{ElasticFit}, a VLM-guided framework for fit-aware object insertion centered on a novel scene-grounded representation.
  Given a language instruction and rendered scene observations, ElasticFit infers structured fitting cues that specify where the object should be grounded, what volume it should occupy, how it should be oriented, and its adaptation mode (rigid placement, uniform scaling, or elastic fitting).
  These cues convert high-level VLM reasoning into explicit 3D constraints that condition object generation and guide downstream geometric fitting.
  ElasticFit then generates a scene-conditioned object prior, reconstructs it in 3D, and refines the mesh through mode-specific fitting while enforcing collision avoidance, contact consistency, and physical grounding.
  In fixed-asset baseline comparisons, ElasticFit improves spatial relation success from 50.8\% to 69.7\% and support success from 48.3\% to 91.7\% over the strongest baseline, while providing novel support for generative "make-it-fit" insertions in complex scenarios.

</details>


### [44] [Protective Perturbations Must Survive the Resize: Scale-Robust Image Immunization against Malicious Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07464)
*Zhongliang Guo,Yan Lin,Yifei Qian,Daizong Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the vulnerability of protective perturbations (designed to prevent malicious photo editing) to unknown downscaling by image editors. The authors model the resize operation as a frequency-selective channel and propose SRIM, a scale-robust optimization method that achieves significantly better protection against various image editing models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protective perturbations for personal photos are optimized at the editor's working resolution, but shared photos have 10+ megapixels and editors first downscale them by unknown factors. This creates a security gap where perturbations become ineffective after downscaling, leaving photos vulnerable to malicious edits.

Method: The authors model resize as a frequency-selective channel and analyze perturbation decay characteristics. They propose SRIM (Scale-Robust Iterative Method) which samples a grid of anchor scales covering the whole range, with weights favoring the currently weakest scale, instead of standard expectation over transformation.

Result: On full-resolution photos (9-30 megapixels) with downscaling factors 2-8, SRIM raises worst-case disruption of FLUX.2-klein edits from 0.192 to 0.463 LPIPS (roughly doubling protection at equal visibility). Against the 9B model and FLUX.2-dev, SRIM achieves worst cases of 0.450 and 0.386 respectively, compared to at most 0.184 for prior protections. It also performs well on InstructPix2Pix.

Conclusion: The scale-robust optimization approach (SRIM) effectively addresses the unknown downscaling vulnerability in protective perturbations, providing strong protection across a wide range of scales and multiple editing models. The worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the scale range width.

Abstract: Protective perturbations aim to stop malicious instruction-guided editing of personal photos, but they are optimized and evaluated at the editor's working resolution, whereas shared photos have 10 megapixels or more and editors first downscale them by an unknown factor. We model this resize as a frequency-selective channel. In this model, a perturbation computed at the native resolution decays with the downscaling factor and is weak even without a resize, and a perturbation computed at a fixed working resolution protects only a window of scales. The best worst-case protection over an unknown range of scales degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range, and averaging over scales does not reach it. Guided by this analysis, we propose SRIM, which samples a grid of anchor scales covering the whole range, with weights that favor the currently weakest scale, at the cost of standard expectation over transformation. On full-resolution photos of 9 to 30 megapixels and downscaling factors from 2 to 8, SRIM raises the worst-case disruption of FLUX.2-klein edits from 0.192 LPIPS, attained by the strongest published protection, to 0.463. At equal visibility, it roughly doubles the protection. The same protected photos also protect against the 9B model and against FLUX.2-dev, with worst cases of 0.450 and 0.386 against at most 0.184 for published protections, and SRIM leads on InstructPix2Pix as well.

</details>


### [45] [LARK: A Low-Cost, Accurate, Occlusion-Resilient, Kalman Filter-Assisted Tracking System for Image-Guided Surgery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07561)
*George Sideris,Justin Cree,Andrew Stirling,Mamadou Ly,Étienne Léger,D. Louis Collins*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LARK is a low-cost multi-camera optical tracking system for image-guided surgery using commodity RGB cameras, achieving sub-millimeter accuracy (0.64-0.73 mm median error) at under $1,000 USD, compared to expensive commercial stereo infrared trackers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial stereo infrared tracking systems for image-guided surgery are accurate but suffer from occlusion issues and are cost-prohibitive for many clinical settings, limiting accessibility for research and practical applications.

Method: Developed LARK, a multi-camera optical tracking system using five commodity RGB cameras with multi-view redundancy and fusion. Two tracking methods were evaluated: multi-view monocular pose fusion and multi-view triangulation. Both methods were tested under varying occlusion levels using a precision-machined grid and anatomical head phantom, with adaptive Kalman filtering employed. Results were compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared system.

Result: With five cameras and adaptive Kalman filtering, LARK achieved median target registration errors of 0.64 mm for point localization (triangulation) and 0.73 mm for trajectory tracking (pose fusion) on the machined grid. Camera-subset experiments demonstrated graceful degradation in adaptive pose-fusion accuracy as fewer views became available. Total hardware cost is under $1,000 USD.

Conclusion: LARK provides a low-cost, accurate alternative to commercial tracking systems for image-guided surgery research, with publicly available hardware designs, software, and datasets. The system achieves sub-millimeter accuracy comparable to gold-standard stereo infrared systems while significantly reducing cost and maintaining performance under occlusion through multi-view redundancy.

Abstract: Image-guided surgery (IGS) depends on accurate tracking of surgical instruments to provide real-time navigation relative to anatomical structures. Commercial stereo infrared trackers are accurate but prone to occlusion and cost-prohibitive for many settings. This work presents LARK, a multi-camera optical tracking system using commodity RGB hardware and multi-view redundancy and fusion. We develop and evaluate two complete tracking methods: multi-view monocular pose fusion and multi-view triangulation. Both methods are assessed under varying occlusion levels using a precision-machined grid and an anatomical head phantom, and compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared system. With five cameras and adaptive Kalman filtering, LARK achieves median target registration errors of 0.64 mm for point localization with triangulation and 0.73 mm for trajectory tracking with pose fusion on the machined grid.
