Camera-subset experiments show graceful degradation in adaptive pose-fusion accuracy as fewer views remain available. With tracking hardware costing under $1,000 USD, LARK provides a low-cost platform for image-guided surgery research. Hardware designs and software are publicly available at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/software/ , and datasets at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/data/ .

</details>


### [46] [AIMS: Anchor-Integrated Multi-View Synthesis for Scalable Novel View Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07566)
*JooHyun Park,HanYoung Jang,HyeongYeop Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AIMS introduces a scalable framework for novel view synthesis that decouples the number of input observations from the number of views processed by the global synthesis model. It uses farthest point sampling to select fixed anchor views, groups nearby observations around anchors, and uses a learnable integrator to fuse information into enriched anchor representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward novel view synthesis methods achieve strong generalization from posed multi-view inputs, but scaling them to large input view sets remains challenging. Transformer-based approaches that jointly process all input-view tokens incur rapidly increasing computation and memory as the number of views grows, while simple view subsampling discards potentially useful observations.

Method: AIMS selects a fixed set of spatially distributed anchor views using farthest point sampling, groups nearby observations around each anchor, and uses a lightweight learnable integrator to fuse their information into enriched anchor representations. This allows additional observations to contribute to synthesis while keeping the downstream global view budget fixed.

Result: AIMS achieves 29.41 dB PSNR on RealEstate10K and 17.73 dB PSNR on ScanNet, with rendering averaging 7.24 ms per view, demonstrating a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off against transformer-based and Gaussian-based baselines.

Conclusion: AIMS provides a scalable solution for multi-view synthesis that maintains quality while keeping computational costs manageable by using anchor-based view integration.

Abstract: Feed-forward novel view synthesis methods achieve strong generalization from posed multi-view inputs, but scaling them to large input view sets remains challenging. Transformer-based approaches that jointly process all input-view tokens incur rapidly increasing computation and memory as the number of views grows, while simple view subsampling discards potentially useful observations. We introduce Anchor-Integrated Multi-View Synthesis (AIMS), a scalable framework that decouples the number of available observations from the number of views processed by the global synthesis model. AIMS selects a fixed set of spatially distributed anchor views using farthest point sampling, groups nearby observations around each anchor, and uses a lightweight learnable integrator to fuse their information into enriched anchor representations. This allows additional observations to contribute to synthesis while keeping the downstream global view budget fixed. Evaluations on RealEstate10K and ScanNet demonstrate a favorable quality--efficiency trade-off against transformer-based and Gaussian-based baselines. AIMS achieves 29.41 dB and 17.73 dB PSNR on the two datasets, respectively, with rendering averaging 7.24 ms per view.

</details>


### [47] [CETUS: How Far Do Representations Trained on Earth Transfer to Cassini SAR of Titan?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07576)
*Kevin Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates transfer learning from Earth to Titan for planetary terrain classification using Cassini SAR images, comparing DINOv2, DOFA, CROMA, classical features, and an untrained vision transformer on a USGS Cassini SAR mosaic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of systematic evaluation of Earth-pretrained representations for planetary terrain classification, specifically applying computer vision advances to Titan's surface mapping.

Method: Trained classifiers on expert geomorphological labels and predicted terrain in geographically separate Titan regions. Tested under logistic regression with varying feature scaling, optimization, and regularization. Also evaluated fine-tuning on Titan data.

Result: Pretrained encoders achieved higher mean macro F1 than classical features under logistic regression. Rankings changed with different hyperparameter settings. Fine-tuning improved DINOv2, degraded DOFA, and showed mixed results for CROMA.

Conclusion: Architectural and input processing differences prevent isolating pretraining effects. Classifier fitting and per-class performance matter critically when assessing representation transfer for planetary mapping. The evaluation is limited to agreement with expert interpretation since the map uses the same radar observations.

Abstract: Cassini synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images reveal the dunes, plains, and lake basins of Titan, providing an instance of representations learned from Earth imagery for planetary terrain classification. Cross-domain Evaluation of Earth-to-Titan Transfer Using SAR (CETUS) compares features from DINOv2, DOFA and CROMA with classical image measurements and features from an untrained vision transformer on the U.S. Geological Survey's Cassini SAR mosaic. The classifiers learn terrain labels from an expert geomorphological map and predict those labels in geographically separate Titan regions. Under logistic regression settings, pretrained encoders achieve higher mean macro F1 than the combined classical features. Encoder rankings change when feature scaling, optimization, and regularization change together. Further training on Titan improves DINOv2 performance, degrades DOFA performance, and leads to mixed results for CROMA under the tested settings. Architectural and input processing differences prevent these comparisons from isolating the effect of pretraining. Classifier fitting and performance on individual terrain classes matter when assessing representation transfer for planetary mapping. Since the map draws partly on the same radar observations, the scores measure agreement with expert interpretation.

</details>


### [48] [REViT-v2: Hierarchical Windowed Roto-reflection Equivariant ViT for Equivariant Feature Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07585)
*Sheir A. Zaheer,Jihwan Moon,Chan Y. Park*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A scalable roto-reflection-group-equivariant vision transformer (REViT-v2) using windowed group-convolutional self-attention and hierarchical feature architecture, capable of scaling to millions of parameters on ImageNet-sized datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for group-equivariant vision transformers that can scale to large parameter counts and practical image sizes (e.g., ImageNet), which has been challenging due to computational constraints.

Method: Developed a Hierarchical Windowed Roto-reflection Equivariant ViT (REViT-v2) combining windowed group-convolutional self-attention with a hierarchical feature architecture to enable scalability.

Result: Successfully demonstrated that the approach scales to group-equivariant ViTs with millions of parameters on practically sized ImageNet images.

Conclusion: REViT-v2 represents a practical implementation of scalable group-equivariant vision transformers, with publicly available code and pretrained weights.

Abstract: We propose a scalable roto-reflection-group-equivariant vision transformer based on windowed group-convolutional self-attention and a hierarchical feature architecture. We demonstrate that our approach can be scaled to group-equivariant vision transformers (ViTs) with millions of parameters and large datasets with practically sized images, i.e., ImageNet. The code and pretrained weights for the proposed Hierarchical Windowed Roto-reflection Equivariant ViTs (REViT-v2) are available at https://github.com/kc-ml2/revit.

</details>


### [49] [Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07684)
*Haipeng Liu,Yang Wang,Meng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Dual-FDM proposes a frequency-disentanglement approach for personalized image generation using dual references (customization and color/style). It addresses text misalignment issues in diffusion models by manipulating different frequency bands (mid-frequency for customization style transfer, low-frequency for color style transfer) within the frequency domain to simultaneously handle foreground customization and background style transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous diffusion-based personalized image generation methods suffer from text misalignment issues: background misalignment for image customization and foreground misalignment for style transfer. This problem stems from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process.

Method: Dual-FDM uses a frequency domain approach with mask strategy to disentangle dual image references. For customization style transfer, it replaces the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, it substitutes the low-frequency band of the background with that from both foreground and background of the color reference. These substituted bands serve as key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of Dual-FDM over state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed Dual-FDM successfully addresses the frequency band entanglement problem in personalized image generation by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy, enabling simultaneous customization style transfer and color style transfer with improved text-image alignment.

Abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.

</details>


### [50] [Unlocking Fine-Grained Perception in CLIP via Structurally-Aware Latent Masked Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07689)
*Juntong Li,Lingwei Dang,Haomin Wu,Ziyan Qiu,Qingxin Xiao,Qingyao Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SALM is an unsupervised framework that enhances CLIP's fine-grained visual perception through structurally-aware latent mask modeling, using dual-matrix alignment for explicit local geometric priors and latent mask modeling for implicit semantic aggregation, without requiring image-text pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CLIP excels in global semantic alignment but lacks fine-grained perceptual capabilities, hindering dense prediction tasks and limiting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Existing methods that incorporate geometric priors often fail to achieve deep alignment for both local spatial structures and global semantics, and may distort the original image-text space.

Method: SALM uses a dual-path design combining explicit and implicit mechanisms: (1) Dual-matrix alignment explicitly calibrates intra-sample spatial correlations and activation intensities to inject local geometric priors; (2) Latent mask modeling guides CLIP to restore missing semantic details from a target model, implicitly aggregating fine-grained structures into the global semantic space. SALM-Self extends this to self-distillation by leveraging CLIP's shallow features which inherently possess strong spatial observational capabilities.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SALM significantly improves performance in dense prediction tasks and boosts CLIP's zero-shot accuracy, effectively enhancing fine-grained understanding capabilities of MLLMs.

Conclusion: SALM successfully synergizes local and global alignment without image-text pairs, unlocking CLIP's intrinsic fine-grained potential through structural awareness. This approach not only improves dense prediction but also enhances MLLMs' visual understanding.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP excel in global semantic alignment but often lack fine-grained perceptual capabilities. This hinders dense prediction tasks and bottlenecks the visual potential of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Existing research has attempted to enhance CLIP's visual representations by incorporating geometric priors from vision-centric models. However, these strategies often struggle to achieve deep alignment for both local spatial structures and global semantics, potentially even distorting the original image-text space. To address these limitations, we propose SALM, an unsupervised embedding alignment framework based on structurally-aware latent mask modeling. SALM effectively synergizes local and global alignment via a dual-path design combining explicit and implicit mechanisms, without requiring any image-text pairs. First, we introduce a dual-matrix alignment strategy that explicitly calibrates intra-sample spatial correlations and activation intensities, thereby effectively injecting local geometric priors. Based on this, we further design a latent mask modeling mechanism to guide CLIP to restore the missing semantic details of the target model, thereby implicitly aggregating fine-grained structures into the global semantic space. Furthermore, driven by the empirical observations that CLIP's shallow features inherently possess strong spatial observational capabilities, we naturally extend SALM to a highly efficient self-distillation paradigm, SALM-Self. This unlocks CLIP's intrinsic fine-grained potential without relying on any external models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SALM not only significantly improves performance in dense prediction tasks but also boosts CLIP's zero-shot accuracy, effectively enhancing the fine-grained understanding capabilities of MLLMs. Project page at https://qzfm.github.io/salm_project_page/.

</details>


### [51] [Anchor-driven Multi-modal Multi-scale Expert Selection for Survival Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07694)
*Tao Zhou,Ying Hu,Huazhu Fu,Yi Zhou,Xiao-Jun Wu,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes AM²ES, a novel framework for cancer survival prediction that integrates histopathological Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) with transcriptomic profiles. It addresses two key limitations in existing methods: the lack of explicit alignment between morphological and molecular features, and the uniform treatment of spatial heterogeneity in WSIs. The framework uses learnable semantic anchors for cross-modal alignment and a hierarchical mixture-of-experts module for adaptive multi-scale feature selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-modal fusion methods for cancer survival prediction suffer from two major limitations: (1) they project features into a shared latent space without explicit alignment, causing entanglement of mismatched morphological and molecular signals; (2) they treat the extreme spatial heterogeneity of WSIs uniformly, lacking mechanisms to adaptively prioritize clinically relevant tissue scales for individual patients.

Method: The proposed AM²ES framework consists of two main components: (1) Anchor-driven Multi-modal Fusion (AMF) module - uses learnable semantic anchors as cross-modal mediators to bridge the semantic gap by enforcing structurally regularized alignment between transcriptomic features and multi-scale pathology representations; (2) Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE) selection module - performs Intra-scale Expert Filtering to identify salient tumor regions within each magnification, and Inter-scale Hierarchy Routing to dynamically weight and select the most informative resolution levels, mimicking a pathologist's diagnostic workflow.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple TCGA cancer cohorts demonstrate that AM²ES achieves state-of-the-art performance while offering fine-grained interpretability by visualizing how specific molecular pathways drive expert routing decisions across tissue scales.

Conclusion: The AM²ES framework successfully addresses the alignment and adaptive selection challenges in multi-modal WSI analysis for survival prediction, achieving superior performance with interpretable insights into how molecular pathways influence tissue morphology at different scales.

Abstract: The integrative analysis of histopathological Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) and transcriptomic profiles holds significant promise for cancer survival prediction. However, existing methods typically project multi-modal features directly into a shared latent space without explicit alignment, leading to the entanglement of mismatched morphological cues and molecular signals. Furthermore, current fusion strategies often treat the extreme spatial heterogeneity of WSIs uniformly, lacking mechanisms to adaptively prioritize clinically relevant tissue scales for individual patients. To address these limitations, we propose an Anchor-driven Multi-modal Multi-scale Expert Selection (AM$^2$ES) framework for survival prediction. Specifically, we present an Anchor-driven Multi-modal Fusion (AMF) module, which introduces learnable semantic anchors as cross-modal mediators to bridge the semantic gap by enforcing a structurally regularized alignment between transcriptomic features and multi-scale pathology representations. Built upon this aligned semantic space, we further design a Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE) selection module to decouple the hierarchical prognostic selection process. Mimicking the pathologist's diagnostic workflow, H-MoE performs (i) Intra-scale Expert Filtering to discriminatively identify salient tumor regions within each magnification, and (ii) Inter-scale Hierarchy Routing to dynamically weight and select the most informative resolution levels. Extensive experiments on multiple TCGA cancer cohorts demonstrate that our AM$^2$ES achieves state-of-the-art performance while offering fine-grained interpretability by visualizing how specific molecular pathways drive the expert routing decisions across tissue scales. The code will be released at https://github.com/taozh2017/AM2ES.

</details>


### [52] [RBMatch: Dual-Level Class Rebalancing for Semi-Supervised Building Footprint Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07698)
*Akil Ahmad Taki,Shaikh Anowarul Fattah*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RBMatch addresses the class imbalance problem in semi-supervised building footprint extraction from remote sensing imagery by jointly regulating pseudo-label generation and unsupervised optimization through three components: ACT, CACBR, and DAL. It achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple datasets and labeling ratios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-supervised learning can reduce annotation costs for building footprint extraction, but severe foreground-background imbalance causes "imbalance leak" - bias toward majority background class in both pseudo-label selection and unsupervised loss optimization. Existing methods only address imbalance at one stage, which is insufficient.

Method: RBMatch is a dual-level class-rebalancing framework with three components: (1) Adaptive Class-specific Thresholding (ACT) for balanced pseudo-label selection, (2) Confidence-aware Class-balanced Reweighting (CACBR) for mitigating class bias in unsupervised loss, and (3) Distribution Alignment (DAL) for matching predicted unlabeled-data distribution to labeled-data prior. The framework combines supervised learning with self-training.

Result: RBMatch consistently achieves the best building IoU and F1-score on WHU, INRIA, and Massachusetts datasets across 1%--10% labeled ratios. On the highly imbalanced Massachusetts dataset at 1% labeling ratio, RBMatch improves IoU by 1.37 points over the strongest baseline. It is the only method to outperform the fully supervised baseline across all twelve dataset--ratio settings.

Conclusion: Addressing class imbalance at both pseudo-label generation and unsupervised optimization stages is essential for effective semi-supervised building extraction. The dual-level rebalancing approach in RBMatch successfully prevents "imbalance leak" and achieves superior performance, especially on highly imbalanced datasets.

Abstract: Accurate building footprint extraction from high-resolution remote sensing imagery is essential for urban planning, disaster response, and environmental monitoring. However, obtaining dense pixel-level annotations is costly, motivating the use of semi-supervised learning (SSL) to leverage unlabeled imagery. In remote sensing, severe foreground--background imbalance poses a particular challenge for self-training, as it can bias pseudo-label generation and the resulting unsupervised optimization toward the majority background class. We show that addressing this imbalance at only one stage is insufficient: balancing pseudo-label selection alone does not prevent background bias from re-emerging during unsupervised loss optimization, a failure mode we term \emph{imbalance leak}. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{RBMatch}, a dual-level class-rebalancing framework that jointly regulates pseudo-label generation and unsupervised optimization. RBMatch combines a supervised learning pathway with a self-training module comprising three components: adaptive class-specific thresholding (ACT) for balanced pseudo-label selection, confidence-aware class-balanced reweighting (CACBR) for mitigating class bias in the unsupervised loss, and distribution alignment (DAL) for matching the predicted unlabeled-data distribution to the labeled-data prior. Experiments on the WHU, INRIA, and Massachusetts building footprint datasets across labeled ratios of 1%--10% show that RBMatch consistently achieves the best building IoU and F1-score among the evaluated methods. The improvement is most pronounced on the highly imbalanced Massachusetts dataset, where RBMatch improves IoU by 1.37 points over the strongest baseline at a 1% labeling ratio and is the only method to outperform the fully supervised baseline across all twelve dataset--ratio settings.

</details>


### [53] [What Frame-Level Labels Can and Cannot Do for Small-UAV Point Detection in Thermal Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07705)
*Wonbin Son,Gyumum Choi,Junil Seo,Hyungjoon Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a learning-based UAV detection method using only frame-level presence/absence labels (no spatial annotations). The approach freezes classification-trained spatial features and trains a readout to produce spatial score maps and point detections. Evaluated on two thermal infrared datasets (CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410), with additional exploration on a visible-light dataset (AOT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the challenge of obtaining spatial annotations when sensor or scene changes make additional labeling burdensome. Aims to learn localization from simple frame-level labels while maintaining detection performance.

Method: Uses an architecture that: (1) freezes spatial features learned through classification training, (2) trains a readout head with frame-level labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. Evaluates hit rates, detection rates under false-alarm constraints, and analyzes training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration.

Result: Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses; readout training extracted them consistently. Distributing labels across more videos improved localization hit rates. Synthesis effects varied by dataset. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints. Failures occurred when target signals were weak relative to background and under cross-dataset transfer.

Conclusion: Provides guidance on: (1) label allocation strategies, (2) spatial representations and readout design, (3) synthesis considerations, and (4) false-alarm control. The method works without external detectors but has limitations with weak targets and cross-dataset generalization.

Abstract: The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has increased the importance of image-based UAV detection. Learning-based detectors are trained on imagery and annotations, with annotation type determining the information available during training. We focus on learning localization from frame-level target presence/absence labels when sensor or scene changes make spatial annotations for additional training burdensome. We analyze the detection capability, learning behavior, and potential applications of an existing architecture for point detection of small UAVs, trained with presence/absence labels and requiring no external detector. The architecture freezes spatial features learned through classification and trains a readout with the same frame labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. On two thermal infrared datasets, CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410, we evaluate localization hit rates and detection rates under false-alarm constraints, analyze the effects of training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration, and compare with bounding-box detectors. We also explore potential applications on Airborne Object Tracking (AOT) using its visible-light imagery and frame labels. Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses, while readout training helped extract them consistently. Distributing similar label counts across more videos yielded higher localization hit rates, while synthesis effects varied by dataset and evaluation criterion. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints, and failures remained when target signals were weak relative to background variation and under cross-dataset transfer. These findings provide guidance on label allocation, spatial representations and readouts, synthesis, and false-alarm control.

</details>


### [54] [Comprehensive Evaluation and Fine-Tuning of Foundational Cell Nuclei Segmentation Models in Renal Pathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07711)
*Ruijie Wu,Junlin Guo,Ruining Deng,Yu Wang,Shilin Zhao,Haichun Yang,Yuankai Huo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses nuclei instance segmentation in renal pathology by combining foundation-model pseudo-labels (Easy), expert annotations of challenging cases (Medium), and consensus failure cases (Hard) to evaluate seven fine-tuning strategies across nine model configurations. LSP-DETR achieved the highest F1 score (0.8725) with Hard-only fine-tuning, while StarDist showed the largest improvement (0.7380 to 0.8332) with Medium-only fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose models struggle with renal pathology nuclei segmentation due to low contrast, dense nuclei, complex morphology, and strong background staining, necessitating improved segmentation approaches.

Method: Extended a human-in-the-loop framework by combining 5,901 Easy pseudo-labels from foundation models, 860 Medium expert-annotated challenging cases, and 198 Hard consensus failure cases. Systematically evaluated seven single-source and mixed-source fine-tuning strategies across nine cell segmentation model configurations.

Result: Fine-tuning improved all models. Medium data appeared in 7 of 9 best-performing strategies. LSP-DETR achieved highest F1 score of 0.8725 with Hard-only fine-tuning. StarDist showed largest improvement (0.7380 to 0.8332) with Medium-only fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Annotations spanning multiple difficulty levels support effective model adaptation for renal nuclei segmentation, though optimal annotation composition remains model-dependent.

Abstract: Accurate nuclei instance segmentation is essential for quantitative renal pathology, yet general-purpose models often struggle with low contrast, dense nuclei, complex morphology, and strong background staining. In this work, we extended a human-in-the-loop framework by combining 5,901 foundation-model-generated pseudo-labels from well-segmented cases (Easy), 860 newly expert-annotated unresolved challenging cases (Medium), and 198 expert-annotated consensus failure cases (Hard). These annotations, spanning different levels of segmentation difficulty, enabled the systematic evaluation of seven single-source and mixed-source fine-tuning strategies across nine cell segmentation model configurations. Fine-tuning improved all models, with Medium data included in seven of the nine best-performing strategies. LSP-DETR achieved the highest F1 score of 0.8725 with Hard-only fine-tuning, while StarDist showed the largest improvement, increasing from 0.7380 to 0.8332 with Medium-only fine-tuning. These findings show that annotations spanning multiple difficulty levels support effective model adaptation, although the optimal annotation composition remains model dependent.

</details>


### [55] [RefRoute: Decoupling Conditioning Cost from References via Compact Residual Conditioning and Spatial Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07720)
*Wanning He,Yuyao Zhang,Yu-Wing Tai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefRoute is a framework for multi-reference image generation that addresses scalability issues in diffusion transformers by using compact residual conditioning and spatially routed attention. It achieves 36.06 Weighted-Ref-VIEScore on ManyRef100 benchmark versus 8.88 for FLUX.2-Klein-9B, with 14-18x speedups at 16 references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-reference image generation requires preserving multiple subject appearances while composing them into coherent scenes, but existing diffusion transformers encode references as dense visual token grids with global attention, making conditioning increasingly expensive as reference count and resolution grow.

Method: Two complementary mechanisms: (1) Compact residual conditioning combines low-resolution latent tokens with lightweight residual features from full-resolution pixels to reduce reference token counts while retaining fine-grained appearance; (2) Condition routing and attention routing align reference tokens with assigned target regions and restrict cross-reference interactions while allowing selective reference access beyond boundaries for scene integration.

Result: RefRoute achieves Weighted-Ref-VIEScore of 36.06 on ManyRef100 vs 8.88 for FLUX.2-Klein-9B. At 16 references, 50-step config achieves 18.3x speedup and 4-step config achieves 14.2x speedup over FLUX baselines, with substantially slower latency growth as reference count increases.

Conclusion: Compact reference representations and spatially routed attention constitute an effective approach to scalable many-reference image generation, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining quality.

Abstract: Multi-reference image generation requires preserving the appearance of multiple subjects while composing them into a coherent scene. However, existing diffusion transformers commonly encode references as dense visual token grids and jointly process them with global attention, making conditioning increasingly expensive as the number and resolution of references grow. We present RefRoute, a framework that addresses both reference representation cost and attention overhead through two complementary mechanisms. Compact residual conditioning combines low-resolution latent tokens with lightweight residual features extracted from full-resolution pixels, reducing reference token counts while retaining fine-grained appearance cues. Condition routing and attention routing align reference tokens with their assigned target regions and restrict cross-reference interactions, while allowing selective reference access beyond region boundaries for scene integration. We further introduce RefRoute-Data for training many-reference generation models and ManyRef100, a benchmark spanning human, object, and mixed compositions with 10-17 references. After many-reference fine-tuning, RefRoute achieves an overall Weighted-Ref-VIEScore of 36.06 on ManyRef100, compared with 8.88 for FLUX.2-Klein-9B. Separate inference-cost evaluations show substantially slower latency growth as the reference count increases: at 16 references, our 50-step and 4-step configurations achieve $18.3\times$ and $14.2\times$ speedups over their corresponding FLUX baselines, respectively. These results establish compact reference representations and spatially routed attention as an effective approach to scalable many-reference image generation.

</details>


### [56] [Structure-aware Keypoint Localization for Videofluoroscopic Swallowing Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07726)
*Kai Zhou,Chuanshen Chen,Runhao Zeng,Meng Dai,Yifan Yang,Jinwu Hu,Daiyuan Li,Mingkui Tan,Fei Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses limitations in automated kinematic analysis of Videofluoroscopic Swallowing Studies (VFSS) by introducing a new dataset (VFSSKep) with extended keypoint annotations including the soft palate, and a novel semi-supervised learning framework (S³KL) that overcomes spatial bias in medical X-ray keypoint localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VFSS analysis methods focus on limited anatomical keypoints (cervical vertebrae, hyoid), ignore critical regions like the soft palate, and only annotate active swallowing segments while discarding abundant non-swallowing data. Additionally, standard semi-supervised learning suffers from spatial bias in medical X-rays with fixed layouts, where models memorize absolute coordinates rather than understanding anatomical structures.

Method: The authors propose two main contributions: (1) VFSSKep dataset extending annotations to the soft palate with large-scale unlabeled data; (2) S³KL framework with two strategies: (a) Structure-Aware Learning to extract high-resolution structural cues for representation learning, and (b) Structural Representation Consistency Learning with block shuffling to enforce invariant structural recognition.

Result: The proposed S³KL achieves state-of-the-art semi-supervised performance. Notably, using only 25% labeled data combined with unlabeled data outperforms fully supervised learning with 100% labeled data.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that incorporating structural awareness and leveraging abundant non-swallowing data through semi-supervised learning can significantly improve keypoint localization in VFSS, reducing annotation requirements while maintaining or exceeding fully supervised performance.

Abstract: Videofluoroscopic Swallowing Study (VFSS) is one of the gold standard for diagnosing swallowing disorders, providing dynamic X-ray imaging of the swallowing process. Automated kinematic analysis in VFSS relies fundamentally on precise anatomical keypoint localization. However, existing studies focus on limited keypoints (e.g., cervical vertebrae or the hyoid) and overlook critical regions such as the soft palate, while annotating only active swallowing segments and ignoring abundant non-swallowing data, resulting in poor data efficiency. Moreover, leveraging this unlabeled data via standard semi-supervised learning is suboptimal, as generic methods are prone to spatial bias. In medical X-rays with fixed layouts, models tend to memorize absolute coordinates rather than understanding anatomical structures. To tackle these challenges, we introduce VFSSKep, a novel dataset that extends annotations to the soft palate and incorporates large-scale unlabeled data. We further propose S$^3$KL, a Structure-aware Semi-Supervised Keypoint Localization framework designed to overcome spatial bias. It integrates a Structure-Aware Learning strategy to extract high-resolution structural cues for structure-aware representation learning, and a Structural Representation Consistency Learning strategy with block shuffling to enforce invariant structural recognition. Experiments show our method achieves state-of-the-art semi-supervised performance, even with unlabeled and 25% labeled data surpassing fully supervised learning with 100% labeled data. Code and data will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/kaai520/S3KL.

</details>


### [57] [Foveated Compression: Selective High-Resolution Preservation for Token-Efficient VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07729)
*Donghyun Han,Jangho Park,Yuseok Bae*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Foveated Compression is a method for vision-language models that allocates a fixed token budget by preserving native-resolution tokens in selected spatial regions while compressing others. It uses a self-distilled Foveated Merger for compression and a lightweight Foveated Selector for region choice. Experiments show that localized fidelity is not universally preferable, and substantial headroom exists in region selection, with complementary bottlenecks identified in region selection and compressed-region fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address the question of where visual fidelity should be preserved under a fixed token budget in vision-language models, since simple image downsampling is a strong compression baseline but doesn't consider where to allocate the limited tokens spatially.

Method: Foveated Compression encodes a full-resolution image once and represents it with a mixture of native- and compressed-resolution visual tokens. Key components include: (1) a behaviorally self-distilled Foveated Merger that compresses local visual tokens while preserving compatibility with native tokens, and (2) a lightweight Foveated Selector that chooses one of nine spatial cells to retain at native resolution using exhaustive budget-matched intervention supervision.

Result: At 11.11% visual tokens, uniform Foveated Compression matches iso-token downsampling. At 20.99%, the learned selector outperforms random and fixed allocation but remains below strong whole-image resizing. A budget-matched oracle achieves 82.73 macro accuracy vs 69.61 for the learned selector. Probing shows that signals predicting compression failure are more accessible after language-model computation than to the prefill-free selector.

Conclusion: Localized fidelity is not universally preferable to whole-image resizing. Substantial headroom (13+ macro accuracy points) exists within the same spatial action space. There are complementary bottlenecks in both region selection and compressed-region fidelity, suggesting future work should address both aspects.

Abstract: Visual tokens are a major source of inference cost in vision-language models, yet simple image downsampling remains a surprisingly strong compression baseline. This raises a complementary question: under a fixed token budget, where should visual fidelity be preserved? We introduce Foveated Compression, which encodes a full-resolution image once and represents it with a mixture of native- and compressed-resolution visual tokens. A behaviorally self-distilled Foveated Merger compresses local visual tokens while preserving compatibility with their native counterparts, and a lightweight Foveated Selector chooses one of nine spatial cells to retain at native resolution using exhaustive budget-matched intervention supervision. At 11.11% visual tokens, uniform Foveated Compression shows no significant paired difference from iso-token downsampling. At 20.99%, the learned selector significantly outperforms random and fixed allocation, but remains below strong whole-image resizing, showing that localized fidelity is not universally preferable. A budget-matched region-choice oracle reaches 82.73 macro accuracy versus 69.61 for the learned selector, revealing substantial headroom within the same spatial action space. Matched probing further shows that signals predicting when compression breaks the answer are substantially more accessible after language-model computation than to the lightweight prefill-free selector. These results expose complementary bottlenecks in region selection and compressed-region fidelity.

</details>


### [58] [Later Is Better: Token Reduction for ViTs Under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07758)
*Hyeongheon Cha,Hyungjun Yoon,Sung-Ju Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Training-free token reduction accelerates vision transformers but suffers accuracy degradation under distribution shift. This paper identifies that the reduction schedule (when tokens are removed across layers) is the key factor governing this gap. The authors propose a simple "late-concentrated power-law schedule" that concentrates token removal in later layers, consistently improving OOD accuracy without extra compute. The method works across 5 token-reduction methods, 9 backbones, multiple corruption types and shift datasets, and two modalities (video and vision-language QA).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training-free token reduction methods for vision transformers are designed and evaluated on clean data, but under real-world distribution shift (e.g., corruptions, noise), their accuracy gap to the uncompressed model widens with the removal rate. The authors identified that this gap is governed by the reduction schedule (the depth profile of token removal), which was previously left fixed as an implementation detail.

Method: The authors introduce a one-parameter late-concentrated power-law schedule that concentrates token removal in later layers of the vision transformer, as opposed to the "flat" schedule that removes tokens uniformly across layers. They also use single-layer probes to investigate the mechanism behind their finding.

Result: On ImageNet-C with DeiT-S, the late schedule closes 83% of the OOD accuracy gap at a 26% compute reduction (+1.17pp), and 99% of it at a lighter 7% reduction (+0.26pp). The gain cannot be attributed to retaining more tokens or using extra compute: held to flat's compute, the late schedule removes more tokens in total and leaves fewer tokens at the end, yet still wins. The effect is broad: holding across five token-reduction methods (ToMe, EViT, ATS, ATC, PiToMe), nine backbones, all ImageNet-C corruption types, eight further shift suites, and two further modalities (video and vision-language QA).

Conclusion: The late-concentrated power-law schedule consistently improves out-of-distribution accuracy over flat schedules at no extra inference cost. The mechanism is that earlier reductions perturb features that pass through more remaining layers, front-loading reduction error in depth. The schedule keeps its gain under six test-time adaptation methods, and needs no per-input or per-domain tuning.

Abstract: Training-free token reduction accelerates vision transformers by removing redundant tokens across layers, recovering most of the original accuracy at a fraction of the compute. These methods, however, are designed and evaluated primarily on clean data, and under real-world distribution shift their accuracy gap to the uncompressed model widens with the removal rate. We show that this gap is governed by the reduction schedule, the depth profile of removal, usually left fixed as an implementation detail. Concretely, we introduce a one-parameter late-concentrated power-law schedule that consistently improves out-of-distribution accuracy over flat at no extra inference cost. On ImageNet-C with DeiT-S, the late schedule closes 83% of that gap at a 26% compute reduction (+1.17pp), and 99% of it at a lighter 7% reduction (+0.26pp). The gain cannot be attributed to retaining more tokens or using extra compute: held to flat's compute, the late schedule removes more tokens in total and leaves fewer tokens at the end, yet still wins. Single-layer probes point to a mechanism: earlier reductions perturb features that pass through more remaining layers, front-loading reduction error in depth. The effect is broad, holding across five token-reduction methods (ToMe, EViT, ATS, ATC, PiToMe), nine backbones, all ImageNet-C corruption types, eight further shift suites, and two further modalities, video and vision-language QA. It is also specific to shift, still positive on clean and rising monotonically to ~4x that at the highest severity 5. The schedule keeps its gain under six test-time adaptation methods, and needs no per-input or per-domain tuning.

</details>


### [59] [From Laboratory to Road: Evaluating Wearable Gaze Accuracy for Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07783)
*William Engel,Fabian Flohr*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first unified framework for quantifying wearable gaze accuracy under real driving conditions. The study found a mean on-road error of 4.58 degrees, which was reduced to 1.10 degrees after applying a calibration offset, suggesting that online recalibration may be necessary for reliable BEV supervision in autonomous driving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations in autonomous driving don't capture behavioral relevance to human drivers. While gaze offers a promising behavioral signal, wearable eye trackers have known accuracy issues due to head motion, illumination changes, and calibration drift - yet these devices are often treated as ground truth. The authors aimed to quantify wearable gaze accuracy under real driving conditions for the first time.

Method: The study combined on-road and indoor experiments. On-road: 41 validated scenes where one driver fixated on a vehicle's license plate, measuring angular difference between plate center and estimated gaze direction. Indoor: Systematic analysis of how distance, illumination, head motion, target motion, and gaze eccentricity affect systematic bias and precision using the same driver and device.

Result: Mean on-road error was 4.58 degrees. Applying an offset estimated from indoor recordings reduced error to 1.10 degrees and improved all 41 scenes. The offset varied between sessions, indicating that reliable BEV supervision requires online recalibration and condition-dependent estimates of gaze uncertainty.

Conclusion: Wearable eye trackers have significant accuracy limitations in real driving conditions. To achieve reliable BEV supervision in autonomous driving, online recalibration and condition-dependent uncertainty estimates are necessary. The study provides the first unified framework for quantifying gaze accuracy under real driving conditions.

Abstract: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations have become a widely used interface between perception and planning in autonomous driving, but they encode what is in a scene, not what is behaviorally relevant to a human driver. Gaze offers a compelling behavioral signal for this gap, yet wearable eye trackers are routinely deployed as if their spatial output were ground truth, despite known sensitivity to head motion, illumination, and calibration drift. We present, to our knowledge, the first unified framework for quantifying wearable gaze accuracy under real driving conditions. Our on-road study contains 41 validated scenes in which one driver fixated a vehicle's license plate. Gaze error is measured as the angular difference between the plate center and the gaze direction estimated by the glasses. Separate indoor studies with the same driver and device systematically analyze how distance, illumination, head motion, target motion, and gaze eccentricity affect both systematic bias and gaze precision. The mean on-road error was 4.58 degrees. Applying an offset estimated from the indoor recordings reduced it to 1.10 degrees and improved all 41 scenes. Because this offset varied between sessions, reliable BEV supervision may require online recalibration and condition-dependent estimates of gaze uncertainty.

</details>


### [60] [Image-Space Refraction Correction for Underwater 3D Reconstruction: Warping Flat-Port Views into Pinhole Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07788)
*Chelim Lim,Tobias Fischer,Emilio Olivastri,Beverley Gorry,Michael Milford,Alejandro Fontan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A method to correct refraction distortion in underwater images captured by consumer-grade cameras in flat-port housings, enabling accurate 3D reconstruction and SLAM without modifying existing downstream algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flat-port underwater camera housings cause refraction that creates bowl-shaped deformation in reconstructed scenes and trajectories, compromising metric accuracy needed for coral reef mapping and seafloor exploration.

Method: Physics-based refraction correction in image space using ray-tracing simulations to characterize refractive distortion. The corrected images can be directly fed into existing reconstruction and SLAM pipelines.

Result: Removes reconstruction deformation, registers more frames, maintains low reprojection error, and generalizes across diverse reconstruction and VSLAM backends compared to conventional and refractive SfM methods.

Conclusion: The proposed refraction correction is downstream-agnostic and broadly applicable to underwater vision pipelines, enabling accurate metric mapping and navigation using low-cost consumer cameras.

Abstract: Consumer-grade cameras in flat-port housings are widely used for underwater exploration and mapping of coral reefs and seafloor habitats due to their low cost and accessibility. However, refraction at flat-port interfaces causes bowl-shaped deformation in reconstructed scenes and camera trajectories, compromising the metric accuracy required for mapping and navigation. To remove the dominant refractive distortion before reconstruction, we introduce a physics-based refraction correction in image space. Our method is downstream-agnostic: the refraction-corrected images can be directly used as input to existing reconstruction and SLAM algorithms. We characterize the refractive distortion through ray-tracing simulations and validate our correction on two real underwater datasets with differing scene structures. Compared with conventional and refractive Structure-from-Motion (SfM), our approach removes reconstruction deformation while registering more frames and maintaining low reprojection error. The correction further generalizes across diverse reconstruction and VSLAM backends, demonstrating its broad applicability to downstream vision pipelines.

</details>


### [61] [Geometry-Constrained Bidirectional Point Cloud Registration for Thin, Sheet-Like Heritage Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07793)
*Yuezhe Zhang,Lei Wei,Jingnan Du,Shuai Wan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A geometry-constrained bidirectional point cloud registration method for reconstructing thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts by independently acquiring front/back surfaces and using thickness-aware constraints to resolve rotational ambiguity and prevent structural collapse during registration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts cannot be suspended or marked due to fragility, requiring independent acquisition of front and back surfaces. Registration is challenging due to limited shared geometric features, scarcity of physical constraints, and risks of rotational ambiguity, instability, and structural collapse during iterative optimization.

Method: The method integrates semantic-guided preprocessing, PCA-based geometric normalization, and a thickness-aware registration strategy. Physical thickness serves as a geometric constraint. Rotational ambiguity is resolved by evaluating global rotation hypotheses refined via point-to-plane ICP, with optimal transformation selected using a geometry-aware fitness criterion consistent with thickness scale.

Result: The method achieves competitive or improved performance in most cases, particularly in projected area consistency and physically plausible front-back alignment. The thickness-aware constraint and rotation hypothesis evaluation reduce the risk of degenerate configurations where surfaces are incorrectly flipped while yielding deceptively acceptable numerical scores.

Conclusion: The proposed approach enables reliable non-contact digitization of delicate and thin heritage artifacts by preserving structural integrity through thickness constraints and preventing registration failures through systematic rotation hypothesis evaluation.

Abstract: Non-contact three-dimensional reconstruction of thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts poses significant geometric and registration challenges. Due to their fragility, these artifacts cannot be suspended or equipped with artificial markers, necessitating independent acquisition of their front and back surfaces. Subsequent registration proves difficult due to the limited number of shared geometric features and the scarcity of explicit physical constraints, which may result in rotational ambiguity, instability, and structural collapse during iterative optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry-constrained bidirectional point cloud registration method specifically tailored for thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts. The method integrates semantic-guided preprocessing, Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based geometric normalization, and a thickness-aware registration strategy. The estimated physical thickness is incorporated as a geometric constraint to preserve structural integrity during registration. Rotational ambiguity is resolved by evaluating a finite set of global rotation hypotheses, each refined using the point-to-plane Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm, with the optimal transformation selected via a geometry-aware fitness criterion consistent with the thickness scale. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive or improved performance in most cases, particularly in projected area consistency and physically plausible front-back alignment. In addition, the thickness-aware constraint and rotation hypothesis evaluation reduce the risk of degenerate configurations in which the two surfaces are incorrectly flipped while still yielding deceptively acceptable numerical scores, supporting reliable non-contact digitization of delicate and thin heritage artifacts. Implementation details are available at https://zyz-nwpu.github.io/GCBPCR/.

</details>


### [62] [Efficient Gaussian Splatting Sequence Compression with Standard Video Codecs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07795)
*Qi Yang,Shuting Xia,Le Yang,Geert Van Der Auwera,Zhu Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes GSCV, a novel Gaussian Splatting sequence compression method that leverages video codecs. It addresses the limitation that existing methods require tracked primitive information, which is often unavailable in practice. The key contribution is an Inter-PLAS method that enhances inter-frame correlation for better video codec performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video-based GS sequence compression relies on Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) and tracked primitive information, which is unavailable in most practical applications. Without tracked information, vanilla PLAS generates images with weak inter-frame correlation due to its stochastic nature, limiting compression performance.

Method: The proposed GSCV method incorporates an Inter-PLAS method to produce close images between I- and P-frames of GS sequences, enhancing inter-frame performance of video codecs. It also implements a new pipeline based on state-of-the-art video codecs with high bit-depth GS images to achieve higher compressibility and quality upper bound.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that GSCV exhibits obviously improved performance over MPEG video and point cloud-based anchors in GS sequence compression.

Conclusion: The GSCV method successfully addresses the limitation of requiring tracked primitive information in GS compression, providing a practical solution with superior compression performance compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: This paper presents a novel effective Gaussian Splatting (GS) sequence Compression method that utilizes the Video codec (GSCV). Existing video-based GS sequence compression relies on the Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) and tracked primitive information to convert GS into smooth 2D videos. However, tracked information is not available for most practical applications, and without it, using the vanilla PLAS can generate images exhibiting weak inter-frame correlation, due to its stochastic nature. GSCV incorporates a simple yet efficient Inter-PLAS method to produce close images between the I- and P-frames of GS, enhancing the inter-frame performance of video codec greatly. GSCV also realizes a new pipeline based on the state-of-the-art video codecs with high bit-depth GS images, achieving higher compressibility while simultaneously providing a higher quality upper bound. Experimental results show that the proposed GSCV exhibits obviously improved performance over MPEG video and point cloud-based anchors in GS sequence compression. The code is available at https://github.com/Qi-Yangsjtu/GSCV.

</details>


### [63] [Towards benchmarking Western Bluebird detection in the wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07802)
*Estela Monserrat Arriaga Santana,Julian Rosas Scull,Ibeth P. Alarcón,Bibiana Montoya,Aylin Sosa Mejía,Hugo Jair Escalante*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a new benchmark dataset for detecting and segmenting Western bluebirds (Sialia Mexicana) in natural environments, comprising over 6,000 high-resolution (4K) images where birds occupy only a small fraction of the scene. The study evaluates supervised detectors, open-vocabulary models, and segmentation approaches, finding that supervised methods generally perform best, though fine-tuned open-vocabulary models like YOLO-World can become competitive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bird monitoring in natural environments is challenging due to small bird size relative to the scene, background clutter, illumination variability, and observer viewpoint variations. Progress is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, realistic datasets essential for understanding behavioral patterns.

Method: The authors created a benchmark dataset with over 6,000 labeled images from 41 recording sessions featuring high-resolution (4K) in-the-wild images. They evaluated supervised detectors (Faster R-CNN, RT-DETR), open-vocabulary models under zero-shot and fine-tuned settings (YOLO-World), and segmentation approaches (Mask R-CNN, YOLOv8-Seg, Grounded-SAM, SAM).

Result: For detection, Faster R-CNN achieved the highest mAP while RT-DETR offered the best precision-recall trade-off. Open-vocabulary models performed poorly in zero-shot settings, but fine-tuning substantially improved performance—YOLO-World achieved highest precision, F1-score, and mAP@0.5. For segmentation, supervised methods significantly outperformed Grounded-SAM; Mask R-CNN achieved highest mask mAP while YOLOv8-Seg provided best precision and fastest inference. Failure analysis revealed that detection failures are caused by a combination of apparent scale, brightness, contrast, clutter, blur, crowding, and recording-session variation—not just object size.

Conclusion: Zero-shot bird detection in cluttered ecological scenes is highly difficult. Domain adaptation is crucial in small-object settings. Supervised detectors remain most reliable overall, though fine-tuned open-vocabulary models can become competitive with supervised methods.

Abstract: Bird monitoring in natural environments is challenging due to the small size of some species of birds relative to the scene, background clutter, variability in illumination, and the observers' viewpoint. Progress is further limited by the scarcity of large-scale, realistic datasets, which are essential for understanding behavioral patterns. To address this gap, we introduce a new benchmark dataset for the detection and segmentation of Western bluebirds (Sialia Mexicana), comprising over 6,000 labeled images from 41 recording sessions. The dataset features high-resolution (4K) in-the-wild images in which birds occupy only a small fraction of the image. We evaluated supervised detectors, open-vocabulary models under zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, and segmentation approaches. Supervised detectors remain the most reliable overall, with Faster R-CNN achieving the highest detection mAP and RT-DETR offering the best precision-recall trade-off. Open-vocabulary models perform poorly in zero-shot settings; however, fine-tuning substantially improves their performance, with YOLO-World becoming competitive with supervised methods and achieving the highest precision, F1-score, and mAP@0.5. For segmentation, supervised methods significantly outperform Grounded-SAM and SAM 3: Mask R-CNN achieves the highest mask mAP, while YOLOv8-Seg provides the best precision and fastest inference. A diagnostic analysis further shows that failures are not explained by object size alone, but by a combination of apparent scale, brightness, contrast, clutter, blur, crowding, and recording-session variation. Overall, our findings highlight the difficulty of zero-shot bird detection in cluttered ecological scenes and underscore the importance of domain adaptation in small-object settings.

</details>


### [64] [CHARTER: Auditing Reference Substitution in Hierarchical Compact-Evidence Evaluation for Computational Pathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07843)
*Hyun Do Jung,Jungwon Choi,Soojung Choi,Yujin Oh,Hwiyoung Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces CHARTER, a reference-aware evaluation framework for assessing compact evidence in digital pathology whole-slide image multiple instance learning models. It addresses the problem that candidate filtering and evaluation reference choices can artificially change measured fidelity and reverse comparative conclusions between candidate strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to expose and address a critical issue in evaluating compact evidence explanations for MIL models: when candidate filtering introduces candidate-conditioned predictions alongside full-bag predictions, and the evaluation reference changes while the target remains the original full-bag prediction, the measured fidelity of compact evidence can change, and comparisons between competing candidate strategies can be reversed. This hidden dependence makes evaluation results unreliable and potentially misleading.

Method: The authors introduced CHARTER with three components: (1) DECLARE - specify intended target and reference; (2) QUANTIFY - measure candidate-induced prediction shift; (3) AUDIT - test stability of comparative conclusions. They conducted experiments across 15 comparisons in a five-seed Random-K audit and a matched native-ranking stress test to demonstrate how reference choices affect evaluation outcomes.

Result: The audit revealed significant issues: 4 out of 15 comparisons showed determinate reversals (where the winning candidate strategy changes depending on reference choice). In the native-ranking stress test, the ACMIL comparison changed from REVERSED to PRESERVED, demonstrating that comparative conclusions are not stable across different reference choices.

Conclusion: CHARTER transforms implicit candidate-filtering and reference choices into an explicit, auditable evaluation specification. This helps researchers distinguish genuine preservation of the intended prediction from apparent gains that are actually induced by changing the prediction being explained, improving the reliability and transparency of compact evidence evaluation in digital pathology.

Abstract: In digital pathology, compact evidence is often used to explain or audit predictions made by whole-slide image multiple instance learning models. In hierarchical compact-evidence pipelines, candidate filtering introduces a strategy-specific candidate-conditioned prediction alongside the original full-bag prediction. If the evaluation reference changes while the intended target remains the original full-bag prediction, however, not only can the measured fidelity of the same compact evidence change, but comparisons between competing candidate strategies can also change. To make this dependence explicit, we introduce CHARTER, a reference-aware evaluation charter that asks researchers to DECLARE the intended target and reference, QUANTIFY candidate-induced prediction shift, and AUDIT the stability of comparative conclusions. Across the 15 comparisons in our main five-seed Random-K audit, 4 showed determinate reversals; in a matched native-ranking stress test, the ACMIL comparison changed from REVERSED to PRESERVED. CHARTER turns otherwise implicit candidate-filtering and reference choices into an auditable evaluation specification, helping distinguish genuine preservation of the intended prediction from apparent gains induced by changing the prediction being explained.

</details>


### [65] [CueRator: Agentic Search for Symbolic Rules to Adapt Frozen Multimodal Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07868)
*Sunchan Park,Beomkwon Cho,Kyeongbo Kong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CueRator is an agentic framework for policy-aware decision-rule discovery that adapts frozen contrastive multimodal encoders by searching for decision rules that convert cross-modal similarities into predictions. It addresses the trade-off between adaptivity and generalization in open-vocabulary audio-visual event perception by combining symbolic formulation with a lightweight per-video policy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for open-vocabulary audio-visual event perception suffer from a trade-off: trained modules adapt well but fail to generalize to unseen categories, while fixed rules generalize but cannot adapt. The authors seek to overcome this limitation.

Method: CueRator pairs a symbolic formulation (for generalization) with a lightweight policy that predicts parameters per video (for adaptivity). A report-guided multi-agent loop discovers the formulation offline by evaluating candidates on their expressive ceiling and whether a trained policy can realize them. The framework uses frozen contrastive multimodal encoders.

Result: On OV-AVEBench, CueRator improves total average from 57.8 to 60.2 and unseen-category performance from 55.8 to 59.9 over the best existing method. The seen-unseen gap is reduced from 7.1 to 1.2. Gains are attributed to both the formulation and the policy, with both feedback signals necessary for effective search. Improvements also generalize to two other audio-visual event perception tasks, and the discovered rule remains competitive across encoders with only policy retraining.

Conclusion: CueRator successfully bridges the adaptivity-generalization trade-off by combining symbolic decision rules with a lightweight policy. The agentic framework with multi-agent search and dual feedback signals enables discovery of effective decision rules that generalize across encoders while maintaining adaptability to new videos.

Abstract: Large language model agents have been used to search over symbolic structures such as programs and equations. We propose CueRator, an agentic framework for policy-aware decision-rule discovery, which adapts frozen contrastive multimodal encoders by searching for the decision rule that converts their cross-modal similarities into predictions. We validate it on open-vocabulary audio-visual event perception, where existing methods involve a trade-off between adaptivity and generalization to unseen categories: trained modules adapt at the cost of generalization, and fixed rules the reverse. The framework pairs a symbolic formulation for generalization with a lightweight policy that predicts its parameters per video for adaptivity. A report-guided multi-agent loop discovers the formulation offline, evaluating each candidate on its expressive ceiling and on whether a trained policy can realize it. On OV-AVEBench, CueRator raises the total average from 57.8 to 60.2 and unseen-category performance from 55.8 to 59.9 over the best existing method, reducing the seen-unseen gap from 7.1 to 1.2. Ablations attribute the gains to both the formulation and the policy and show that both feedback signals are necessary for effective search. CueRator also improves over the respective baselines on two further audio-visual event perception tasks, and the discovered rule remains competitive across encoders with only the policy retrained. Code is available at https://github.com/cvsp-lab/cuerator.

</details>


### [66] [Revar3r: gauge-aware perturbation uncertainty for feed-forward 3d reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07883)
*Sammam Mahdi,Fariha Binta Salim,Rakin Bin Rabbani,Aniqua Nusrat Zereen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReVar3R addresses uncertainty estimation in frozen 3D vision models (VGGT, π3, MASt3R) by deriving a closed-form error-independent variance term that grows with scene extent (||x_p||^2). The method registers predictions to a common similarity frame before computing per-point variance, without retraining. It outperforms built-in confidence in 15/18 conditions across six datasets, though trained evidential heads better calibrate magnitude within their training domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training-free perturbation uncertainty fails when outputs contain unobserved symmetry—run-to-run variation reflects symmetry rather than error. Existing alternatives have trade-offs: built-in confidence underperforms in most conditions, while trained evidential heads require model-specific supervision. For point maps, an error-independent variance term grows with scene extent and can overwhelm the desired signal.

Method: ReVar3R derives a closed-form, error-independent variance term that grows with scene extent (||x_p||^2 signature). It robustly registers predictions to a common similarity frame before computing per-point variance, without retraining or modifying the frozen model. Optional calibration and fusion use a held-out split. Tested across VGGT, π3, and MASt3R backbones on six datasets.

Result: Simulation reproduces the ||x_p||^2 signature; all 30 real VGGT view-sets tested exhibit this predicted signature. The estimator lowers AUSE below built-in confidence in 15 of 18 conditions. Staged evaluation: 11/18 wins for label-free core, 12/18 for label-free equal-weight fusion, 14/18 with held-out weights, 15/18 with built-in signal. Against trained evidential heads: the head calibrates magnitude better and leads in its training domain, while ReVar3R transfers across backbones without adaptation.

Conclusion: ReVar3R provides a training-free, backbone-agnostic uncertainty estimator that improves point filtering through better ranking. Limitations: it does not detect stable systematic bias, aid novel-view synthesis, or transfer calibration across domains. The method offers a practical trade-off: less precise magnitude calibration than trained approaches but superior cross-domain transferability without model-specific supervision.

Abstract: A correctly reconstructed distant point appears uncertain even when a frozen 3D model processes equivalent inputs because its output frame rotates fractionally. This exposes a weakness of trainingfree perturbation uncertainty: when outputs contain an unobserved symmetry, run-to-run variation potentially reflects symmetry rather than error. Existing alternatives have trade-offs: built-in confidence is outperformed in most evaluated conditions, while trained evidential heads require modelspecific supervision. For point maps, this research derives a closed-form, error-independent variance term that grows with scene extent and potentially overwhelms the desired signal. Simulation reproduces the effect; all 30 real VGGT view-sets tested exhibit its predicted $\|x_p\|^2$ signature. ReVar3R robustly registers predictions to a common similarity frame before computing per-point variance, without retraining or modifying the frozen model. Optional calibration and fusion use a held-out split. Across VGGT, π3, and MASt3R on six datasets, the same estimator on every backbone lowers AUSE below built-in confidence in 15 of 18 conditions. The staged evaluation yields 11 of 18 wins for the label-free core, 12/18 for label-free equal-weight fusion, 14/18 with held-out weights, and 15/18 when the built-in signal is included. Against a trained evidential head, the result is a trade-off: the head calibrates magnitude better and leads in its training domain, whereas ReVar3R transfers across backbones without adaptation. Its ranking improves point filtering, but it does not detect stable systematic bias, aid novel-view synthesis, or transfer calibration across domains.

</details>


### [67] [Unsupervised Long-Tailed Adaptation of Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07903)
*Keliang Chen,Yaxin Hou,Hui Liu,Yuheng Jia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Unsupervised Long-Tailed Adaptation (ULTA), a new scenario where vision-language models are adapted to downstream tasks using unlabeled data with long-tailed distributions. The key finding is that unlike supervised long-tailed learning, ULTA causes head-class performance degradation. The proposed MARS method addresses this through Boundary-Preserving Alignment and Margin-aware Self-Refinement, achieving 4.71% average accuracy improvement across nine datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world data distributions are often long-tailed, but existing methods assume uniform unlabeled data distribution. This leads to a contrasting phenomenon where head-class performance drops sharply in ULTA, distinct from supervised long-tailed learning where tail classes suffer most. The distributional mismatch erodes head-class boundaries and pushes head samples into confusable classes.

Method: The paper proposes MARS (Margin-Aware Refinement with Structural alignment) with two key components: 1) Boundary-Preserving Alignment - uses zero-shot VLM as fixed visual reference to suppress probability increases lacking visual support; 2) Margin-aware Self-Refinement - employs dynamic adjustment strategy to refine tail and confusable classes while preventing prediction bias.

Result: MARS outperforms state-of-the-art methods on nine benchmark datasets, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 4.71 percentage points.

Conclusion: The paper successfully formalizes the ULTA problem and demonstrates that addressing head-class boundary erosion through visual reference alignment and dynamic margin refinement can effectively handle unsupervised long-tailed adaptation challenges.

Abstract: Adapting vision-language models to downstream tasks has achieved remarkable success by leveraging pseudo-labels generated from unlabeled data. Existing methods typically assume a uniform unlabeled data distribution, and thus the resulting pseudo-label distribution is likewise uniform. However, real-world data distributions are often long-tailed. To tackle this, we formalize a new scenario termed Unsupervised Long-Tailed Adaptation (ULTA). Under this scenario, existing methods exhibit a contrasting phenomenon: head-class performance drops sharply, which is distinct from supervised long-tailed learning where tail classes suffer the most. In particular, we uncover that the distributional mismatch not only erodes head-class boundaries, but also pushes head samples into confusable classes, reinforcing the model's inherent bias. To address these issues, we propose a novel model called Margin-Aware Refinement with Structural alignment (MARS). Specifically, we mitigate head-class boundary erosion via Boundary-Preserving Alignment, which takes the zero-shot VLM as a fixed visual reference to suppress probability increases that lack visual support in the training targets. Building upon this, we introduce Margin-aware Self-Refinement, which employs a dynamic adjustment strategy to refine tail and confusable classes while preventing prediction bias. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that MARS outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 4.71 percentage points.

</details>


### [68] [Diverse Motion Customization via Control-based Dynamic Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07911)
*Youngyoon Choi,Kihyun Kim,Jeongwoo Shin,Joonseok Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A new training framework called Control-based Motion Customization (CMC) that addresses content leakage in video generation by using Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC) to steer generative dynamics toward desired motion while avoiding collapse toward the reference video.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generation suffers from content leakage where appearance attributes from reference videos unintentionally propagate into generated outputs. This occurs because the learning objective is formulated as direct regression on the reference, causing the generative process to collapse toward the reference video.

Method: The paper proposes using Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC) to formalize the problem - steering generative dynamics toward desired motion while keeping the output within the pre-trained model's prompt-conditional distribution (where appearance is determined by text prompt, not reference). Additionally, they introduce a timestep-adaptive motion cost that focuses only on early generative stages to improve efficiency.

Result: CMC effectively mitigates content leakage while achieving competitive motion fidelity. The timestep-adaptive approach accelerates training by 2.5 times. The method preserves the diversity of the base model across diverse scenarios.
