Motivation: Facial affect models are almost exclusively trained on adult data but are increasingly applied to children in education, health, and developmental research. This creates potential risks as models may not generalize well to child faces, which have different morphological features.

Method: Controlled multi-model audit using five AffectNet-pretrained expression models (EmoNet, EmotiEffLib, DDAMFN++, OpenFace 3.0, LibreFace) tested across four child image datasets, the AffectNet-8 validation set, and two spontaneous child video datasets through a shared harness. Linear probe analysis on frozen features was used to diagnose where the performance gap originates.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Child gap is model-agnostic - all architectures degrade from posed to naturalistic faces and share fear→surprise confusion; (2) Gap is concentrated in open-mouth faces (AU26 jaw drop), South-Asian children, with smaller averted-gaze penalty, while closed-mouth, White/Black children, and direct gaze perform normally - bias tracks expression morphology and specific populations, not skin tone; (3) Gap is diagnosable - linear probe on frozen features achieves 0.75-0.91 on unseen children vs 0.48-0.66 zero-shot, indicating the gap lies in the classifier head, not representation. Dimensional valence/arousal regression degrades sharply under domain shift. Recalibrating only the head on small target data recovers +0.13 to +0.28 on the two largest child sets across all five models, though gains are in-distribution and don't transfer across child collections.

Conclusion: The child gap in facial affect recognition is a systematic, diagnosable, and partially remediable problem. The bias is not due to skin tone but rather expression morphology (open-mouth/surprise) and specific populations (South-Asian children). The gap resides in the classifier head, making targeted recalibration effective. The paper will release the evaluation harness and analysis code while keeping child face data license-locked.

Abstract: Facial affect models are trained almost entirely on adults, yet are increasingly applied to children in education, health, and developmental research. We present a controlled, multi-model audit of five AffectNet-pretrained expression models (EmoNet, EmotiEffLib, DDAMFN++, OpenFace 3.0, LibreFace) on children, across four child image datasets, the AffectNet-8 validation set, and two spontaneous child video datasets, through one shared harness. Three findings emerge. First, the child gap is model-agnostic: every architecture degrades from posed to naturalistic faces and shares the fear$\rightarrow$surprise confusion. Second, it is concentrated and corroborated across all five models: open-mouth faces (read as surprise, correlating with the AU26 jaw drop) and South-Asian children degrade systematically, with a smaller averted-gaze penalty, while closed-mouth faces, White and Black children, and direct gaze do not; the bias tracks expression morphology and specific populations, not skin tone. Third, the gap is diagnosable: a linear probe on frozen features reaches 0.75-0.91 on unseen children versus 0.48-0.66 zero-shot, so it lies largely in the classifier head, not the representation, whereas dimensional valence/arousal regression degrades sharply under domain shift. Building on this, recalibrating only the head on a little target data recovers $+0.13$ to $+0.28$ on the two largest child sets across all five models at negligible adult cost, though the gain is in-distribution and does not transfer across child collections. We will release the harness, per-sample predictions, and analysis code; the child face data stays license-locked and is never redistributed.

</details>


### [91] [Event Detection in Table Tennis Videos using 2D Keypoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08286)
*Rainer Lienhart,Daniel Kienzle,Shin'ichi Satoh,Anastasiia Bilinska*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EventNet is a two-stage pipeline for automatic, frame-accurate event detection in table tennis videos. It uses 2D keypoint extraction (players' upper-body poses, table corners, ball center) combined with a keypoint transformer, followed by a transformer encoder that predicts time-to-event values for each frame. The method achieves 91.16% F1 score on Latte-MV and 73.08% on TTHQ dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D ball trajectory and spin estimation methods require key events (ball-racket contacts) to be identified in advance, making them difficult to apply to longer, unedited video recordings. This limitation motivates the need for an automatic event detection approach.

Method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) Extract 2D keypoints of upper-body poses for both players, table corners, and ball center. Use a small keypoint transformer to combine them into a compact viewpoint-robust representation. (2) Process temporal sequences with a transformer encoder predicting two time-to-event values for each frame (distance to next and previous ball-racket contact). Novelties include a temporal cosine-like target signal, viewpoint augmentation via 3D reprojection, and frame-rate augmentation.

Result: Achieves F1 score of 91.16% and mean frame deviation of 0.42 on Latte-MV dataset; 73.08% F1 score and 1.16 mean frame deviation on challenging TTHQ dataset.

Conclusion: 2D keypoint-based temporal modeling with EventNet architecture is a promising and practical approach for automatic event detection in table tennis videos, demonstrating robustness and generalization through extensive ablation studies.

Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of automatic, frame-accurate event detection in table tennis videos. Current methods for estimating 3d ball trajectories and ball spin typically require that key events, such as ball-racket contacts, have already been identified in advance. This requirement makes it difficult to apply these methods to longer, unedited video recordings. To overcome this limitation, we propose EventNet, a two-stage pipeline to detect key events: (1) 2d keypoints are extracted of the upper-body poses for both players, table corners and ball center. A small keypoint transformer combines them into a compact representation that is robust to changes in viewpoint, lighting, and background clutter. (2) The temporal sequences of these frame-based representations are processed by a transformer encoder that predicts two time-to-event values for each frame, indicating how close the current frame is to the next and previous ball-racket contact. One novelty is a new, temporal cosine-like target signal. Furthermore, we introduce viewpoint augmentation via 3D reprojection and frame-rate augmentation to improve robustness and generalization. Our extensive ablation study gives deeper insights into the importance of various architectural and training aspects. Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves an F1 score of 91.16% and a mean frame deviation between ground truth and predicted frame of 0.42 on the Latte-MV dataset and 73.08% / 1.16 on the challenging TTHQ dataset. Overall, our work demonstrates that 2d keypoint-based temporal modeling with our EventNet architecture is a promising and practical approach for automatic event detection in table tennis videos.

</details>


### [92] [Catastrophic Forgetting in Sequential Thermal Anti-UAV Detection: The Role of Scale-Conditioned Gradient Imbalance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08315)
*Khac Duc Giang Nguyen,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates catastrophic forgetting in continual learning for thermal infrared counter-UAV detection systems. YOLOMG (YOLOv5-based detector) is trained sequentially across three anti-UAV benchmarks of increasing scale difficulty. The study compares naive fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, and Scale-Stratified Herding (SSH) to address the stability-plasticity trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counter-UAV systems based on thermal infrared detection require accurate performance as operational datasets evolve. However, sequential fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks, a problem insufficiently characterized in this domain. The research aims to measure the stability-plasticity trade-off and identify the mechanism behind forgetting.

Method: YOLOMG (YOLOv5-based detector) runs as a single thermal-infrared stream with motion channel disabled. Experiments train sequentially across three benchmarks: Anti-UAV-RGBT (Stage 1), Anti-UAV410 (Stage 2), and CST Anti-UAV (Stage 3). Three approaches are evaluated: (1) Naive fine-tuning, (2) Knowledge distillation from a frozen teacher, and (3) Scale-Stratified Herding (SSH) using a 300-exemplar buffer balanced across four UAV size strata. Per-stratum analysis examines detection performance by target scale.

Result: Naive fine-tuning on CST yields Forgetting Measure (FM) = -0.605 against Stage 1 baseline, representing 90% capability loss, with -0.572 occurring in Stage 3 alone. Knowledge distillation achieves FM = -0.033 ± 0.004 across three seeds (95% retention). SSH roughly halves forgetting (FM = -0.605 to -0.311) and maintains non-zero large-target detection. Random-stratified replay performs comparably (FM = -0.221). Notably, large-target detection collapses to near zero within the first epoch despite high inter-stage cosine similarity (0.987) over weights, suggesting scale-conditioned gradient imbalance rather than weight drift as the forgetting mechanism.

Conclusion: Scale-conditioned gradient imbalance, not weight drift, is the primary mechanism causing catastrophic forgetting in scale-varying drone detection. Knowledge distillation provides strong retention (95%), while scale-stratified replay methods (SSH and random-stratified) effectively mitigate forgetting. The lack of a Stage 2 no-KD control limits causal attribution for KD results, and replay experiments require multi-seed validation.

Abstract: Counter-UAV systems based on thermal infrared detection must stay accurate as operational datasets evolve, yet sequential fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks, a problem that remains insufficiently characterized in this domain. This continual-learning study measures the stability-plasticity trade-off in YOLOMG, a YOLOv5-based detector run as a single thermal-infrared stream with the motion channel disabled, trained sequentially across three anti-UAV benchmarks of rising scale difficulty: Anti-UAV-RGBT, Anti-UAV410, and CST Anti-UAV. Naive fine-tuning on CST yields a Forgetting Measure of -0.605 against the Stage 1 ceiling, corresponding to a 90% capability loss, with -0.572 occurring in Stage 3 alone. In contrast, knowledge distillation from a frozen teacher is associated with FM = -0.033 +/- 0.004 across three seeds, corresponding to 95% retention. Because no Stage 2 no-KD control is included, this result establishes retention under KD training rather than a causal KD effect. Per-stratum analysis shows large-target detection collapsing to near zero within the first epoch, despite an inter-stage cosine similarity of 0.987 over the gradient-updated weights, pointing to scale-conditioned gradient imbalance, rather than weight drift, as a candidate mechanism. Scale-Stratified Herding (SSH), a 300-exemplar buffer balanced across four UAV size strata, roughly halves the forgetting (FM = -0.605 to -0.311) and keeps large-target detection non-zero. An ablation attributes the gain primarily to scale stratification rather than herding: random-stratified replay performs at least as well (FM = -0.221 versus -0.311 for SSH). These replay results are single-seed and should therefore be treated as preliminary.

</details>


### [93] [Transferable Spatial Temporal Coherence Adversarial Attack on Black-Box Vision Language Models for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08331)
*Heyam Bin Jahlan Areej Alhothali Abeer Alhothali*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces STCA (Spatial Temporal Coherence Adversarial Attack), a novel black-box adversarial attack targeting video Vision Language Models (VLMs) used in autonomous driving. The attack uses a three-stage approach: modalities expansion (caption-guided frame selection), spatial attack, and temporal coherence disruption. Experiments on BDD100K and nuScenes datasets show high attack success rates against Video LLaVA-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Dolphin models, revealing significant safety vulnerabilities in autonomous driving VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid integration of VLMs into sensitive autonomous driving systems introduces critical safety vulnerabilities. While adversarial robustness has been studied for image-based models, the susceptibility of VLMs to temporally-aware adversarial attacks against video in driving contexts remains unexplored and poses a distinct, under-examined threat.

Method: The proposed STCA attack comprises three stages: (1) Modality expansion using caption-guided frame selection to target semantically significant frames; (2) Spatial attack to craft effective perturbations while preserving high SSIM; (3) STCA attack using motion-guided mask to disrupt cross-frame temporal coherence. The attack operates under a black-box threat model, relying solely on transferability from a white-box surrogate model.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that the spatial attack achieves high attack success rate (ASR) with high SSIM. The findings reveal that existing video language models remain highly susceptible to adversarial attacks in autonomous driving scenarios.

Conclusion: Existing video language models used in autonomous driving are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, underscoring the urgent need for robust defense mechanisms for VLM models in safety-critical applications.

Abstract: The rapid integration of Vision Language Models (VLMs) into sensitive systems introduces critical safety vulnerabilities that remain unexplored in exist studies. While adversarial attack robustness has been extensively studied for image-based models, the susceptibility of VLMs to temporally-aware adversarial attacks against video in driving context poses a distinct and under examined threat. In this paper, we introduce novel adversarial attack against video targeting VLM models used for autonomous driving scenes named Spatial Temporal Coherence Adversarial Attack (STCA). Our attack comprise from three stages: modalities expansion, Spatial attack, and STCA attack. In modalities expansion, we propose caption-guided frame selection method in order to ensure that adversarial perturbation target the most semantically significant frames. Secondly.In spatial attack, we craft effective perturbation and preserve high similarity. Then the perturbed video generated fed into STCA stage that disrupt cross-frame temporal coherence using motion guided mask. Our method operate under black box threat model against victim target VLMs, relying solely on transferability from white-box surrogate model.We conduct our experiments on the BDD100K and nuScenes autonomous driving datasets across three VLM models: Video LLaVA-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Dolphin. Experimental results demonstrate spatial attack achieves an ASR with high SSIM. Our finding reveal that existing video language model, remain highly susceptible to adversarial attack in autonomous driving scenarios, underscoring the urgent need for robust defense for VLM models.

</details>


### [94] [Digital Twin-Driven Real2Sim2Real: Simulator-Conditioned Generation via Paired Driving-Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08339)
*Hojun Lim,Hyeongseok Jeon,Donghyun Kim,Soonyoung Jung,Heecheol Yoo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes DT-R2S2R, a digital-twin-driven Real2Sim2Real pipeline that reduces the cost of manual data collection and annotation for camera-based 3D perception in autonomous driving. By reconstructing driving clips in a georeferenced digital twin and conditioning a diffusion model on aligned simulator renderings, the method generates photorealistic training data without requiring target-region real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camera-based 3D perception for autonomous driving requires large annotated datasets, but deploying to new target regions traditionally needs expensive data collection and annotation. Existing generative augmentation methods face a trade-off: label-conditioned methods consume annotations they aim to replace, while simulator-conditioned methods lack visual grounding to specific real environments.

Method: The method combines two pipelines: (1) DT-R2S (Real2Sim2Real) - reconstructs recorded driving clips inside a georeferenced digital twin; (2) DT-S2R - conditions a diffusion model on geometrically aligned simulator renderings to create a digital twin-grounded Sim2Real model. This synthesizes photorealistic driving images from low-cost yet georeferenced simulator data across both reconstructed and novel simulator scenes within digital-twin coverage.

Result: DETR3D achieves 93.18% of mAP obtained by a target-region real-data oracle without using target images for detector training. Moreover, simple co-training with existing out-of-target real data outperforms the oracle.

Conclusion: DT-R2S2R can substantially reduce the cost of manual on-site data collection and annotation in digital twin-available districts, providing a practical foundation for scaling 3D perception for autonomous driving.

Abstract: Camera-based 3D perception for autonomous driving relies heavily on large annotated datasets, and deploying such a system to a new target region typically requires data collection and annotation. Generative augmentation has been proposed to reduce this cost, but existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off: label-conditioned methods consume the very annotations they aim to replace, while simulator-conditioned methods offer free annotations but lack visual grounding to specific real environments. This work investigates the extent to which a digital-twin-driven Real2Sim2Real pipeline (DT-R2S2R) can substitute for target-region real data. By reconstructing recorded driving clips inside a georeferenced digital twin (DT-R2S), we condition a diffusion model on geometrically aligned simulator renderings, establishing a digital twin-grounded Sim2Real model (DT-S2R). As a result, DT-S2R synthesizes photorealistic driving images given low-cost yet georeferenced simulator data across both reconstructed and novel simulator scenes within digital-twin coverage. The efficacy of generated data is verified on diverse 3D detectors. DETR3D, especially, reports 93.18% of mAP obtained by a target-region real-data oracle, without employing target images for detector training. Furthermore, simple co-training with existing out-of-target real data outperforms the oracle. Thus, DT-R2S2R can substantially reduce the cost of manual on-site data collection and annotation in digital twin-available districts, providing a practical foundation for scaling 3D perception.

</details>


### [95] [DIPrune: Task-Aware Token Pruning with Dual Importance for Efficient Multimodal Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08341)
*Shuo Yang,Changbai Li,Linlin Yang,Huobin Tan,Rongyu Chen,Tongfei Chen,Tian Wang,Sheng Xu,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses semantic degradation in training-free pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by proposing DIPrune, a dual-importance scoring framework that jointly considers intra-layer static features and inter-layer dynamic semantic evolution to preserve tokens crucial for deep reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training-free pruning methods for MLLMs suffer from semantic degradation due to task-agnostic design or unreliable attention estimates. The root cause is that salient tokens in shallow layers persistently suppress emerging semantic ones through numerical inertia, leading to premature discarding of signals crucial for deep reasoning.

Method: The authors reformulate training-free pruning as a minimization of distortion in the final task loss and derive a tractable token-wise upper bound as a surrogate objective. This formulation reveals a previously neglected inter-layer term accounting for gradients across layers. DIPrune implements this with a dual importance scoring mechanism: (1) intra-layer static feature saliency and (2) inter-layer dynamic semantic evolution.

Result: Extensive experiments on LLaVA and Qwen-VL demonstrate that DIPrune consistently achieves state-of-the-art results.

Conclusion: By jointly optimizing intra-layer static features and inter-layer dynamic semantic evolution, DIPrune effectively addresses the semantic degradation issue in training-free pruning for MLLMs, preserving tokens crucial for deep reasoning while reducing computational overhead.

Abstract: Recent training-free pruning approaches for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) effectively cut computational overhead by exploiting visual redundancy or text-vision attention. However, they frequently suffer from semantic degradation due to their task-agnostic design or unreliable attention estimates. Based on our empirical analysis, we have found that this issue arises because salient tokens in shallow layers persistently suppress emerging semantic ones through numerical inertia, leading to premature discarding of signals crucial for deep reasoning. To address the aforementioned issue, from the task-oriented aspects, we first reformulate training-free pruning as a minimization of the distortion in the final task loss and derive a tractable, token-wise upper bound to serve as a surrogate objective. Specifically, this formulation inherently reveals a previously neglected inter-layer term that accounts for gradients across layers. Accordingly, for the implementation, we propose DIPrune, a rank-based framework that employs a dual importance scoring mechanism to jointly optimize intra-layer static feature saliency and inter-layer dynamic semantic evolution. Extensive experiments on LLaVA and Qwen-VL demonstrate that DIPrune consistently achieves state-of-the-art results.

</details>


### [96] [PolarScale: A Physics-Grounded Benchmark for Radiometrically Consistent RGB-to-Stokes Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08346)
*Beibei Lin,Tingting Chen,Xin Zhang,Wenhao Zhao,Dongjun Li,Zifeng Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PolarScale is a benchmark that evaluates explicit scale estimation in polarization imaging from normalized intensity inputs. It addresses the limitation that current polarization inference methods divide out the radiometric scale, making full Stokes reconstruction impossible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polarization imaging provides physical cues beyond intensity imaging but typically requires specialized hardware. Existing methods infer polarization from RGB-like inputs but only predict normalized Stokes components or relative descriptors, from which the radiometric scale needed for full Stokes reconstruction has been divided out. This scale is not physically identifiable from the normalized input.

Method: PolarScale is built on existing trichromatic full-Stokes measurements. It takes per-scene normalized total-intensity image s0 (scene-referred linear image, not consumer sRGB) as input and asks models to predict: normalized Stokes components, AoLP/DoLP/DoCP descriptors, and a per-scene scale. Evaluation includes dataset-conditioned semantic scale estimation against constant-scale control, along with angular, self-consistency, and physical-bound metrics. Tested across seven restoration-based and generative backbones with three prediction strategies.

Result: Strongest restoration models estimate scale with 3.6-4.3% mean relative error versus 5.7% for constant control, violating physical bounds on fewer than 0.25% of pixels. Two generative baselines collapse to near-zero scale. Explicit descriptor supervision improves descriptor accuracy (23.66 vs 18.88 dB PSNR for MAE). Predicted full-Stokes representations improve diffuse/specular separation, material segmentation, and glare classification, though in diffuse/specular separation the learned scale performs only on par with constant control.

Conclusion: Scale estimation in polarization imaging is challenging but achievable with restoration models (achieving ~3.6-4.3% error vs 5.7% baseline). Generative models struggle significantly with this task. The predicted full-Stokes representations have practical value for downstream vision tasks including material segmentation and glare classification, though the benefit of learned scale over constant scale is task-dependent.

Abstract: Polarization imaging provides physical cues beyond intensity imaging but typically requires specialized hardware. Recent methods infer polarization from RGB-like inputs, yet predict only normalized Stokes components or relative descriptors, from which the radiometric scale needed for full Stokes reconstruction has been divided out. We introduce PolarScale, a benchmark that makes this scale an explicit prediction and evaluation target. Built on existing trichromatic full-Stokes measurements, PolarScale takes the per-scene normalized total-intensity image $s_0$ (a scene-referred linear image, not a consumer sRGB photograph) and asks models to predict normalized Stokes components, AoLP/DoLP/DoCP, and a per-scene scale. Because the scale is divided out of the input, it is not physically identifiable; PolarScale therefore evaluates dataset-conditioned semantic scale estimation against a constant-scale control, together with angular, self-consistency, and physical-bound metrics. Across seven restoration-based and generative backbones and three prediction strategies, the strongest restoration models estimate the scale with 3.6-4.3% mean relative error versus 5.7% for the constant control and violate physical bounds on fewer than 0.25% of pixels, whereas two generative baselines collapse to a near-zero scale; explicit descriptor supervision improves descriptor accuracy (23.66 vs. 18.88 dB PSNR for MAE). Predicted full-Stokes representations improve diffuse/specular separation, material segmentation, and glare classification, although in diffuse/specular separation the learned scale performs only on par with the constant control.

</details>


### [97] [Test-Time Adaptation of Quantized ViTs via Single-Pass Quantizer-Aligned Recalibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08358)
*Hyeongheon Cha,Young D. Kwon,Sung-Ju Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: QuAR is a test-time adaptation method for quantized vision transformers that recalibrates activations at quantizer inputs to map test distribution statistics back toward source calibration, without backpropagation or parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training quantization makes ViTs brittle under distribution shift. Existing TTA methods either require backpropagation (incompatible with quantized inference) or incur overhead from extra forward passes/parameter updates. A key quantization-specific failure mode—activation distribution shifting relative to frozen quantizer ranges, distorting code distribution—is not directly addressed.

Method: QuAR performs single-pass recalibration at the input to frozen quantizers, mapping the test stream's running per-channel statistics back toward source calibration statistics. No backpropagation or model parameter updates are involved.

Result: On ImageNet-C with ViT-B, QuAR achieves highest mean accuracy among state-of-the-art backprop-free TTA methods at 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-bit precision. Outperforms strongest baseline by 2.28 points at 8 bits and 4.00 at 3 bits, with 46% lower latency and only 0.17 MB memory overhead (0.01% of peak inference memory). Maintains advantage across continual streams, non-i.i.d. label shift, seven OOD suites, and three other backbones.

Conclusion: QuAR effectively addresses quantization-specific distribution shift by restoring proper quantizer code distribution. The gain derives from reduced per-channel mismatch at quantizers. The method is practical for edge deployment due to minimal overhead and single-pass nature.

Abstract: Post-training quantization is a standard route to fitting vision transformers (ViTs) into edge compute and memory budgets, yet quantized models become especially brittle under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses such shifts without labels, but most existing approaches are poorly aligned with the constraints of quantized inference. Prevailing TTA methods recover accuracy through backpropagation, while backprop-free methods often still incur overhead from extra forward passes or parameter updates, and lightweight feature- or logit-level methods recover only part of the loss. Across these approaches, a quantization-specific failure mode that amplifies the drop is not directly targeted: under shift, activations occupy frozen quantizers' calibrated ranges differently, distorting their code distribution. We propose Quantizer-Aligned Recalibration (QuAR), a single-pass TTA method tailored to quantized ViTs that neither backpropagates nor updates any model parameters. QuAR recalibrates activations at the input to a frozen quantizer, mapping the test stream's running per-channel statistics back toward the source calibration. On ImageNet-C with ViT-B, QuAR achieves the highest mean accuracy among state-of-the-art backprop-free TTA methods at 3-, 4-, 6- and 8-bit weight/activation precision, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.28 points at 8 bits and 4.00 at 3 bits, with 46% lower latency and a memory overhead of only 0.17 MB (0.01% of peak inference memory). Analysis and diagnostics trace the gain to a reduced per-channel mismatch at these quantizers, which restores the code distribution the baselines leave unchanged or distort further. A single fixed configuration remains ahead across continual streams, non-i.i.d. label shift, seven out-of-distribution suites, and three other backbones.

</details>


### [98] [A Stevens's Power Law Check-up of GPT-5.5's Image-Based Visualization Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08365)
*Kaichun Yang,Jian Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: We adapt Stevens's power law to measure the innate ability of AI models to read visualizations, which can reveal the built-in perceptual mechanisms of algorithmic models. In our pilot study, models see no legend. A model first views a reference visual representation and estimates its magnitude, then estimates the magnitude of each subsequent image of the same representation relative to that reference. Our evaluation of twelve visual variables makes how algorithmic models read visual encodings measurable, comparable with human perception, and more interpretable to humans.

### [99] [UniCounting: Instance-Aware Proposal Consolidation for Image-Query-Free Multi-Category Counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08379)
*Jinshi Liu,Pan Liu,Lei He,Weichao Luo,Rui Qian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniCounting is a novel image-query-free multi-category counting method that predicts complete category-count vectors from RGB images without knowing which categories appear. It uses frozen SAM 2.1 for segmentation, DINOv2/OpenCLIP for features, and a lightweight 3,267-parameter relation head trained to predict same-instance affinities. The approach outperforms calibrated OWLv2-All80 on COCO clean500 in ℓ1 error and absent-class false mass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current visual counting methods typically count a single specified target given an image-specific exemplar, text query, or target category. This paper proposes a new paradigm: fixed-vocabulary image-query-free multi-category counting, where given only an RGB image, the model predicts a complete category-count vector without being told which categories appear.

Method: UniCounting casts counting as instance-aware structural inference over an over-complete proposal set. It uses frozen SAM 2.1 for mask generation, frozen DINOv2 and OpenCLIP for relation and category features. A 3,267-parameter category-shared relation head is trained to predict same-instance affinities from instance-mask-derived supervision. Sparse graph construction, representative selection, labeling, and background-margin admission convert admitted components into counts with replayable group evidence. Only the relation head is trained, without count or density-map targets.

Result: On COCO clean500, UniCounting achieves lower point-estimate vector ℓ1 error and absent-class false mass than calibrated OWLv2-All80, with comparable micro presence F1. Under a matched decoder, the learned relation reduces both errors relative to mask containment, mask IoU, CLIP, and DINO, while revealing a fragmentation-merge trade-off. Transfer diagnostics are reported on OmniCount-sub, FSC-147, and CARPK.

Conclusion: UniCounting achieves lower point-estimate vector ℓ1 error and absent-class false mass than calibrated OWLv2-All80 on COCO clean500, with comparable micro presence F1. The learned relation head reduces errors relative to mask containment, mask IoU, CLIP, and DINO. The approach also shows transfer potential on OmniCount-sub, FSC-147, and CARPK datasets.

Abstract: Visual counting is commonly formulated as counting a single specified target, with a model receiving an image-specific exemplar, text query, or target category and returning a single count. We instead study fixed-vocabulary image-query-free multi-category counting. A global vocabulary is fixed for each run, and, given only an RGB image, the model predicts a complete category--count vector without being told which categories appear. We present UniCounting, which casts counting as instance-aware structural inference over an over-complete proposal set. Generic segmenters produce duplicate masks, partial views, and proposals from neighboring instances; semantic scores can name them but cannot determine which denote the same object. Frozen SAM~2.1 generates masks, while frozen DINOv2 and OpenCLIP provide relation and category features. A 3,267-parameter category-shared relation head predicts same-instance affinities from instance-mask-derived supervision. Sparse graph construction, representative selection, labeling, and background-margin admission then convert each admitted component into one count with replayable group evidence. Only the relation head is trained, without count or density-map targets. On COCO clean500, UniCounting obtains lower point-estimate vector $\ell_1$ error and absent-class false mass than calibrated OWLv2-All80, with comparable micro presence F1. Under a matched decoder, the learned relation reduces both errors relative to mask containment, mask IoU, CLIP, and DINO, while revealing a fragmentation--merge trade-off. We also report transfer diagnostics on OmniCount-sub, FSC-147, and CARPK.

</details>


### [100] [UP-MOPD: Update Projection in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08398)
*Taojie Zhu,Jing Jin,Yuan Xia,Chenyang Ding,Qunshan He,Wanke Xia,Tao Sun,Yan Chen,Jian Wang,Jinjie Gu,Tao Feng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UP-MOPD addresses conflicting gradients in multi-teacher on-policy distillation by projecting optimizer updates rather than gradients. This handles the issue where AdamW's momentum, adaptive scaling, and weight decay can turn corrected gradients into updates that increase domain loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation combines expertise from different domains, but conflicting gradients hinder this integration. While gradient corrections directly constrain parameter updates under plain SGD, optimizers like AdamW can transform corrected gradients into updates that increase domain loss due to momentum, adaptive scaling, and weight decay. Existing gradient-level corrections fail with adaptive optimizers.

Method: UP-MOPD works in two stages: (1) Let the original mixed gradient update the optimizer state and generate a candidate displacement, (2) Project only violating candidates before they are committed to parameters. The projection finds the unique feasible update closest to the candidate in Euclidean distance.

Result: UP-MOPD improves IFEval-loose accuracy by 2.96 points over vanilla M-OPD late in training. It achieves an average score of 60.03 across eight metrics, compared with 59.00 for gradient projection and 59.15 for update rejection. On a public benchmark covering mathematics, code, and instruction following, it achieves the best average across six tasks (32.67), leads on LiveCodeBench v5, and ties for the best IFEval result.

Conclusion: Projecting optimizer updates rather than gradients is an effective approach to reduce interference between domains in multi-teacher on-policy distillation, outperforming gradient projection and update rejection methods.

Abstract: On-policy distillation from multiple teachers combines expertise from different domains in a single student, but conflicting gradients can hinder this integration. Gradient corrections directly constrain parameter updates under plain SGD. With optimizers such as AdamW, however, momentum, adaptive scaling, and weight decay can turn a corrected gradient into an update that increases a domain loss to first order. To address this gap, we propose Update Projection for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (UP-MOPD). UP-MOPD lets the original mixed gradient update the optimizer state and generate a candidate displacement, then projects only violating candidates before they are committed to the parameters. The projection gives the unique feasible update closest to the candidate in Euclidean distance. In experiments combining medical and general domains, UP-MOPD improves IFEval-loose accuracy late in training by 2.96 points over vanilla M-OPD. It achieves an average score of 60.03 across eight metrics, compared with 59.00 for gradient projection and 59.15 for update rejection. On a public benchmark covering mathematics, code, and instruction following, it achieves the best average across six tasks (32.67), leads on LiveCodeBench v5, and ties for the best IFEval result.These results support projecting optimizer updates to reduce interference between domains.

</details>


### [101] [GeoPID: Decomposing and Steering Visual Information in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08401)
*Seulgi Kim,Zhixiong Zhang,Xinwei Zhang,Jie Ling,Ronn Shaw*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GeoPID is a training-free framework that addresses vision-language models' tendency to over-rely on textual context by analyzing multimodal information geometrically. It decomposes visual-textual representations into Redundant, Modality-Unique, and Synergistic components, then applies targeted intervention to amplify vision-unique representations during inference, achieving 7.63% average relative accuracy gain without model updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models (VLMs) tend to under-use visual information and over-rely on textual context, which limits their visual grounding capabilities. Existing methods typically require training or fine-tuning, making them computationally expensive.

Method: GeoPID uses geometric analysis to decompose information into three components: Redundant (common to both modalities), Modality-Unique (specific to each modality), and Synergistic (combined information). It analyzes geometric relationships between visual and textual representation subspaces across 22 VLMs and 14 benchmarks. A targeted intervention technique selectively amplifies visual representations along the vision-unique subspace during inference.

Result: Correct predictions exhibit stronger vision-unique components when questions strongly require visual grounding. The intervention technique enhanced visual grounding capabilities without any additional model parameter updates, achieving an average relative accuracy gain of 7.63%.

Conclusion: GeoPID demonstrates that geometric analysis of multimodal representations can effectively identify and remedy VLMs' over-reliance on textual context. The training-free intervention provides a practical approach to improving visual grounding without requiring model fine-tuning.

Abstract: While recent vision-language models (VLMs) have shown outstanding performance across diverse applications, they tend to under-use visual information and over-rely on textual context. In this work, we propose \textsc{GeoPID}, a training-free framework that analyzes multimodal information within VLMs from a geometric perspective. \textsc{GeoPID} decomposes information into Redundant, Modality-Unique, and Synergistic components through the geometric relationships between visual and textual representation subspaces. Through an extensive analysis across 22 VLMs and 14 benchmarks, we confirm that correct predictions exhibit stronger vision-unique components when questions strongly require visual grounding. Building on this geometric analysis, we introduce a targeted intervention technique that selectively amplifies visual representations along the vision-unique subspace during inference. As a result, visual grounding capabilities were enhanced without any additional model parameter updates, achieving an average relative accuracy gain of 7.63\%.

</details>


### [102] [Decoy and disclosure radii of invariant shape descriptors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08410)
*Tanush Shaska,Lubjana Beshaj*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the security vulnerabilities of rotation-invariant descriptors used for surface recognition. The authors demonstrate that these descriptors have large "fibers" (sets of different shapes producing identical descriptors), allowing adversarial "decoy" surfaces to bypass matchers while being geometrically distinct from the enrolled surface. The analysis uses spherical harmonics to represent star-shaped surfaces and examines the dimension of decoy families at various truncation levels (L=4,6,8,16), with practical testing on asteroid (101955) Bennu shape models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be security analysis of biometric/shape recognition systems. When a recognition system uses rotation-invariant descriptors, it can only distinguish surfaces up to the "fiber" of the descriptor - all shapes in the same fiber appear identical to the matcher. The authors want to measure this fiber's size (radius) to understand: (1) how vulnerable the system is to decoy attacks (distant shapes that pass as matching), and (2) how much enrolled shape information is exposed to anyone with access to the stored descriptor. This has implications for secure recognition systems and understanding the fundamental limits of shape matching.

Method: The methodology involves: (1) Mathematical analysis using spherical harmonics (truncated to degree L with n coefficients) to represent star-shaped surfaces; (2) Computing the generic fiber dimension for descriptors of rank r, which equals n-3-r modulo rotations; (3) Analyzing the "standard pool" of band powers, bispectra, and degree-three band invariants; (4) Testing odd bispectra as an alternative; (5) Applying exact and interval arithmetic for certification; (6) Practical validation using: (a) synthetic decoys matching 32 invariants at L=6 with relative precision 2×10^-18, and (b) radar shape model data from asteroid (101955) Bennu.

Result: Key findings: (1) Standard pool admits decoy families of dimension 5, 13, and 20 at L=4, 6, and 8 respectively; (2) Descriptor rank first reaches n-3 at L=16, but a "mirror decoy" persists at every L; (3) Odd bispectra remove the mirror decoy generically for L≥4; (4) At fixed mean radius, the pool determines enclosed volume exactly but cannot determine clearance requirements; (5) At L=6, a decoy matches all 32 invariants to relative precision 2×10^-18 at orbit distance 0.87 times the norm of the enrolled tuple; (6) For asteroid Bennu: the pool recovers the modeled volume, misses the handedness, and leaves the keep-out radius uncertain by more than 7 meters.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that rotation-invariant descriptors based on spherical harmonics have significant security vulnerabilities: they admit large families of decoy shapes that can pass as matching while being geometrically distinct. The standard pool of invariants (band powers, bispectra) provides insufficient security at practical truncation levels. Odd bispectra offer improved security by removing mirror decoys. The authors demonstrate these vulnerabilities are not just theoretical - they verified them with exact arithmetic and on real asteroid shape data. The practical implications include: systems using such descriptors cannot reliably distinguish between shapes with different clearance properties, and an adversary could potentially craft decoy objects that bypass recognition while having different physical characteristics. This work has implications for security systems, object recognition, and any application where shape discrimination is critical.

Abstract: A recognizer that compares rotation-invariant descriptors sees a surface only up to the fiber of the descriptor. We measure this fiber by its radius in the orbit distance from the enrolled surface. A large radius admits decoys, that is, distant shapes that pass the matcher. A small radius discloses the enrolled shape to anyone who captures the stored value. For star-shaped surfaces truncated to spherical harmonics of degree at most $L$, with $n$ coefficients, a descriptor of generic rank $r$ has generic fibers of dimension $n-3-r$ modulo rotations. The standard pool of band powers, even bispectra, and three invariants of the degree-three band therefore admits decoy families of dimension $5$, $13$, $20$ at $L=4,6,8$. Its rank first reaches $n-3$ at $L=16$, and a mirror decoy remains at every $L$. The odd bispectra remove the mirror decoy generically for $L \geq 4$. Yet at fixed mean radius the same pool determines the enclosed volume exactly, and it does not determine whether a surface meets a clearance requirement. We certify two cases by exact and interval arithmetic. At $L=6$ a decoy matches all $32$ invariants to relative precision $2 \cdot 10^{-18}$ at orbit distance at least $0.87$ times the norm of the enrolled tuple. For the radar shape model of asteroid (101955) Bennu, the pool recovers the modeled volume, misses the handedness, and leaves the keep-out radius uncertain by more than $7 \, \mathrm{m}$.

</details>


### [103] [Image Bitstream Fine-grained Understanding for Privacy-Friendly AIoT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08414)
*Zhen Yu,Wenyang Liu,Kejun Wu,Chengwang Xiao,Renjie Qiao,Chengtao Cai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Bitstream Fine-grained Generator (BFG), a foundation model for Image Bitstream Fine-grained Understanding (IBFU) that performs fine-grained classification and caption generation directly from encoded image bitstreams without pixel reconstruction, enabling privacy-friendly AIoT applications. The method includes a Bitstream Semantic Encoder (BSeE) and Fine-grained Semantic Generator (FSeG), trained on a new Corrupted-bitstream Fine-grained Understanding dataset (CFU-D).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional visual understanding requires full image decoding to pixels, which poses privacy risks in AIoT applications. IBFU aims to perform semantic analysis directly on encoded bitstreams without pixel reconstruction, reducing visual exposure in the processing pipeline while maintaining fine-grained understanding capabilities.

Method: BFG consists of two components: (1) Bitstream Semantic Encoder (BSeE) that directly extracts semantic representations from encoded image bitstreams without pixel reconstruction, and (2) Fine-grained Semantic Generator (FSeG) that transforms bitstream semantics into detailed natural-language descriptions via autoregressive generation. The model is trained and evaluated on CFU-D, a large-scale dataset containing both intact and corrupted bitstreams across multiple corruption types and severity levels.

Result: BFG maintains stable performance under bitstream corruption. On Stanford Dogs Caption dataset, the average CIDEr score only drops from 0.6339 to 0.6077, while vision-language models (Qwen-VL-Chat, BLIP-2, GLM, Gemini, GPT) suffer severe performance degradation.

Conclusion: BFG provides a practical paradigm for privacy-friendly fine-grained understanding in AIoT, demonstrating robust performance even with corrupted bitstreams. This approach successfully reduces visual exposure while maintaining accurate fine-grained caption generation.

Abstract: Image Bitstream Fine-grained Understanding (IBFU) aims to directly perform fine-grained classification and semantic description generation from encoded image byte sequences. In contrast to conventional pixel-domain visual understanding, IBFU conducts semantic analysis without fully decoding images into the pixel domain. Since pixel-level visual content is not explicitly reconstructed during inference, this paradigm reduces visual exposure within the processing pipeline and suits privacy-friendly Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) applications. In this paper, we propose Bitstream Fine-grained Generator (BFG), a novel foundation model tailored for IBFU. BFG consists of two main components: a Bitstream Semantic Encoder (BSeE) and a Fine-grained Semantic Generator (FSeG). BSeE directly models semantic representations from encoded image bitstreams without explicit pixel reconstruction, while FSeG transforms the extracted bitstream semantics into detailed natural-language descriptions through autoregressive generation. To train BFG and comprehensively evaluate IBFU in practical AIoT scenarios, where image bitstreams may suffer corruption during transmission and storage, we construct a large-scale Corrupted-bitstream Fine-grained Understanding dataset (CFU-D), containing both intact bitstreams and corrupted variants across multiple corruption types and severity levels. Experiments show that BFG maintains stable fine-grained caption generation under bitstream corruption. For example, the performance only has slight change from 0.6339 to 0.6077 in terms of average CIDEr score on Stanford Dogs Caption dataset, while vision-language models, such as Qwen-VL-Chat, BLIP-2, GLM, Gemini, and GPT suffer severe performance decrease. This paper provides a practical paradigm for privacy-friendly fine-grained understanding in AIoT.

</details>


### [104] [Ariadne's Thread of LipSync: Unraveling Forgeries via Inconsistency between Lip Motions and Head Poses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08417)
*Tianyi She,Jiawei Liu,Weifeng Liu,Hanqing Zhao,Weiming Zhang,Kejiang Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LipDA is a novel framework for detecting and attributing LipSync forgeries by exploiting the inherent biological coupling between lip movements and head poses. It uses feature contrast between authentic and forged videos for detection, and captures temporal dynamics and audio-visual synchronization patterns for model attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defense strategies struggle against advanced LipSync generation methods because they overlook an important biological coupling between lip movements and head poses in natural speech videos. Advanced LipSync methods achieve better lip synchronization while eliminating visual artifacts, making detection challenging.

Method: The framework uses two main approaches: (1) For detection, it quantifies the discrepancy between lip and pose features by contrasting authentic versus forged videos; (2) For attribution, it captures unique temporal dynamics and audio-visual synchronization patterns that serve as model fingerprints for source tracing.

Result: LipDA achieves over 97% AUC in detection and 97.5% accuracy in model attribution on two challenging LipSync datasets and a proposed large-scale multi-generator dataset (LipSync-A).

Conclusion: The proposed LipDA framework significantly outperforms existing methods by leveraging the biological inconsistency between head poses and lip movements, providing both effective detection and accurate model attribution capabilities for LipSync forgeries.

Abstract: Recent advances in LipSync generation technology have led to the creation of highly realistic videos, posing severe societal risks. However, existing defense strategies struggle against LipSync forgeries, as advanced LipSync generation methods not only achieve better lip synchronization but also eliminate visual artifacts. An important reason is that they overlook an inherent biological coupling between lip movements and head poses in natural speech videos. In this paper, we propose LipDA, a novel framework for joint LipSync Detection and Attribution, which takes advantage of the inconsistency between head and lip. For detection, the framework learns to quantify this discrepancy by contrasting lip and pose features from authentic versus forged videos. For attribution, our method is designed to capture the unique temporal dynamics and audio-visual synchronization patterns that act as the fingerprint of models, enabling source tracing. We conduct extensive experiments on two challenging LipSync datasets as well as our own proposed large-scale and multi-generator dataset. LipDA achieves over 97\% AUC in detection and 97.5\% accuracy in model attribution, significantly outperforming existing methods. Code and the proposed LipSync-A dataset are available at https://github.com/AnsonShe/LipDA.

</details>

### [105] [GAMEGO: Training Game-Dev Agents with Synthetic Trajectories Anchored in Real-World Assets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06910)
*Haoyue Yang,Jingyao Li,Zhengfan Wu,Jing Liu,Xuanle Zhao,Kang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GameGo is a framework that transforms brief game ideas into detailed Product Requirements Documents (PRDs) for training coding agents to generate browser-based games end-to-end. It includes GameGoData (55,060 development trajectories) and GameGoBench (124 game queries), with GameGoCoder outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Problem: Generating complex games directly from sparse user queries forces coding agents to make underspecified assumptions, resulting in incomplete mechanics, disconnected gameplay flows, and limited visual aesthetics. Prior approaches rely on complex multi-turn workflows or static benchmarks.

Method: 1) GameGo framework: Transforms brief game seeds into comprehensive PRDs using industry game-development practices. 2) Task-specific dynamic compression: Maximizes information density while preserving instruction following to retain core gameplay constraints without restricting design exploration. 3) Construction of GameGoData: 55,060 development trajectories across 2D, 2.5D, and 3D games. 4) GameGoBench: 124 diverse game queries for benchmarking. 5) Training GameGoCoder on GameGoData.

Result: GameGoCoder outperforms matched baselines and is comparable to frontier models across gamedev benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed GameGo framework successfully enables scalable, direct end-to-end real-world game synthesis from sparse user queries by systematically expanding game seeds into detailed PRDs, addressing the challenge of underspecified assumptions in LLM-based game generation.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in web front-end execution, with browser-based game generation emerging as a particularly prominent frontier. While previous efforts frequently rely on complex multi-turn workflows or focus on static game evaluation benchmarks, this work targets direct end-to-end real-world game synthesis driven by coding agents. However, generating complex games directly from sparse user queries often forces coding agents to make underspecified assumptions, yielding incomplete mechanics, disconnected gameplay flows, and limited visual aesthetics. To resolve this issue, this paper presents GameGo, a scalable framework that systematically transforms brief game seeds into comprehensive Product Requirements Documents grounded in industry game-development practices. To retain core gameplay constraints without restricting design exploration, GameGo uses task-specific dynamic compression to maximize information density while preserving instruction following. Based on this pipeline, GameGoData is constructed with 55,060 development trajectories across 2D, 2.5D, and 3D games, alongside GameGoBench, a benchmark comprising 124 diverse game queries. Training GameGoCoder on GameGoData yields a model that outperforms matched baselines and is comparable to frontier models across gamedev benchmarks. All code, datasets, and models will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [106] [Text2Dashboard: A Governed Agent Architecture for Natural-Language Dashboard Generation over Enterprise DataBrain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06914)
*Yiou Wu,Zezhi Tang,Ningwei Bai,Liuhaichen Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Text2Dashboard is a DataBrain-specific prototype that converts natural-language analytic requests into inspectable dashboards, combining LLM-based action proposals with deterministic software control for execution, state management, and fault handling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of turning natural language analytic requests into actionable, inspectable dashboards by combining AI model reasoning with deterministic software control for reliability and auditability.

Method: The system uses schema-constrained model decisions with typed tools, persistent state, and deterministic Hooks for approval, audit, checkpointing, recovery, and failure handling. The pipeline resolves entities, discovers metadata, enforces read-only SQL, composes dashboards, and applies static checks, dynamic preflight, and browser inspection.

Result: Metadata selection: 4/4 passed. SQL tasks: 4/4 met semantic criteria, 2/4 met exact output-column contract. Dashboard tasks: 4/4 single-panel passed, one two-panel task passed, one existing-dashboard refinement passed. All ten fault scenarios met specified outcomes. Model inference accounted for over 97% of runtime.

Conclusion: The system demonstrates successful natural-language-to-dashboard conversion with deterministic control, but results are small and DataBrain-specific, not establishing production readiness, general text-to-SQL accuracy, or efficiency advantage over manual construction.

Abstract: Text2Dashboard is a DataBrain-specific prototype that turns natural-language analytic requests into inspectable dashboards. An installable Codex plugin and standalone Agent Runtime combine schema-constrained model decisions with typed tools, persistent state, and deterministic Hooks for approval, audit, checkpointing, recovery, and failure handling. The pipeline resolves entities, discovers metadata, enforces read-only SQL, composes dashboards, and applies static checks, dynamic preflight, and browser inspection. The model proposes actions while deterministic software controls execution and records state transitions.
  We evaluate the workflow on frozen real-DataBrain tasks and controlled Hook faults. Strict success was 6/8 on metadata and SQL tasks: metadata selection passed 4/4, all four SQL tasks met semantic criteria, and 2/4 met the exact output-column contract. The final release passed 4/4 single-panel dashboard tasks, one two-panel task, and one existing-dashboard refinement; a parameterised task exceeded its step limit. All ten fault scenarios met their specified outcomes without unapproved external side effects. Model inference accounted for over 97\% of observed runtime in every reported group. These small, DataBrain-specific results do not establish production readiness, general text-to-SQL accuracy, or an efficiency advantage over manual dashboard construction.

</details>


### [107] [FluidPD: In-Place Elasticity for SLO-Aware Prefill-Decode Disaggregated LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06917)
*Kartik Ramesh,Kaidi Fu,Zihan Zheng,Jiahuan Yu,Fabio Oliveira,Carlos Costa,Minjia Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FluidPD is a P/D-disaggregated LLM serving system that provides SLO-aware in-place elasticity through two mechanisms: FluidToken handles transient prefill-to-decode imbalance by offloading prefill computation to decode workers, while FluidRole handles sustained imbalance by reassigning workers between roles without model reload. Both mechanisms are guided by lightweight pressure indices. The system improves SLO attainment by up to 94.6 percentage points over static SGLang on Azure production traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing P/D-disaggregated LLM serving systems use fixed prefill/decode worker ratios, but real-world workloads exhibit dynamic prefill-to-decode demand ratios (short bursts and sustained shifts). This causes latency SLO violations even when idle capacity exists elsewhere. Existing autoscaling reacts slowly, requires spare GPUs, and doesn't address short-timescale phase imbalance directly.

Method: FluidPD introduces two complementary mechanisms: (1) FluidToken - offloads a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers when decode-side slack is available, handling transient imbalance; (2) FluidRole - reassigns running workers between prefill and decode roles in-place, avoiding model reload and engine restart, handling sustained imbalance. Both mechanisms are guided by lightweight pressure indices that expose prefill and decode-side resource pressure before SLO violations occur.

Result: Across production Azure trace workloads, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment over static SGLang by up to 94.6 percentage points, demonstrating that SLO-aware in-place P/D elasticity improves service quality without provisioning additional workers.

Conclusion: SLO-aware in-place P/D elasticity is feasible and effective. By dynamically balancing prefill/decode workloads within existing resources using FluidToken and FluidRole mechanisms guided by pressure indices, FluidPD significantly improves service quality without requiring additional GPU provisioning or slow autoscaling reactions.

Abstract: Prefill-decode disaggregation is becoming a common architecture for LLM serving because it separates two phases with distinct execution patterns and SLO objectives. Existing systems typically combine a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio with request routing across workers. However, real-world workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio. As a result, a configuration that is well provisioned at one time may quickly become mismatched, causing latency SLO violations even when idle capacity exists elsewhere. Existing autoscaling mechanisms can add capacity, but they react slowly, require spare GPUs, and do not directly address short-timescale phase imbalance.
  We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system that provides SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidPD introduces two complementary mechanisms. FluidToken handles transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers when decode-side slack is available. FluidRole handles sustained imbalance by reassigning running workers between prefill and decode roles in place, avoiding model reload and engine restart. Both mechanisms are guided by lightweight pressure indices that expose prefill and decode-side resource pressure before they appear as SLO violations. Across production Azure trace workloads, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment over static SGLang by up to 94.6 percentage points, demonstrating that SLO-aware in-place P/D elasticity improves service quality without provisioning additional workers.

</details>


### [108] [Anchor Divergence for Semantic Geometry in Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06919)
*Akash Kannan,Kiho Park,Victor Veitch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Anchor Divergences" - a method to define context-specific semantic geometries on fixed representations by mapping probability distributions over "anchors" to Bregman geometries, enabling contrastive representations to be specialized for different semantic similarity criteria (e.g., object identity, visual style, clinical relevance).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cosine similarity provides a single fixed geometry for measuring similarity, but semantic similarity is inherently context-dependent—two items may be similar for multiple reasons (same object, same style, same clinical finding). Existing methods lack a principled way to specify context-specific geometries.

Method: The authors establish a correspondence between probability distributions over "anchors" and Bregman geometries on representation space, combining contrastive learning, exponential families, and information geometry. This correspondence allows modeling the anchor distribution to directly control the geometry.

Result: Experiments on retrieval tasks demonstrate that anchor divergences provide an effective and efficient way to specify context-specific semantic similarity, outperforming fixed geometry approaches.

Conclusion: Contrastive representations naturally encompass a family of geometries that can be specialized to particular semantic structures. Anchor Divergences offers a principled, flexible framework for adapting similarity metrics to specific contexts without retraining the underlying representations.

Abstract: This paper concerns how semantic context determines geometry in learned vector representations. Similarity is typically measured using cosine similarity, which provides a single fixed geometry. Semantic similarity, however, is inherently context dependent: two images may be similar because they depict the same object, share a visual style, or are relevant to the same clinical finding. We show that contrastive representations naturally encompass a family of geometries that can be specialized to particular semantic structure. The key idea is to use an interplay between contrastive learning, exponential families, and information geometry to establish a correspondence between probability distributions over "anchors" and Bregman geometries on the representation space. We use this correspondence to define "Anchor Divergences", a method for specifying context-specific semantic geometries on fixed representations. Under this correspondence, modeling the anchor distribution models the geometry itself. Experiments on retrieval show that anchor divergences provide an effective and efficient way to specify context-specific semantic similarity.

</details>


### [109] [RadOnc-Agent: An LLM-Orchestrated Framework for AI Workflows Across the Radiotherapy Care Pathway](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06923)
*Caiwen Jiang,Shuoyang Wei,Songlin Zhao,Junyu Li,Jingyuan Chen,Wei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadOnc-Agent is an agentic AI framework that orchestrates 26 radiotherapy functions across four clinical phases through a conversational interface, using an LLM to map clinical intent to schema-constrained function calls while preserving patient and workflow context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI capabilities in radiotherapy are fragmented across clinical stages, software environments, and data modalities, which contrasts with the longitudinal nature of radiotherapy workflows from treatment decision-making through follow-up.

Method: The framework formalizes radiotherapy into four clinical phases and provides 26 callable functions. An LLM controller maps clinical intent to schema-constrained calls, preserves patient/workflow context, and routes requests to specialist services. Evaluation included: 2,600 single-function requests (7,800 repeat executions), 200 synthetic cross-stage scenarios (600 executions), and 120 real workflow instances from 60 patient records (360 clean executions).

Result: The system achieved 98.79% function selection accuracy for single-function requests, 96.50% completion for scripted cross-stage workflows, and 96.67% for real-patient workflows. Ablations showed: removing longitudinal state reduced cross-stage completion from 96.50% to 84.00%; disabling schema/identity validation increased mismatched backend dispatch from 0% to 95.28%.

Conclusion: The findings establish technical feasibility of an LLM-orchestrated architecture for coordinating heterogeneous radiotherapy capabilities across longitudinal workflows. Important caveats: does not establish clinical correctness, clinical utility, or prospective benefit.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced individual radiotherapy tasks, yet these capabilities remain separated across clinical stages, software environments and data modalities. This fragmentation contrasts with the longitudinal radiotherapy workflow from treatment decision-making through follow-up. Here we present RadOnc-Agent, an agentic artificial-intelligence framework that formalizes radiotherapy into four clinical phases and provides 26 callable functions through a conversational interface. A large-language-model controller maps clinical intent to schema-constrained calls, preserves patient and workflow context, and routes requests to specialist services. We evaluated system execution using 2,600 single-function requests (7,800 repeat executions), 200 prespecified synthetic cross-stage scenarios spanning four phases (600 executions), and 120 workflow instances from 60 de-identified patient records (360 clean executions) representing decision-to-planning and planning-to-adaptation. RadOnc-Agent selected the intended function in 98.79% of single-function executions, completed 96.50% of scripted cross-stage workflows, and completed 96.67% of real-patient workflow executions. In comparative ablations, removing longitudinal state reduced cross-stage completion from 96.50% to 84.00%, while disabling schema and identity validation increased mismatched backend dispatch from 0% to 95.28% in a replay/test evaluation. These findings establish the technical feasibility of an LLM-orchestrated architecture for coordinating heterogeneous radiotherapy capabilities and information across longitudinal workflows; they do not establish clinical correctness, clinical utility or prospective benefit.

</details>


### [110] [Metonymic Circuits for Abstract Concept Grounding in Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06928)
*Jing Ding,Ziqiao Ma,Jiayuan Mao,Joyce Chai,Freda Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how Vision Transformers learn to ground abstract concepts (e.g., "angry") when direct training evidence is limited, proposing a metonymic grounding mechanism where concrete "anchor" concepts (e.g., "fire") bridge visual signals to abstract semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key motivation is to understand how vision models can recognize abstract concepts despite limited direct referential evidence in training data. The authors hypothesize that models use concrete, interpretable anchor concepts as a bridging mechanism—a metonymic process where abstract predictions are derived from concrete visual cues.

Method: The researchers apply Transcoders (a type of autoencoder) on CLIP and DINO vision encoders to decompose intermediate features. These features are then associated with semantic labels for concrete concepts, and their contributions are traced through circuits underlying abstract concept recognition. Experiments are conducted on a curated icon dataset, with causal interventions used to validate the functional role of metonymic intermediates.

Result: The study reveals structured metonymic circuits in Vision Transformers: (1) perceptual primitives dominate early layers, (2) object-like anchors precede abstract targets in the processing hierarchy, and (3) images containing rendered text recruit a distinct perceptual-to-textual route. Causal interventions confirm that these metonymic intermediates are functionally involved in grounding abstract concepts.

Conclusion: The findings support the existence of a metonymic grounding mechanism in Vision Transformers, where abstract concept recognition relies on concrete anchor concepts. This provides a mechanistic explanation for how limited training data can still enable abstract concept understanding through intermediate interpretable features, with implications for model interpretability and understanding semantic grounding in visual models.

Abstract: We study how Vision Transformers ground abstract concepts (e.g., angry) when training data provide limited direct referential evidence. We hypothesize a metonymic grounding mechanism in which abstract predictions are driven by concrete, interpretable anchor concepts (e.g., fire) that bridge visual signals to abstract semantics. By applying Transcoders on CLIP and DINO vision encoders, we recover intermediate features that can be associated with semantic labels for more concrete concepts, and trace their contributions in circuits underlying abstract concept recognition. Experiments on a carefully curated icon dataset reveal structured metonymic circuits, in which perceptual primitives dominate early layers and object-like anchors precede abstract targets. Images containing rendered text instead recruit a distinct perceptual-to-textual route. Causal interventions further validate that metonymic intermediates are functionally involved in grounding abstract concepts.

</details>


### [111] [Principles that Guide, Actions that Inform: Agent Evolution via Knowledge Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06964)
*Bowen Ye,Yongchao Xu,Junkai Ma,Xiang Yin,Wenzhao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAGA is a framework enabling LLM agents to continuously evolve from experience by transforming interaction trajectories into hierarchical knowledge (episodes → procedures → principles), with principles instantiated into task-specific guidance that refines actions through corrective feedback and resampling, creating an execution-abstraction feedback loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning for LLM agent adaptation requires parameter access and high computational costs, limiting flexibility for large-scale/closed-source models. Existing external memory methods focus on experience representation but keep knowledge tightly coupled with specific tasks, preventing generalization. The key challenge is transforming concrete interactions into abstract, reusable knowledge that guides future decisions beyond individual experiences.

Method: SAGA progressively transforms interaction trajectories into three levels of abstraction: (1) episodic descriptions, (2) reusable procedures, and (3) principles with explicit applicability conditions while maintaining links to execution evidence. Retrieved principles are instantiated into task-specific guidance and used to refine candidate actions through corrective feedback and resampling, creating an execution-abstraction feedback loop where accumulated knowledge guides future interactions and new experiences update hierarchical memory.

Result: Experiments on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld demonstrate improved task performance. Ablation studies highlight the importance of contextual instantiation and action regulation for leveraging principle-level knowledge.

Conclusion: SAGA successfully enables LLM agents to evolve from experience without parameter modification by implementing a hierarchical knowledge abstraction approach. The execution-abstraction feedback loop allows agents to generalize from concrete interactions to reusable principles, with ablation studies confirming that contextual instantiation and action regulation are critical components for effective principle-level knowledge utilization.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interactive environments, yet their ability to continually evolve from experience remains limited. Although fine-tuning enables adaptation, its dependence on parameter access and high computational costs restrict its flexibility, especially for large-scale and closed-source LLMs. External memory offers an alternative by allowing agents to accumulate experience without modifying model parameters. However, existing methods mainly focus on experience representation and organization, while the acquired knowledge remains tightly coupled with specific tasks and contexts, limiting generalization. A key challenge is how to transform concrete interactions into abstract and reusable knowledge that guides future decisions beyond individual experiences.
  To address this challenge, we propose SAGA (\underline{\textbf{S}}elf-evolving \underline{\textbf{A}}gents through Experience-\underline{\textbf{G}}rounded \underline{\textbf{A}}bstraction), a framework for experience-grounded knowledge abstraction and utilization in LLM agents. SAGA progressively transforms interaction trajectories into episodic descriptions, reusable procedures, and principles with explicit applicability conditions, while maintaining links to execution evidence. Retrieved principles are instantiated into task-specific guidance and used to refine candidate actions through corrective feedback and resampling. This creates an execution--abstraction feedback loop, where accumulated knowledge guides future interactions and new experiences continuously update hierarchical memory. Experiments on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld demonstrate improved task performance, with ablation studies highlighting the importance of contextual instantiation and action regulation for leveraging principle-level knowledge.

</details>


### [112] [AegisFlow: A Multi-Agent Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Remediation and Self-Healing in Fragile Data Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06971)
*Muhammad Bilal Awan,Zubair Hussain,Abdul Shahid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AegisFlow is an agentic self-healing framework for data pipelines that uses Watchdog and Repair agents to automatically detect and fix failures caused by schema drift, API changes, or DOM modifications. It employs Parallel Shadow Patching based on the MAPE-K loop to generate and test patches in digital twin environments, achieving 98.1% MTTR improvement and 92% patch success rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional data pipelines are brittle and frequently fail due to upstream schema drift, API contract changes, or website DOM modifications. Current observability tools only raise alerts for human engineers, resulting in high Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) and operational fatigue.

Method: AegisFlow uses a Watchdog agent to collect runtime telemetry and a Repair agent to automatically create, test, and deploy code patches based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It employs a non-intrusive execution model called Parallel Shadow Patching based on the Monitor, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Knowledge (MAPE-K) loop to generate and verify patches in digital twin environments. The framework is deployment-agnostic and can be deployed as a plugin into existing pipeline orchestration systems.
