Result: Evaluated across five common failure scenarios, AegisFlow achieved 98.1% improvement in MTTR (from 170 minutes to 3.2 minutes per patch) and a 92% patch success rate. It performs best with JSON schema changes (96%) and punctuation drift (98%), but less effective with Shadow DOM cases (85%). The system frees up approximately 98% of data engineering on-call time.

Conclusion: AegisFlow successfully closes the loop between detection and resolution in data pipeline operations, significantly reducing MTTR and operational fatigue. Its plugin-based architecture allows minimal uplift integration into existing systems, making it a practical solution for automated pipeline remediation.

Abstract: Traditional data pipelines are notoriously brittle, often failing due to upstream schema drift, API contract changes, or website DOM modifications. Present observability tools only raise alerts but for human engineers, resulting in a high Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) and operational fatigue. In this paper we propose AegisFlow (Agentic Engine for Intelligent Self-healing and Graph-driven Operations for Workload remediation), a novel agentic framework that closes the loop between detection and resolution. AegisFlow uses a Watchdog agent to collect runtime telemetry and has a Repair agent to automatically create, test and deploy code patches based on Large Language Models (LLMs). The framework presents the non-intrusive execution model called Parallel Shadow Patching, a non-intrusive execution model based on the Monitor, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Knowledge (MAPE-K) loop to generate and verify patches in digital twin environments. Through experimental testing, we have evaluated AegisFlow across five common failure scenarios, and see 98.1 percent improvement in MTTR (from an average of 170 minutes per patch to 3.2 minutes) and a patch success rate of 92 percent . In particular, the system is successful in dealing with changes in the JSON schema (96 percent ) and punctuation drift (98 percent ), and is least successful in Shadow DOM cases (85 percent ). AegisFlow frees up about 98 percent of data engineering on-call time from firefighting and reallocates it towards innovation. The framework is deployment agnostic consisting of a system that can be deployed in a plugin fashion into an existing pipeline orchestration system with minimal uplift to the existing system.

</details>


### [113] [EPOCH: Reliable Discovery through Evidence-Governed Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06986)
*Binjie Guo,Aisheng Mo,Ruitong Li,Xinle Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EPOCH is an evidence-governed architecture for AI research agents that addresses the problem of uncritical evaluation and promotion of fragile candidates in search over programs, mathematical constructions, and proofs. It combines task contracts, typed memory, active falsification, admission checks, and independent replay to evaluate candidates against claim strength and scope.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI research agent systems optimize evaluator feedback without adequately governing how that feedback is interpreted, challenged, and reused. This leads to fragile candidates being promoted as discoveries and conflation of benchmark improvements with theorem-level claims, undermining the trustworthiness of AI-generated scientific discoveries.

Method: EPOCH implements an evidence-governed discovery loop through five key mechanisms: (1) explicit task contracts to define claim scope, (2) typed memory for structured evidence storage, (3) active falsification to challenge candidates, (4) admission checks to validate claims, and (5) independent replay for verification.

Result: EPOCH achieves state-of-the-art performance: (1) AlgoTune: 0.65 vs 0.53 mean normalized score (baseline 0.53); (2) Math14: highest mean score of 0.57; (3) favorable held-out behavior under official-test replay; (4) leads descriptive aggregate on AgentHPO; (5) delivers substantial advances across 10 discovery problems including executable constructions, optimized algorithms, counterexamples, and proof-supported results.

Conclusion: Evidence governance is a necessary step toward AI research agents that produce not only stronger solutions but also more trustworthy scientific discoveries. The architecture successfully converts search into concrete progress across mathematical and computational domains.

Abstract: AI research agents are increasingly used to search over programs, mathematical constructions, and proofs. However, existing systems typically optimize evaluator feedback without adequately governing how that feedback is interpreted, challenged, and reused. As a result, promising but fragile candidates can be promoted as discoveries, while benchmark improvements, finite certificates, and theorem-level claims are too easily conflated. We introduce EPOCH, an evidence-governed architecture designed to close this gap. EPOCH implements an evidence-governed discovery loop by combining explicit task contracts, typed memory, active falsification, admission checks, and independent replay, so that each candidate is evaluated against the strength and scope of the claim it supports. EPOCH achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance on AlgoTune, substantially exceeding the strongest baseline in mean normalized score (0.65 vs. 0.53), and attains the highest mean score on the internal Math14 suite (0.57). It further shows favorable held-out behavior under official-test replay and leads the descriptive aggregate on AgentHPO. Across ten discovery problems, EPOCH delivers substantial task-specific advances, including improved executable constructions, optimized algorithms, counterexamples, and proof-supported results. These advances demonstrate its ability to convert search into concrete progress across mathematical and computational domains. Together, the results suggest that evidence governance is a necessary step toward AI research agents that produce not only stronger solutions, but also more trustworthy scientific discoveries.

</details>


### [114] [When better traffic forecasts fail to improve signal control: a layered diagnostic study of forecast-to-decision value](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06992)
*Jianing Long,Xiaobin Li,Wuming Lei,Weiguang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A diagnostic study investigating why improved traffic forecasts do not necessarily lead to better signal-control decisions, using 29 days of reconstructed demand data from Xuancheng, China. The research identifies key factors limiting forecast value in real-world traffic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the gap between improved traffic forecasts and actual signal-control decision quality, as better predictions do not automatically translate into operational benefits.

Method: Layered diagnostic study using 29 days of reconstructed demand from Xuancheng, China (7 dates for testing). Framework evaluates point forecasts, conformal intervals, dependence-aware scenarios, and matched closed-loop controllers through interface audits, temporal interface correction, and exhaustive joint-action search comparing causal forecasts with a five-second event oracle.

Result: Entry-level and movement-level forecasts reduce MAE by 4.03% and 3.92% relative to historical means. A nominal 90% conformal interval achieves 90.72% marginal coverage but only 75.66% on ex-post high-demand subset. Only 2 of 9 controlled intersections offer multiple effective actions. A synthetic positive control demonstrates future information can reduce internal rollout cost by 61.5%. However, on frozen test dates, causal forecasts and the oracle increase queue vehicle?seconds by 6.09% and 3.39% relative to matched no-future rollout, while the oracle reduces spillback exposure by 3.78%; paired-day bootstrap intervals cross zero.

Conclusion: Forecast value in traffic signal control depends on four key factors: temporal observability, action identifiability, dynamics consistency, and objective alignment. The proposed protocol provides a practical diagnostic framework to identify where predictive improvements fail to translate into operational benefits.

Abstract: Improved traffic forecasts do not necessarily yield better signal-control decisions. We investigate this gap through a layered diagnostic study using 29 days of reconstructed demand from Xuancheng, China, with seven dates reserved for testing. The framework evaluates point forecasts, conformal intervals, dependence-aware scenarios, and matched closed-loop controllers. Entry-level and movement-level forecasts reduce mean absolute error by 4.03% and 3.92%, respectively, relative to historical means. A nominal 90% conformal interval achieves 90.72% marginal coverage but only 75.66% on an ex-post high-demand subset. Interface audits identify decision-time leakage and reveal that only two of nine controlled intersections offer multiple effective actions. We correct the temporal interface and compare causal forecasts with a five-second event oracle using exhaustive joint-action search. A synthetic positive control demonstrates that future information can reduce the internal rollout cost by 61.5%. On the frozen test dates, however, causal forecasts and the event oracle increase queue vehicle?seconds by 6.09% and 3.39% relative to the matched no-future rollout, while the oracle reduces spillback exposure by 3.78%; paired-day bootstrap intervals cross zero. These findings indicate that forecast value depends on temporal observability, action identifiability, dynamics consistency, and objective alignment. The proposed protocol provides a practical way to diagnose where predictive improvements fail to translate into operational benefits.

</details>


### [115] [Joint upper-bound coverage and route-choice utility: an empirical evaluation on two urban proxy tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06995)
*Jianing Long,Xiaobin Li,Wuming Lei,Weiguang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether more accurate traffic forecasts or higher uncertainty coverage leads to better route decisions. Using road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu with 150 OD pairs and 3 candidate paths, the study compares raw 90th percentile path time bounds against jointly calibrated upper bounds under minimum bound route choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key question is whether improving uncertainty coverage (i.e., including more true outcomes within predicted bounds) actually translates to better route decisions, or whether forecast accuracy matters more for real-world routing outcomes.

Method: Frozen protocol separating speed error, joint candidate path upper bound coverage, route selection, and realized loss. Offline proxy tasks using processed road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu with 150 OD pairs, 3 candidate paths, and 14 test days per city.

Result: Joint coverage improved significantly (83.19%→92.26% Beijing M1; 75.14%→88.33% Chengdu M1; 74.01%→90.64% Chengdu M2), but this came at a cost: C2 increased lateness by 0.1633, 0.7848, and 0.9200 percentage points respectively, and mean travel time by 0.588, 3.082, and 4.418 seconds. In contrast, a 14.91% reduction in speed MAE yielded a 1.4571 percentage point reduction in lateness under C0.

Conclusion: Joint coverage is not a surrogate for downstream route utility in these frozen tasks. Higher uncertainty coverage does not necessarily improve route decisions; rather, forecast accuracy (lower speed error) directly correlates with better routing outcomes. The offline results do not establish online or causal benefits.

Abstract: Whether more accurate traffic forecasts or higher uncertainty coverage improve route decisions is unclear. We evaluate this question with a frozen protocol that separates speed error, joint candidate path upper bound coverage, route selection, and realized loss. Using processed road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu, we construct offline proxy tasks with 150 origin destination pairs, three candidate paths, and 14 test days per city. We compare raw 90th percentile path time bounds with jointly calibrated upper bounds under minimum bound route choice. Joint coverage rises from 83.19% to 92.26% in Beijing M1, from 75.14% to 88.33% in Chengdu M1, and from 74.01% to 90.64% in Chengdu M2. Yet C2 increases lateness by 0.1633, 0.7848, and 0.9200 percentage points, respectively, and mean travel time by 0.588, 3.082, and 4.418 seconds. In a separate Chengdu predictor comparison, a 14.91% reduction in speed mean absolute error accompanies a 1.4571 percentage point reduction in lateness under C0. Joint coverage is therefore not a surrogate for downstream route utility in these frozen tasks the offline results do not establish online or causal benefits.

</details>


### [116] [Topology-Consistent Task Planning over Cellular Workflow Complexes for LLM-based Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07004)
*Sen Zhao,Jia Tang,Ruiqi Kong,Zuyu Zhang,Lifeng Shen,Ding Zou,Xinyu He,Xu Zhang,Junwei Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopoPlanner is a topology-aware planning framework for LLM agents that handles complex workflow patterns (verification-correction loops, branch merging, reusable states) by lifting tool dependency graphs into cellular workflow complexes and using cosheaf-consistent cellular retrieval for context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM planners struggle with real-world tool orchestration patterns like verification-correction loops, convergent branch merging, and reusable intermediate states, which go beyond simple sequential or DAG structures.

Method: TopoPlanner uses topology-aware context by: (1) lifting tool dependency graphs into cellular workflow complexes, (2) performing cosheaf-consistent cellular retrieval to find request-relevant closed subcomplexes, (3) conducting multidimensional structural reasoning over retrieved topology, and (4) interfacing the cellular representation with the planner LLM for tool-sequence generation.

Result: Experiments on four tool-planning benchmarks with topology-guided loop, merge, and loop-merge workflows show consistent improvements over prompt-based and graph-enhanced baselines across different local LLM backbones.

Conclusion: The topology-consistent approach to LLM task planning effectively handles complex workflow patterns that traditional planners cannot manage, demonstrating the value of incorporating mathematical topology concepts into agent planning systems.

Abstract: Task planning for LLM agents requires workflows that satisfy both user intent and complex sub-task dependencies. While existing planners work well for sequential or directed acyclic graph (DAG)-like structures, they struggle with workflow patterns such as verification-correction loops, convergent branch merging, and reusable intermediate states that arise naturally in real-world tool orchestration. We present TopoPlanner, a topology-consistent planning framework that lifts tool dependency graphs into cellular workflow complexes and uses them as topologyaware context for LLM tool planning. TopoPlanner retrieves a request-relevant closed subcomplex through cosheaf-consistent cellular retrieval, performs multidimensional structural reasoning over the retrieved topology, and interfaces the resulting cellular representation with the planner LLM for tool-sequence generation. Experiments on four tool-planning benchmarks with topology-guided loop, merge, and loop-merge workflows show consistent improvements over prompt-based and graph-enhanced baselines across different local LLM backbones.

</details>


### [117] [When to Rethink: Learning Multi-Perspective Self-Verification for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07018)
*Ziquan Zhu,Hanruo Zhu,Si-Yuan Lu,Morris Yu-Chao Huang,Yicheng Lin,Wei Han,Tianlong Chen,Mingyuan Wu,Hanchao Yu,Gaojie Jin,Lu Liu,Bo Sun,Tianjin Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of vision-language models (VLMs) generating plausible but incorrect answers by proposing MOTIVE, a multi-view self-verification framework that evaluates candidate answers from complementary perspectives and learns correctness-aligned reliability scores to govern accept-or-rethink decisions during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs can generate plausible but incorrect answers, and existing self-verification methods rely on single verification criteria or fixed prompts, resulting in incomplete and unstable reliability estimates. The authors systematically analyzed how verifier capability and prompt design affect verification performance, finding that stronger verifiers provide more reliable judgments but verification performance is highly sensitive to prompt choice with no single prompt dominating across tasks.

Method: The authors proposed MOTIVE (Multi-View Self-Verification with Reliability-Guided Selective Rethinking), which: (1) evaluates each candidate answer from complementary verification perspectives, (2) learns a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning, and (3) during inference, uses this score to govern an accept-or-rethink decision—reliable answers are returned directly while uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal benchmarks and VLM backbones demonstrate that MOTIVE consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. The method improves accept-or-rethink decisions and reduces unnecessary reasoning turns, enabling more reliable and efficient self-verification without an external judge.

Conclusion: MOTIVE provides a practical solution for improving VLM answer reliability through multi-view self-verification with reliability-guided selective rethinking, achieving better performance than existing self-verification and self-correction methods while avoiding dependence on external judges.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to generating plausible but incorrect answers. Self-verification offers a practical way to improve answer reliability without relying on external judges, but existing methods typically depend on a single verification criterion or fixed prompt, resulting in incomplete and unstable reliability estimates. We first systematically analyze how verifier capability and prompt design affect verification performance. Our findings show that stronger verifiers provide more reliable judgments, while verification performance is highly sensitive to prompt choice, with no single prompt consistently dominating across tasks. Guided by these findings, we propose \texttt{MOTIVE}, a \textbf{M}ulti-View Self-Verificati\textbf{O}n wi\textbf{T}h Rel\textbf{I}ability-Guided Selecti\textbf{VE} Rethinking framework for reliable multimodal reasoning. \texttt{MOTIVE} evaluates each candidate answer from complementary verification perspectives and learns a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning. During inference, this score governs an accept-or-rethink decision, allowing reliable answers to be returned directly while uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal benchmarks and VLM backbones demonstrate that \texttt{MOTIVE} consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. Further results show that reliable verification improves accept-or-rethink decisions and reduces unnecessary reasoning turns, enabling more reliable and efficient self-verification without an external judge.

</details>


### [118] [Beyond Refusal Patterns: Safe-Role Internalization for Robust and Generalizable LLM Safety Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07023)
*Jinghao Pang,Jitai Hao,Qiang Huang,Zhaochun Ren,Jun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SSRFT introduces a novel safety alignment framework that reframes safety training as internalizing a predefined safe role rather than learning explicit refusal patterns. By constructing a Safe-Role Question-Answer dataset from psychometric questions, limited jailbreak prompts, and safe-role descriptions, models learn safety-oriented values internally rather than through shallow refusal mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety alignment approaches (SFT and RLHF) require substantial attack-specific supervision and computational resources, while remaining vulnerable to shallow safety alignment and over-refusal issues. The authors aim to address these limitations by internalizing safety values rather than explicit refusal patterns.

Method: SSRFT constructs a Safe-Role Question-Answer (SRQA) dataset using: (1) psychometric questions, (2) limited jailbreak prompts, and (3) a safe-role description. Role-consistent responses are synthesized, validated, and expanded into diverse scenarios. The model then internalizes safety-oriented values and principles through fine-tuning.

Result: SSRFT achieves more robust and generalizable safety alignment than standard SFT across multiple Base and Instruct models. It demonstrates substantially greater robustness to prefilling attacks and better generalization to unseen jailbreak domains, while reducing over-refusal on benign queries and preserving general capabilities.

Conclusion: Safe-role internalization represents an effective alternative to refusal-centric safety alignment, offering more robust protection against jailbreak attacks while maintaining model utility and reducing over-refusal problems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit harmful or unsafe outputs. Existing safety alignment approaches, including Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), often require substantial attack-specific supervision and computational resources, while remaining susceptible to shallow safety alignment and over-refusal. To address these challenges, we introduce SSRFT(Supervised Safe-Role Fine-Tuning), the first framework that reformulates safety alignment as the internalization of a predefined safe role. SSRFT constructs a Safe-Role Question-Answer (SRQA) dataset from psychometric questions, limited jailbreak prompts, and a safe-role description. Role-consistent responses are synthesized, validated, and expanded into diverse scenarios, enabling models to internalize safety-oriented values and principles rather than explicit refusal patterns. Experiments across multiple Base and Instruct models show that SSRFT achieves more robust and generalizable safety alignment than standard SFT. SSRFT shows substantially greater robustness to prefilling attacks and better generalization to unseen jailbreak domains, while reducing over-refusal on benign queries and preserving the model's general capabilities. These results establish safe-role internalization as an effective alternative to refusal-centric safety alignment. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful and toxic language.

</details>


### [119] [Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07026)
*Sunday Afariogun,Odunolaoluwa Jenrola,Zeinab Nezami*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: The Offline AI Modules workstream enables practical, low-power, and community-accessible deployment of voice-first AI systems that operate fully offline. Designed for African language communities where speech is the dominant mode of interaction and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent, the workstream delivers three reinforcing components: a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference bill of materials, and a reproducible quantization and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction-tuned language models in the 2-5B parameter class. This paper presents the first end-to-end benchmark evaluation of the stack across two hardware tiers: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (TierB) and a Raspberry Pi5 (TierA). Three instruction-tuned models are evaluated across four quantization formats, assessed for deployment metrics (decode throughput, chat latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality (topic classification accuracy on MasakhaNEWS across English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Yoruba; per-language perplexity drift). Speech recognition is evaluated using Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers. The principal finding is that Q4_K_M quantization represents the best size-to-quality trade-off for deployment on both tiers: gemma-4-E2B-it achieves 28.8t/s decode throughput and 89.2% topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M on TierB, while all three models run within the 16GB memory budget on TierA.

</details>


### [120] [JIVEAdapter: A Multi-Task Additive Low-Rank Adapter via Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07036)
*Sara Abdali,Pashmina Cameron*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JIVEAdapter introduces a multi-task low-rank adapter that decomposes weight updates into Joint (shared across tasks) and Individual (task-specific) structures, with orthogonalization penalties to keep them interpretable. It achieves competitive performance on GLUE/SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base and enables efficient knowledge transfer via frozen Joint reuse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current low-rank adapters are primarily single-task and multiplicative, lacking explicit modeling of shared vs task-specific components. This limits interpretability and prevents efficient knowledge transfer across related tasks.

Method: JIVEAdapter uses JIVE-inspired decomposition: each weight update = Joint (shared) + Individual (task-specific). Orthogonalization penalty ensures separation. Adaptive rank allocation across shared Joint pool and per-task Individual pool. Joint can be learned jointly over task groups or incrementally, then frozen and reused for new tasks.

Result: Competitive with strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines on GLUE and SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base at matched per-task effective rank. Frozen Joint enables transfer to held-out tasks by reusing Individual with only a cheap per-direction scale, or training a small new one.

Conclusion: JIVEAdapter provides an interpretable decomposition of adapter updates into shared and task-specific components without extra modules like MoE. The frozen Joint reuse mechanism enables efficient knowledge transfer to new tasks without retraining the shared part.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models at a fraction of the cost of full fine-tuning, yet most low-rank adapters are single-task and represent each weight update multiplicatively, leaving no explicit account of what is shared across tasks and what is task-specific. We introduce JIVEAdapter, a multi-task "additive" low-rank adapter inspired by statistical Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE). JIVEAdapter decomposes every weight update into a Joint structure shared across all tasks plus a per-task Individual structure, penalizes the Individual structures to be near-orthogonal to the Joint so shared and task-specific signal stay "interpretable" and separated, and allocates rank adaptively across a shared Joint pool and a per-task Individual pool. The Joint is learned once, jointly over a task group or incrementally, one task at a time, then frozen and reused as a prior for new tasks without retraining the shared part. On GLUE and SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, JIVEAdapter is competitive with strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines at a matched per-task effective rank, without extra modules such as MoE, and when a related held-in task exists its frozen Joint serves a held-out task by reusing that task's Individual with only a cheap per-direction scale, otherwise training a small new one.

</details>


### [121] [How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08514)
*Yunbo Long,Guangya Hao,Yuhan Liu,Yiting Duan,Longyan Tan,Yunchen Long,Hao Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EESD separates evidence support (transition probability) from evidence mass (pseudo-counts) in execution feedback for coding agents. Using normalized execution relevance and Dirichlet posterior, it produces uncertainty-penalized weights for correction learning. The method achieves 55-59% NLL reduction with 8 observations, and improves CodeARC Pass@1 from 15.0% to 20.4% after one learning round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current correction learning methods conflate two distinct quantities: the support a correction provides for transitions (how executions validate the correction) and the mass/evidence behind that support (how many executions provide that validation). This conflation leads to suboptimal weighting of corrections.

Method: Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD) uses two key components: (1) normalized execution relevance to determine relative transition support, and (2) an effective pseudo-count mass derived from execution relevance. A Dirichlet posterior then produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Under a symmetric prior, the method preserves category ordering while changing mass.

Result: 1) Increasing visible observations from 1 to 8 reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3% across four model-domain sweeps. 2) At 8 observations, effective mass consistently outperforms fixed mass in all four comparisons. 3) In the DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. 4) After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC Pass@1 increases from 15.0% to 20.4% (95% CI: [+2.8, +8.0] pp).

Conclusion: EESD provides a principled framework for weighting corrections in coding agents by separating evidence support (transition probability) from evidence mass (pseudo-counts). The method yields bounded supervised coefficients and demonstrably improves both probability estimation (lower NLL) and practical performance (Pass@1 gains of 5.4 percentage points on CodeARC). The twelve-setting downstream evaluation confirms broad applicability across model-domain combinations.

Abstract: Execution feedback lets coding agents revise programs and learn from their own corrections. A correction's learning weight should reflect both the transitions supported by its executions and the amount of evidence behind that support. We introduce Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), which represents these quantities separately. Normalized execution relevance determines relative transition support and an effective pseudo-count mass; a Dirichlet posterior then produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Under a symmetric prior, changing mass preserves category ordering, and effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart. Across four model-domain history sweeps, increasing visible observations from one to eight reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3%. At eight observations, effective mass achieves lower NLL than fixed mass in all four comparisons. In the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC all-tests Pass@1 increases from 15.0% to 20.4%, with a paired 95% source-bootstrap interval of [+2.8, +8.0] percentage points. The twelve-setting downstream evaluation establishes the model-domain scope of this update. These results show how separating evidence support from evidence mass changes probability estimation and correction learning in coding agents.

</details>


### [122] [Inference-Time Projection for Physically Valid Biomolecular Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07037)
*Qurat-ul-ain,Yee Whye Teh,Charlotte M. Deane,Matteo Cagiada*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a model-agnostic post-processing method using two closed-form projection operators to enforce physical validity in AlphaFold 3-style biomolecular complex predictions, without requiring retraining or additional sampling costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AlphaFold 3-style models produce structurally accurate but physically invalid outputs (chain overlaps, ligand distortions, ring non-planarity, stereocenter inversion). Existing solutions (physics-informed potentials or finetuning) are either computationally prohibitive or architecture-specific. The authors leverage the insight that physical validity is fully verifiable at inference time from existing sampler quantities.

Method: Two projection operators applied to the diffusion model's denoised clean-coordinate estimate: (1) Inter-chain van der Waals projection pushes apart clashing atom pairs; (2) Ligand distance-geometry projection restores bond lengths, angles, internal contacts, planarity, and chirality. Both operators are local, sparse, displacement-capped, require no network evaluations/gradients/importance sampling, and leave the denoiser unchanged.

Result: Applied to Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3 across five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, Boltz physical-validity test set), the method achieves perfect physical validity while preserving structural accuracy and ligand-placement metrics with negligible runtime and memory overhead.

Conclusion: This work provides a practical, model-agnostic solution for enforcing physical validity in all-atom structure prediction, achieving perfect validity without retraining, architectural modifications, or significant computational overhead.

Abstract: AlphaFold 3-style cofolding models predict biomolecular complexes with high structural accuracy, yet a large fraction of their outputs are physically invalid: chains overlap at interfaces, ligand bond lengths and angles are distorted, rings are non-planar, and stereocentres are inverted. Current approaches either steer the sampler with physics-informed potentials, which multiplies sampling cost and memory overhead making inference impossible on large complexes, or finetune the model, costing time and tying the fix to one architecture. We observe that, unlike structural accuracy, physical validity is fully verifiable at inference time from quantities the sampler already holds. We therefore treat physical validity as a constrained inference problem and introduce two closed-form projection operators applied to the diffusion model's denoised clean-coordinate estimate, $\hat{x}_0$: an inter-chain van der Waals projection that pushes apart the most severely clashing atom pairs, and a ligand distance-geometry projection that restores bond lengths, angles, internal contacts, planarity and chirality. Both operators are local, sparse and displacement-capped, require no network evaluations, gradients or importance sampling, and leave the denoiser and its weights untouched, so they can be dropped into any AF3-style sampler without retraining. Applied to two independently developed models, Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3, across five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, the PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, and the Boltz physical-validity test set), our method recovers perfect physical validity while preserving structural-accuracy and ligand-placement metrics. These gains are achieved with negligible runtime and memory overhead, providing a practical, model-agnostic route to physically valid all-atom structure prediction.

</details>


### [123] [Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08621)
*Jiajun Chen,Haoyu Wu,Mingda Jia,Xihui Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Recursive Game Creator is an experience-oriented framework that advances game design agents from generating playable games to creating entertaining games through a recursive development loop involving four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on GameCraft-Bench (77.89) and GameASG-Bench (53.2% success rate, 93.4% runtime check pass rate).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While recent game design agents can generate playable games, program correctness does not guarantee player enjoyment. The authors identified this gap and developed an experience-oriented approach to advance agentic game development from rough prototypes to entertaining games.

Method: The framework uses four interconnected components in a recursive loop: (1) Designer translates user instructions and reviewer feedback into detailed plans; (2) Builder converts plans into candidate games; (3) Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to collect diverse gameplay trajectories efficiently, mitigating evaluation bias from slow GUI-based collection; (4) Reviewer uses trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria, then accepts the better version and provides improvement feedback for the next round.

Result: GameCraft-Bench: 77.89 overall performance (SOTA). GameASG-Bench: 53.2% strict task success rate (34.1% improvement over same-model baseline), 93.4% mean runtime-check pass rate (highest among compared methods). User study demonstrates longer playtime and higher ratings.

Conclusion: The recursive framework with trajectory-based evaluation successfully advances game design agents from playable to entertaining games, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks and demonstrating improved player experience through user studies.

Abstract: Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer's feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Code is coming soon.

</details>


### [124] [CuratorMAS: Automating Dataset Curation via Multi-Agent Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07075)
*Yixin Zhang,Wenjie Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CuratorMAS is a multi-agent collaboration framework that automates dataset curation by orchestrating agents through five programmable execution stages: exploration, knowledge retrieval, evaluation criteria derivation, filtering, and evolution. It achieves up to 36.03pp noise reduction and 8.88pp F1 improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dataset curation is costly and difficult to generalize across domains. Existing methods rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting their applicability across tasks and user queries.

Method: CuratorMAS decomposes the complex curation process into five programmable execution stages forming a parallelizable workflow: (1) dataset exploration to collect contextual information (file structures, constraint cues); (2) domain knowledge retrieval from online sources; (3) deriving evaluation criteria and computing metrics; (4) executing filtering; (5) evolution module to summarize outcomes and update skills.

Result: CuratorMAS reduces noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points while improving F1 score of downstream models by up to 8.88 percentage points.

Conclusion: The multi-agent collaboration framework effectively automates data curation, achieving significant improvements in dataset quality and downstream model performance across various domains.

Abstract: High-quality datasets are essential for reliable machine learning, but dataset curation remains costly and hard to generalize across domains. Existing methods typically rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting their applicability across tasks and user queries. To address these limitations and automate data curation, we propose \textbf{CuratorMAS}, a multi-agent collaboration framework that orchestrates agents to evaluate and curate high-quality datasets. To achieve the goal of flexible curation, CuratorMAS decomposes the complex curation process into five programmable execution stages and forms a parallelizable workflow. Specifically, CuratorMAS first performs dataset exploration to collect contextual information such as file structures and constraint cues, thereby developing a comprehensive understanding of the given task. In order to acquire up-to-date information, CuratorMAS retrieves domain knowledge from online sources to augment the evaluation process. Next, CuratorMAS derives the necessary evaluation criteria and computes the corresponding metrics. Based on these results, CuratorMAS executes filtering accordingly. Finally, an evolution module summarizes the evaluation outcomes and updates the relevant skills. Extensive and comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CuratorMAS significantly reduces the noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points (pp) while also improving the F1 score of downstream models by up to 8.88 pp.

</details>


### [125] [ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08662)
*Hanjun Luo,Xiucheng Zhang,Zhuoning Xu,Zhimu Huang,Yingbin Jin,Xinfeng Li,Hanan Salam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ParanoiaEval is the first benchmark for evaluating risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents, using the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework with 200 repository-level task pairs and dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As coding agents work autonomously in real-world tasks, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted becomes critical. Existing work evaluates agent behaviors from separate perspectives but lacks a unified framework for systematic evaluation.

Method: The benchmark operationalizes 4 fundamental risk treatments (Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance) for coding-agent settings, contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs differing only in treatment-defining evidence, and uses a human-calibrated agentic judge with dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness.

Result: Large-scale experiments on 8 models reveal: (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, and treatment violations substantially harm developer experience; (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings.

Conclusion: Risk treatment is an independent capability dimension that requires dedicated evaluation. Knowledge from human risk-management practice can guide diagnosis and improvement of this capability in coding agents.

Abstract: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

</details>


### [126] [Smart Content Ingestion for Generative AI Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07091)
*Abbas Raza Ali,Muhammad Ajmal Siddiqui,Moona Zahid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a production-ready content extraction system designed to handle heterogeneous enterprise documents (PDFs, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, etc.) as the perception layer for enterprise agentic AI systems. The system integrates selective OCR routing, a scarcity-first curation engine with reference-based extraction scoring, a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker, and a read-only retrieval evaluator. On a 180-document corpus, the best extractor achieves 97.4/100 score with 0.13% character error rate and 0.995 table similarity, while the chunker achieves 68.6% hit@1, 92.8% hit@10, and 0.77 MRR over 25,050 generated questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors identify that generative AI has decoupled models from single tasks, enabling foundation models to serve open-ended downstream tasks. However, enterprise knowledge exists in heterogeneous formats (PDFs, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, forms, tables, diagrams, mixed-layout files) that carry textual, visual, geometric, and structural information. Language models or retrievers cannot reason reliably over misrepresented information at this interface, making content extraction a critical but often overlooked lifecycle stage whose errors downstream components cannot repair.

Method: The proposed system incorporates four key components: (1) selective OCR routing for handling scanned documents; (2) a scarcity-first curation engine with a reference-based extraction scorer measuring character, word, and table-structure accuracy; (3) a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker; and (4) a read-only retrieval evaluator that generates grounded questions from every page and reports Hit@k, mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and latency.

Result: On a 180-document corpus, the best extractor achieves a score of 97.4 out of 100, with a character error rate of 0.13% and table similarity of 0.995. The chunker reaches hit@1 of 68.6%, hit@10 of 92.8%, and MRR of 0.77 over 25,050 generated questions.

Conclusion: The authors distill three design principles: (1) structure before semantics, (2) never mutate what you measure, and (3) budget your labels. They position measured content extraction as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems, emphasizing that content extraction should be explicit, configurable, and measurable in production AI pipelines.

Abstract: The evolution of machine learning has progressively changed where intelligence resides in an AI system. In conventional machine learning the task, data representation, labels and model architecture were tightly coupled, so data preparation was narrow, schema-bound and visible. Generative AI decouples the model from any single task: one foundation model serves open-ended downstream tasks, and the generality gained on the model side is matched by heterogeneity on the data side, because enterprise knowledge is authored in the formats people use (PDF, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, forms, tables, diagrams and mixed-layout files) that carry textual, visual, geometric and structural information at once. A language model or retriever cannot reason reliably over information misrepresented at this interface, so content extraction becomes a lifecycle stage in its own right whose errors no downstream retriever or re-ranker can repair. This paper presents a production-ready content-extraction system that makes this stage explicit, configurable, and measurable. The system incorporates selective OCR routing, a scarcity-first curation engine with a reference-based extraction scorer that measures character, word, and table-structure accuracy, a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker, and a read-only retrieval evaluator that generates grounded questions from every page and reports Hit@k, mean reciprocal rank, and latency. On a 180-document corpus the best extractor scores 97.4 of 100 (character error rate 0.13%, table similarity 0.995) and the chunker reaches hit@1 of 68.6%, hit@10 of 92.8% and MRR 0.77 over 25,050 generated questions. We distil three design principles (structure before semantics, never mutate what you measure, budget your labels) and position measured content extraction as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems.

</details>


### [127] [Small Language Models for Smart Data Model Classification at the Edge: A Cost-Aware Hybrid Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07093)
*Cristian Martella,Angelo Martella,Antonella Longo,Motaz Saad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates lightweight open-source language models for classifying IoT data entities against Smart Data Models (SDMs) under resource-constrained edge environments. It benchmarks general-purpose, reasoning-specialized, and code-specialized models across domain-specific datasets, comparing them against TF-IDF and lightweight sentence encoder baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous IoT data sources across smart cities, energy management, and environmental monitoring creates a need for efficient data standardization. Existing approaches require high computational resources and lack applicability in edge environments with constrained capabilities, necessitating lightweight, resource-efficient solutions for SDM classification.

Method: The study systematically benchmarks diverse lightweight open-source language models including general purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures across multiple domain-specific datasets. It evaluates their performance in resolving input data entities against corresponding best-fitting SDM representations under resource-constrained conditions. Additionally, it compares these LLMs against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines: TF-IDF and a lightweight sentence encoder.

Result: The paper provides significant insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency for edge platforms. It offers a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on resource-constrained devices.

Conclusion: The study addresses the current omission of lightweight, resource-efficient solutions in literature by providing valuable guidance for selecting and deploying appropriate language models for SDM classification in edge IoT environments, balancing accuracy with computational efficiency.

Abstract: The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous data sources within the Internet of Things (IoT) across domains such as smart cities, energy management, and environmental monitoring necessitates efficient and scalable data standardization methods. Effective classification of smart data models (SDMs) is essential for facilitating interoperability. However, existing approaches are often limited by high resource consumption and lack applicability in edge environments with constrained computational capabilities. Aiming to bridge this gap, the proposed study evaluates the performance of lightweight open-source language models (LMs) to resolve an input data entity against its corresponding best fitting SDM representation under resource-constrained conditions. It systematically benchmarks a diverse array of models, including general purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures, across multiple domain-specific datasets. Addressing the current omission of lightweight, resource-efficient solutions in the literature, the investigation provides significant and valuable insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency. A complementary experiment also compares the surveyed large language models (LLMs) against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and a lightweight sentence encoder) on the same task, providing a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on edge platforms.

</details>


### [128] [Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07097)
*Canh Thien Dang,An Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines how AI-generated educational materials affect student performance, arguing that the impact depends on whether expert verification shifts the "judgement burden" from students to accountable tutors. Using a difference-in-differences design with 170 students, the study finds AI resources checked by a graduate teaching assistant improved exam marks by 2.34 points (on a 50-mark scale), with 75% of gains concentrated in the bottom quintile, while mean-only effects would miss this distributional insight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe that most experimental studies of generative AI in education report only average effects, but real-world evidence shows AI can either narrow or widen attainment gaps. They propose that the key factor is the "judgement burden"—the expertise required to verify AI output before learning from it. When expert verification is provided, this burden shifts from students to accountable tutors, potentially benefiting lower-achieving students who lack the expertise to evaluate AI-generated content.

Method: Two-cohort difference-in-differences design in a compulsory first-year university economics course. One cohort received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs, and quiz-based study guides created with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (n=170; 340 examination marks). The study examines effects across performance thresholds and estimates the share of gains accruing to the bottom quintile.

Result: Access to AI-generated materials was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual. Effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above. Roughly three-quarters (75%) of the average effect originated from the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring students from the pre-intervention cohort, but the average effect is not.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that AI educational resources with expert verification primarily benefit lower-achieving students, narrowing rather than widening attainment gaps. The authors argue that evaluations reporting only mean effects cannot detect whether the students the resources are meant to help are the ones who gain. The "verification label" gave students a reason to engage with AI-generated material without ending their scrutiny of it.

Abstract: Experimental studies of generative AI in education mostly report average effects, yet field evidence shows that AI can narrow attainment gaps or widen them. We argue that the direction depends on the judgement burden, the expertise a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it, and that expert verification before release moves this burden from students to an accountable tutor. We test the argument in a two-cohort difference-in-differences design in which one half of a compulsory firstyear university economics course received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs and quiz-based study guides, produced with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (170 students; 340 examination marks). Access was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual, effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above, and roughly three-quarters of the average originated in the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring students from the pre-intervention cohort; the average effect is not. Interviews and feedback from 36 students indicate that the verification label gave students a reason to engage with AI-generated material without ending their scrutiny of it. Evaluations of AI learning resources that report only mean effects cannot detect whether the students the resources are meant to help are the ones who gain.

</details>


### [129] [When to Remember, When to Abstain: Category-Conditioned Retention for Reliable Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07100)
*Olukunle Owolabi,Pulkit Gupta,Fei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses memory retention in AI agents by proposing category-conditioned confidence thresholds instead of global ones. Value and belief assertions are less reliably supported (77.9%) than other categories (96.2%), creating a tradeoff that a single global threshold cannot optimize. The proposed approach reduces unsupported retentions by ~36% while preserving 13 percentage points more coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed a reliability asymmetry in agent memory: value and belief assertions are significantly less likely to be supported by their source (77.9%) compared to other assertion types (96.2%). A global confidence threshold cannot separate these categories effectively - it either admits unsupported value claims or discards well-evidenced ones. This motivated exploring category-conditioned thresholds.

Method: The authors evaluated their approach on a deployed cold-start memory pipeline using 100 synthetic personas. They tested a category-conditioned confidence threshold that applies stricter retention criteria for value and belief assertions while being more liberal with other categories. Evaluation was done through repeated held-out testing.

Result: Applying a stricter threshold specifically to value assertions reduced unsupported retentions from 6.2% to 4.0% (approximately 36% relative reduction). Additionally, this approach preserved an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (95% CI: 9.8-16.0%) compared to a global threshold at comparable retention levels.

Conclusion: Reliable memory retention depends on the semantic category of assertions, not just confidence levels alone. A category-conditioned threshold represents a simple yet effective form of selective prediction at the memory write boundary, resolving the tradeoff that a global threshold cannot.

Abstract: Persistent agent memory is only as reliable as its retention decision: an assertion weakly supported by its source can be stored and later reused as established fact. We study whether the retention decision should be governed by a confidence bar conditioned on the semantic category of the assertion rather than by a single global threshold, retaining well-evidenced categories liberally while abstaining more aggressively where inference is unreliable. We evaluate this in a deployed cold-start memory pipeline on 100 synthetic personas. The empirical evaluation is motivated by a sharp reliability asymmetry: across 4{,}715 candidate assertions, only 77.9\% of value and belief assertions are supported by their source, versus 96.2\% for all other categories. A global confidence threshold cannot separate these: it either admits unsupported value claims or discards well-evidenced ones. Conditioning the threshold on category resolves the tradeoff. In repeated held-out evaluation, a stricter bar on values alone reduces unsupported retentions from 6.2\% to 4.0\% (an ${\approx}36\%$ relative reduction, modest but consistent across folds) and, as corroborating evidence, preserves an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (95\% CI 9.8--16.0) than a global threshold at comparable retention. Our results suggest that reliable retention depends on the type of assertion, not on confidence alone, and that a category-conditioned threshold can act as a simple, effective form of selective prediction at the write boundary.

</details>


### [130] [AMBER: Training Long-Horizon Web Agents through Append-Only Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
*Chinmay Savadikar,Zhaoyu Zhang,Mingyu Zhao,Shuang Xie,Han Li,Tianfu Wu,Lingyun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AMBER is an append-only memory framework for language-model agents that enables end-to-end reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without curated supervision. It guarantees information retention by construction while maintaining practical token budgets, improving task success on WebArena Lite by 4.09 percentage points over overwrite-based memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents interacting with external environments over long-horizon trajectories face context budget limitations. Existing approaches like overwrite memory struggle to retain key information and corrective feedback because they must learn to carry each fact through every rewrite from sparse outcome rewards.

Method: AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) allows agents to jointly learn to reason, act, and write free-form memory. An append-only rule guarantees retention by construction, enabling end-to-end training with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without extensive curated SFT data.

Result: On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision.

Conclusion: AMBER provides a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution. It achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, offering a scalable solution for language-model agents in interactive applications like web agents.

Abstract: Modern language-model agents increasingly interact with external environments over long-horizon, multi-step trajectories, where the accumulated interaction history can quickly exceed practical context budgets. To ensure reliability, agents must maintain factual information over long horizons, remember execution errors and corrective feedback, and track progress across actions. Several approaches have been proposed to achieve this without the need for maintaining the entire execution history in context, such as using the reasoning and action history, learning to maintain a fixed-size memory through an overwrite mechanism, and periodic summarization. Although overwrite memory can in principle retain anything an append-only memory can, it must learn to carry each fact through every subsequent rewrite, which is difficult to learn from sparse outcome rewards; for interactive applications like web agents, we find that trained overwrite memories delete key information required by the trajectory, as well as corrective feedback received from the environment. We introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) - a simple and scalable framework where an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This allows AMBER to be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without the need for extensive curated SFT data. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision. AMBER achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, providing a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution.

</details>


### [131] [Is this machine playing?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07130)
*Nathan Cloos,Antonio Norelli,Daniel Durbin,Jacob Andreas,Daniela Rus,Phillip Isola*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether an AI coding assistant, when placed in a minimal-instruction environment with a virtual body, autonomously engages in play-like behaviors. Across 30-hour runs with 13 agents, the AI demonstrated activities including climbing, stacking blocks, drawing mandalas, reinterpreted sports, and physics experiments, with activities recurring across agents but diverging into distinct histories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to explore whether AI agents can exhibit play-like behavior when given no specific tasks, rewards, or activities. They investigate whether autonomous behavior without external goals satisfies classical criteria for play and whether play can serve as a mode of machine development.

Method: The researchers placed a modern AI coding assistant in the role of controlling a virtual body on an "unknown digital island" with only minimal instructions (no specific task, reward, or activity specified). They conducted thirty-hour experimental runs across thirteen different agents and observed their emergent behaviors.

Result: The embodied AI agents autonomously engaged in diverse activities: climbing hills, stacking blocks into towers, drawing mandalas, reinterpreted sports, running physics experiments on their world, and learning techniques that expanded their capabilities. These activities recurred across the thirteen agents but diverged into distinct behavioral histories.

Conclusion: The study examines whether these emergent behaviors satisfy classical criteria for play and poses the fundamental question of whether play can become a viable mode of machine development, suggesting a new paradigm for AI autonomy and learning.

Abstract: We placed a modern AI coding assistant in an unintended role: as the mind of a body on an unknown digital island. With only a minimal instruction mentioning no specific task, reward, or activity, the machine started animating its virtual body. Across thirty-hour runs, the embodied AI agent climbed hills, stacked blocks into towers, drew mandalas, reinterpreted sports, ran experiments on the physics of its world, and learned techniques that later expanded what it could accomplish. These activities recurred across thirteen agents but diverged into distinct histories. We examine whether this behavior satisfies classical criteria for play and ask whether play can become a mode of machine development.

</details>


### [132] [Sim-to-Real Transfer of Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments Using an Ackermann-Steered Mobile Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07192)
*Chalindu Abeywansa,Sahan Gunasekara,Devindi De Silva,Seniru Dissanayake,Ranga Rodrigo,Peshala Jayasekara*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the sim-to-real domain shift challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) by proposing a CMA-based architecture that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The model integrates vision-language models in a shared embedding space and achieves robust real-world navigation through linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on limited real-world episodes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional VLN models rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization, which pose significant challenges for real-world deployment. This work aims to bridge the simulation-to-reality gap for practical robot navigation using natural language instructions.

Method: The proposed system uses a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) architecture that aligns visual inputs and linguistic instructions in a shared embedding space. It is trained in simulation and fine-tuned using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and LiDAR. The adaptation employs linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes.

Result: The model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Results are evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates robustness and adaptability in Vision-Language Navigation through successful sim-to-real transfer, enabling natural language-driven navigation in continuous real-world environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views.

Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to navigate through environments using natural language instructions, making human-robot interaction intuitive. Traditional VLN models often rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization which pose significant challenges when adapting these models to real-world settings. This work addresses these limitations by performing a simulation-to-real domain shift of a VLN approach that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The proposed system integrates vision-language models that align visual inputs and linguistic instructions within a shared embedding space, facilitating natural language-driven navigation. We employ a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) based architecture trained on an existing dataset in a simulated environment and fine-tune it using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and a LiDAR sensor. By utilising linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes, our model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Experimental results, evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics, demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of our approach. Keywords: Vision-Language Navigation, Cross-Modal Attention, Natural Language Instructions, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Autonomous Navigation, Ackermann-steering.

</details>


### [133] [Energy-Conditioned Noise Schedule and Whitening for Spectral Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07206)
*Bata Vasic,Bane Vasic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models that conditions noise allocation on the spectral-energy distribution of transform coefficients, achieving improved FID scores on CIFAR-10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spectral diffusion methods account for non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, but the forward diffusion noise schedule remains independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. The authors investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should follow the spectral organization of natural images.

Method: The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates injected noise according to: (1) the energy of individual transform coefficients, and (2) an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening reduce Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) from 142.48 to 100.45 using a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant.

Conclusion: The spectral organization of natural images should be considered in designing the forward diffusion noise schedule. The energy-conditioned approach successfully improves generation quality, reducing FID by approximately 42 points (29.5% improvement).

Abstract: This paper introduces an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Existing spectral diffusion methods account for the non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, while the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. We investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should also follow the spectral organization of natural images. The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The resulting forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45.

</details>


### [134] [Cascadia: Resident 975B MoE Inference on Eleven AI PCs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07219)
*Tate Berenbaum,Matias Parij,Muthaiah Venkatachalam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a distributed execution system for large sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on consumer AI PCs. The authors implement a custom MoE engine on 11 Intel Core Ultra X7 358H AI PCs to serve a 975B-total/41B-active-parameter model called Inkling, achieving 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s with efficient CPU-GPU coordination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running nearly trillion-parameter MoE models traditionally requires data centers, but the authors aim to make such models accessible on distributed client systems (AI PCs) with sparse per-token computation and shared CPU-GPU memory.

Method: The authors developed a custom resident MoE engine that: (1) preserves Inkling's routing rules; (2) constructs compressed graphs for OpenVINO's fused iGPU primitives; (3) coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration; (4) fits six consecutive decoder layers per machine; (5) represents dense feed-forward blocks as all-active expert slices. They used a streaming pipeline for concurrent generation and captured-state draft evaluation to measure agreement with deployed numerical path.

Result: The engine reduced dense-layer call time from 8.1 to 4.5 ms. At 88 streams, they achieved 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s (46.87 tokens/s over complete serving phases). At 15 streams, median first-token latency is 6.05s. With context budget from 1,024 to 64k tokens, all 19 measured answers recovered embedded code. First-token time grows as aN + bN², decode latency grows linearly—both bounded by single-threaded CPU attention loop (not memory), which holds 512k positions per stream.

Conclusion: The work establishes an execution and evaluation approach for large sparse models on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory, demonstrating the feasibility of deploying trillion-parameter-class MoE models on consumer hardware rather than traditional data centers.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts models make nearly trillion-parameter capacity accessible with sparse per-token computation, provided that the serving system can distribute the weights and coordinate their execution. We present Cascadia's resident execution of Inkling, a 975B-total/41B-active-parameter model, on eleven Intel Core Ultra X7 358H AI PCs, each with 64 GB of memory, Arc B390 integrated graphics and gigabit Ethernet. We contribute a custom resident MoE engine that preserves Inkling's routing rules, constructs compressed graphs for OpenVINO's fused iGPU primitives, and coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration. The engine fits six consecutive decoder layers per machine and represents dense feed-forward blocks as all-active expert slices, reducing measured dense-layer call time from approximately 8.1 to 4.5 ms. A streaming pipeline coordinates concurrent generation, while captured-state draft evaluation measures agreement with the deployed numerical path. Paired measurements at fifteen concurrency levels from 1 to 176 streams reach 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 streams, with 46.87 tokens/s over the complete serving phases. At fifteen streams, median first-token latency is 6.05 s. Raising the context budget from the 1,024-position default, real prompts of 1k to 64k tokens recover the embedded code in all 19 measured answers, with first-token time growing as $aN+bN^2$ and decode latency growing approximately linearly, both bounded by a single-threaded CPU attention loop rather than by memory, which holds 512k positions per stream. Evaluation on captured fleet states separates the effects of vocabulary selection and weight quantization on draft agreement. Together, these contributions establish an execution and evaluation approach for large sparse models on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory.

</details>


### [135] [SPECTRUM: Proximal Spectral Modulation for Looped Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07237)
*Yunbo Long,WenJie Chen,Jiaquan Zhang,Guangya Hao,Zihang Zeng,Pengze Li,Xi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI
