TL;DR: Looped Self-Distillation (LSD) is a self-evolution framework where a model learns from its own outputs without external assessment. The key finding is that while correctness can improve, the breadth of correct implementations may contract. SPECTRUM addresses this by re-estimating loss-sensitive key/value geometry and converting it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. This approach retains 89.9% of initial model's correct AST richness compared to 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that models learning from their own outputs inherit not just correctness but also which solutions they produce. This leads to a contraction in the diversity of correct implementations even as overall correctness improves. The motivation is to establish correct-solution retention as a complementary objective to recursive self-improvement.

Method: SPECTRUM re-estimates loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor at each round and converts it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. All generated completions train a single student, whose subsequent inference requires no intervention.

Result: After five rounds on MBPP, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the initial model's 64-sample correct AST richness, compared with 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation and 65.5% for a subspace-projection control. The advantage persists at matched correct-sample counts. Transfer benefits observed on HumanEval+ and APPS Intro without further training or recalibration.

Conclusion: Correct-solution retention is a complementary objective of recursive self-improvement (RSI). Generation-time intervention can improve the solution repertoire retained by subsequent students. The approach successfully maintains diversity of correct implementations while improving correctness.

Abstract: A model that learns from its own outputs inherits more than their correctness: it inherits which solutions it produces. We formulate Looped Self-Distillation, a self-evolution framework for code generation in which a model repeatedly generates and learns from its own raw outputs, under a fixed information budget, without ongoing external assessment or test-based selection of the generated samples. We identify a consequential separation: correctness can improve while the breadth of correct implementations contracts. We introduce SPECTRUM, which re-estimates loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor at each round and converts it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. All generated completions train a single student, whose subsequent inference requires no intervention. After five rounds of experiments on MBPP, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the initial model's 64-sample correct AST richness, compared with 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation and 65.5% for a subspace-projection control. The advantage persists at matched correct-sample counts. Without further training or recalibration, the resulting student also achieves higher matched-correct richness than Vanilla SD on HumanEval+ and APPS Intro, demonstrating transfer of the diversity benefit. These findings establish correct-solution retention as a complementary objective of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and show that generation-time intervention can improve the solution repertoire retained by subsequent students.

</details>


### [136] [Can Semantic Geometry Teach an AI Judgement?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07249)
*Thomson D. Nguy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses how AI agents can determine which rules to follow when multiple conflicting rules (permits, conditions, exceptions, obligations) exist in natural language. The authors tested geometric approaches (vector representations of actions and policies) across four studies but found these did not enable reliable pre-action judgment. A lexical router in a synthetic study successfully identified governing/blocking policies (97.7% reduction in policy checks) but still failed to correctly distinguish permissible from non-permissible actions. The key finding: identifying relevant policies does not solve the problem of interpreting them. The authors propose a revised hypothesis: judgment requires building a consequence graph connecting actors, authorities, policy conditions, exceptions, and action outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that AI agents face implicit rule conflicts in natural language—following one rule may cause them to miss another that should block an action. The authors sought to enable agents to distinguish between permissible and non-permissible actions rather than refusing all unresolved actions (which is overly restrictive) or blindly acting (which risks violating rules).

Method: The authors tested geometric approaches: representing actions and policies as vectors to see if their geometry could identify governing policies and interpret an action's relation to them. They conducted four empirical studies and a final synthetic study. They also tested a lexical router pipeline and a downstream mechanism that received all policies.

Result: Geometric approaches failed to establish reliable pre-action judgment across four studies. The lexical router recovered every governing and blocking policy while reducing median policy checks by 97.7%, but the pipeline escalated all 2,304 test actions—including those it should have allowed. Supplying every policy to the downstream mechanism changed no decisions. Finding the policies had not solved the problem of interpreting them.

Conclusion: The authors concluded that their initial hypothesis was wrong. Judgment in AI agents requires developing a consequence graph that explicitly connects: (1) the actor and authority to policy conditions, (2) exceptions, and (3) the changes an action would produce. Follow-on studies will investigate whether making these relationships explicit helps agents distinguish when to act, stop, or seek review.

Abstract: How can an AI agent determine what rules to follow? One rule permits an action. Another imposes a condition, exception, or conflicting obligation. Deterministic systems can resolve those relationships when they have been specified. When they remain implicit in language, an agent can follow one rule while missing another that should stop it. Refusing every unresolved action avoids that risk, but also blocks permissible actions.
  We wanted the agent to make the distinction and still act. Our initial hypothesis was that geometric measurements could supply a basis for judgment. We represented actions and policies as vectors, then tested whether their geometry could identify governing policies and interpret the action's relation to them.
  Across four studies, the tested approaches did not establish reliable pre-action judgment. In the final synthetic study, a lexical router recovered every governing and blocking policy while reducing median policy checks by 97.7%. The composed pipeline nevertheless escalated all 2,304 test actions, including those it should have allowed. Supplying every policy to the same downstream mechanism changed no decision. Finding the policies had not solved the problem of interpreting them.
  This result led us to revise our hypothesis: judgment in AI agents requires developing a consequence graph. Such a graph would connect the actor and authority to policy conditions, exceptions, and the changes an action would produce. Follow-on studies will ask whether making those relationships explicit helps the agent distinguish when to act, stop, or seek review.

</details>


### [137] [Internalizing Agent Experience into Diffusion Model Weights via On-Policy Context Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07250)
*Wenxuan Wang,Zekai Liu,Weinan Zhang,Yu Cheng,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: D-OPCD distills agent-improved prompt knowledge into diffusion model weights via on-policy context distillation, enabling the model to retain harness benefits without running the full agent harness. Combined with Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), it raises direct-generation scores from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks and enables continual co-evolution between model and harness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agentic harnesses improve Text-to-Image generation through external prompt refinement but require running the full harness each time. The goal is to internalize this harness knowledge into the diffusion model's weights so benefits persist without the harness.

Method: 1) Use a Text-to-Image agent with Auto Skill Evolver (ASE) to generate improved prompts
2) Treat agent-improved prompts as privileged context
3) Apply On-Policy Context Distillation to transfer harness knowledge into diffusion model weights
4) Enable iterative co-evolution: after distillation, the saturated harness evolves new skills

Result: Average direct-generation score increased from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks. A second ASE round on the updated generator further improved performance by 1.83 points over a skill-free harness.

Conclusion: D-OPCD successfully internalizes agent harness capabilities into diffusion model weights, enabling the model to benefit from harness improvements without running the full harness. This enables a co-evolution paradigm where model and harness continuously improve each other through iterative distillation rounds.

Abstract: Wrapping an image generation model in an agentic harness can effectively boost Text-to-Image task performance: the harness can leverage memory, skills, workflow orchestration, result verification, and iterative refinement to continually construct and revise prompts, thereby eliciting better images. These gains, however, remain external to the diffusion model and are realized only while the full harness runs. We propose Diffusion On-Policy Context Distillation (D-OPCD), which treats the agent-improved prompt as privileged context and distills the knowledge encoded in the agent harness into the weights of the diffusion model, so that the model retains part of the harness's benefit when conditioned on the original query alone. Using a Text-to-Image agent equipped with our proposed Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), we show that D-OPCD can internalize harness capabilities into the generator's weights, raising the average direct-generation score from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks. With this knowledge absorbed into the weights, the harness can shed its saturated skills and resume evolving: a second ASE round on the updated generator improves on a skill-free harness by additional 1.83 points, pointing toward text-to-image systems in which harness and model keep improving each other through continual co-evolution.

</details>


### [138] [MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07257)
*Sumanyu Muku*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemMux is a local runtime system that provides runtime verification for multi-agent coding environments, enabling per-agent memory attribution, complete process reclamation, escaped-process detection, and bounded memory footprint under overcommit, outperforming tmux and raw-process baselines in experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal multiplexers and agent managers were built for window arrangement, not resource governance. When multiple coding agents run simultaneously, there's no standard tool to: attribute memory to specific agents, confirm terminated agents' descendants are fully reclaimed, detect escaped child processes, or prevent OOM kills that discard uncommitted work.

Method: MemMux transforms resource governance into checkable observable signals through a claims-disciplined benchmark. It provides: per-agent memory attribution, complete reclamation verification, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead tracking. The system was evaluated against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads, with additional testing on real Claude Code sessions.

Result: Under a binding 7.5 GiB memory budget on Linux, MemMux keeps the fleet under budget with zero swap usage. In contrast, ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at 2x the RAM ceiling, and spill ~2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of terminated agents' process subtrees (vs. 50% stranded in baseline). It detects all 10 escaped children. However, CPU overhead at 1Hz attribution scan is 0.6% at one agent but 2.7% at ten agents, exceeding the 2% target. Real Claude Code sessions show 100% attribution and low overhead.

Conclusion: MemMux successfully provides runtime verification for agent-hosting substrates, enabling observable signals for resource governance. It outperforms existing tools in memory management, process reclamation, and escaped-process detection, though CPU overhead at scale slightly exceeds the target. The engine, benchmark, and one-command reproducer are released.

Abstract: Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. The tools they reach for, terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers, were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an OOM kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: an agent-hosting substrate should continuously emit observable signals an operator or auditor can check while agents run. We present MemMux, a local runtime that turns resource governance into checkable signals (per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead), with a claims-disciplined benchmark against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux keeps the fleet under budget (7.5 GiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it, and it alone surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). We report the cost: the 1 Hz attribution scan runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and a one-command reproducer.

</details>


### [139] [Verifying Coordination in Parallel Coding Agents: NP-Bench and a Scheduling Planner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07261)
*Sumanyu Muku*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses coordination failures in multi-agent LLM coding systems where individual agents pass tests but merged results fail. The authors propose a proactive planning approach that schedules work items based on declared scopes, partitions work into disjoint scopes, and orders merges along the producer-consumer graph. Evaluation on NP-Bench shows significant improvements: clean-integration rate increases from 1/9 to 9/9, merge conflicts drop from 13 to 0, and live contract change scenarios achieve 1.0 success on frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coordination tools for multi-agent coding systems are reactive—they detect conflicts only after wasted work. At agent speed, these warnings arrive too late. The authors recognize that coordination should be proactive rather than reactive, treating the problem as scheduling rather than conflict detection.

Method: The authors recast coordination as a scheduling problem: (1) take each work item's declared scope, (2) partition work into disjoint scopes, and (3) order merges along the producer-consumer graph upfront. This planner is built into "Nerveplane" and evaluated using NP-Bench—a three-arm benchmark (no coordination, reactive detection, proactive planning) that verifies integration via real git merges in both deterministic simulation and live agent experiments.

Result: The proactive planner achieves dramatic improvements: clean-integration rises from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios; merge conflicts reduce from 13 to 0. On live breaking contract changes, clean-integration improves from 0 to 1.0 on frontier models and 0.6 on small models. Cross-session memory drops repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00. A negative finding: routing facts to agents does not improve long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales—the value is cost and capacity, not attention. Benefits persist across different model capabilities because the advantage comes from work allocation, not model reasoning.

Conclusion: Proactive planning through scope partitioning and merge ordering effectively solves multi-agent coordination failures. The approach is model-agnostic—the benefits come from how work is allocated rather than from improvements in model reasoning. Future work could explore more sophisticated scope declaration mechanisms and producer-consumer graph inference.

Abstract: A team of coding agents can look fine agent by agent yet fail as a team: each passes its own tests while the merged result is broken, and single-agent evaluation never catches it. As teams run several LLM coding agents in parallel on one codebase, the agents collide: two rewrite the same function, one codes against a contract a teammate just changed, and integration fails after the work is done. Most coordination tools react (watch for a conflict, then warn), but at agent speed the warning arrives after the wasted edit. We recast the problem as scheduling: take each work item's declared scope, partition the work into disjoint scopes, and order merges along the producer->consumer graph, all up front. We build this planner into Nerveplane and evaluate it with NP-Bench, an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark (no coordination; reactive detection; proactive planning) that verifies integration off a real git merge, both in a deterministic simulation and with live agents. The planner lifts clean-integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and cuts merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with a gap that grows in the number of agents. On a live breaking contract change it rescues an outcome both baselines miss on every seed: the clean-integration rate rises from 0 (no coordination and reactive detection) to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small one, while agents respect assigned scopes (0/5 leakage). A cross-session memory drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on strong and weak models alike. We also report a negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales; its value is cost and capacity, not attention. Across two capability tiers and two vendors, the benefit did not shrink as models got stronger, because it comes from how work is allocated, not model reasoning.

</details>


### [140] [Does the Model Use the Feature? Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07270)
*Tong Che,Yilong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes empirical tests to determine whether LLM internal features are actually used by the model for computation or merely correlate with behaviors. The tests evaluate features at natural values: installation (copying feature values between inputs with/without behavior), removal (opposite of installation), and downstream rescue (restoring feature after upstream edit). Applied to three representation types, the tests reveal that features capable of strongly steering behavior don't necessarily transfer that behavior when intervention stays within natural range, challenging the assumption that steering demonstrates mechanistic use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches interpret LLM internal features as mechanisms when they track concepts and manipulation changes behavior. However, steering can push features far outside their natural range, where effects may not reflect the model's own computation. This raises a fundamental question: does steering demonstrate the model actually uses a feature, or merely that the feature correlates with behavior?

Method: The authors propose an empirical framework with three tests: (1) Installation - copying a feature's value from an input showing a behavior into a matched input that doesn't; (2) Removal - the reverse of installation; (3) Downstream rescue - restoring the feature after an upstream edit. These tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs rather than artificial steering values. Applied to three representation types: (a) published unknown-entity latent, (b) dense known-unknown directions in Gemma and Llama, (c) released subject-verb agreement feature set.

Result: The tests reveal sharp separations between installation and removal effects. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values transfers only a small fraction of the natural known-unknown abstention contrast. Dense known-unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal. The subject-verb agreement feature set's ability to reproduce and restore behavior depends on how values are written into the model. Across all three cases, strong steering capability does not guarantee the feature is actually used by the model in natural computation.

Conclusion: Tracking a concept and steering a behavior do not by themselves demonstrate that the model uses a feature for its natural computation. Each conclusion about feature mechanism holds only for the specific intervention tested. This challenges the common interpretation of LLM features as mechanistic and emphasizes the need for careful causal analysis within natural value ranges before claiming functional roles for internal representations.

Abstract: Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. Yet steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model's own computation. We examine this inference and propose an empirical contract whose tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs. One test copies a feature's value from an input that shows a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal); the other restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it. Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known--unknown abstention contrast. Dense known--unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama, and how fully a released subject--verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model. Tracking a concept and steering a behavior therefore do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature, and each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested.

</details>


### [141] [A Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07274)
*Mohammadreza Sediqin,Shivali Dalmia,Srinivasa Karthikeya Reddy Kovvuri,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current agent benchmarks only report whether a task was completed correctly, but not whether the result is trustworthy (earned honestly, reproducible, etc.). This paper introduces a "Trust Layer" framework that adds post-hoc verification to benchmark scores by checking four properties: grading logic support, traceable computation, completion claim accuracy, and result stability across runs. Testing five agent configurations on 108 tasks revealed significant issues - only 22.6% of passing runs clear all four trust checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks only measure capability (what an agent can do) but don't verify actual execution (what it actually did). An agent could receive credit without having legitimately earned it through proper computation, or produce results that wouldn't reproduce on re-run. This gap between measurement and verification needs to be addressed.

Method: The Trust Layer framework uses saved artifacts for the first three checks (grading logic verification, traceable computation detection, completion claim matching) and re-runs the agent for stability testing. Model judgments only label evidence under majority voting, while all verdicts follow deterministic rules without modifying recorded scores. Applied to five agent configurations on 108 tasks from the "Agents' Last Exam" benchmark.

Result: All five models showed passing runs with no traceable computation (rates varying tenfold), confirmed false completion claims, and unstable results (18-46% of tasks don't stay in one score band over five runs). Only 22.6% of recorded passes clear all four trust checks (95% CI 15.0-32.6, n=84).

Conclusion: Measuring agent capability and verifying actual execution are fundamentally different problems. Current benchmarks only address the first; this paper demonstrates the need for trust verification layers to ensure benchmark scores reflect genuine, reproducible agent performance.

Abstract: Deterministic benchmark scores show that an agent received credit, but not whether that credit was earned, reported honestly, or would hold on a second run. We introduce a Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation, an additive post-hoc framework that reports, beside each recorded score, whether it should be believed. It verifies four properties: whether the result is supported by the benchmark's own grading logic, whether a passing answer was earned through traceable computation, whether the agent's completion claim matches what occurred, and whether the result is stable under repeated execution. The first three use only saved artifacts; the fourth re-runs the agent. Model judgments only label evidence under majority voting; all verdicts follow deterministic rules and never modify the recorded score. Applied to five agent configurations on 108 tasks from Agents' Last Exam, every model shows passing runs with no traceable computation (at rates varying tenfold), confirmed false completion claims, and unstable results: 18-46% of tasks do not stay in one score band over five runs. Only 22.6% of recorded passes clear all four checks (95% CI 15.0-32.6, n=84). Measuring what an agent can do and verifying that it did it are different problems, and current benchmarks address only the first.

</details>


### [142] [The Right Memory in the Wrong Context: Verifying Retrieval Admissibility in Long-Term Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07309)
*Zi Wang,Xingqiao Wang,Emmanuel Addai,Devika Ambekar,Xiaowei Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical security and privacy issue in long-term-memory agents: the potential retrieval of inadmissible information (belonging to other principals, violating policy, or having incompatible lifecycle states). The authors propose a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that classifies memory-query pairs as admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved, tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure, and links exposure to target-level disclosure. Evaluation on two benchmarks (RHELM and MemOps) shows significant improvements in anchor recall and recall feasibility, while dramatically reducing computational costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term-memory agents can retrieve relevant but inadmissible information—data belonging to another principal, violating policy, or reflecting incompatible lifecycle states. This is dangerous because standard metrics (recall and final-answer accuracy) don't reveal this problem: a route can appear safe by missing required evidence, while correct answers may follow inadmissible prompt exposure. No existing framework verifies admissibility of retrieved content.

Method: The authors introduce a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that: (1) assigns each memory-query pair one of three statuses—admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved; (2) compares routes at matched required-evidence recall with bounds for unresolved cases; (3) tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure while linking exposure to target-level disclosure. Evaluation involves post-hoc top-20 reanalysis of frozen rankings from RHELM and MemOps benchmarks (3,767 queries), a 72-case development diagnostic, and 16 controlled exposure scenarios across three readers.

Result: Key results: (1) Top-20 anchor recall increased from 0.432 to 0.533; (2) 80% recall feasibility improved from 0.237 to 0.311; (3) Exact similarity evaluations decreased by 98.3%; (4) In the 72-case diagnostic, released-metadata reference preserved required evidence while text-only verifiers failed to detect violations under the 1% false-denial limit; (5) Across 1,523 paired cases, namespace routing showed judged-accuracy gains of 0.053-0.068; (6) In 16 controlled exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% CIs excluded zero for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]).

Conclusion: The results motivate separate verification of candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure. The framework successfully improves retrieval quality metrics while dramatically reducing computational costs. The findings highlight the importance of verifying not just recall but also the admissibility of retrieved information in long-term-memory systems.

Abstract: Long-term-memory agents can retrieve relevant information that is inadmissible for the current request because it belongs to another principal, violates policy, or reflects an incompatible lifecycle state. Recall and final-answer accuracy do not reveal this: a route can appear safe by missing required evidence, while a correct answer may follow inadmissible prompt exposure. We introduce a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that assigns each memory-query pair one of three statuses (admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved), compares routes at matched required-evidence recall with bounds for unresolved cases, and tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure while linking exposure to target-level disclosure. We evaluate its stages on separate, non-pooled populations. A post-hoc top-20 reanalysis of frozen rankings from two public long-term-memory benchmarks, RHELM and MemOps, covers 3,767 queries. All released anchors lie within trusted query namespaces; with within-namespace scores unchanged, off-namespace filtering cannot lower their ranks. Top-20 anchor recall increases from 0.432 to 0.533, 80% recall feasibility from 0.237 to 0.311, and exact similarity evaluations decrease by 98.3%. In a frozen 72-case development diagnostic, a released-metadata reference preserves required evidence, whereas neither text-only verifier detects violations under the 1% required-anchor false-denial limit. Across 1,523 paired benchmark-native cases, namespace routing is associated with judged-accuracy gains of 0.053-0.068 across three readers; recall also changes, so this comparison is observational. In 16 controlled exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% confidence intervals excludes zero for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]). Results motivate separate verification of candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure.

</details>


### [143] [Understanding and Mitigating Inference-Time Overreliance Using Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07311)
*Luoxi Tang,Yuqiao Meng,Nilesh Auradkar,Muchao Ye,Dazheng Zhang,Zhaohan Xi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies "memory over-reliance" as a failure mode in LLM agents where correctly stored and retrieved memories distort inference when only partial evidence transfers to the current task. The authors propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls reuse at read time to mitigate this issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical failure mode in LLM agents with agentic memory: even when memories are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved, they can still distort inference. This is particularly problematic under partial query-memory overlap, where only part of the past experience transfers to the current task.

Method: The authors first conducted benchmark experiments across different memory architectures to identify when memory becomes misleading. They then proposed MEMTRIM, a framework that: (1) indexes memory evidence at write time, and (2) controls memory reuse at read time by removing repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information. MEMTRIM is plug-and-play, requires no retraining, and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory systems.

Result: Memory is useful when past experience fully transfers to the current task, but becomes misleading under partial query-memory overlap. MEMTRIM successfully reduces memory over-reliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory across models and memory settings.

Conclusion: Memory over-reliance is a significant failure mode in LLM agents that occurs under partial evidence transfer. MEMTRIM provides a practical solution that addresses this issue without requiring retraining, making it applicable to existing memory-augmented systems.

Abstract: Agentic memory allows LLM agents to reuse past experience, yet retrieved memories can also distort inference even when they are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. We study this failure mode, which we call memory over-reliance. Across benchmarks and memory architectures, we find that memory is useful when past experience transfers to the current task, but can become misleading when only part of the evidence transfers. Failures are strongest under partial query-memory overlap, a pattern further confirmed by controlled experiments thatvary the amount of overlapping evidence. Motivated by this finding, we propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls its reuse at read time. MEMTRIM removes repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information, requires no retraining, and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory systems.Experiments show that MEMTRIM reduces memory overreliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory across models and memory settings.

</details>


### [144] [Rule-Based Languages for Neurosymbolic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07313)
*Stefania Dumbrava,Efthymia Tsamoura*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey paper examines logic programming as the symbolic backbone of neurosymbolic AI systems, reviewing three major rule-based languages (Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs) across semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanisms. The authors analyze over 50 systems and applications across databases/programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics, providing a decision matrix for matching application scenarios to appropriate formalisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing adoption of logic programming as the symbolic component in neurosymbolic AI systems necessitates a systematic review of available formalisms and their suitability across different application domains.

Method: Survey and comparative analysis of over 50 recent systems and applications, examining three rule-based languages (Datalog, answer set, probabilistic logic programs) along four axes: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanism.

Result: Analysis reveals distinct usage patterns of formalisms across four research areas (databases/programming languages, machine learning, vision, robotics), with a decision matrix mapping application scenarios to required features.

Conclusion: The paper provides practical guidance for selecting appropriate logic programming formalisms for neurosymbolic AI applications and outlines open research problems in the field.

Abstract: Logic programming is increasingly used as the symbolic component of neurosymbolic AI systems. We survey the main rule-based languages in this setting, namely Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs, along four axes: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanism. We analyse over 50 recent systems and applications, comparing formalism usage across four research areas: databases and programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics. We provide a decision matrix mapping application scenarios to required features and close by outlining open problems.

</details>


### [145] [Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization: Learning to Reason with Adaptive Rationale Scaffolding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07342)
*Hoang Phan,Minh Pham,Chau Pham,Chinmay Hegde,Trung Le,Qi Lei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RGPO introduces a framework that uses ground-truth rationales as temporary scaffolds to address reward sparsity in on-policy reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning, adapting guidance to the model's capability while preserving exploration freedom.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning is limited by reward sparsity—when models fail to discover correct trajectories, they receive insufficient learning signal. Existing methods requiring off-policy data to match RL task format or rely on rejection sampling from stronger models are restrictive.

Method: RGPO uses rationales as temporary scaffolds rather than fixed imitation targets. It allows the model to generate improved responses guided by rationales, then transfers only higher-reward, model-generated solutions back to the unguided setting. This preserves exploration while adaptively leveraging ground-truth information based on the model's current capability.

Result: RGPO consistently improves performance over RLVR baselines in both language-only and vision-language reasoning settings. Ablation studies confirm that adaptive rationale guidance is a key contributor to these gains.

Conclusion: RGPO offers a practical and general approach for reducing reward sparsity, stabilizing reinforcement learning, and improving reasoning in both text-only and multimodal models without requiring off-policy data to match the RL task format.

Abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning has become a central paradigm for improving the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, its effectiveness is often limited by reward sparsity: when a model fails to discover correct trajectories for difficult problems, the optimization process receives little useful signal and may stagnate. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by incorporating off-policy demonstrations, expert traces, or model-generated solutions, but they typically require the auxiliary data to match the format of the reinforcement-learning task, often relying on rejection sampling from stronger models to obtain suitable training trajectories. We introduce Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization (RGPO), a framework that adaptively leverages ground-truth rationale information according to the model's current capability while preserving its freedom to explore. Rather than treating reference solutions as fixed imitation targets, RGPO uses them as temporary scaffolds: rationales help the model generate improved responses, after which only higher-reward, model-generated solutions are transferred back to the original unguided setting. This design allows training to exploit available ground-truth information without requiring off-policy data to follow the same format as the RL task. Across both language-only and vision-language reasoning settings, RGPO consistently improves performance over RLVR baselines, and ablation studies show that adaptive rationale guidance is a key contributor to these gains. These results suggest that RGPO offers a practical and general approach for reducing reward sparsity, stabilizing reinforcement learning, and improving reasoning performance in both text-only and multimodal models.

</details>


### [146] [Trajectory-Retrieval Speculative Decoding: When Does a Model's Own History Help?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07350)
*Yuyang Dai,Yushun Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the inefficiency of long chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models by proposing Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR), which reuses previously generated continuations from the model's history to reduce sequential decoding costs while maintaining output quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning increases sequential decoding cost while creating a growing history of potentially reusable continuations. The authors investigate when this history can supply useful drafts and complement an existing drafter through controlled source comparisons.

Method: TLAR retrieves approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory and uses recent verification outcomes to adapt retrieval activation and candidate width. It combines retrieved continuations with model-generated drafts in a shared candidate tree, preserving the target model's output distribution through exact verification.

Result: Across code debugging, mathematics, and open-ended writing, the evaluation shows trajectory-specific reuse. Combining TLAR with strong retrieval baselines improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets and increases end-to-end throughput over the draft-model baseline.

Conclusion: The findings support generated trajectories as runtime memory for adaptive inference, demonstrating that reusing continuation history can significantly improve efficiency in chain-of-thought reasoning.

Abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning increases sequential decoding cost while creating a growing history of potentially reusable continuations. We investigate when this history supplies useful drafts and complements an existing drafter. Controlled source comparisons reveal trajectory-specific reuse, motivating our method Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR). TLAR retrieves approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory and uses recent verification outcomes to adapt retrieval activation and candidate width. TLAR combines retrieved continuations with model-generated drafts in a shared candidate tree, preserving the target model's output distribution through exact verification. Across code debugging, mathematics, and open-ended writing, our evaluation connects source reuse, incremental acceptance, and execution cost. Combining TLAR with strong retrieval baselines improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets and increases end-to-end throughput over the draft-model baseline. These findings support generated trajectories as runtime memory for adaptive inference.

</details>


### [147] [Evaluating Escalation Signals for LLM Routing: Targets, Controls, and Five Ways to Fool Yourself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07354)
*Ramin Pishehvar,Andrea Morandi,Mahesh Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of when to escalate queries from small to large language models, using semantic entropy as a prediction signal. The authors discover that semantic entropy works well on GSM8K (AUROC 0.871) but found that an earlier positive result on a synthetic benchmark was misleading—a simple question difficulty heuristic performed equally well. Their main contribution is a checklist of validation checks to prevent reporting such spurious results, including verifying signals add real information beyond question difficulty, checking different definitions of "escalation worked," and accounting for the true cost of live sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to find a cheap signal that predicts whether escalating from a small to a large language model would improve answer quality, without actually calling the large model first. Semantic entropy (measuring meaning disagreement in model samples) is a natural candidate since high disagreement often signals unreliable answers.

Method: The authors tested semantic entropy across three benchmarks and two model families. They compared semantic entropy against a simple question-difficulty-only baseline on a synthetic benchmark. They also proposed a cheaper alternative using cached past outcomes and developed a method to predict whether this approach will work on new datasets.

Result: On GSM8K, with a small/large model pair ~12x apart in size, semantic entropy achieved AUROC 0.871 for distinguishing small model's mistakes and improved routed accuracy by up to nine points at matched cost. However, the synthetic benchmark result proved misleading—a simple rule based only on question difficulty (no model involved) matched semantic entropy almost exactly. The authors successfully predicted a collapse from AUROC 0.908 to chance level (0.518) on a new dataset using their validation method.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that semantic entropy is a useful escalation signal but requires careful validation. The authors provide a general checklist for evaluating escalation signals: (1) score a cheap question-only difficulty estimate alongside any signal to reveal whether it adds real information; (2) consider multiple definitions of "escalation worked"; (3) check if benchmark leaves room for improvement over always using the large model; and (4) account for the true cost of live sampling. They demonstrate the practical value of these checks by correctly forecasting performance collapse on a new dataset.

Abstract: Deciding when to escalate a query from a small language model to a larger one requires a cheap signal that predicts, before the large model is called, whether escalating would help. Semantic entropy, originally developed to detect hallucinations, is a natural candidate: it measures how much a model's sampled answers disagree in meaning, and high disagreement often signals an unreliable answer. We test it across three benchmarks and two model families. On GSM8K, with a small/large pair about twelve times apart in size, semantic entropy reliably distinguishes the small model's mistakes (AUROC 0.871) and improves routed accuracy over random escalation by up to nine points at matched cost. An earlier strong-looking result on a synthetic benchmark proved misleading: a simple rule based only on question difficulty, with no model involved, matched semantic entropy almost exactly. This paper's main contribution is a set of checks that catch this before it is reported as real. We show that scoring a cheap, question-only difficulty estimate alongside any signal reveals whether the signal adds real information or just tracks how hard a question looks; that two reasonable definitions of "escalation worked" can produce very different results on the same data; that a benchmark can leave almost no room for any signal to beat simply always using the large model; and that the true cost of live sampling can make routing more expensive than calling the large model directly. For a cheaper alternative that reuses cached past outcomes, we show how to predict whether it will work on a new dataset -- confirmed by correctly forecasting a collapse from AUROC 0.908 to chance level (0.518) ahead of time. We offer these as a general checklist for evaluating escalation signals.

</details>


### [148] [Evaluate the Stack, Not the Layer: Do Deterministic and LLM Gates for Agent Actions Fail Independently?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07359)
*Chenglin Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper challenges the common assumption that errors multiply when stacking runtime gates for agent tool calls. Testing 1,119 labeled agent actions from three corpora with one deterministic rule layer and four LLM judges, the authors find that judges compose to only 1.2-1.4 layers (not 2 layers as would be expected under multiplicative error assumption), and rule layer plus one judge composes to 1.86-2.09 layers. The study also reveals significant methodological issues, including a model versioning problem that reversed five conclusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research investigates whether the common assumption that errors multiply when stacking runtime gates for agent tool calls is valid. This assumption underlies much of the design of safety and quality control systems in AI agent frameworks, but has not been empirically tested at scale.

Method: The authors tested 1,119 labeled agent actions from three corpora using a stack consisting of one deterministic rule layer and four LLM judges (three re-collected with the served model recorded on every call). They analyzed the stack as "multiplication-equivalent layers" (n_mult) with floor under perfect coupling. The study compared two miss definitions: STRICT (escalation to human scored as not stopped) and PRIMARY (escalation scored as caught).

Result: Under STRICT miss definition: any two judges compose to about 1.2 to 1.4 layers (φ median +0.430, 6 of 6 pairs significant, floors 1.02 to 1.17). The rule layer plus one judge composes to 1.86 to 2.09 layers (φ median +0.014, 0 of 4 significant, floors 1.01 to 1.09). Under PRIMARY, the bands are 1.21 to 1.57 and 1.80 to 2.13. Solo accuracy did not predict what a layer adds: a cloud rule pack lowered the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% but added no new joint coverage. The difficulty share of judge coupling was 31.8% to 61.8% depending on probe and miss definition. A third-vendor judge landed in the judge band. One judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50 of 112 batches, concentrated on the external corpus.

Conclusion: The multiplicative error assumption is not supported: gates compose more efficiently than predicted. The study also documents a significant methodological issue where model versioning problems overturned a pre-declared analysis rule and reversed five conclusions, demonstrating the importance of careful experimental control in LLM evaluation. Both original and reversed conclusions are reported.

Abstract: Runtime gates for agent tool calls are stacked on the assumption that their errors multiply. We test it on 1,119 labelled agent actions from three corpora, without an adaptive adversary. The stack has one deterministic rule layer and four LLM judges, three of them re-collected with the served model recorded on every call. We read each stack as a number of multiplication-equivalent layers, n_mult, with its floor under perfect coupling. Under the STRICT miss definition (escalation to a human scored as not stopped), any two judges compose to about 1.2 to 1.4 layers (φ median +0.430, 6 of 6 pairs significant, floors 1.02 to 1.17). The rule layer plus one judge composes to 1.86 to 2.09 layers (φ median +0.014, 0 of 4 significant, floors 1.01 to 1.09). Under PRIMARY (escalation scored as caught) the bands are 1.21 to 1.57 and 1.80 to 2.13. Intervals separate on the pooled data, point estimates split on each corpus, and a third-vendor judge lands in the judge band. Solo accuracy does not predict what a layer adds: a cloud rule pack lowers the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% and adds no new joint coverage. The difficulty share of judge coupling is not identifiable: 31.8% to 61.8% depending on the probe and the miss definition. One judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50 of 112 batches, concentrated on the external corpus. That event overturned a pre-declared analysis rule, and the scoring of review verdicts reversed five conclusions. We report both.

</details>


### [149] [MemCo: Memory-Centric Collaboration for Generalizing LLM Agents to Unseen Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07376)
*Xinting Liao,Siyan Liu,Rabab K. Ward,Holger R. Roth,Xiaoxiao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemCo is a memory-centric collaboration framework that enables LLM agents to generalize to unseen interactive environments by maintaining complementary local and global memory spaces, preserving environment-specific details locally while transferring transferable workflows globally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory designs for LLM agents operate in isolation, making it expensive to collect enough trajectories to populate memory. While shared-memory approaches pool episodic memories across tasks, they suffer from granularity issues—retrieved memories can be too specific (losing current grounding) or too coarse (failing to support next actions).

Method: MemCo maintains complementary local and global memory spaces: local memory preserves environment-specific details, while global memory stores transferable workflows induced from local trajectories. During online interaction, MemCo routes relevant local and global memories based on the agent's current state and decision phase, enabling agents to reuse others' experience without blindly transferring environment-specific details.

Result: Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that MemCo improves task success and reduces redundant exploration compared with isolate-memory and shared-memory baselines.

Conclusion: MemCo successfully enables LLM agents to generalize to unseen interactive environments through dual memory spaces that balance specificity and transferability, improving performance while reducing redundant exploration.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in interactive environments, where they need to make sequential decisions through observation, action, and feedback. Although memory can help agents reuse experience, existing work designs memory in isolation, where collecting enough trajectories to populate it is expensive. Existing shared-memory approaches mitigate isolated experience by pooling episodic memories across tasks and environments. However, retrieving shared memory is challenged by the granularity, where retrieved memories can be either too specific to preserve current grounding or too coarse to support the next action. In this work, we propose MemCo, a memory-centric collaboration framework for generalizing LLM agents to unseen interactive environments. It maintains complementary local and global memory spaces, preserving environment-specific details locally while promoting transferable workflows induced from local trajectories to global memory. During online interaction, MemCo routes relevant local and global memories in terms of the agent's current state and decision phase, enabling agents to reuse the experience of other agents without blindly transferring environment-specific details. Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that MemCo improves task success and reduces redundant exploration compared with isolate-memory and shared-memory baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/SYannL/nvdamas.

</details>


### [150] [Defense-in-Depth for LLMs: Evaluating Memory Gates Against Activation-Induced and Memory-Induced Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07403)
*Ritvij Sharma,Russell Dlugosz,Ryan Zhou,Maheep Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses memory-induced sycophancy in LLMs, where retrieved user history causes models to favor stored user beliefs over objective evidence. The authors propose a 2×2 defense framework combining internal activation steering with external memory handling, and evaluate it across four open-weight models on MemSyco-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term memory enables personalized context in LLMs but introduces a vulnerability: retrieved user history can induce sycophancy, causing models to prioritize stored user beliefs over factual accuracy. Existing defenses operate on retrieved context without joint evaluation with internal behavioral bias.

Method: The authors extracted sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and evaluated four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench. They tested three new configurations (rewriting every memory, Router Gate that keeps/rewrites/drops each memory, and dropping all memory) plus two MemSyco baselines, using three LLM judges for evaluation.

Result: Selective Router Gate filtering preserves substantially more accuracy than complete memory removal. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering (α=-1.5) reduced sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while accuracy moved from 43.99% to 43.31%. The reduction was consistent across all three judges but not statistically significant (paired p=0.08 to 0.63 on 149 items).

Conclusion: External memory filtering is the effective component of the defense design. The data does not show that inverse steering adds meaningful benefit beyond memory filtering alone. The Router Gate approach provides a better accuracy-sycophancy tradeoff than complete memory removal.

Abstract: Long-term memory allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain personalized context across interactions, but retrieved user history can induce memory-induced sycophancy, causing models to favor stored user beliefs over objective evidence. Existing defenses primarily operate on retrieved context and are rarely evaluated jointly with internal behavioral bias. We introduce a $2 \times 2$ defense-in-depth framework separating internal activation steering from external memory handling. We extract sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and evaluate four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench (answers for all 1,550 items; defense conditions judged on a fixed 250-item subsample), with three LLM judges. Three of the five configurations are new (rewriting every memory, a Router Gate that keeps, rewrites, or drops each memory, and dropping all memory); the other two are MemSyco's baselines. Selective Router Gate filtering preserves substantially more of MemSyco's average accuracy than complete memory removal, and this separation persists when the models are steered toward sycophancy. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering ($α= -1.5$) lowers judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while average accuracy moves from 43.99% to 43.31%; this reduction has the same direction under all three judges but is not statistically significant (paired $p = 0.08$ to $0.63$ on 149 items). External memory filtering is the part of the design that holds up; our data do not show that inverse steering adds to it.

</details>


### [151] [2d-fet-bench: from spatial reasoning to fet design on flakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07423)
*Dunzhi Zhou,Chengyu Zhu,Gang Qiu,Caiwen Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: 2D-FET-Bench V2 is a benchmark of 128 layout tasks for evaluating language-model agents at designing field-effect transistor (FET) layouts on exfoliated 2D material flakes. The benchmark uses microscopy-derived flake contours and tests whether AI agents can generate correct GDSII layouts from textual device specifications. Best model (GPT5.6-Luna with ReAct-3) achieves 62.3% pass rate, 80.5% coverage, and 43.8% consistency, with expert acceptance rates of 56.4-63.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual FET layout design on 2D flakes is time-consuming and flake-specific. This paper addresses the lack of executable benchmarks to test whether language-model agents can reliably perform this flake-specific construction task, which is important for automating semiconductor device design.

Method: The benchmark comprises 128 layout tasks built from microscopy-derived flake contours, including hole-containing flakes and multi-flake tasks. Each task provides textual device specifications and contour coordinates. Agents generate typed polygon and path operations rendered to GDSII format. A deterministic verifier checks geometric and structural requirements, with an integrity check ensuring contours remain unchanged. Evaluation tested six models and seven workflow/scaffold variants of GPT5.6-Luna with five attempts per task.

Result: Scripted reference layouts pass all 128 tasks, confirming all tasks are solvable. GPT5.6-Luna with ReAct-3 achieves the best performance: 62.3% pass@1, 80.5% task coverage (solved at least once), and 43.8% consistency (solved in all five attempts). ReAct-3 outperforms Plan-and-Execute by 27.0 pass@1 points at 2.46x token cost. Expert audit of verifier-passing layouts shows 56.4% to 63.5% acceptance rates across five ReAct-3 configurations.

Conclusion: Language-model agents can perform FET layout construction on 2D flakes with moderate success, but significant room for improvement remains. ReAct-3 reasoning workflow substantially outperforms simpler planning approaches, though at higher computational cost. The benchmark successfully evaluates geometric and structural FET layout construction capabilities of AI agents.

Abstract: Field-effect transistor (FET) layouts on exfoliated two-dimensional flakes are typically drawn by hand for each flake, placing contacts and gates to match its position and outline in optical micrographs. To our knowledge, no executable benchmark tests whether language-model agents can perform this flake-specific construction reliably. We introduce 2D-FET-Bench V2, a benchmark of 128 layout tasks built from microscopy-derived flake contours, including hole-containing flakes and multi-flake tasks. Each task supplies a textual device specification and contour coordinates. An agent generates typed polygon and path operations rendered to GDSII. A deterministic verifier checks geometric and structural requirements, and a separate integrity check verifies that the supplied contours remain unchanged. Scripted reference layouts pass all 128 tasks, showing that every task is solvable. We evaluate six models and seven workflow and scaffold variants of GPT5.6-Luna, with five attempts per task. The best-performing configuration in the six-model panel, GPT5.6-Luna with ReAct-3, passes 62.3% of attempts and solves 80.5% of tasks at least once (coverage) and 43.8% in all five attempts (consistency). ReAct-3 exceeds the one-pass Plan-and-Execute by 27.0 pass@1 points at 2.46 times the tokens. An expert audit of one sampled verifier-passing layout per covered task, across five ReAct-3 configurations, accepts 56.4% to 63.5% of them. The benchmark evaluates geometric and structural FET layout construction.

</details>


### [152] [Adaptive Gait Biofeedback With Participant-Held-Out Modeling and Participant-Specific Updating in Chronic Ankle Instability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07428)
*Jaeyoon,Kim,Veronika Lebisova,Jeniya Sultana,Jaeyoung Cho,Jaeho Jang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study evaluated an adaptive gait biofeedback system using temporal convolutional networks for chronic ankle instability. The model achieved high AUROC (0.948) and sensitivity (0.941) but low specificity (0.366). The adaptive group showed improved frontal-plane ankle angle at Post compared to controls, but limitations include the nonrandomized design and inability to establish causal benefits or independent clinical classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate an adaptive gait biofeedback system for chronic ankle instability using a temporal convolutional classifier. The study addresses whether model performance and human response can support repeated practice in rehabilitation.

Method: Temporal convolutional classifier trained on protocol-defined, angle-derived GOOD/BAD gait-cycle labels. Used participant-held-out leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation across 20 participants. Seven participants in the adaptive-intervention group completed 9 sessions over 3 weeks, with one motion-capture recording analyzed per session. Models were updated after failed sessions and compared offline. Frontal-plane ankle angle was compared between the adaptive group (n=7) and 10 controls at Baseline, Post, and 7-day Retention.

Result: Mean fold-level AUROC was 0.948, sensitivity was 0.941, and specificity was 0.366. Mean BAD-class F1 was higher in candidate models by 0.187 on same-session validation subset and 0.118 on first subsequent recording. At Post, the adaptive group had a baseline-adjusted frontal-plane ankle angle 5.168 degrees lower than controls (95% CI: 1.766-8.569 degrees lower); the Retention contrast was uncertain.

Conclusion: The findings characterize population-model discrimination and offline participant-specific updating during repeated biofeedback use, alongside a nonrandomized Post frontal-plane ankle angle association. However, it does not establish independent clinical gait classification or a causal benefit of updating.

Abstract: Adaptive gait biofeedback may support repeated practice in chronic ankle instability, but its evaluation must address model performance and human response. We evaluated a temporal convolutional classifier on protocol-defined, angle-derived GOOD/BAD gait-cycle labels using participant-held-out leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation in 20 participants. Seven participants in the adaptive-intervention group completed nine sessions over three weeks, with one motion-capture recording analyzed per session. Models updated after failed sessions were compared offline with their parent models on the same-session validation subset used for candidate selection and the first subsequent adaptive-session recording. Frontal-plane ankle angle was compared between the adaptive group and 10 sequentially enrolled controls at Baseline, Post, and 7-day Retention. Across 20 held-out folds, mean fold-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.948, sensitivity for angle-threshold-exceeding BAD cycles was 0.941, and specificity for angle-threshold-meeting GOOD cycles was 0.366. Mean BAD-class F1 was higher in candidate models by 0.187 on the same-session subset and 0.118 on the first subsequent recording. At Post, the adaptive group had a baseline-adjusted frontal-plane ankle angle 5.168 degrees lower than controls (95% confidence interval, 1.766-8.569 degrees lower); the Retention contrast was uncertain. These findings characterize population-model discrimination and offline participant-specific updating during repeated biofeedback use, alongside a nonrandomized Post frontal-plane ankle angle association. They do not establish independent clinical gait classification or a causal benefit of updating.

</details>


### [153] [When Does AI Supervision Help? A Role-Aware Study of Network Fraud Decision Management with Blockchain Auditability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07434)
*Saviz Changizi,Nasibeh Mohammadzadeh,Mohammad Shojafar,Rahim Tafazolli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates when a second AI component improves network fraud detection through a role-aware Decider-Supervisor framework with blockchain auditability. The study compares primary-only versus supervised decisions across four configurations combining centralized ML, federated meta-models, and LLM variants. Results show that AI supervision value depends on role assignment, calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than merely having a second model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical question in AI-assisted fraud detection: when does adding a second AI component improve decision-making versus simply adding operational burden? The authors aim to determine the conditions under which AI supervision provides genuine benefit in network fraud detection systems.

Method: The study employs a role-aware Decider-Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations combining: (1) centralized machine learning, (2) Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and (3) Base or Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) large language model variants. Evaluation metrics include non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, conditional calibration, traffic-mix and review-capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures.

Result: The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, leaving the non-hard population as the main AI decision setting. Conditional validation calibration does not produce a consistently transferable supervisory advantage on deployment replay. DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive supervised configuration but still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, while exposing a pre-finalisation single-write limitation.

Conclusion: The value of AI supervision in fraud detection depends on multiple factors—role assignment, calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls—rather than on the presence of a second model alone. Simply adding a second AI component does not guarantee improved performance; careful consideration of these contextual factors is essential for effective AI supervision in network fraud detection systems.

Abstract: When does a second artificial intelligence (AI) component improve a primary network-fraud decision rather than add operational burden? We study this question through a role-aware Decider-Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations that combine centralised machine learning, a Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and Base or Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) large language model variants. The analysis compares primary-only and supervised decisions using non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, conditional calibration, traffic-mix and Review-capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls. The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, leaving the non-hard population as the main AI decision setting. Conditional validation calibration does not produce a consistently transferable supervisory advantage on deployment replay. DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive supervised configuration, but it still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, while exposing a pre-finalisation single-write limitation. The results show that the value of AI supervision depends on role assignment, calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than on the presence of a second model alone.

</details>


### [154] [Auditable Claims about AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07459)
*Yue Zhao,Jiate Li,Li Li,Yi Nian,Jinbo Liu,Xiaolin Zhou,Xiyang Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses how to verify claims made about AI agents (e.g., "every email is human-approved") by making them auditable. The authors propose that auditable claims must specify: the policy, its scope, the records that would verify it, who writes them, and a decision rule. They extend the Auditable Agents framework to cover claims rather than just single actions, with three additional conditions for agents. The paper provides practical tools including a claim-check table for six common claims and a worked case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to automatically record events, but does not specify which records can verify specific claims about an AI agent. Organizations make various claims about their AI agents (human approval, logging, safety), but there's no standardized way to verify these claims. This creates a gap in AI governance and accountability.

Method: The authors adapt the preconditions of an assurance engagement to define "auditable claims." They extend the Policy Checkability dimension of their Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims. They prove theoretically that support is impossible without each condition (under explicit models). They apply the method to six common claims using NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts as anchors, and provide a worked case following one claim through five evidence states.

Result: The paper produces: (1) a definition of auditable claims with four required elements (policy, scope, records, record-writer) plus a decision rule, (2) three additional conditions for agents (coverage by independent record, authorization bound to action arguments, completeness beyond integrity), (3) a claim-check table applying the method to six common claims, and (4) a worked case study demonstrating the approach.

Conclusion: The paper provides a practical framework for making AI agent claims verifiable. It offers tools for operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters to assess and validate claims about AI agent behavior, addressing the gap between regulatory requirements (EU AI Act) and practical verification methods. The authors conclude with practice recommendations for different stakeholders.

Abstract: Organizations make claims about their AI agents: a person approves every external email, every action is logged, an evaluation shows the agent is safe to deploy. Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to allow the automatic recording of events but does not say which records settle a given claim. The position is one sentence: to be checked, a claim about an agent must first name its policy, its scope, the records that would settle it, and who writes them. Adapting the preconditions of an assurance engagement, we call a claim auditable when these elements and a decision rule are fixed before any verdict and the records are obtainable. This extends the Policy Checkability dimension of our Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims. Agents add three conditions: coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity. Under an explicit model, we prove that support is impossible without each wherever its hypotheses hold. A claim-check table applies the method to six common claims, anchored in current NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts. A worked case follows one claim through five evidence states. We close with a practice box and steps for operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters.

</details>


### [155] [COMPASS: Finding Where Reasoning Lives in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07469)
*Pratyay Dutta,Kowshik Thopalli,Vivek Narayanaswamy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: COMPASS is an inference-time activation steering method that uses the model's own answer correctness as a signal to identify reasoning-promoting attention heads. It outperforms baselines, improving GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points while using 20-70% fewer tokens than CoT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reasoning elicitation methods require predefined characterizations (CoT prompts, contrastive directions, or SAE features). This paper aims to show that a much simpler signal—the correctness of the model's own direct answer attempts—suffices to decode a latent reasoning direction within model activations.

Method: COMPASS identifies reasoning-carrying attention heads using a logit-space attribution score and steers their activations along the "correctness direction" (derived from the model's own answer attempts). Only per-head activation statistics are needed, no gradient-based fine-tuning.

Result: Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, COMPASS outperforms activation-steering baselines. It improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average, approaches CoT accuracy with 20-70% fewer generated tokens, and transfers to unseen benchmarks without re-fitting. Ablations confirm both the correctness direction and a small subset of heads are necessary.

Conclusion: The correctness of a model's own direct answer attempts is a sufficient signal for eliciting reasoning. The reasoning direction is decodable in most attention heads, but only a small subset can be effectively intervened upon. This provides a simple, efficient, and transferable method for improving LLM mathematical reasoning at inference time.

Abstract: Explicitly eliciting reasoning substantially improves LLM performance. Existing approaches require a predefined characterization of reasoning, whether through CoT prompt design, contrastive CoT directions, or via SAE derived reasoning features. For mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, we show that a much simpler signal suffices, which is the correctness of the model's own direct answer attempts. This signal yields a latent direction that elicits reasoning. This direction is decodable within the activations of most attention heads, but only a small subset of them can be effectively intervened. We introduce COMPASS, an inference-time steering method that identifies these heads using a logit-space attribution score and steers their activations along the correctness direction, requiring only per-head activation statistics. Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, COMPASS outperforms the activation-steering baselines we compare against, improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average, and approaches CoT accuracy with 20-70\% fewer generated tokens. Interventions transfer without re-fitting to unseen benchmarks, and ablations show that both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads.

</details>


### [156] [PsyCIDRA: A Dual-Agent Framework for Psychiatric Interviewing and Diagnostic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07473)
*Milad Mohammadi,Fatemeh Akrami Shamsabadi,Zahra Mohseni,Amirhossein Safdarian,Malekfarhad Malek,Hadi Moradi,Hesham Faili*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PsyCIDRA is a dual-agent LLM framework that combines free-form psychiatric interviewing with diagnostic reasoning. It uses an interviewer agent with tools for notes, skills, and ICD-11 retrieval, and a diagnostic reasoning agent that reports hypotheses with supporting/conflicting/missing evidence. Evaluation shows improved diagnostic agreement over direct prompting (60.5% vs 51.9% rank-1 accuracy on 81 cases; 79.6% vs 65.4% agreement with psychologists on 101 human participants).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
