Motivation: Large language models show promise in clinical reasoning, but their ability to conduct interactive psychiatric interviewing—guiding an evolving conversation for diagnostic assessment—remains less studied. Current approaches lack frameworks that link free-form interviewing with systematic diagnostic reasoning.

Method: PsyCIDRA is a dual-agent framework: (1) Interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry; (2) Diagnostic reasoning agent receives the completed transcript and reports hypotheses with supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, withholding final hypotheses when insufficiently supported. Evaluation used patient profiles from PsyCPG: (1) Simulation across 4 models on 53 evaluation cases; (2) 81 held-out simulated cases; (3) Blinded study with 101 human participants in separate arms comparing PsyCIDRA vs direct prompting.

Result: Across four models on 53 evaluation cases, PsyCIDRA achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% vs 51.9%. In a blinded study of 101 human participants, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, compared with 65.4% for direct prompting.

Conclusion: LLM agents can assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety together, this study contributes to understanding the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.

Abstract: Large language models show promise in clinical reasoning, but psychiatric interviewing requires guiding an evolving conversation. Their ability to carry out this interactive assessment remains less studied. We present PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework linking free-form psychiatric interviewing with diagnostic reasoning for expert review. Its interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry. Its diagnostic reasoning agent then receives the completed interview transcript and reports hypotheses alongside supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, withholding a final hypothesis when none is sufficiently supported. Using patient profiles generated with PsyCPG, we first evaluate PsyCIDRA in simulation. Across four models on 53 evaluation cases, it achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% versus 51.9%. In a blinded study of 101 human participants in separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, compared with 65.4% for direct prompting. Together, these findings support the potential of LLM agents to assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety together, this study contributes to understanding the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.

</details>


### [157] [In With the Old: Enhancing 'Classical' Document Automation with Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07480)
*Marc Lauritsen,Hannes Westermann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores the integration of traditional expert system-based document automation services with modern generative AI approaches to enhance software-based legal assistance systems. Preliminary experiments using large language models to identify and fix issues in laypeople's legal texts are also reported.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to leverage the strengths of both symbolic/expert system approaches and generative AI to improve legal assistance systems. Traditional expert systems have been used for legal knowledge representation and reasoning, but may have limitations that generative AI could address.

Method: The study discusses the theoretical benefits and challenges of combining expert system-style document automation with generative AI approaches. Preliminary experiments were conducted using large language models to identify and fix issues in texts written by laypeople.

Result: The abstract reports on preliminary experiments but does not provide specific quantitative results. The focus appears to be on exploring the possibilities and identifying potential benefits and challenges of the integration approach.

Conclusion: The paper suggests that there are possible benefits to combining traditional symbolic legal assistance approaches with generative AI, though challenges exist. The integration could enhance both types of approaches, but further research is needed to validate the proposed framework.

Abstract: Software-based legal assistance systems have leveraged many different forms of knowledge representation and reasoning. This article explores how document automation services rooted in expert system style and other symbolic approaches can usefully enhance and be enhanced by current generative AI approaches. We discuss the possible benefits and challenges, and report on preliminary experiments in using large language models to identify and fix issues in texts written by laypeople.

</details>


### [158] [Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07497)
*Meher Chaitanya,Tianyi Zhou,Aristides Gionis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how much spectral detail the Muon optimizer needs. The authors find that 94-97% of singular modes lie below a noise edge, yet collectively contribute positively to training. They propose BulkBoost, a two-band reweighting framework that separates the "bulk" (noisy modes below the edge) from "spikes" (informative modes above the edge), achieving better performance than fine-grained spectral profiles with just a single bulk-to-spike gain parameter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon optimizer uses a "flat profile" giving equal weight to all singular directions. Recent optimizers like Freon use fine-grained spectral maps with per-mode gains. This paper questions whether such detailed spectral information is necessary, hypothesizing that most singular modes are noise but collectively beneficial.

Method: The authors introduce BulkBoost with two variants: (1) fixed-rank variant with hand-tuned parameters, and (2) noise-calibrated variant using split-minibatch gradient differences with Marchenko-Pastur theory to estimate the noise edge. Both variants reweight the bulk (modes below noise edge) versus spikes (modes above edge) through a single shared gain parameter while preserving Frobenius norm of each matrix's unreweighted direction.

Result: Across 30 continued-pretraining settings (Pythia-14M to 410M, six corpora), two-band reweighting outperforms fine-grained power-law profiles (Freon) and Spectra. Compared to Muon's flat profile: Freon reduces loss by 0.022% on average, while BulkBoost variants achieve 0.073-0.147% reduction. The noise-calibrated variant performs best.

Conclusion: Useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional. A single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as fine-grained spectral profiles, suggesting that most spectral detail in optimizers is unnecessary. The bulk of singular modes, despite being noisy individually, collectively contribute positively and should be upweighted relative to spike modes.

Abstract: Muon combines current and past gradients into matrix momentum. For $M=UΣV^\top$, the idealized polar update $Q=UV^\top$ gives every singular direction the same weight. We refer to this as the flat profile. Several recent optimizers replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that give each direction its own gain. We ask how much of this spectral detail a Muon update needs. Our spectral diagnostics show that approximately $94$--$97\%$ of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient.
  We introduce BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko--Pastur reference edge for Muon's Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk's relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix's unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. Across 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia-14M to 410M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon and outperforms Spectra. Measured against Muon's flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by $0.022\%$ of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of $0.073$--$0.147\%$. These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles.

</details>


### [159] [MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07505)
*Ming Yin,Sixun Dong,Yudong Liu,Wen-Yun Yang,Yunjiang Jiang,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation in long-history recommendation systems where user histories contain multi-scale semantic structure (short-term intent, medium-term interests, long-term preferences) but are compressed into monolithic cached memories that unevenly preserve these temporal scales. The authors propose MARS, a multi-resolution user memory with recurrent state tracks for different half-lives and a sparse routing reader that selectively materializes relevant temporal resolutions for candidate scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address "temporal aliasing" - a failure mode where linear probes recover recent and mid-range content far worse than long-range content when using monolithic cached memories. This is important because real user histories exhibit multi-scale semantic structure, and existing methods fail to preserve all temporal scales evenly, degrading recommendation quality especially for longer histories.

Method: MARS uses two key components: (1) A multi-resolution memory that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives, preserving information at multiple temporal scales; (2) A sparse routing reader that materializes compact seed memories by selecting relevant temporal resolutions for each seed, maintaining fixed-size candidate scoring. The approach is evaluated on three public datasets with component-matched ablations and paired tests.

Result: MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains that grow with history length. Component-matched ablations show that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond what hard-window memories or added capacity provide. The advantage widens after within-user behavioral shifts, with only ~1.02x the baseline's warm-cache serving latency for 1,000 candidates per user.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that handling multi-scale temporal structure in user histories is crucial for long-history recommenders. MARS successfully addresses temporal aliasing through multi-resolution memory and sparse routing, achieving better performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The approach is particularly effective for longer histories and scenarios with behavioral shifts.

Abstract: Long-history recommenders often compress each user's history into a compact, candidate-independent memory that is cached and reused to score large candidate pools. We show that real user histories exhibit multi-scale semantic structure, with short-lived intent, medium-term interests, and long-term preferences coexisting in one sequence, and that monolithic cached memories preserve these scales unevenly: linear probes recover recent and mid-range content far worse than long-range content. We call this failure mode \textit{temporal aliasing}. We propose \textbf{MARS}, a multi-resolution user memory that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives, and a sparse routing reader that materializes compact seed memories by selecting the relevant temporal resolutions for each seed, preserving fixed-size candidate scoring. MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains that grow with history length. Component-matched ablations with paired tests show that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond what hard-window memories or added capacity provide. The advantage of MARS over its interface-matched baseline also widens after within-user behavioral shifts, at about $1.02\times$ that baseline's warm-cache serving latency for $1{,}000$ candidates per user.

</details>


### [160] [On Open-Ended Information Seeking for Information Elicitation Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07509)
*Victor De Lima,Grace Hui Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how different large language models (LLMs) make value judgments about information in agentic elicitation tasks, and how these varying judgments shape sequential information-seeking behavior. The authors examine 11 LLMs across multiple families and parameter scales using a controlled simulation environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Information elicitation is an open-ended problem where elicitors must continuously decide which information to pursue as new information emerges. While agentic elicitation delegates these decisions to foundation models, how model choice affects information-seeking behavior remains understudied. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically examining how different LLMs evaluate information value and how these differences impact the resulting information-seeking patterns.

Method: The authors conducted a multi-stage study: (1) Examined value judgments across 11 LLMs using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives; (2) Developed a controlled elicitation simulation where different models encounter the same information space with the same selection rule, isolating judgments from question generation and respondent behavior; (3) Characterized breadth-depth behavior emerging from model-specific preferences; (4) Examined how interaction history changes evaluation and selection of prospective information; (5) Tested robustness through sensitivity analyses and ablations over opportunities available, response labels, interaction history presence, and redundancy relevance.

Result: The study reveals that judgments about information value vary significantly across LLMs from different model families and parameter scales. These differences shape sequential information-seeking behavior in measurable ways. Interaction history was found to change both the evaluation and subsequent selection of prospective information. The findings were validated through comprehensive sensitivity analyses and ablations.

Conclusion: Model choice significantly impacts information-seeking behavior in agentic elicitation. Different LLMs exhibit distinct preferences for breadth vs. depth in information gathering, and these preferences are modulated by interaction history. The controlled simulation methodology provides a robust framework for studying LLM decision-making in information-seeking tasks.

Abstract: Information elicitation is an open-ended information-seeking problem in which an interaction can unfold in many potentially valuable directions, requiring an elicitor to continually determine which information to pursue as new information emerges. In agentic elicitation, these decisions may be delegated to a foundation model, yet how model choice shapes the resulting information-seeking behavior remains understudied. We study how judgments about information value vary across LLMs and how these differences shape sequential information seeking. We first examine these judgments across 11 LLMs spanning multiple model families and parameter scales, using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives. We then develop a controlled elicitation simulation in which different models encounter the same information space and use the same selection rule, isolating these judgments from question generation and respondent behavior. Using this setting, we characterize the breadth-depth behavior that emerges from model-specific information-seeking preferences over the course of elicitation. We further examine how interaction history changes the evaluation and subsequent selection of prospective information. We test the robustness and boundaries of these findings through sensitivity analyses and ablations over the opportunities available to the elicitor, the response labels used to operationalize information-seeking preferences, the presence of interaction history, and whether redundancy is explicitly relevant to the assessment. The project code, data, and trajectory files are available at https://github.com/infosenselab/open-elicitation.

</details>


### [161] [From Local Evidence to Safety Verdicts: Causal Tracing in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07514)
*Faezeh Dehghan Tarzjani,Mevan Wijewardena,Alexander Romanus,Sampad Mohanty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces SSU-Bench, a dataset designed to investigate where vision-language models make joint safety judgments when combining images with text prompts. The study uses intervention techniques to trace how internal model states between paired inputs (safe/unsafe combinations) affect safety verdicts, finding that earlier decoder layers are more responsive to input changes while later layers handle final token decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand where in vision-language models the joint safety judgment occurs - specifically, how models combine image and text inputs to recognize safety risks that neither modality reveals alone. The key question is: at what internal layer does this joint decision-making become accessible?

Method: The researchers created SSU-Bench with matched safe/unsafe image-text combinations using single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated regions. They used three vision-language models and transferred internal states between paired inputs, measuring resulting changes in safety verdicts. They also estimated directions from other examples and used linear readouts of final-token states.

Result: Interventions at changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective later. Directions from other examples produce similar late-layer effects. A linear readout of final-token state predicts the model's own verdict (including incorrect judgments), and cross-model comparisons reveal similarities in counterfactual change patterns.

Conclusion: The findings identify a recurring transition in where interventions can influence joint safety verdicts, distinguishing between a readable model decision and a correct safety judgment. This suggests a consistent pattern across models in how safety decisions emerge from joint image-text processing.

Abstract: A vision-language model may need to combine an image with a prompt to recognize a safety risk that neither reveals alone. Where does this joint safety judgment become accessible inside the model? We introduce SSU-Bench, a dataset of matched safe and unsafe image-text combinations constructed using single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated intended regions. Using three vision-language models, we transfer internal states between paired inputs and measure the resulting change in the safety verdict. Across models and both types of counterfactual, interventions at the changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective later. Directions estimated from other examples produce similar late-layer effects. A linear readout of the final-token state also predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect judgments, and cross-model comparisons reveal similarities in the patterns of counterfactual change. These findings identify a recurring transition in where interventions can influence a joint safety verdict and distinguish a readable model decision from a correct safety judgment.

</details>


### [162] [Grounding What Shapes the Plan: Rethinking Groundedness for Physical Intelligence in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07521)
*Minkyoung Cho,Zewei Zhou,Wenhao Ding,Shuhan Tan,Boyi Li,Yuxiao Chen,Yan Wang,Zheng Lian,Min-Hung Chen,Chaowei Xiao,Zhuoqing Mao,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone,Yulong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GroundAct addresses the gap between grounded reasoning and actual driving actions by using entities as the unit of grounding with reference tokens, enabling grounded planning that connects reasoning to plan execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current driving models ground reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures, but this grounding doesn't ensure desirable driving outcomes. The fundamental question is: what should groundedness mean when the model outputs an action?

Method: GroundAct introduces entities as the unit of grounding. A lightweight reference token keeps each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning. Only the referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal correct the plan, creating an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does (grounded planning).

Result: GroundAct shows strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, with closed-loop results extending this evidence to driving in simulation.

Conclusion: The concept of "grounded planning" provides an explicit path from reasoning grounds to plan actions, demonstrating practical value in both open- and closed-loop driving scenarios including normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical conditions.

Abstract: Driving models increasingly ground reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures. These advances make reasoning more faithful to the driving scene, but leave a fundamental question unresolved: what should groundedness mean when the model ultimately outputs an action? Correctly grounded reasoning does not, by itself, ensure desirable driving outcomes. We introduce GroundAct, which starts from a simple premise: driving unfolds through physical entities and their interactions. Entities therefore become the unit of grounding; a lightweight reference token keeps each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning; and only the referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal correct the plan. The result is an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does, which we call grounded planning. To assess its practical value, we evaluate GroundAct in both open- and closed-loop settings. GroundAct shows strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, with closed-loop results extending this evidence to driving in simulation.

</details>


### [163] [A Systematic Investigation of Bias in Large Language Models for Advertising Relevance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07544)
*Weiwei Wang,Yinchuan Xu,Jialu Gao,Youkow Homma,Jian Jiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates fairness in LLM-based relevance judgments for advertising queries, examining how advertiser identity, language, and demographic wording affect fairness. Using GPT-4o and a fine-tuned Qwen-7B model, the study finds that relevance assessments can be altered by advertiser identity or input language, and demographic comparisons reveal stereotypical patterns. Mitigation effectiveness depends on advertiser information relevance and training data distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs are increasingly used to judge ad-query relevance, the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention. This study addresses this gap by systematically examining potential biases in LLM-based relevance assessment systems for advertising.

Method: The study uses a counterfactual framework to examine fairness across three dimensions: (1) advertiser identity and popularity, (2) input language, and (3) demographic wording. Two models are evaluated: GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model fine-tuned for relevance prediction. Data sources include real advertising logs for advertiser and language experiments, and controlled synthetic queries for demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit contexts. Both inference-time and training-time mitigation strategies are tested.

Result: Both models show fairness issues: (1) Changing advertiser identity or input language can alter relevance assessments; (2) Demographic comparisons reveal patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly involving gender and occupation; (3) Mitigation effectiveness varies depending on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in training data.

Conclusion: LLM-based relevance judgment systems for advertising exhibit fairness concerns across multiple dimensions. The effectiveness of mitigation strategies depends on specific contextual factors. These findings help advertising practitioners identify fairness risks and develop appropriate mitigation methods for LLM relevance systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge how well an advertisement matches a query, but the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention. We conduct a systematic study of fairness in relevance judgments made by LLMs for queries and advertisements. Our counterfactual framework examines the effects of advertiser identity and possible popularity, input language, and demographic wording. We study GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model trained specifically for relevance prediction. The advertiser and language experiments use query and advertisement pairs sampled from real advertising logs. Controlled synthetic queries are used to study demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit. For both models, changing the advertiser identity or input language can alter the relevance assessment. Selected demographic comparisons also show patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly those involving gender and occupation. We further study mitigation during model inference and training. The results indicate that its effectiveness depends on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in the training data. These findings can help advertising practitioners identify fairness risks and develop suitable mitigation methods for LLM relevance systems.

</details>


### [164] [Decoupled Multi-Agent Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07556)
*Xinle Wu,Yao Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeOrch introduces a two-stage planner for language-model multi-agent systems that separates worker-agnostic task decomposition from worker selection, using a lightweight matcher with contextual bandit adaptation to enable transfer learning and proper credit assignment without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learned orchestration approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome, which limits transfer and obscures credit assignment.

Method: DeOrch uses a two-stage planner: (1) decomposes tasks without worker information, then (2) selects collaboration operations using worker-identity-free matchability feedback. A lightweight matcher estimates worker suitability from behavior on a fixed probe set and adapts online with a contextual bandit, allowing new workers without retraining.

Result: DeOrch outperforms prior automatic MAS orchestration methods with fewer worker calls, remains effective when transferred to unseen worker pools without retraining, and shows consistent gains from both components across diverse in- and out-of-distribution tasks.

Conclusion: Separating worker-agnostic planning from worker selection enables effective transfer to unseen worker pools and proper credit assignment, with the contextual bandit-based matcher providing adaptable worker suitability estimation without retraining.

Abstract: Learned orchestration can automatically construct effective language-model multi-agent systems, but existing approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome, limiting transfer and obscuring credit assignment. We introduce DeOrch, which separates worker-agnostic planning from concrete worker selection. Its two-stage planner first decomposes the task without worker information, then chooses collaboration operations using compact, worker-identity-free matchability feedback from the pool, enabling conditional credit assignment to decomposition and collaboration decisions. A lightweight matcher estimates worker suitability from behavior on a fixed probe set and adapts online with a contextual bandit, allowing new workers to be incorporated without retraining the planner or matcher. Across diverse in- and out-of-distribution tasks, DeOrch outperforms prior automatic MAS orchestration methods with fewer worker calls than competing learned orchestrators, remains effective when transferred to an entirely unseen worker pool without retraining, and shows consistent gains from both components.

</details>


### [165] [Navigating Route Latent Space for Synthesizable Molecular Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07560)
*Tao Li,Tuan Vinh,Monika Raj,Yuan Fang,Zhichun Guo,Carl Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RouteFlow proposes a novel framework for synthesizable molecular design by searching over a continuous route latent space instead of discrete molecular spaces. It uses reward-guided flow matching with cycle-consistency stabilization to efficiently navigate toward high-property molecules while preserving synthesizability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Goal-directed molecular design has advanced rapidly, but a significant proportion of designed molecules are difficult to synthesize, limiting real-world utility. Prior methods either project molecules back to synthesizable analogs (causing deviation from target) or optimize in discrete synthesis spaces (lacking continuous landscape for efficient search). The authors argue the limitation comes from the search space rather than the optimizer.

Method: RouteFlow reformulates synthesizable molecular design as search over a continuous route latent space where each latent maps back to a complete synthesis route, inherently preserving synthesizability. It uses reward-guided flow matching as an efficient sampler to steer toward high-property regions. A cycle-consistency mechanism is introduced to stabilize fine-tuning and keep optimization on-manifold of real synthesis routes.

Result: Across 16 optimization tasks from Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow achieves the best sample efficiency among synthesizability-aware baselines, with the best synthetic accessibility and the highest retrosynthesis success rate. The cycle-consistency mechanism reliably keeps optimization on-manifold while improving target properties.

Conclusion: RouteFlow supports effective synthesizable molecular discovery by maintaining synthesizability throughout the optimization process while achieving superior performance in sample efficiency, synthetic accessibility, and retrosynthesis success rate compared to existing synthesizability-aware baselines.

Abstract: Goal-directed molecular design has advanced rapidly, yet a substantial proportion of designed molecules remain difficult to synthesize in practice, limiting their real-world utility. Prior synthesizability-aware methods either project generated molecules back to synthesizable analogs that deviate from the intended target, or optimize directly in discrete synthesis spaces that lack a continuous landscape for efficient search. We argue that this limitation mainly comes from the search space rather than the optimizer. To address this, we propose RouteFlow, a framework that reformulates synthesizable molecular design as a search over a continuous route latent space, where each latent maps back to a complete synthesis route and synthesizability is inherently preserved. To navigate this space, we adopt reward-guided flow matching as an efficient sampler that steers toward high-property regions. Since reward optimization may push latents off the manifold of real synthesis routes, where decoding becomes unreliable, we further introduce a cycle-consistency mechanism to stabilize fine-tuning. Across 16 optimization tasks from Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow achieves the best sample efficiency among synthesizability-aware baselines, with the best synthetic accessibility and the highest retrosynthesis success rate. Our results also confirm that the proposed cycle-consistency reliably keeps optimization on-manifold while improving target properties, supporting effective synthesizable molecular discovery.

</details>


### [166] [Unanimously Wrong: Certified Abstention from How Medical LLM Consensus Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07570)
*Xiaoyang Wang,Tianrui Wang,Christopher C. Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework for agentic medical QA systems that detects when consensus is wrong by analyzing how the consensus was formed, not just whether agreement exists. It uses process features, rationale semantic entropy, and active probing to achieve 0.696 AUROC in distinguishing correct from incorrect unanimous votes, with 9.0% observed selective risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current systems rely on agreement as a proxy for correctness, but unanimous votes can be wrong when all samples share the same misconception. Agreement-based signals only read the final state and discard how consensus was reached, making them unable to flag when everyone is wrong.

Method: ProbeGuard uses: (1) Process features tracing agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation; (2) Rationale semantic entropy for unanimous votes to check if reasons behind the vote cohere; (3) Active probe to retrieve counter-evidence and test consensus survival; (4) Stratified Learn-then-Test calibration to convert scores into distribution-free bounds on selective risk.

Result: On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong (undetectable by agreement-based signals). Process signals raise discrimination from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers 6/10 unanimous-layer questions at 9.0% observed selective risk, and 9/10 with in-domain calibration data.

Conclusion: Process-based signals that trace how consensus forms can effectively detect incorrect unanimous consensus in medical QA systems, providing certified bounds on selective risk that agreement-based signals cannot achieve.

Abstract: In clinical practice, agreement among independent experts is treated as evidence of reliability, and multi-round consensus has become a core mechanism of agentic medical question-answering systems. When such a system must decide whether to trust its own answer, the prevailing signal is again agreement, now among the sampled answers. But agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong, returning the same incorrect answer on every sample, and on these questions agreement-based signals carry no information. The cause is that these signals read only the final state of the consensus and discard how it was reached. Agreement that was reached by resolving disagreement with evidence looks identical, at the end, to agreement that was present from the first sample because every sample shares one misconception. ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework that bases the abstention decision on how the consensus formed. Process features trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration then converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk. We evaluate ProbeGuard on three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference, with a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong, and no agreement-based signal can flag them. Process signals raise the discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at an observed selective risk of 9.0%, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.

</details>


### [167] [Cooperating with Future Collaborators: Multi-Agent RL under Staggered Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07578)
*Jianglin Qiao,Siyi Hu,Thien Hoang Nguyen,Zehong Cao,Salah Sukkarieh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses staggered participation (SP) in cooperative MARL, where agents act at different times and earlier agents leave information for later agents. It proposes SPL (Staggered Participation Learning) with prospective acquisition supervision for early agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. Across 60 benchmark comparisons, SPL achieves 14.1% higher task completion on average.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many cooperative tasks, agents participate at different times (staggered participation), creating cross-time, cross-agent learning dependencies. Earlier agents' actions affect returns through information provided to later agents. This setting requires: (1) identifying useful information for future decisions, and (2) learning how later agents should use it. Existing MARL methods assume concurrent participation and fail to address this.

Method: The proposed SPL is a training-time augmentation with two components:
1. Prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents - guides them to acquire useful information for future decisions
2. Outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents - teaches them how to effectively use information from earlier agents
Evaluated on multiple policy-based MARL backbones, MPE/RWARE environments, and various staggered-participation patterns.

Result: Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average improvement of 14.1%. Gains extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.

Conclusion: SPL successfully addresses the staggered participation problem in cooperative MARL by training earlier agents to provide useful information and later agents to leverage it effectively. The consistent improvements across diverse settings (algorithms, time scales, embodiment types) demonstrate the method's generalizability and effectiveness.

Abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are often trained under concurrent participation, while in many tasks some agents act earlier and leave task-relevant information that becomes useful to agents participating later. We study this setting as staggered participation (SP), which introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency because an early action may affect the return through the information it provides and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP therefore requires both identifying what information is useful for future decisions and learning how later agents should use it. We propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that addresses these two parts with prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average difference of 14.1%. The gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.

</details>


### [168] [LOGIC: An LLM Benchmark for Intent-Grounded Change Impact in Aerospace Electrical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07580)
*Muhammad Faraz Shoaib,Muhammad Qasim,Raisulhaq Mohammed Rizwan,Rahmatullah Safdar,Muzammil Adnan Shaik,Abdul Aleem Mohammed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LOGIC is a benchmark and evaluation framework for aerospace electrical design change propagation. It uses language models to ground engineering requests in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before propagating selected changes through a typed traceability graph, separating candidate-selection errors from downstream propagation errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Problem: Aerospace electrical-design revisions contain multiple genuine changes, but engineering requests may only authorize a subset. Propagating every detected difference produces overly broad impact reports, making it difficult to identify truly affected elements.

Method: LOGIC contains 168 scenarios (144 selection, 24 abstention cases). It evaluates three 7-8B language models against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods using a typed electrical traceability graph. The framework separates candidate selection from downstream propagation to distinguish error types.

Result: On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases: gate-only structured evidence achieves candidate F1 of 1.0000 vs 0.9677 for token-lexical matching. On 12 relational-paraphrase cases: token-lexical F1 is 0.1772, gate-only F1 is 0.0000, vs 0.5000-0.6400 for LLMs. Model grounding degrades as candidate inventories grow from 4 to 64 changes. An exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raises strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 and reduces unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, but decreases coverage by 16.0-27.1 percentage points.

Conclusion: Combining literal evidence and language-model reasoning with engineering review is recommended when intent cannot be established reliably. Strict evidence gating suppresses false positives but can remove correct semantic selections; a hybrid approach balances precision and recall.

Abstract: Aerospace electrical-design revisions can contain multiple genuine changes, although an engineering request may authorize only a subset. Propagating every detected difference can therefore produce overly broad impact reports. We present LOGIC, a controlled benchmark and evaluation framework in which locally deployable language models ground a request in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before selected changes are propagated through a typed electrical traceability graph. This separation permits candidate-selection errors to be distinguished from downstream propagation errors. LOGIC contains 168 scenarios, including 144 selection and 24 abstention cases. We evaluate three 7--8B models against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods, with an oracle-root upper bound. On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, gate-only structured evidence achieves candidate F1 of 1.0000, compared with 0.9677 for token-lexical matching. On 12 relational-paraphrase cases, token-lexical F1 is 0.1772 and gate-only F1 is 0.0000, compared with 0.5000--0.6400 for the large language models. Model grounding degrades as candidate inventories grow from 4 to 64 changes, while affected-element and typed-path accuracy remain comparatively stable when frozen selections are replayed over graphs of approximately 1K to 100K nodes. Strict evidence gating suppresses false positives but can remove correct semantic selections. An exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raises strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 for all three models and reduces unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, while decreasing answerable-case coverage by 16.0--27.1 percentage points. Four of six conflicting requests remain unsafe for each model. These findings support combining literal evidence and language-model reasoning with engineering review when intent cannot be established reliably.

</details>


### [169] [Representation Bias, Correction Transfer, and Resolution Sensitivity in Three-Dimensional Mitochondrial Morphometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07582)
*Farouk Ganiyu Adewumi,Timothy Oladunni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an empirical reliability assessment of 3D mitochondrial morphometry, identifying systematic measurement biases in quantitative imaging pipelines. Using 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library and 2,728 test objects, the study finds that occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference volumes by 3.665% despite high ICC (0.994). A controlled label-pipeline reimplementation reduces volume error by 1.57 percentage points (~45% of the inflation). Frozen regression reduces median error from 3.481% to 0.664%, but calibrated error bounds only cover 92.1% overall and 49.2% in low-occupancy subgroups. Resolution sensitivity testing shows significant changes in surface area (-10.60%) and sphericity (+11.76%) when coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative imaging pipelines can produce precise but systematically different measurements of the same object. The motivation is to provide quantitative checks for distinguishing processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences, without establishing biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

Method: The study used 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy and 2,728 previously unused objects for validation. For resolution sensitivity analysis, 550 rat-cortex objects from the MitoEM resource were used. Methods included: occupancy-derived volume measurement vs. reference mesh volumes, boundary analysis, controlled label-pipeline reimplementation (removing depth offset), frozen regression using occupancy-derived features, and testing different in-plane spacing (8 to 24 nanometers).

Result: 1. Occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average despite ICC of 0.994
2. Boundary analysis identifies outward label displacement of 0.00304 normalized units
3. Removing depth offset reduces volume error by mean of 1.57 percentage points (~45% of mean reproduced inflation)
4. Frozen regression reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664%
5. Calibrated error bound covers only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in low-occupancy subgroup
6. Coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nm changes median surface area by -10.60% and sphericity by +11.76%, despite rank correlation of 0.994

Conclusion: The results provide quantitative checks for distinguishing processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences. The study demonstrates that: (1) high correlation (ICC 0.994) does not guarantee accuracy - systematic bias exists; (2) partial correction is possible through pipeline intervention (~45% of error reduced); (3) accuracy and uncertainty transfer must be evaluated separately; (4) resolution significantly affects morphological descriptors even when rank correlation remains high. The study does not establish biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

Abstract: Quantitative imaging pipelines can produce precise but systematically different measurements of the same object. We present an empirical reliability assessment of three-dimensional mitochondrial morphometry that connects representation bias, a controlled processing intervention, correction transfer, and resolution sensitivity. Using 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy, we find that occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average despite an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.994. Boundary analysis identifies an outward label displacement of 0.00304 normalized units. In a controlled label-pipeline reimplementation, removing the depth offset reduces volume error in all 55 analyzed objects by a mean of 1.57 percentage points, approximately 45% of mean reproduced inflation; the source of the remainder is not isolated. A frozen regression using occupancy-derived features reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664% in 2,728 previously unused objects from the same resource. However, its calibrated error bound covers only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in a low-occupancy subgroup, demonstrating that accuracy and uncertainty transfer must be evaluated separately. In 550 rat-cortex objects from the MitoEM resource, coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nanometers changes median surface area by minus 10.60% and sphericity by plus 11.76%, despite a rank correlation of 0.994. These results provide quantitative checks for distinguishing processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences, without establishing biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

</details>


### [170] [Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation with Cross-Platform User History](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07588)
*Yu Xia,Jiangfan Zhang,Jun Xiao,Julian McAuley,Xiangjun Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation, where a personal LLM agent mediates platform rankings using cross-platform user history. The authors propose MediateRec benchmark and PAMO training method to balance beneficial rescues against harmful overrides when the agent has less information than the platform.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern recommendation systems are shifting from platform-centric to user-governed personalization. A key challenge is that platforms have more information than the personal agent, so mediation must balance correcting wrong recommendations (rescues) vs incorrectly overriding correct ones (harmful overrides).

Method: 1) MediateRec benchmark: scalable proxy cross-platform environments + real cross-platform test under controlled platform-agent information boundary. 2) PAMO training: counterfactually masks cross-platform history to estimate personal mediation support, then reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor.

Result: Personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, but even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently improves over matched outcome-only RL across seen/unseen platforms and on real cross-platform test, achieving better rescue-harm balance.

Conclusion: The paradigm of user-governed personalization via personal LLM agents is promising but requires careful training (like PAMO) to balance the trade-off between beneficial rescues and harmful overrides. The theoretical guarantees on advantage mass preservation provide a foundation for effective mediation.

Abstract: Modern recommendation is shifting from platform-centric personalization toward user-governed personalization, where a personal LLM agent can act on the user's behalf across services. We formalize this emerging paradigm as Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation: a platform recommender ranks a candidate set using platform-local information, and a personal agent uses user-authorized cross-platform history to mediate the resulting ranking and produce the final top-K slate. Such mediation is nontrivial: the platform ranking can encode strong population evidence that the personal agent cannot observe, so effective mediation must therefore balance beneficial rescues against harmful overrides. To study this trade-off, we introduce MediateRec, a benchmark that includes scalable proxy cross-platform environments and a real cross-platform test under a controlled platform-agent information boundary. To train the agent to use cross-platform history effectively, we further propose Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization (PAMO), which counterfactually masks that history to estimate personal mediation support and reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor. We theoretically prove that PAMO preserves cutoff-level advantage mass and is locally optimal among first-order reallocations that preserve this mass without lowering average platform-relative value. Experiments on MediateRec show that personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, yet even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently improves over matched outcome-only RL across seen and unseen target platforms and on the real cross-platform test, while achieving a better rescue-harm balance.

</details>


### [171] [LSC-DPO: Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07592)
*Yang Qu,Yusheng Han,Chengjia Feng,Handan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LSC-DPO addresses the diminishing sensitivity problem in Direct Preference Optimization by dynamically controlling the learning signal through a sigmoid-based mechanism. It uses log-space analysis for stable tracking and introduces a signal-budget compensation rule to reduce performance variation across different coefficient initializations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The DPO loss becomes progressively less sensitive to further changes as the scaled preference margin grows during training, limiting the effectiveness of continued training.

Method: 1) Loss-level geometric analysis of DPO to identify sigmoid factor as learning signal; 2) Dynamic regulation of learning signal near target regime; 3) Log-space analysis for stable tracking; 4) Signal-budget compensation rule to adjust target learning signal based on transient trajectory differences.

Result: LSC-DPO consistently improves over DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH. The compensation rule substantially reduces performance variation across coefficient initializations.

Conclusion: The learning-signal perspective provides a new understanding of DPO training dynamics. By dynamically controlling the learning signal and compensating for transient differences, LSC-DPO achieves more consistent and improved performance across different initialization settings.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a standard reward-model-free approach for aligning language models with preference data. However, as the scaled preference margin grows during training, the logistic DPO loss becomes progressively less sensitive to further changes. We study DPO from a loss-level geometric perspective and identify the sigmoid factor as a learning signal that characterizes the local sensitivity of the objective. Based on this view, we propose Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization (LSC-DPO), which dynamically regulates the learning signal near a target regime. A log-space analysis establishes conditions for stable tracking of the target learning-signal regime. Experiments on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH show that LSC-DPO consistently improves over DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines. We further find that different coefficient initializations induce distinct transient learning-signal trajectories even when their later signal levels become similar. Based on this observation, we derive a signal-budget compensation rule that adjusts the target learning signal to compensate for these transient differences. The resulting compensation substantially reduces performance variation across coefficient initializations.

</details>


### [172] [Beyond Scalar IoU: Structured Verification from Rollout Groups for Video Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07601)
*Youngjae Cho,Won Young Jhoo,Jongsuk Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SUTURE introduces a novel verification method for reinforcement learning in video temporal grounding that exploits the joint structure of rollout groups at two scales: disagreement across rollouts for target reweighting and coverage at each position for reward redistribution. It decomposes into standard IoU term plus a covariance correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing overlap verifiers in RLVR for video temporal grounding score each rollout independently, leaving the joint structure of the rollout group unused, which limits the informativeness of the verification signal.

Method: SUTURE conditions verification on the rollout group and exploits its structure at two complementary scales: (1) disagreement across rollouts controls target reweighting strength, (2) coverage at each position determines where reward mass is redistributed. The verifier admits exact decomposition into standard IoU term and a covariance correction determined by the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic identifies preferences for responses covering less supported target regions.

Result: Across five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE improves grounding performance at every reported IoU threshold. The trained policy shows less video-start anchoring in reasoning traces - for later events, the first temporal mention more often overlaps the annotated target.

Conclusion: The joint structure of a rollout group can support a more informative temporal verifier, enabling better video temporal grounding performance and more accurate reasoning traces.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a natural framework for adapting pretrained models to video temporal grounding, where generated temporal intervals can be scored directly against ground truth intervals. Yet existing overlap verifiers typically score each rollout independently, leaving the joint structure of the rollout group unused. We introduce SUTURE, which conditions verification on the rollout group and exploits its structure at two complementary scales: disagreement across rollouts controls how strongly the target is reweighted, while coverage at each position determines where reward mass is redistributed. We show that the resulting verifier admits an exact decomposition into the standard IoU term and a covariance correction determined by the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic finds a preference for responses covering relatively less supported target regions in the analyzed groups. Across five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE improves grounding performance at every reported IoU threshold. Its trained policy also shows less video-start anchoring in reasoning traces: for later events, the first temporal mention more often overlaps the annotated target. Together, these results show that the joint structure of a rollout group can support a more informative temporal verifier.

</details>


### [173] [VALSE: Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficient Inference in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07606)
*Jia-Dong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents VALSE (Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficiency), a theoretical framework and practical method for per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping in deep neural networks. The approach uses a lightweight difficulty estimator to score inputs from early layers, with per-layer gates selectively skipping redundant layers to activate only necessary depth for each sample.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to reduce computational costs during deep learning inference by dynamically adapting the network depth for each input sample. Rather than processing all layers for every input, the method aims to skip redundant layers while maintaining model performance, making inference more efficient.

Method: The paper establishes a theoretical framework through three main approaches: (i) deriving a closed-form Expected FLOPs formula (theorem 2) as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities; (ii) analyzing function-space relationships through superset (theorem 10) and strict inclusion (theorem 11) theorems with a separating example; and (iii) establishing structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (proposition 6). Practically, VALSE uses a lightweight difficulty estimator from early layers and per-layer gates to selectively skip arbitrary middle layers.

Result: The three foundational results are: (i) a closed-form Expected FLOPs formula quantifying computational cost of arbitrary per-sample skip schedules; (ii) proof that skip-layer models are strictly contained in yet meaningfully approximate the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example; and (iii) identification of structural duality between vertical depth-wise sparsity (VALSE) and horizontal width-wise sparsity (MoE). Feasibility is preliminarily assessed at prototype scale.

Conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for vertical adaptive layer skipping, positioning VALSE as the orthogonal counterpart to MoE architectures. The framework enables per-sample dynamic depth adaptation, promising computational efficiency gains while maintaining model expressiveness. Future work includes scaling the prototype and further theoretical development.

Abstract: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for vertical adaptive layer skipping, proving three foundational results: (i) an Expected FLOPs formula (theorem 2) giving a closed-form expression for the computational cost of arbitrary per-sample skip schedules as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities; (ii) function-space superset (theorem 10) and strict inclusion (theorem 11) theorems showing that skip-layer models are strictly contained in---yet meaningfully approximate---the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example; and (iii) a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (proposition 6), positioning vertical depth-wise sparsity as the orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity. Building on this theory, we propose VALSE (Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficiency), a per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping method: a lightweight difficulty estimator scores each input from the first few layers, and per-layer gates selectively skip redundant layers---including arbitrary middle layers while retaining deeper ones---so that only the necessary depth is activated for each input, whose feasibility is preliminarily assessed at prototype scale.

</details>


### [174] [BioStudyBench: Evaluating Agents on Post-Cutoff Biomedical Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07614)
*David Li,Shaamil Karim,Christian Gensbigler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BioStudyBench evaluates whether AI agents can replicate published biomedical study findings using public data. The benchmark contains 25 long-horizon analysis tasks from PubMed records, testing agents' ability to find data, search literature, and perform analysis. Access to data and tools improves pass rates by 47 percentage points, with closed-weight models (94.7%) outperforming open-weight models (81.3%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of AI agents in biomedical domains do not consistently separate analysis capabilities from prior knowledge or retrieval of published answers. There is a need to benchmark AI agents' ability to conduct genuine data-driven analysis rather than relying on training-time knowledge.

Method: BioStudyBench was constructed from 404,019 PubMed records (published July-September 2026), semi-automatically filtered to 25 long-horizon analysis tasks. Agents receive neutral research questions without data files, requiring them to find and download relevant public data, search literature through tools with pre-cutoff dates, and report findings through data analysis. Experiments compare performance with and without access to data and tools across eight models.

Result: Access to data and tools raises pass rate by 47 percentage points on average over the no-data baseline. Open-weight models across sizes trail closed-weight models, with the best open-weight model passing 81.3% of tasks versus 94.7% for the best closed-weight model.

Conclusion: AI agents can substantially benefit from access to data and tools to replicate biomedical study findings. Closed-weight models outperform open-weight models, though the gap may close with continued development. The benchmark provides a rigorous test of AI agents' genuine analytical capabilities versus prior knowledge retrieval.

Abstract: We evaluate whether AI agents can match the reported findings of published biomedical studies using public data. Existing evaluations do not consistently separate analysis from prior knowledge or retrieval of the published answer. We introduce BioStudyBench, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon analysis tasks drawn from studies first published between July and September 2026, after the developer-reported knowledge cutoffs of the models we evaluate, semi-automatically filtered down from 404,019 PubMed records. In each task, the agent receives a neutral research question but no data files, so it must find and download the relevant public data, search the literature through tools that return only records dated before its cutoff, and report findings through data analysis. To measure gains over prior knowledge, we run every task both with and without access to data and tools. Across eight models, access to data and tools raises the pass rate by 47 percentage points on average over the no-data baseline. Open-weight models across sizes trail closed-weight models, with the best open-weight model passing 81.3% of tasks against 94.7% for the best closed-weight model.

</details>


### [175] [Explore, Then Commit: Measurement-Efficient Scientific Law Discovery with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07620)
*Kautik Mandve,Dileepa Fernando*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates an "explore-then-commit" protocol for AI-driven scientific law discovery, where a large language model proposes hypotheses, a programmatic planner gathers measurements, and a prompt synthesizes the final law. Across 576 trials on 12 physics modules, the protocol with interpreter access achieves significant measurement savings (8.6 vs 22.5 for GPT-4.1-mini) and error reduction (RMSE from 2.514 to 0.202), though symbolic accuracy gains are inconsistent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific law discovery requires selecting measurements and converting evidence into governing equations. Current approaches may be inefficient in measurement acquisition. The researchers aimed to develop a measurement-efficient protocol that reduces the number of data points needed while maintaining accuracy.

Method: The study evaluated an explore-then-commit protocol combining: (1) structured probes, (2) automatic numerical diagnostics, (3) restricted measurement batches, and (4) optional interpreter access. They compared 8 configurations across 12 physics modules using GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-4.1, totaling 576 NewtonBench trials. An additional audit retained incomplete/invalid submissions for coverage-sensitive analysis.

Result: Interpreter-enabled planners showed major improvements: measurement usage dropped from 22.5 to 8.6 (GPT-4.1-mini) and 43.0 to 8.9 (GPT-4.1) on medium tasks. Mean magnitude-based RMSLE fell from 2.514 to 0.202 (GPT-4.1-mini) and 0.626 to 0.149 (GPT-4.1). Measurement savings occurred in every module, though symbolic accuracy gains were inconsistent across modules. Random acquisition performed competitively with disagreement scoring.

Conclusion: The complete protocol (with interpreter access) is a promising measurement-efficient configuration for scientific law discovery. However, causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks remain unresolved. Unequal batch constraints prevent attributing savings solely to acquisition quality.

Abstract: Scientific law discovery requires selecting measurements and converting evidence into a governing equation. We evaluate an explore-then-commit protocol in which a large language model proposes hypotheses, a programmatic planner gathers measurements, and a fresh prompt synthesizes the final law from fixed observations. The protocol combines structured probes, automatic numerical diagnostics, restricted measurement batches, and optional interpreter access. Across 576 NewtonBench trials, we compare eight configurations on 12 physics modules using GPT-4.1-mini and a medium-difficulty GPT-4.1 replication. On medium tasks, interpreter-enabled planners use 8.6 versus 22.5 measurements per trial for GPT-4.1-mini and 8.9 versus 43.0 for GPT-4.1. Their mean magnitude-based root-mean-squared logarithmic error falls from 2.514 to 0.202 and from 0.626 to 0.149, respectively. An additional audit retains incomplete and invalid submissions in a coverage-sensitive analysis. Observed symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent across modules, and random acquisition is competitive with disagreement scoring. Measurement savings occur in every module, but unequal batch constraints prevent attributing them solely to acquisition quality. These results support the complete protocol as a promising measurement-efficient configuration, while leaving its causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks unresolved.

</details>


### [176] [Learning to Outgrow a Theory: Experimental Discovery Beyond the Initial Hypothesis Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07627)
*SiYuan Ma,Albert Gao,Chunzheng Zhu,Xin Yan,Wenlong Zhang,Wenxin Zhang,Luqi Gong,Tianlin Li,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "experimental model-class revision," a method where a discovery policy jointly proposes structural edits to a hypothesis space and diagnostic experiments to test those edits. It addresses a failure mode in current scientific discovery systems where candidate disagreement collapses when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism. The method couples a class-level distinguishability objective with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current model class is rejected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scientific discovery systems optimize experiments within a fixed hypothesis space, which fails when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism. In such cases, candidate disagreement can collapse even while the model class is systematically wrong. This limitation prevents discovery systems from revising their own hypothesis spaces when needed.

Method: The method proposes a joint policy that simultaneously proposes structural edits and diagnostic experiments to test whether those edits are necessary. It couples a class-level distinguishability objective (where one shared parameterization must explain all selected experiments) with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current class is rejected.

Result: On 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the joint policy achieves 89.5% exact recovery with a budget of 32 real experiments, improving the strongest matched baseline by 10.0 percentage points while requiring fewer executed experiments and candidate fits. When the true mechanism is outside the edit grammar, it detects library insufficiency in 88% of cases with a 5.5% false-support rate. The method transfers across unseen mechanism combinations, held-out but expressible primitives, parameter extrapolation, and shifted experiment costs. Revision gains also transfer to ODEBench, ODEBase model-library tasks, and DiscoverPhysics worlds.

Conclusion: The results support treating deciding what mechanisms a theory should make expressible and where to collect evidence as a single sequential decision problem. This unified approach significantly improves scientific discovery compared to fixed hypothesis space methods, with strong transfer learning capabilities across various domains and tasks.

Abstract: Scientific discovery systems typically optimize experiments within a fixed hypothesis space. This creates a failure mode when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism: candidate disagreement can collapse even while the model class is systematically wrong. We formulate experimental model-class revision, in which a discovery policy jointly proposes a structural edit and a diagnostic experiment that tests whether that edit is necessary. The method couples a class-level distinguishability objective, in which one shared parameterization must explain all selected experiments, with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current class is rejected. On 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the joint policy reaches 89.5% exact recovery with a budget of 32 real experiments, improving the strongest matched baseline by 10.0 percentage points while requiring fewer executed experiments and candidate fits. The learned revision-experiment pairing transfers across unseen mechanism combinations, held-out but expressible primitives, parameter extrapolation, and shifted experiment costs; when the true mechanism is outside the edit grammar, it detects library insufficiency in 88% of cases with a 5.5% false-support rate. Revision gains also transfer to ODEBench and ODEBase model-library tasks, as well as DiscoverPhysics worlds. These results support a view of scientific discovery in which deciding what mechanisms a theory should make expressible and where to collect evidence are treated as a single sequential decision problem.

</details>


### [177] [Measuring climate backlash in Twitter and Reddit archives: Lexical definitions, recorded responses and participant turnover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07634)
*Wentao Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes Twitter and Reddit archives to study resistance to climate action, examining how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields, and observation boundaries shape conclusions about climate backlash. The study processes full archives without sampling and applies transparent lexical rules to link frame co-occurrence to temporal and response models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social media archives are commonly used to study resistance to climate action, but different measurement approaches (words, response counters, observed participants) may not capture the same social process. The authors aim to understand how these measurement choices affect what can be claimed about climate backlash.

Method: The study processes all registered files from four Twitter and Reddit archives without sampling, applying transparent, non-exclusive lexical rules. It links frame co-occurrence to source-specific temporal and response models, separates event-period changes among returning authors from participant turnover, and examines various lexical and author-based patterns.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Renewable-energy terms accompany cost-related language on Reddit; (2) Narrower backlash phrases reduce cross-source contrasts and reverse the Paris Agreement contrast; (3) Cross-discourse history does not improve forecasts; (4) Denial/hoax terms correlate with higher Twitter likes while Reddit responses depend on frame, outcome, and author; (5) Around the 2019 climate strike, both returning-author expression and participant turnover increased protest-language shares; (6) Archive endpoint prevents Climate Twitter migration inference; (7) Most crossed-cluster estimates lack released intervals and covariance estimates fail, restricting formal inference.

Conclusion: The contribution is an archive-based account of how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields, and observation boundaries shape claims about climate backlash—rather than measuring individual opposition, persuasion, or advocacy-induced backlash. The study highlights the methodological limitations and measurement consequences in social media research on climate politics.

Abstract: Social media archives are often used to study resistance to climate action, but words, response counters and observed participants do not measure the same social process. We examine four supplied Twitter and Reddit archives by processing all registered files without sampling and applying transparent, non-exclusive lexical rules. The study links frame co-occurrence to source-specific temporal and response models, then separates event-period changes among returning authors from participant turnover. Renewable-energy terms accompany cost-related language on Reddit, yet narrower backlash phrases sharply reduce cross-source contrasts and reverse the sign of the Paris Agreement contrast in submissions. Cross-discourse history does not improve eligible primary-context forecasts. Denial/hoax terms are associated with higher recorded Twitter likes, whereas Reddit response associations depend on frame, outcome and author specification. Around the 2019 global climate strike, returning-author expression and participant turnover both contribute to increased protest-language shares. An archive endpoint prevents the corresponding Climate Twitter migration inference. Most crossed-cluster estimates lack released intervals, and joint author/month response covariance estimates fail, restricting formal inference. These results show how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields and observation boundaries shape what can be claimed about climate backlash. The contribution is an archive-based account of these measurement consequences, rather than a measure of individual opposition, persuasion or advocacy-induced backlash.

</details>


### [178] [Learning Explainable Representations of Complex Game-playing Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07638)
*Abhijeet Krishnan,Colin M. Potts,Arnav Jhala,Harshad Khadilkar,Shirish Karande,Chris Martens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a human cognition-inspired approach for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures based on sequences of gameplay actions, demonstrated in chess and grid-based environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human players develop abstractions for game concepts and strategies to improve performance, but understanding other players' strategies requires significant time and effort. The paper aims to automate this process by training RL agents to synthesize executable strategies from gameplay data.
