Method: The authors propose a strategy similar to human cognition for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures based on sequences of gameplay actions. Methods are presented to automatically learn such programs from gameplay data for chess and grid-based environments.

Result: The learned strategies produce effective actions and can be learned from gameplay data.

Conclusion: The approach successfully demonstrates that RL agents can learn executable strategies that produce effective actions in both chess and grid-based environments, providing a human cognition-like framework for strategy synthesis.

Abstract: As part of learning to play complex games, human players develop develop abstractions for concepts and strategies of gameplay consistent with game rules to improve their performance. These concepts are applied to explain other players' actions, and to inform their own actions in-game. Understanding other players' strategies is a crucial part of such improvement, but requires time and effort. In this paper, we propose a strategy similar to human cognition for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures based on sequences of gameplay actions. We present methods to automatically learn such programs to play chess and to solve tasks in a grid-based environment. We show that the learned strategies produce effective actions, and can be learned from gameplay data.

</details>


### [179] [Towards the Automatic Synthesis of Interpretable Chess Tactics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07640)
*Abhijeet Krishnan,Chris Martens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a symbolic sub-policy model for interpreting reinforcement learning agents in chess, using domain knowledge and patterns from an inductive logic programming system called PAL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art RL agents can outperform human experts at games but their strategies are not interpretable. The authors aim to interpret these strategies to provide human players with valuable insights for improving their play.

Method: The authors propose a symbolic sub-policy model for playing chess inspired by chess tactics. They incorporate domain knowledge to improve interpretability and adapt patterns learned by an inductive logic programming system called PAL to derive their model. They also contribute a divergence metric to evaluate the model against a random baseline.

Result: The model found a set of tactics that is able to suggest moves of similar playing strength to a human beginner. The authors also proposed a computational evaluation scheme by augmenting an off-the-shelf engine with the model.

Conclusion: This is preliminary work demonstrating that symbolic, domain-knowledge-informed approaches can capture meaningful chess tactics at a beginner level. Future work could explore more sophisticated tactics and evaluation methods.

Abstract: State-of-the-art reinforcement learning agents are capable of outperforming human experts at games like chess, Go and StarCraft II. These agents do not simply take advantage of their digital hardware in being able to react and calculate faster than humans, but employ better strategies that lead to more victories. Interpreting these strategies would give human players valuable insight into how to improve their play. In this preliminary work, we propose a symbolic sub-policy model for playing chess. Inspired by chess tactics, our model attempts to incorporate domain knowledge to improve interpretability. We adapt patterns learned by an inductive logic programming system called PAL to derive our model. We contribute a divergence metric to evaluate our model against a random baseline, and find a set of tactics that is able to suggest moves of similar playing strength to a human beginner. Finally, we propose a computational evaluation scheme for the model by augmenting an off-the-shelf engine with it.

</details>


### [180] [Matching Object or Relation? Tracing Abstract Reasoning Inside VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07646)
*Gouki Minegishi,Hiroki Furuta,Takeshi Kojima,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates why Vision Language Models (VLMs) fail at abstract reasoning tasks despite performing well on visual benchmarks. Using the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm combined with mechanistic analysis, the study identifies four factors (capability tier, model scale, object count, and absence of per-object noise) that enable VLMs to achieve relational matching. The key finding is that abstract reasoning in VLMs is implemented by two competing circuits: an early circuit processing surface features and a late circuit processing abstract relations. Analysis on ARC-AGI-1 confirms the relational circuit's broader importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Language Models excel on visual benchmarks but systematically fail on tasks requiring abstract reasoning. Existing benchmarks document this failure but cannot explain why it happens or identify which cognitive capability is missing. This gap motivates the adoption of the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology, combined with mechanistic analysis of model internals to understand the underlying mechanisms of abstract reasoning in VLMs.

Method: The study uses the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm paired with mechanistic analysis. It evaluates a parametrically controlled stimulus set across frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3). Methods include: per-layer representational similarity analysis to examine how representations evolve across network layers; causal mediation analysis to identify the underlying mechanisms; and ablation experiments on ARC-AGI-1 to test whether the identified relational circuit is recruited beyond controlled stimuli.

Result: The study identifies four levers that shift VLMs toward relational matching: capability tier, model scale, number of objects per scene, and absence of per-object stimulus noise. Together these produce a developmental-like trajectory mirroring the human "relational shift." Mechanistic analysis reveals two competing circuits: an early circuit organizing images by surface object features, and a late circuit organizing them by abstract relations. Ablating relational heads on ARC-AGI-1 degrades performance more than ablating random heads, confirming the relational circuit's importance beyond the controlled stimuli.

Conclusion: VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by two competing neural circuits—an early feature-based circuit and a late relation-based circuit. The relational circuit identified through RMTS is recruited beyond the controlled stimuli, as demonstrated by its importance in ARC-AGI-1 performance. This mechanism-level view provides a foundational understanding of how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs and offers a step toward understanding the computational basis of relational cognition in artificial systems.

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel on visual benchmarks but fail systematically on tasks requiring abstract reasoning. Existing benchmarks document this failure but cannot say \emph{why} it happens or which cognitive capability is missing. We close this gap by adopting the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology and pairing it with a mechanistic analysis of the model's internals. On a parametrically controlled stimulus set evaluated across frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3), we identify four levers that shift VLMs toward the relational match---capability tier, model scale, the number of objects per scene, and the absence of per-object stimulus noise---together producing a developmental-like trajectory that mirrors the human \emph{relational shift}. Opening up the model, a per-layer representational similarity analysis and a causal mediation analysis reveal that VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by two competing circuits: an early circuit that organises images by their surface object features, and a late circuit that organises them by their abstract relation. Extending the analysis to ARC-AGI-1, we find that ablating the relational heads identified on RMTS degrades performance more than ablating random heads, indicating that the relational circuit is recruited beyond our controlled stimuli. We hope this mechanism-level view serves as a step toward understanding how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs.

</details>


### [181] [Where Rules End and Judges Begin: Measuring the Judgment Boundary in Multi-Agent Systems Security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07657)
*Shaswata Mitra,Raj Patel,Subash Neupane,Sudip Mittal,Md Rayhanur Rahman,Shahram Rahimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DEFER is a cascade-based defense system for LLM-based multi-agent systems that combines 28 deterministic checks with a panel of four judges, reducing attack success rates from ~30% to ~3% while addressing limitations of single-attack evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MAS defenses are evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, leading to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. There is a need for comprehensive defense mechanisms that can handle diverse adversarial content.

Method: The study organizes defenses into five principles and implements DEFER (DEterristic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment) as a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. Tested across four independent domains.

Result: Attack success rates dropped from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%. 78% of blocked attacks were handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain. A risk-score approval gate was found to inaccurately approve most attack proposals but few legitimate ones.

Conclusion: The rules-based approach provides security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges handle those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, particularly in accurately assessing threats, highlighting the challenges in threat assessment for MAS.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, often encountering adversarial content. Current defenses for MAS are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which can lead to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. This study organizes defenses into five principles, implementing them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment), which includes a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. In independent testing across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%, with 78% of blocked attacks handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain, illustrating that the rules provide security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges manage those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, such as a risk-score approval gate that inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, highlighting the challenges in assessing threats accurately.

</details>


### [182] [Massive Activation Gating Channel in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07661)
*Minjia Mao,Shi Chen,Bowen Yin,Xiao Fang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies a single channel (MAGC) in the input embedding that controls massive activations in LLMs. When this channel's value exceeds a threshold, the FFN output exhibits massive activations due to a quadratic form reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Massive activations are pervasive in LLMs, but the mechanism by which tokens develop these exceptionally large magnitudes as they propagate through pretrained models was poorly understood. This work aims to uncover the underlying mechanism.

Method: The authors examined six LLMs across four model families and different model sizes. They identified the Massive Activation Gating Channel (MAGC) - a fixed-position channel in the input embedding to the spike FFN - and provided theoretical analysis showing that when MAGC value is sufficiently large/small, the FFN output asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form mixing columns of the down-projection matrix.

Result: The existence and effect of MAGC was verified across all six LLMs tested. The theoretical explanation demonstrates that the columns of the down-projection matrix exhibit massive activation shapes, causing the output to exhibit massive activations when MAGC threshold is crossed.

Conclusion: Massive activations in LLMs are controlled by a single gating channel (MAGC) in the input embedding. This finding provides a clear mechanistic understanding of massive activations and could inform techniques for managing or mitigating this phenomenon in LLMs.

Abstract: Massive activations, a phenomenon in which a small number of hidden channels exhibit exceptionally large magnitudes, are pervasive in large language models (LLMs). However, the mechanism by which a token develops massive activations as it propagates through a pretrained LLM remains poorly understood. In this paper, we find that the emergence of massive activations is controlled by a single channel in the input embedding to a spike feed-forward network (FFN). The position of this channel is fixed for a particular LLM. We name this channel the massive activation gating channel (MAGC). When the value of the MAGC is sufficiently large (or small, depending on the LLM), the output of the spike FFN exhibits massive activations. Examining six LLMs across four model families and different model sizes, we verify the existence and effect of MAGC. We further provide a theoretical explanation of the mechanism by which MAGC induces massive activations. When the value of MAGC is sufficiently large (or small), the output of a spike FFN asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form that mixes a few columns of the down-projection matrix of the FFN. Since these columns exhibit the shape of massive activations, the output therefore exhibits massive activations.

</details>


### [183] [EIO-Agents: The Missing Semantic Layer for AI Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07675)
*Fouad Bousetouane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EIO-Agents is an open specification for AI agent evaluation that addresses the lack of semantic standards in current evaluation practices. It consists of two layers: the Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) providing semantic structure through typed evidence, claims, and decision rules, and the Portable Evaluation Record (PER) preserving the complete evidence-to-decision chain as a verifiable artifact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents are being deployed in critical environments without a shared semantic standard for evaluation. Current methods (scores, traces, judge outputs, jury findings) lack specifications for what evidence supports claims, what claims can establish, or how claims lead to decisions. This creates accountability gaps in readiness and release decisions.

Method: The authors introduce a two-layer specification: (1) EIO - a semantic ontology with typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and decisions (PASS/REVIEW/BLOCK); (2) PER - a canonical, content-addressed representation preserving the evidence-to-decision chain that can be re-derived, explained, and verified.

Result: The specification provides a semantic contract that defines what evidence means and what it can prove, complementing scores (which summarize), juries (which interpret), and traces (which record). The PER serves as a portable and verifiable system of record for evaluations.

Conclusion: As AI agents assume greater operational responsibility, evaluation must become an accountable artifact whose meaning, evidence, limitations, and decisions can be independently checked. EIO-Agents transforms evaluation from a collection of scores and verdicts into a verifiable, auditable record.

Abstract: AI agents are entering production in increasingly consequential environments without a shared semantic standard for what their evaluations actually mean. Scores, traces, judge outputs, and multi juror findings are increasingly used to justify readiness and release decisions, yet they often do not specify what evidence supports a claim, what that evidence can establish, or how the claim leads to a decision. We introduce EIO-Agents, an open specification for interoperable AI agent evaluation built on two layers. The Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) provides the semantic layer through typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and PASS, REVIEW, or BLOCK decisions. The Portable Evaluation Record (PER) provides the system of record: a canonical, content addressed representation of one evaluation that preserves the evidence to decision chain and can be re derived, explained, and verified. Scores summarize, juries interpret, and traces record, but none of them define what the evidence means or what it can prove. EIO provides that missing semantic contract, while PER preserves the resulting evaluation as a portable and verifiable system of record. As AI agents assume greater operational responsibility, evaluation must become more than a collection of scores and verdicts; it must become an accountable artifact whose meaning, evidence, limitations, and decisions can be independently checked.

</details>


### [184] [BluffJAX: Adversarial Imperfect Information Games in JAX](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07686)
*Aryaman Reddi,Jan Peters,Carlo D'Eramo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BluffJAX is an open-source suite of adversarial imperfect information games implemented in JAX, featuring canonical implementations of games like Texas Hold'Em Poker, Kuhn Poker, Bluff, Stud Poker, and Kemps, designed for high simulation throughput and GPU parallelization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to address the lack of diverse, high-performance game environments for studying game-theoretic methods in reinforcement learning, particularly for imperfect information games that present unique challenges.

Method: The authors implemented games in JAX to leverage GPU acceleration and parallelization, creating canonical implementations of various poker variants and lesser-known games, while benchmarking RL, tree search, and game-solving algorithms.

Result: BluffJAX achieves scaling of up to hundreds of millions of samples per second in single and multi-GPU settings, demonstrating superior throughput and memory efficiency compared to existing CPU and GPU-based libraries.

Conclusion: The suite provides a valuable benchmark platform for future research in game-theoretic RL methods, with the variety of game mechanics and difficulties intended to foster novel research directions.

Abstract: We introduce BluffJAX: an open-source suite of adversarial imperfect information games in JAX. We provide canonical implementations of games designed for high simulation throughputs and parallelization on GPU accelerators. Our suite consists of well-studied benchmarks such as Texas Hold'Em Poker and Kuhn Poker, as well as games that have not been previously studied in reinforcement learning research, such as Bluff, Stud Poker, and Kemps. We hope that implementing a variety of game mechanics and difficulties will introduce new challenges and foster novel research directions in game-theoretic methods for RL. We benchmark the throughput performance and memory usage of our environments in single and multi-GPU settings, demonstrating scaling of up to hundreds of millions of samples per second, and motivating the usage of BluffJAX over related GPU and CPU-based libraries. We benchmark reinforcement learning, tree search, and game-solving algorithms in JAX in order to provide users with baseline results and facilitate future comparisons.

</details>


### [185] [On the Boundary of Admission Gates: An Injected-Truth Study of Falsification-First Selection in Quantitative Strategy Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07701)
*Tianlun Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in strategy research: distinguishing genuine profitable rules from statistical flukes (search luck). The authors propose using "admission gates" - statistical criteria that must be met before accepting a strategy as valid. They introduce an injected-truth protocol to test whether these gates actually work. The key findings are that while gates can eliminate false discoveries in weak-signal environments, they also drastically reduce adoption rates (to 1-7%), and critically, using absolute returns rather than excess returns causes gates to reject all candidates, including true signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the replication crisis in quantitative finance/strategy research. The authors identify that strategy research conflates two distinct problems: (1) finding a profitable rule, and (2) demonstrating that the finding is not due to search luck. Despite the widespread use of statistical gates (thresholds) to filter strategies, there has been no rigorous testing of whether these gates actually work or what their costs are.

Method: The authors introduce an "injected-truth protocol" with a random-admission control. This approach adopts strategies at the same rate as the gate being tested. Only if the gate outperforms this random control does it carry actual information (rather than merely raising a threshold). They test this across synthetic and real-calibrated panels.

Result: Three key results: (1) In the weak-signal regime, gates eliminate false discoveries but reduce adoption to only 1-7%; (2) When signals are strong, gates add no value; (3) Most critically, criteria computed on absolute returns (rather than excess returns relative to a benchmark) silently reject every candidate, including true signals - a potentially fatal flaw in common practice.

Conclusion: The conclusion suggests that admission gates, as commonly implemented, may be overly conservative or fundamentally flawed. The finding that absolute return criteria reject all candidates (including true signals) is particularly concerning, as it suggests current practices in strategy validation may be systematically dismissing valid strategies. The paper implies that more careful consideration of what constitutes meaningful statistical evidence in strategy research is needed.

Abstract: Strategy research conflates two problems: finding a profitable rule, and establishing that the finding is not search luck. The latter calls for admission gates -- statistical criteria that must be satisfied before a conclusion is adopted -- yet whether gates work, and at what cost, remains untested. We introduce an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control that adopts at the same rate as the gate; only if the gate beats this control does it carry information rather than merely raise a threshold. Across synthetic and real-calibrated panels, gates eliminate false discoveries in the weak-signal regime but cut adoption to 1--7%, and add nothing when signals are strong. Most importantly, criteria computed on absolute rather than excess returns silently reject every candidate, including true signals. Keywords: multiple testing, backtest overfitting, strategy admission, injected-truth validation, excess returns, false discovery rate

</details>


### [186] [AgentMemGate: Addressing Speculation Contamination in Conversational Assistant Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07707)
*Chirag Sharma,Benjamin Fowlersmith,Karime Maamari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses "speculation contamination" in conversational AI assistants with long-term memory, where stated plans (e.g., "I might move to Seattle") are incorrectly recorded as facts. The authors propose AgentMemGate, a write-time gate that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other, preventing speculations from entering memory until verified.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory benchmarks fail to detect speculation contamination because they don't probe intermediate memory state and include few unresolved speculations. This is a practical problem: users mentioning future plans get recorded as current facts, leading to incorrect system behavior in subsequent conversations.

Method: The authors propose AgentMemGate, a write-time gate mechanism for profile-store memory. It classifies extracted statements into four categories: speculation, completed event, correction, or other. Speculations are kept outside memory with governing conditions for later promotion or deletion. They also create a dataset of multi-session conversations where plans are confirmed, abandoned, or left unresolved.

Result: On a 147-conversation held-out set, Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination (87.5% to zero) and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the harder held-out set, gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% and task accuracy rises by 9 to 13 percentage points. Field matching is identified as the main remaining bottleneck.

Conclusion: AgentMemGate effectively eliminates speculation contamination in conversational AI memory systems. The key insight is that classifying statements at write-time prevents false facts from entering memory. The main remaining challenge is field matching - realistic speculations often don't match any profile field and never reach the gate for classification.

Abstract: Conversational AI assistants with long-term memory extract facts from user messages into a store consulted in later conversations. A stated plan can enter that store as fact: a user who might move to Seattle may be recorded as already living there. We call this speculation contamination. Final-state memory benchmarks miss this error because they do not probe intermediate state and include few unresolved speculations. We present AgentMemGate, a write-time gate for profile-store memory that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other. Speculations remain outside memory, with conditions governing later promotion or deletion. We also contribute a dataset of multi-session conversations in which plans are confirmed, abandoned, or left unresolved. On our 147-conversation held-out set, Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination relative to the identical ungated pipeline (87.5% to zero for the most exposed extraction style) and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the harder held-out set, gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% and task accuracy rises by 9 to 13 percentage points. Our analysis identifies field matching as the main remaining bottleneck: realistic speculations often match no profile field and never reach the gate. We release our datasets, prompts, and evaluation code.

</details>


### [187] [Evidence Before Sampling: Interpretable Implicit Negative Candidate Discovery for Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07708)
*Shreya Rajpal,Sonia Sharma,Swapnil Parekh,Lisa Li,Jeyendran Balakrishnan,Nagaraj Janardhana,Andrew Mattarella-Micke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes "implicit negative candidate discovery" - a method to identify high-quality negative samples in recommender systems by encoding observed customer behavior patterns as symbolic rules, scoring them, and using LLM to interpret rules aligned with business objectives. The method improves negative sample quality in industrial B2B and public datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In recommender systems, explicit negative feedback is often unavailable. Traditional negative sampling treats all unobserved interactions as negatives, but missing interactions don't explain why users are uninterested. This is especially problematic in business recommendation where negative signals should be interpretable and aligned with business objectives.

Method: 1) Formulate implicit negative candidate discovery to identify unobserved interactions supported by observed customer behavior. 2) Encode behavioral patterns as symbolic rules. 3) Score rules based on support, informativeness, and product relevance. 4) Rank retained rules by evidence. 5) Use LLM to interpret retained rules using business objectives and domain knowledge. 6) Combine interpretations with statistical evidence in final report.

Result: In industrial B2B setting and 5 public datasets: Candidate-quality evaluations show higher precision than baselines. Symbolic selection improves downstream test PR-AUC by 12.5% over random selection with 4 negatives per positive. Negative candidate validity can be evaluated separately from downstream recommendation performance.

Conclusion: The proposed method enables evidence-based, business-aligned, and explainable negative selection, improving both interpretability and model training in sparse, skewed, real-world recommendation settings. The distinction between candidate validity and downstream performance enables more effective negative sample selection.

Abstract: Recommender systems learn from observed user-item interactions, but explicit negative feedback is often unavailable. Since deep learning models require negative signals for training, negative sampling methods typically treat selected unobserved interactions as negatives. However, a missing interaction does not explain why a user is uninterested in an item or whether there is sufficient evidence to label it negative. This is especially important in business recommendation, where negative signals should be interpretable and aligned with business objectives. We formulate implicit negative candidate discovery to identify unobserved interactions supported by observed customer behavior. We encode these patterns as symbolic rules, score them based on support, informativeness, and product relevance, and rank the retained rules by evidence. An LLM then interprets the retained rules using business objectives and domain knowledge; the interpretations are combined with the statistical evidence in the final report. We evaluate our method in an industrial B2B setting and across five public recommendation datasets. Candidate-quality evaluations in the industrial setting and three public datasets show higher precision than the evaluated baselines, while symbolic selection improves downstream test PR-AUC by 12.5% over random selection with four negatives per positive example in the industrial task. Our results show that negative candidate validity can be evaluated separately from downstream recommendation performance. This distinction enables evidence-based, business-aligned, and explainable negative selection, improving both interpretability and model training in sparse, skewed, real-world recommendation settings.

</details>


### [188] [PERSIST: Who-What-When Memory Across Sessions for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07725)
*Achira Lin,Siyuan Hou,Wenyi Yu,Xinnian Zhao,Haoyu Niu,Wang Geng,Longshuai Xiao,Shihai Xiao,Mangsuo Zhao,Chao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PERSIST is a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When to enable voice assistants to answer questions about earlier conversations and adapt to individual users based on past interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern voice assistants are often shared by multiple users and need to answer questions about earlier conversations (e.g., "When did I originally plan to leave?") or adapt behavior based on past interactions. This requires identifying the current speaker, recovering relevant past state, and distinguishing it from later revisions - capabilities beyond simple topical retrieval.

Method: PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism combining semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time interaction, it reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone to avoid query-audio re-encoding. The authors also introduce SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types.

Result: PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy on SpokenTrace and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% (with BGE-large) to 82.10%. Retrieval latency is reduced from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms.

Conclusion: The 3W joint scoring mechanism effectively combines semantic content, speaker identity, and temporal state for persistent memory in multi-speaker dialogue systems. The optimization for real-time interaction makes the system practical for full-duplex interaction. SpokenTrace provides a useful diagnostic benchmark for evaluating memory, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking capabilities.

Abstract: Modern voice assistants may be shared by multiple users and should be able to answer questions about earlier conversations such as "When did I originally plan to leave?" or adapt their behavior to individual users based on past interactions. This requires more than retrieving a topically similar passage: the assistant must identify the current speaker, recover the relevant past state, and distinguish it from later revisions. We present PERSIST, a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When. PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism that combines semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time full-duplex interaction, PERSIST further reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone, avoiding query-audio re-encoding and reducing retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms. We also introduce SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking. On SpokenTrace, PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% with BGE-large to 82.10%.

</details>


### [189] [How Well Do LLMs Reason with Noisy Evidence? An Active Visual Reasoning Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07751)
*Bach Nguyen,Zhaonan Li,Mau Son Nguyen,Sanika Chavan,Nilay Kumar,Hong Anh Nguyen,Khoa Vo,Ben Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VisualNoiseQA is a benchmark for evaluating active reasoning in LLMs under noisy visual feedback, where a text-only LLM must query a stochastic VLM sensor and use self-consistency-based uncertainty signals to decide what to ask and when to stop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing active reasoning benchmarks assume trustworthy environmental feedback or introduce noise without calibrated uncertainty signals. This leaves open how LLMs should reason when evidence itself is uncertain. Real-world agents must gather information from noisy, unreliable tools and sensors.

Method: 1) Build a text-only LLM reasoner that iteratively queries an off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor
2) Draw multiple samples per query and expose empirical uncertainty via self-consistency
3) Enable the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide next actions and termination
4) Automatically construct by starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, retaining only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable

Result: Evaluated multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning.

Conclusion: VisualNoiseQA provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning under noisy visual feedback.

Abstract: Real-world reasoning rarely reduces to static question answering: agents must actively gather information from tools and sensors that are often noisy and unreliable. Yet most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume that environmental feedback is trustworthy, or introduce noise without exposing an explicit, calibrated uncertainty signal, leaving open how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. We introduce VisualNoiseQA, a novel benchmark for active reasoning under noisy visual feedback. A text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, we draw multiple samples and expose an empirical uncertainty signal via self-consistency, enabling the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. Our construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, we retain only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable. We evaluate multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. VisualNoiseQA thus provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning.

</details>


### [190] [ST-Bench: A Spatial-Temporal Benchmark for Multi-Agent System Generation on Scientific Research Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07763)
*Qi Cheng,Rongchao Dong,Shengyu Chen,Licheng Liu,Dan Lu,Zhengzhang Chen,Wei Cheng,Yiqun Xie,Haifeng Chen,Xiaowei Jia,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ST-Bench evaluates whether LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) outperform single agents on scientific data analysis tasks. Testing 5 MAS methods against single-agent baselines on 100 Earth science tasks (2,067 queries), 9/10 MAS configurations exceed the single-agent baseline, with the strongest achieving nearly 3x the composite score. The advantage comes primarily from coverage (more queries producing realistic outputs) rather than quality improvement. Best MAS requires ~4x inference time, but a more economical version captures most benefit at <2x cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid progress of LLM-based MAS has shown advantages over single agents on coding, math, and QA tasks with binary success signals. However, it was unknown whether this advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis, which is more complex and requires nuanced evaluation. This study addresses that gap.

Method: ST-Bench benchmark: 100 data science tasks from published Earth science studies (hydrology, agriculture, wetland methane), expanded to 2,067 queries grounded in additional published studies, validated by domain experts. Evaluated 5 MAS generation methods under 2 training protocols against single-agent baselines using the same GPT-5 backbone.

Result: 9 of 10 MAS configurations exceed the cheapest single-agent baseline. Strongest MAS achieves nearly 3x composite score. The gain is primarily from coverage (producing realistic numerical metrics on larger fraction of queries), while quality conditional on realistic output is comparable to single-agent. Strongest configuration requires ~4x inference time; economical workflow captures majority of benefit at <2x cost.

Conclusion: MAS specialization confers measurable benefit on scientific data analysis, but the benefit is conditional rather than universal. The advantage stems from increased coverage rather than improved output quality, suggesting MAS are better at attempting more queries successfully rather than producing higher-quality results on the same queries.

Abstract: The rapid progress of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) has shown that they largely outperform single agents on coding, math, and QA tasks, where executable tests provide a binary success signal. Whether this advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis remains untested. We introduce ST-Bench, a benchmark designed to answer two questions: whether MAS outperform single agents on complex scientific data analysis tasks, and if so, by how much and at what additional cost. ST-Bench contains 100 data science tasks adapted from published Earth science studies across hydrology, agriculture, and wetland methane research, expanded into 2,067 queries grounded in additional published studies and validated by domain experts. Using ST-Bench, we evaluate five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols, against single-agent baselines on the same GPT-5 backbone. Nine of the ten MAS configurations exceed the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. This gain is primarily attributable to coverage: trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries, while the quality of those metrics, conditional on producing realistic output, is comparable to that of the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration requires approximately four times the single-agent inference time, whereas a more economical workflow captures the majority of the benefit at less than twice the cost. MAS specialization confers measurable benefit on scientific data analysis, but the benefit is conditional rather than universal.

</details>


### [191] [OTel: Open Telco AI Datasets, Benchmarks, and Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07766)
*Farbod Tavakkoli,Gregory Diamos,Kenneth Church,David Kanter,Mark Austin,Imtiaz Karim,Mirza Masfiqur Rahman,Merouane Abdelkader Debbah,Zeinab Nezami,Ali Maatouk,Leandros Tassiulas,Rex Ying,Nick Sorros,Louis Powell,Nikolaos Vasiloglou,Ashish Vaswani,Somanshu Singla,Adarsh Chaluvaraju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource that releases derived telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, together with 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines spanning 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. Each baseline starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

</details>


### [192] [Quantization Effects on Tool-Failure Recovery Vary Across Prompts and Evaluation Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07781)
*Yuhe Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Post-training quantization's effect on language model agent robustness is highly sensitive to evaluation methodology. One prompt, one task set, and one scoring policy cannot establish stable conclusions about 8-bit vs 4-bit quantized agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training quantization reduces deployment costs for language model agents, but its effect on recovery from temporary tool failures remains unclear. The authors investigate whether evaluation methodology choices (prompts, task selection, scoring policy) can reverse conclusions about quantized agent robustness.

Method: Compared 8-bit and 4-bit variants of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on twenty deterministic tool-use tasks and five prompts. Tested recovery from temporary tool failures under different evaluation targets, scoring policies (lenient vs strict output parsing), and task selection criteria.

Result: The 8-bit vs 4-bit recovery comparison reverses across prompts and evaluation targets. For Llama: differences range from 0 to +20.2 percentage points. For Qwen: range from -50.0 to +35.0 points. Full-pipeline estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, but Qwen results change direction across prompts. Evaluation target choice can reverse results: under one prompt, scoring only clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points; scoring same tasks for both gives no difference; scoring full pipeline favors 8-bit by 28.3 points. Strict output parsing (which 8-bit Llama violates far more often) turns +28.3 into -15.0 for Llama while leaving Qwen unchanged.

Conclusion: Evaluations should: (1) compare variants on matched tasks, (2) report full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, (3) state scoring policies explicitly, and (4) quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites. A single evaluation configuration cannot establish stable conclusions about quantized-agent robustness.

Abstract: Post-training quantization reduces the cost of deploying language-model agents, but its effect on recovery from temporary tool failures can depend on how recovery is evaluated. We compare 8-bit and 4-bit variants of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on twenty deterministic tool-use tasks and five prompts. The 8-bit-4-bit recovery comparison changes direction across prompts and evaluation targets. On tasks that both variants complete without faults under the same prompt, the difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points for Llama and from -50.0 to +35.0 points for Qwen. Full-pipeline point estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, whereas the Qwen comparison changes direction across prompts. The evaluation target can also reverse the result. For Llama under one prompt, scoring each variant only on its own clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points; scoring the same tasks for both variants gives no difference, while scoring the full pipeline favors 8-bit by 28.3 points. Executor leniency is a third such choice. Rescoring the same logs with strict output parsing, which 8-bit Llama violates far more often than 4-bit Llama under that prompt, turns that +28.3 into -15.0 while leaving Qwen essentially unchanged. These findings show that one prompt, one screened task set, and one scoring policy do not establish a stable conclusion about quantized-agent robustness. Evaluations should compare variants on matched tasks, report full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, state the scoring policy, and quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites.

</details>


### [193] [Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference: What It Costs, What It Buys, and When You Can Tell](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07782)
*Hochan Son,Kyungdoe Han,Jaehan Koh,Xiaowu Dai,Wenlu Xu,Guang Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates a three-tier agent architecture for long-context inference, comparing decomposition (splitting inference across cooperating agents) against single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. The key findings show decomposition reduces peak KV cache memory (14.3 MiB vs 35.5 MiB), but the persistent memory tier provides no accuracy benefit across eight controlled experiments (n=100 each), with a null result the authors argue is structural due to how single-question benchmarks evaluate memory recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to measure whether a persistent memory tier (storing and recalling reasoning traces) actually improves accuracy in agent systems, as many papers report ablations showing accuracy gains from such tiers but lack rigorous measurement of both memory costs and accuracy effects.

Method: The authors used a three-tier agent architecture and measured both peak KV cache memory and accuracy across eight controlled dataset pairs (n=100 per arm). They identified four measurement corrections needed: three that inflated apparent benefits and one that made a null effect appear resolvable.

Result: Decomposition reduced peak KV working set to 14.3 MiB per query versus 35.5 MiB (single-pass) and 35.3 MiB (retrieval-augmented). The persistent tier showed no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]) but cost +0.368 MiB [+0.167, +0.590] of peak cache.

Conclusion: The null result for the persistent tier is structural: single-question benchmarks provide each item with its own evidence and score independently, requiring resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. The paper provides conditions an agent-memory ablation must satisfy and detection procedures that need no knowledge of specific defects.

Abstract: Decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents bounds the active KV cache per call rather than total evidence, which matters when KV-cache memory binds. Many such systems add a persistent tier storing and recalling reasoning traces, usually validated by an ablation reporting an accuracy gain. We measure both on one three-tier agent architecture. Decomposition delivers: peak KV working set of 14.3 MiB per query against 35.5 and 35.3 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. The persistent tier does not: across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm it costs +0.368 MiB [+0.167, +0.590] of peak cache and produces no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]). We argue the null is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. Reaching it took four measurement corrections -- three inflating the apparent benefit, the fourth making an effect that size look resolvable -- none visible in the results table. We give the conditions an agent-memory ablation must satisfy and detection procedures that need no knowledge of the specific defect.

</details>


### [194] [Attacca: Goal-Directed Control under State Continuity for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07785)
*Gyusik Seo,Jaehong Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Attacca addresses the challenge of visual goal-conditioned policies in continuous long-horizon embodied tasks where targets may not be visible. The method trains policies on complete search-to-interact trajectories using context-decoupled goal sampling, dense current-view grounding via target-mask prediction, and behavioral-phase conditioning to distinguish Search, Approach, and Interact stages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual goal-conditioned policies are evaluated on isolated interactions where targets are visible, but fail in continuous long-horizon execution where targets may be outside the field of view, the agent's position changes, and the world may be modified by previous tasks.

Method: Attacca uses three key techniques: (1) Context-decoupled goal sampling to pair demonstrations with class-compatible masked goal images from different worlds, removing direct scene/pose correspondence; (2) Target-mask prediction head for dense current-view grounding providing auxiliary supervision beyond action imitation; (3) Behavioral-phase conditioning that teaches the policy to distinguish Search, Approach, and Interact stages and adapt control accordingly.

Result: Attacca achieves 39.0-47.5% clean success, improving 1.7-2.4x over the strongest baseline. On long-horizon tasks, it attains 54%, 30%, and 28% completion, yielding up to 7x improvement.

Conclusion: Attacca significantly advances visual goal-conditioned policies for embodied agents in long-horizon tasks, demonstrating substantial improvements over baselines through context-decoupled training, dense grounding, and behavioral-phase conditioning.

Abstract: A central capability of embodied agents is to accomplish complex objectives through sequences of interdependent tasks. Yet existing visual goal-conditioned policies underlying these agents are typically evaluated on isolated interactions where the target is already visible, and thus do not capture the conditions that arise during continuous long-horizon task execution. In such settings, each task begins from the state left by the previous one: the agent may end at a different position and orientation, the world may have been modified, and the next interaction target may lie outside the current field of view. As a result, agents relying on such policies may struggle to proceed to the next task when they cannot ground their target in the current observation. To address this challenge, we propose Attacca, a new approach that trains visual goal-conditioned policies on complete search-to-interact trajectories using goal images decoupled from the execution environment. Attacca uses context-decoupled goal sampling to pair each demonstration with a class-compatible masked goal image from another world, removing direct scene and pose correspondence. It learns dense current-view grounding through a target-mask prediction head, providing auxiliary supervision beyond action imitation. We further introduce behavioral-phase conditioning that teaches the policy to distinguish Search, Approach, and Interact stages and adapt its control as execution progresses. We evaluate Attacca on multiple short- and long-horizon embodied tasks in Minecraft. Our method achieves 39.0-47.5% clean success, improving over the strongest baseline by 1.7-2.4x. On long-horizon tasks, it attains 54%, 30%, and 28% completion, yielding up to a 7x improvement.

</details>


### [195] [OOPMAS: Object-Oriented Multi-Agent Systems for Query-Level Workflow Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07787)
*Qi Cheng,Shengyu Chen,Wei Cheng,Yiqun Xie,Xiaowei Jia,Haoyu Wang,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OOPMAS is a training-free framework that generates agent sets and coordination workflows at the individual query level, using object-oriented class definitions for agents and a dynamic skill library for in-context improvement without fine-tuning. It achieves 89.6% accuracy on a mixed-task benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MAS design methods operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow applied uniformly to all queries. This fails under realistic conditions because query difficulty varies within tasks, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. There is a need for query-level granularity in MAS design.

Method: OOPMAS uses object-oriented class definitions to represent agents with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state. Workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without gradient updates or fine-tuning.

Result: On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.

Conclusion: OOPMAS demonstrates that query-level granularity in MAS design significantly improves performance across heterogeneous tasks. The training-free approach with dynamic skill library enables in-context improvement without fine-tuning, and the framework scales consistently across different LLM backbones.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown strong performance across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering. However, existing methods for automating MAS design mostly operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow per benchmark that is applied uniformly to all queries. This assumption fails under realistic conditions. Query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. We introduce OOPMAS, a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, and workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.

</details>


### [196] [Illusory Pattern Perception Drives Spurious Inference in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07791)
*Peihua Mai,Zhuoyan Shao,Xinbao Qiao,Meng Zhang,Xinyue Zhou,Yan Pang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in Large Language Models (LLMs), finding that LLMs exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans, including over-associating positive attributes with majority groups and constructing causal narratives from ambiguous events. The mechanism is analyzed using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), revealing that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation drive these illusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Illusory pattern perception is a well-documented human cognitive tendency to infer meaningful relationships in random data, leading to reasoning errors. However, whether LLMs exhibit such perceptual tendencies and their underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, which is critical for understanding LLM reliability.

Method: The study adapts classic psychological paradigms to three tasks with direct empirical comparison to human behaviors. A feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) is developed to analyze internal representations and uncover the mechanism behind these behaviors.

Result: LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. Models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and show increased tendencies to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. Holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to the emergence of illusory perceptions.

Conclusion: These findings highlight a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning, emphasizing the need to address this issue in LLM development and deployment.

Abstract: Illusory pattern perception is a well-documented human cognitive tendency to infer meaningful relationships in data that is actually random. Such a tendency, often described as "connecting the dots" where none exist, can result in systematic reasoning errors. This paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit such perceptual tendencies, which can lead to systematic errors in downstream applications. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in LLMs, adapting classic psychological paradigms to three tasks with direct empirical comparison to human behaviors. We find that LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. In particular, models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and show increased tendencies to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. To uncover the mechanism behind these behaviors, we develop a feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to analyze internal representations. Our results reveal that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to the emergence of illusory perceptions. These findings highlight a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning. Code available at https://github.com/NusIoraPrivacy/illusory.

</details>


### [197] [Thin Evidence, Thick Priors: How Language Models Substitute Identity for Missing Financial Facts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07798)
*Saanvi Khetan,Sankar Balasubramanian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how large language models fill in missing financial information when giving investment advice, testing how identity factors (gender, household size, etc.) influence recommendations when users provide varying levels of financial detail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People increasingly consult LLMs for financial advice but rarely provide complete financial information. This creates a "gap" that the model must fill with assumptions, and the paper seeks to understand how identity factors influence the advice when financial evidence is withheld.

Method: Experimental design using 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, varying 100 financial profiles, 138 personas, and 7 disclosure conditions (from 8 facts to none). Measured equity allocation recommendations and analyzed statistical significance with cluster bootstrapping.

Result: The gap between personas with identical finances rises from 4.78 to 10.34 percentage points as financial facts are removed. Identity explains 5% of variation at full disclosure vs 96% with no disclosure. Household size is the only attribute whose influence grows reliably. The model invents financial details (incomes, debts, savings) when not provided, more often unfavorably for larger households. Gender appears as a small standing gap not closed by full disclosure.

Conclusion: Advisory systems built on LLMs should be audited at the disclosure levels users actually reach and judged across the whole identity space rather than one attribute at a time. The model compensates for missing information by inferring identity-based patterns, which can introduce bias.

Abstract: People increasingly ask large language models what to do with their money, yet seldom describe their finances in full. This paper asks what a model does with the gap. Holding finances fixed and changing only who the investor is said to be, we grade the financial evidence in the prompt from eight facts to none and measure how far the recommended equity allocation moves. Across 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, built from 100 financial profiles, 138 personas and seven disclosure conditions, the average gap between two personas with identical finances rises from 4.78 percentage points at full disclosure to 10.34 points with no financial facts. A two-way cluster bootstrap counting duplicated prompts once places the ratio at 2.16 (95% interval 1.69 to 2.79), and the rise is already 1.69-fold with a single fact left. Identity explains 5% of within-profile variation in advice at full disclosure and 96% with no disclosure. Household size is the only attribute whose influence grows reliably as evidence is withdrawn. Once standard errors are clustered on the persona, the unit to which identity was assigned, most attribute-specific interactions reported in the conference version lose significance, and gender instead appears as a small standing gap that full disclosure does not close. Stating risk appetite alone brings the swing into the range seen with two to seven generic facts. With no facts, the model's one-line rationale cites incomes, debts and savings it was never told, and these invented finances turn adverse more often for larger households. Inside the network, gender is linearly decodable at every layer, and ablating the gender direction at five layers leaves the aggregate identity swing unchanged. Advisory systems built on such models should be audited at the disclosure levels users actually reach, and judged across the whole identity space rather than one attribute at a time.

</details>


### [198] [ThinkFuse: Trajectory-Aware Test-Time Fusion for Small Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07803)
*Myunghoon Kang,Jungseob Lee,Jaehyung Seo,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ThinkFuse is a training-free test-time fusion framework that identifies unstable reasoning segments in small reasoning models by comparing segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level trends, and selectively intervenes by fusing auxiliary reasoning paths to recover from erroneous reasoning paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small reasoning models (SRMs) often fail to recover once their reasoning enters an erroneous path. Existing test-time fusion methods rely on local fusion signals that can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations and may reinforce unstable reasoning trajectories.

Method: ThinkFuse compares segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level uncertainty trends to identify unstable reasoning points, then fuses auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory for selective intervention.

Result: ThinkFuse outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks with consistent gains across model-family combinations. It remains robust with a smaller primary model, requires fewer fusion triggers, and generates fewer tokens.

Conclusion: ThinkFuse provides an efficient training-free solution for improving reasoning reliability in SRMs through selective intervention, balancing performance gains with computational efficiency.

Abstract: Small reasoning models (SRMs) have shown strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by generating extended chain-of-thought trajectories, but they often fail to recover once their reasoning enters an erroneous path. Existing test-time fusion methods rely on local fusion signals to determine when to trigger fusion, which can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations and may reinforce unstable reasoning trajectories. We propose ThinkFuse, a training-free test-time fusion framework that selectively intervenes in unreliable reasoning segments. ThinkFuse compares segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level uncertainty trends to identify unstable reasoning points and fuse auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ThinkFuse outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains across model-family combinations, and remains robust with a smaller primary model. Our analysis shows that ThinkFuse requires fewer fusion triggers and generates fewer tokens, highlighting the efficiency of selective triggering. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ThinkFuse.

</details>


### [199] [Do I Need the Cloud? Uncertainty-Aware Step-Level Handoff for Small Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07816)
*Abolfazl Younesi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEPGATE is an uncertainty-aware handoff framework for local small language models (SLMs) that selectively escalates challenging agent steps to stronger models. It scores each local SLM action and decides whether to escalate, achieving 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation on single-step tasks, and 69.0% trajectory success with only 30.0% cloud actions on multi-turn tasks, significantly outperforming local-only and random escalation baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models are attractive for local agent controllers due to reduced latency and deployment footprint, but structured tool errors can cause failures. Existing routers select a model once per query, while agents have sequential decision points whose difficulty dynamically changes based on intermediate observations. This work aims to bridge the performance gap between local SLMs and stronger cloud models at matched cloud-action rates.

Method: STEPGATE uses an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each local SLM action and selectively escalates challenging steps to a stronger model (Qwen2.5-7B). The framework was evaluated on a 52-task held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split and a separate multi-turn evaluation, comparing against local-only, random escalation, query-level routing, and strong-only baselines.

Result: On single-step tasks, Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B pair achieves 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation vs 67.3% local-only and 75.4% random escalation (33.8%). On multi-turn tasks, STEPGATE achieves 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing. Strong-only achieves 82.0% at 100% cloud actions.

Conclusion: Step-level escalation recovers a large performance gap to the stronger Qwen2.5-7B backend at matched cloud-action rates while transmitting fewer tokens remotely. Limitations include evaluation on one model family, single stronger backend, scripted tasks, small test sets, and risk tiers serving as research annotations rather than formal safety guarantees.

Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are attractive as local agent controllers because they reduce remote inference, latency, and deployment footprint, yet structured tool errors can cause an agent step to fail. Existing routers typically select a model once per query. However, agents expose sequential decision points whose difficulty dynamically changes based on intermediate observations. We propose STEPGATE, an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each local SLM action and selectively escalates challenging steps to a stronger model. On a 52-task held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split, the Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B pair attains 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation, versus 67.3% local-only and 75.4% random escalation (which uses 33.8% escalation). In a separate multi-turn evaluation, STEPGATE achieves 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing (strong-only achieves 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions). These results suggest that step-level escalation recovers a large share of the performance gap to the stronger Qwen2.5-7B backend at a matched cloud-action rate while transmitting fewer tokens remotely. However, our evaluation is limited to one model family, a single stronger backend, and scripted tasks. Furthermore, the test sets are small, multi-turn comparisons rely on paired intervals and statistical tests, and our risk tiers serve as research annotations rather than formal safety guarantees.

</details>


### [200] [Agentic Semantic Sensing for Resource-Adaptive AI-RAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07829)
*Zhongqin Wang,Xiaoqi Zhang,Nan Yang,Kai Wu,J. Andrew Zhang,Y. Jay Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Agentic SemS, a closed-loop framework for AI-enabled radio access networks that dynamically controls sensing configurations and observation duration based on evolving task-level evidence, using profile-conditioned causal Transformers with key-value caching and a semantic utility network for value-of-information-based decision making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic sensing formulations operate open-loop with fixed sensing configurations that cannot adapt to evolving evidence. This limits efficiency in AI-RANs where task-relevant information needs dynamic acquisition within communication-feasible constraints.

Method: The proposed Agentic SemS framework uses: (1) a profile-conditioned causal Transformer that updates semantic belief from streaming observations with key-value caching for efficient state updates; (2) a semantic utility network estimating task-level benefit of observations under each feasible profile; (3) continuation utilities supporting both next-profile selection and semantic early exit; (4) interpretation via conditional mutual information for value-of-information.

Result: On Widar3.0 with six emulated sensing profiles, Agentic SemS reduces normalized cumulative sensing cost by 25.33% while achieving 85.79% Macro-F1 compared to full-sequence High. Semantic early exit provides an additional 12.35% cost reduction over adaptive sensing without early exit, with only a 0.97-percentage-point Macro-F1 decrease.

Conclusion: Agentic SemS successfully enables closed-loop, adaptive semantic sensing in AI-RANs, dynamically balancing sensing cost and task performance through profile selection and early exit mechanisms, demonstrating significant resource efficiency gains with minimal accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: Semantic sensing (SemS) acquires task-relevant information rather than reconstructing complete physical information. Existing SemS formulations typically operate open loop: sensing configurations and observation schedules are fixed before inference and cannot respond to evolving task-level evidence. We propose Agentic SemS, a closed-loop framework for AI-enabled radio access networks (AI-RANs) that controls sensing within a communication-feasible profile set. A profile-conditioned causal Transformer updates the semantic belief from streaming observations, while key-value caching enables efficient state updates across profile changes without repeatedly processing the complete history. A semantic utility network estimates the task-level benefit of acquiring the next observation block under each feasible profile after accounting for sensing cost. The resulting continuation utilities jointly support next-profile selection and semantic early exit, adapting sensing configuration and duration to evolving evidence. The expected semantic gain is further related to conditional mutual information, providing a value-of-information interpretation of continued online sensing. Experiments on Widar3.0 with six emulated sensing profiles show that, in comparison with full-sequence High, the resource-efficient Agentic setting reduces normalized cumulative sensing cost by 25.33% while achieving 85.79% Macro-F1. At the same utility checkpoint, semantic early exit provides a further 12.35% cost reduction over adaptive sensing without early exit, with a 0.97-percentage-point Macro-F1 decrease.

</details>


### [201] [DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07835)
*Jie Ren,Jiakang Yuan,Chenyu Huang,Hezeer Ma,Jiayuan Fan,Tao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DHCG is a novel framework that reframes LLM-based multi-agent systems as a partially observable Markov decision process, dynamically determining composition and scale. It uses three modules (Planner, Worker, Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph based on query and execution feedback, with action-aware preference optimization for training the Planner.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution.

Method: DHCG coordinates three modules: Planner generates distinct roles tailored to current reasoning needs and routes relevant information; Worker executes tasks; Generator constructs dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph. The system can finalize early or expand progressively. Action-aware preference optimization trains the Planner for better decisions.

Result: DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance, improving 13.06 points over single-agent baseline and outperforming static/dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. Shows generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

Conclusion: Dynamically determining both composition and scale of multi-agent systems during execution, guided by feedback, enables more effective problem-solving than static or less adaptive approaches. The hierarchical collaboration graph approach provides a promising direction for complex reasoning tasks.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

</details>


### [202] [RA-MoWE: Workflow-Affinity Embeddings for Query Clustering and Agentic Workflow Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07851)
*Qi Cheng,Shengyu Chen,Wei Cheng,Yiqun Xie,Haoyu Wang,Haifeng Chen,Xiaowei Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RA-MoWE is a framework that addresses the tradeoff between optimizing a single workflow for all tasks versus searching for new workflows for each query.
