It uses workflow-affinity embeddings to cluster queries and generate reusable expert workflows, improving task performance while reducing LLM calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key problem is that a workflow optimized for an entire task collection overlooks differences in reasoning strategies needed by individual queries, while searching for a new workflow for every query is computationally expensive. The authors seek to balance between workflow specialization and efficiency.

Method: RA-MoWE uses workflow-affinity embeddings that record how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves each query, revealing similarities in effective reasoning strategies. These embeddings are used to cluster queries, and each cluster's queries and average embedding initialize and refine a specialized workflow through execution feedback. An embedding encoder predicts these embeddings from query text, enabling new queries to select a generated expert without executing reference workflows first.

Result: On a 300-query test set from four benchmarks (mathematics, science, and programming), RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among reference workflows, while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference.

Conclusion: The framework successfully balances workflow specialization and computational efficiency by leveraging workflow-affinity embeddings for query clustering and expert workflow generation, achieving both improved performance and reduced computational cost.

Abstract: Agentic workflows enable large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks by coordinating reasoning, tool use, and verification. However, a workflow optimized for an entire task collection can overlook differences in the reasoning strategies that individual queries need, while searching for a new workflow for every query repeats costly optimization. To address this tradeoff, we introduce RA-MoWE, a framework that uses workflow-affinity embeddings to cluster queries and guide the generation of reusable expert workflows. Each embedding records how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves a query, revealing similarities in which reasoning strategies are effective. RA-MoWE uses each cluster's queries and average embedding to initialize and refine a specialized workflow through execution feedback. An embedding encoder predicts these embeddings from query text, allowing new queries to select a generated expert without first executing the reference workflows. On a 300-query test set drawn from four benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and programming, RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among the reference workflows, while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference.

</details>


### [203] [WorkflowOps: Learning Agent Collaboration Priors for Multi-Agent Workflow Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07860)
*Qi Cheng,Shengyu Chen,Wei Cheng,Zhengzhang Chen,Xiaowei Jia,Haoyu Wang,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorkflowOps is a multi-agent workflow orchestration framework that learns from historical workflows to improve agent collaboration and dynamically expands its agent pool by creating specialized agents when capability gaps are detected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent systems for complex knowledge work are currently memoryless—each new task is executed from scratch without leveraging prior successful executions, leading to inefficient agent collaboration and repeated decomposition efforts.

Method: Three coupled mechanisms: (1) Transition probability matrix capturing pairwise agent collaboration frequencies for DAG workflow construction via intra-layer ordering optimization, probability-thresholded edge suggestion, and transitive reduction; (2) Sufficiency-driven agent creation loop detecting capability gaps through semantic matching and generating specialized agents via LLM while injecting them into the collaboration matrix; (3) Layered semantic matching using pre-trained sentence embeddings as first pass with LLM verification only for low-confidence cases.

Result: Improves end-to-end pass rates over recent workflow-construction baselines, with the largest gains on structured, decomposable tasks where past agent handoff patterns transfer. Reduces LLM routing calls by over 80% compared to pure-LLM approaches.

Conclusion: WorkflowOps successfully enables multi-agent systems to learn from historical workflows, creating a memoryful orchestration layer that improves agent collaboration through learned priors and dynamically expands capabilities on demand, achieving significant performance gains on complex, decomposable tasks.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex knowledge work, yet their orchestration layers remain largely memoryless: each new task is decomposed, assigned, and executed from scratch with no benefit from prior successful executions. We present WorkflowOps, a multi-agent workflow orchestration framework that learns agent collaboration priors from historical workflows and expands its agent pool on demand to cover new capability requirements. Our approach introduces three coupled mechanisms. First, a transition probability matrix captures pairwise agent collaboration frequencies from past workflows and applies them as soft guidance during DAG workflow construction through intra-layer ordering optimization, probability-thresholded edge suggestion, and transitive reduction for parallelism maximization. Second, a sufficiency-driven agent creation loop detects capability gaps via semantic matching scores, generates specialized agents through an LLM, and simultaneously injects them into the collaboration matrix, so that newly created agents are immediately usable with predicted collaboration priors. Third, a layered semantic matching strategy uses pre-trained sentence embeddings for fast, deterministic capability matching as a first pass, invoking LLM verification only for low-confidence cases, thereby reducing LLM routing calls by over 80\% compared to pure-LLM approaches. Experiments on mixed code, math, and question-answering suites show that WorkflowOps improves end-to-end pass rates over recent workflow-construction baselines, with the largest gains on structured, decomposable tasks where past agent handoff patterns transfer.

</details>


### [204] [Self-Referenced Social Preferences: Cooperation without Observing Others Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07881)
*Mohamed Ayman Mohamed,Harshil Kotamreddy,Marcos Menon Jose*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces self-referenced social preferences for multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents learn their own reward model and apply it to assess others' outcomes from their own perspective, without requiring access to others' private reward signals. The approach is evaluated on three sequential social dilemmas (Escape Room, Clean Up, Commons Harvest), demonstrating that cooperative behavior can emerge without explicit reward sharing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key motivation addresses a fundamental limitation in existing social preference approaches for MARL: they require agents to observe peers' rewards, which is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios where agents can only observe others' behavior and outcomes, not their private reward signals. The authors draw an analogy to human social interactions where we can observe others' actions and outcomes but not their internal reward valuations.

Method: The proposed method involves two main components: (1) Each agent learns a model of its own reward function through self-supervised learning; (2) Agents apply this self-reward model to other agents' observed transitions to assess what outcomes those agents would receive from the agent's own perspective. This creates "self-referenced assessments." The authors explore two integration methods: (a) modifying the learning reward by incorporating these assessments, and (b) using assessments to weight policy updates. They compare two types of social preferences: inequity aversion and purely benevolent preferences.

Result: Across all three environments (Escape Room requiring volunteering, Clean Up requiring public-good contribution, and Commons Harvest requiring resource restraint), agents with self-referenced social preferences learned cooperative behavior without observing others' rewards. The approach succeeded even in settings where independent learners fail to cooperate. Notably, these agents frequently achieved more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with access to true rewards. The effectiveness of integration method depended on the social preference type: inequity aversion worked best when combined with reward modification and value look-ahead, while benevolent preferences benefited from policy-update weighting. The policy-update approach also continued to support cooperation under partial observability.

Conclusion: The key conclusion is that explicit access to other agents' reward signals is not necessary for learning cooperative behavior in multi-agent systems. Social preferences can be grounded in self-referenced assessments of others' outcomes derived from their observed behavior, using the agent's own learned reward model. This makes the approach more applicable to real-world scenarios where private reward information is unavailable, while still achieving effective cooperation and often more equitable outcomes than methods with full reward access.

Abstract: Social preferences can promote cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning, but existing approaches often require agents to observe the rewards of their peers. In many real-world interactions, however, an agent can, as humans do, observe others' behavior and outcomes without access to their private reward signals. We introduce self-referenced social preferences, in which each agent learns a model of its own reward, applies it to other agents' observed transitions to assess their outcomes from its own perspective, and feeds these self-referenced assessments into standard social preferences. We study two ways to incorporate these assessments: modifying the learning reward, or using them to weight policy updates. We evaluate the approach on three sequential social dilemmas, Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest, which require volunteering, public-good contribution, and resource restraint, respectively. Across all three environments, agents learn cooperative behavior without observing others' rewards, including in settings where independent learners fail to cooperate, and frequently achieve more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with access to true rewards. The effective integration point depends on the social preference: inequity aversion works best in the reward together with a value look-ahead, whereas a purely benevolent preference benefits from policy-update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy-update approach continues to support cooperation. These results show that explicit access to other agents' reward signals is not necessary for learning cooperative behavior: social preferences can instead be grounded in self-referenced assessments of others' outcomes derived from their observed behavior.

</details>


### [205] [ShanLiangRen: A Nutrition Agent for Personalized Daily Meal Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07886)
*Miao Xie,Xiao Zhang,Yuan Wang,Ruixin Zhu,Chunli Lv*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents ShanLiangRen, a nutrition agent system for personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning. It transforms user requirements into constrained planning instances, uses retrieval-augmented generation to identify candidate meals from large recipe databases, and employs LLM-based iterative refinement guided by Pareto principles to generate executable meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dietary nutrition planning is crucial for chronic disease management and health maintenance. However, personalized constraints and multidimensional nutritional goals often conflict, and user requirements evolve with feedback. This creates a substantial gap between generic dietary guidelines and executable meal plans that users can actually follow.

Method: The system employs a three-stage approach: (1) Transformation of dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes, and natural language requirements into individualized constrained planning instances; (2) Exact retrieval-augmented generation to shrink the feasible candidate set from large-scale ingredient and recipe spaces; (3) Pareto-guided refinement where an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and constraint verification feedback.

Result: The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, along with nutrition compliance reports showing constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. The system has been released online as a WeChat Program.

Conclusion: The proposed ShanLiangRen system successfully bridges the gap between generic dietary guidelines and executable personalized meal plans by combining retrieval-augmented generation with LLM-based iterative refinement, providing users with practical, nutritionally balanced dietary plans.

Abstract: Dietary nutrition planning plays an important role in chronic disease management and maintaining a healthy body. In applications, it must simultaneously satisfy personalized constraints and reasonable multidimensional nutritional goals. These two aspects often conflict, and user constraints evolve with feedback, resulting in a substantial gap between generic guidelines and executable plans. To bridge this gap, we first propose the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP). To tackle MDP, we develop a nutrition agent, ShanLiangRen. The system first transforms dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes and natural language requirements into an individualized constrained planning instance. It then employs an exact retrieval-augmented generation method to shrink the feasible candidate set from a large scale ingredient and recipe space. Finally, it adopts a refinement guided by Pareto principles, where an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and feedback from constraint verification. The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, together with reports on nutrition compliance that show constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. We have released the system online as a WeChat Program, ShanLiangRen. A demo video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=652OtY5VlGA.

</details>


### [206] [Textual Environmental Context and Spatial Graphs for LLM-Based Regional SST Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07895)
*Xiong Li,Xiaowei Zhou,Yanwei Yu,Qian Cui,Junyu Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel framework combining large language models with graph neural networks for regional multi-step sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, using static and dynamic graphs to encode spatial dependencies without serializing the full SST grid as text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SST forecasting depends on heterogeneous conditions including local temporal persistence, regional spatial dependence, and environmental conditions that evolve with the forecast date. The challenge is how to present these conditions to an LLM without serializing the full SST grid as text.

Method: Formulated forecasting as conditional numerical generation: historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental records, and static ocean knowledge form textual context, while regional spatial state is supplied through continuous graph-derived prefixes. A static graph encodes persistent geographic-climatological relations, and a dynamic graph encodes recent SST correlations and localized tropical-cyclone influence. Two GNNs produce target-node representations mapped via spatial-prefix fusion and injected into LLM input. A rule-based module provides post-hoc contextual explanations.

Result: The complete configuration achieves the best MAE and R² among compared methods over ten forecast steps on SST forecasting in the South China Sea.

Conclusion: The proposed LLM-based framework with graph-derived spatial prefixes successfully integrates temporal, spatial, and environmental factors for regional SST forecasting, achieving superior numerical accuracy while providing source-linked contextual explanations through a rule-based module.

Abstract: Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting depends on local temporal persistence, regional spatial dependence, and environmental conditions that evolve with the forecast date. We study how these heterogeneous conditions can be presented to a large language model (LLM) for regional multi-step forecasting without serializing the full SST grid as text. We formulate forecasting as conditional numerical generation: historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental records, and static ocean knowledge form a textual context, while regional spatial state is supplied through continuous graph-derived prefixes. A static graph encodes persistent geographic--climatological relations, and a dynamic graph encodes recent SST correlations and localized tropical-cyclone influence. Two graph neural networks produce a target-node representation that is mapped by a spatial-prefix fusion and injected into the LLM input. On SST forecasting in the South China Sea, the complete configuration achieves the best MAE and $\Rtwo$ among the compared methods over ten forecast steps. Alongside the numerical forecast, a rule-based module matches predicted trends and environmental-factor directions with knowledge entries to return source-linked, post-hoc contextual explanations.

</details>


### [207] [Isotropic Yet Undecodable: The Sequential Content-Sufficiency Gap in Latent-Predictive Text Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07906)
*K. P. Santoso,N. Z. Fadil,F. P. Harsanti,R. V. H. Ginardi,G. N. Iyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates sequential content sufficiency— whether neural representations retain ordered target information from their inputs. The authors propose CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases and canonical-token supervision, and demonstrate that geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access in text settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand whether representations retain ordered target information from their inputs, which is crucial for sequential content sufficiency. The authors identify gaps in current understanding of how representation geometry relates to information preservation, particularly in text settings.

Method: The authors use an information-theoretic decomposition separating input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. They construct recoverable views where perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity coexist with zero target information, and establish limits imposed by deterministic canonical anchors. Token log-loss provides a one-sided information-loss bound, and fixed-penalty ridge analysis shows why rank alone cannot determine prediction risk. The proposed CANOPE framework uses ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization.

Result: On 40,000 validation sequences, latent-agreement (PL0) and token-grounded (PL2) have nearly identical pooled ranks but reach 13.5% and 98.8% positional Recall@1 under strong natural corruption when correct target length is provided. On 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with trained MatchaTTS readout yields 21.54% WER on corrupted text, versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93%.

Conclusion: Geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access in text settings. The paper demonstrates that positional Recall@1 and word error rate are more informative metrics than pooled ranks for evaluating sequential content sufficiency.

Abstract: We study sequential content sufficiency by investigating whether a representation retains the ordered target information available in its input. An information-theoretic decomposition separates input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. We construct recoverable views where perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity coexist with zero target information, and establish limits imposed by deterministic canonical anchors. Token log-loss provides a one-sided information-loss bound; a fixed-penalty ridge analysis shows why rank alone cannot determine prediction risk. These results motivate CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization. On 40,000 validation sequences, latent-agreement (PL0) and token-grounded (PL2) have nearly identical pooled ranks but reach 13.5% and 98.8% positional Recall@1, respectively, under strong natural corruption when the correct target length is provided. On 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with a trained MatchaTTS readout yields 21.54% word error rate (WER) on corrupted text, versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93%. These results show that geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access in the text settings studied here.

</details>
