### [208] [Extending Music Annotation Schemas: Zero-Shot Prediction or Few-Shot Adaptation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06920)
*Christos Plachouras,Emmanouil Benetos,Johan Pauwels*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of accommodating new musical attributes in commercial music catalogs by comparing zero-shot prediction (audio-language models) versus supervised adaptation across different annotation budgets, using the MGPHot dataset as a benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial music catalogs need to accommodate new musical attributes as needs evolve, but expert annotation is expensive. It is unclear which methodological approach is most effective for accommodating new attributes and backfilling existing tracks.

Method: The authors propose a benchmark based on the MGPHot popular music annotation dataset to simulate music schema extension. They investigate three approaches: (1) zero-shot prediction with audio-language models, (2) learning new attributes from pretrained representations, and (3) adapting models trained on existing annotations. These are evaluated across different annotation budgets.

Result: Supervised adaptation outperforms zero-shot prediction even with small annotation budgets. However, frozen representation reuse remains the most effective approach for modest budgets without requiring the tuning needed by deeper adaptation.

Conclusion: For practical music annotation systems, supervised adaptation is generally more effective than zero-shot approaches, but frozen representation reuse offers a good balance of performance and simplicity for modest annotation budgets.

Abstract: Automatic music annotation is typically tackled under the assumption of a fixed annotation schema. In practice, commercial music catalogs often need to accommodate new musical attributes as needs evolve. Given that expert music annotation is expensive, it is not evident which methodological approach is most effective at accommodating new attributes and backfilling existing tracks; audio-language models promise zero-shot prediction, but at what annotation budget does supervised adaptation become more compelling?
  We propose a benchmark based on the MGPHot popular music annotation dataset for simulating music schema extension across different annotation budgets. We investigate zero-shot prediction with audio-language models, learning new attributes from pretrained representations, and adapting models trained on existing annotations. Our results suggest that supervised adaptation is more effective than zero-shot prediction even with small annotation budgets, while frozen representation reuse remains the most effective approach for modest budgets without the tuning required by deeper adaptation.

</details>


### [209] [AdaLoop: Adaptive-Depth Latent Reasoning for Audio Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06949)
*Lee Seung-woo,Bowen Qi*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AdaLoop introduces adaptive computational depth to audio language models by learning how many refinement steps each audio-question pair needs, using a lightweight recurrent module with a learned halting mechanism that exits when the representation is ready.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large audio language models answer questions about speech, sound, and music but accuracy drops on fine-grained acoustic analysis tasks (e.g., comparing speaker pitches). Current models use the same computational depth for all tasks, regardless of complexity. This inefficiency wastes resources on simple tasks while potentially under-processing complex ones.

Method: AdaLoop adds a lightweight recurrent module (<3% of base model parameters) that plugs into any audio encoder-LM pair without modifying either component. A shared transformer block iterates over the audio representation, guided by the question. A learned halting mechanism determines when to exit the loop based on whether the representation is ready for answering.

Result: Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR benchmarks, AdaLoop raises average accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 points, with largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks requiring deeper reasoning.

Conclusion: AdaLoop successfully enables adaptive computational depth in audio language models, achieving significant accuracy improvements on fine-grained acoustic tasks while maintaining efficiency through learned, task-dependent iteration counts. The method is model-agnostic and computationally lightweight.

Abstract: Large audio language models answer questions about speech, sound, and music, yet their accuracy drops sharply on tasks that need fine-grained acoustic analysis. Judging which of two speakers has the higher pitch demands iterative signal-level reasoning that a content question does not. Current models spend the same computational depth on both. We introduce AdaLoop, a lightweight recurrent module that learns how many latent refinement steps a given audio--question pair requires. A shared transformer block iterates over the audio representation, guided by the question, while a learned halting mechanism exits the loop once the representation is ready. AdaLoop adds fewer than 3\% of the base model's parameters and plugs into any audio encoder--language model pair without modifying either component. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, AdaLoop raises the average accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 points, with the largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks where the model learns to apply deeper reasoning.

</details>


### [210] [Where Does the Audio Jailbreak Live? A Controlled Frequency-Depth Audit of AdvWave-P on Qwen2-Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07005)
*Boyuan Chen,Minseok Kim,Sohaila Abdulsattar,Minghao Shao,Siddharth Garg,Ramesh Karri,Muhammad Shafique*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper audits frequency and decoder-depth claims for AdvWave-P, an additive audio jailbreak attack on Qwen2-Audio. Using STFT-domain frequency masking on 520 AdvBench prompts, the study finds that energy share predicts band ranking (rho=0.95), masking any band reduces attack success, and audio-span divergence correlates with band necessity (coefficient rising from +0.63 to +0.93 across layers). The 7520-7960 Hz band at 16-band resolution leaves ASR at 0.10, requiring matched controls for confirmation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to verify and validate frequency and decoder-depth claims for AdvWave-P audio jailbreak on Qwen2-Audio. They investigate which frequency bands are critical for attack success and whether audio-span representations can predict band necessity, while addressing potential labeling biases through validation.

Method: The study uses STFT-domain masking to manipulate frequency components of adversarial perturbations. It tests multiple frequency partitions: standard eight-band (energy-share), equal-Hz, equal-energy, and finer 16-band equal-energy. Attack success rate (ASR) is measured across 520 AdvBench prompts. Validation uses Rogan-Gladen sensitivity estimation (0.87) for the primary condition. Re-optimization pilots test single/two-band supports and random supports covering ~50% STFT bins. Audio-span divergence is analyzed using regression models across model layers.

Result: Primary judge labels 76.7% of adversarial inputs as jailbreaks. Energy share strongly predicts eight-band ranking (Spearman's rho=0.95). Masking any tested band reduces attack success. At 16-band equal-energy resolution, masking 7520-7960 Hz band leaves ASR at 0.10. Re-optimization pilot shows single-band ASRs of 0.00-0.40, two-band at 0.25, while random supports achieve mean ASR of 0.86. Audio-span divergence coefficient rises from +0.63 (projector output) to +0.93 at layer 30 (contrast +0.293, 95% CI [0.11, 0.51]). Contiguous removal is more damaging in lower bands; both removal types approach floor in upper bands.

Conclusion: The results support partition-aware auditing of frequency claims. The fine-resolution top-band result (7520-7960 Hz with ASR=0.10) remains unresolved without matched controls. The audio-span divergence association is not a causal localization, and single-layer patching does not establish a causal layer. Broader generality remains open to future investigation.

Abstract: We audit frequency and decoder-depth claims for AdvWave-P, an additive audio jailbreak, on Qwen2-Audio. The protocol masks frequency components of the perturbation in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain and measures attack success and audio-span representations. On 520 AdvBench prompts, the primary judge labels 76.7% of adversarial inputs as jailbreaks. A condition-blind, single-annotator validation yields a Rogan-Gladen sensitivity estimate of 0.87 for this condition (about 0.83-0.95 with validation-rate uncertainty); this correction is not applied to masked conditions. The apparent frequency ranking depends on the partition: energy share alone predicts the standard eight-band ranking (Spearman's rho = 0.95), and equal-Hz and equal-energy partitions show that masking any tested band can sharply reduce attack success. At a finer 16-band equal-energy resolution, however, masking the narrow 7520-7960 Hz band leaves ASR at 0.10, which remains unresolved without a matched control. Matched-energy scattered-removal tests show that contiguous removal is more damaging in lower bands, while both forms approach the floor in upper bands. Global rescaling leaves ASR near baseline but tests amplitude sensitivity rather than frequency location. In a re-optimization pilot (n = 20), tested single- and two-band supports reach ASRs of 0.00, 0.25, and 0.40, while random supports covering about half the STFT bins reach a mean of 0.86. In a prompt- and energy-adjusted model, audio-span divergence is associated with band necessity, with the coefficient rising from +0.63 at the projector output to +0.93 at layer 30 (contrast +0.293, 95% CI [0.11, 0.51]). This association is not a causal localization, and single-layer patching does not establish a causal layer. The results support partition-aware auditing of frequency claims, leaving the fine-resolution top-band result and broader generality open.

</details>


### [211] [ImpactMat: Continuous Material Estimation for Inverse Impact Sound Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07061)
*Hyebin Cho,Bumsoo Kim,Joon son Chung*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces ImpactMat, a dataset and benchmark for inverse impact sound rendering, along with a feed-forward model that predicts material parameters from impact sound recordings, enabling automatic material parameter estimation without manual tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current impact sound renderers rely on fixed material presets (wood, plastic, steel), limiting the range of expressible sounds. Manually adjusting material parameters requires expertise in material acoustics, making it difficult for users to create custom impact sounds.

Method: The authors introduce ImpactMat, a dataset and benchmark of single and blended material impact sounds paired with ground-truth material parameters. They propose a feed-forward model that predicts material parameters from one or more recordings, using blended materials to learn smooth transitions between material types.

Result: The method outperforms competitive baselines and enables re-rendering from real recordings without manual parameter tuning.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully predicts material parameters from impact sounds, allowing practical renderers to recreate similar material responses without requiring expertise in material acoustics. The project page is available at https://material-from-impact.github.io/material-from-impact/.

Abstract: Impact sound rendering synthesizes the sound produced when a 3D object is struck, but practical renderers often rely on fixed material presets such as wood, plastic, or steel. These presets limit the range of impact sounds a renderer can express, while manually adjusting the underlying material parameters remains difficult without expertise in material acoustics. We therefore study inverse impact sound rendering: predicting material parameters from a reference impact sound so that a simulator can recreate a similar material response. To support this task, we introduce ImpactMat, a dataset and benchmark of single and blended material impact sounds paired with ground-truth material parameters. We further propose a feed-forward model that predicts these parameters from one or more recordings, using blended materials to learn smooth transitions between material types. Experiments show that our method outperforms competitive baselines and enables re-rendering from real recordings without manual parameter tuning. The project page is available https://material-from-impact.github.io/material-from-impact/.

</details>


### [212] [Neural Representations, Natural Connections: What Transfers From Human Speech Foundation Models to Animal Vocalizations?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07107)
*Tomás Arias-Vergara,Christopher Hauer,Héloïse Brotier,Elmar Nöth,Andreas Maier,Lee Koren*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 15 frozen pretrained encoders from speech, speaker verification, animal bioacoustics, and general audio domains for cross-species transfer in animal bioacoustics tasks. Speech-pretrained models generally perform comparably or better than animal-pretrained models, with no systematic benefit from increased language coverage or animal-domain pretraining. Transfer performance is highly layer-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the promise of speech-pretrained models in animal bioacoustics, the factors governing their cross-species transfer effectiveness remain poorly understood, creating a gap in knowledge needed to optimize model selection for bioacoustics applications.

Method: The authors evaluated 15 frozen encoders spanning monolingual/multilingual speech, speaker verification, animal bioacoustics, and general audio domains on caller identification (4 species) and call-type classification (3 species). They conducted controlled comparisons to assess the impact of language coverage and animal-domain pretraining.

Result: Speech-pretrained models showed differences ranging from -0.027 to +0.119 UAR compared to animal-pretrained models. Speech significantly outperformed in 3 of 7 settings (p<0.01) with no significant difference in the remaining 4. No systematic advantage was found from increased language coverage or animal-domain pretraining. Frozen speaker-verification embeddings transferred poorly. Raw-waveform models peaked at early layers while patch-spectrogram models peaked at deeper layers.

Conclusion: Speech-pretrained models transfer effectively to animal bioacoustics tasks, often matching or exceeding animal-pretrained models. Language coverage and animal-domain pretraining provide no systematic advantage. Layer selection is critical and depends on the model architecture (raw-waveform vs. patch-spectrogram).

Abstract: Speech-pretrained models have shown promise in animal bioacoustics, but the factors governing their cross-species transfer remain poorly understood. We evaluate 15 frozen encoders spanning monolingual and multilingual speech, speaker verification, animal bioacoustics, and general audio on caller identification across four species and call-type classification across three. Differences between the strongest speech- and animal-pretrained representations range from $-0.027$ to $+0.119$ UAR; speech is significantly better in three of seven settings ($p<0.01$) and not significantly different in the remaining four. Controlled comparisons show no systematic advantage from increased language coverage or animal-domain pretraining, while frozen speaker-verification embeddings transfer poorly. The results also show that transfer is strongly layer-dependent: raw-waveform models peak early, whereas patch-spectrogram models peak deeper.

</details>


### [213] [Exposing and Mitigating Neural Codec Vulnerabilities in Audio Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07216)
*Abdullah,Awais Khan,Khalid Mahmood Malik*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in audio deepfake detection (ADD): existing detectors are vulnerable to neural audio codec compression artifacts. The authors expose this vulnerability in SOTA ADD models and propose PCL-NET, which uses a pairwise consistency objective to disentangle codec artifacts from real-vs-fake decisions, reducing average EER from 28.67% to 12.77%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ADD systems are designed for vocoder-based synthesis but fail against neural audio codec compression. Neural codecs serve dual roles (compression and resynthesis) in modern ALM-based speech synthesizers, producing distinct artifacts from traditional post-hoc perturbations. This vulnerability remains unexplored, and current SOTA models misclassify legitimately compressed bona fide speech as fake.

Method: The authors constructed the Audio Neural Codec-Spoof dataset by applying seven neural codec algorithms to existing ADD benchmarks as a controlled proxy for codec-based generation. They proposed PCL-NET (Pairwise Consistency Learned Network), which fine-tunes a pretrained XLS-R (300M) encoder using a pairwise consistency objective that minimizes representation distance between an utterance's uncompressed and codec-compressed versions, effectively disentangling codec artifacts from the real-versus-fake decision.

Result: PCL-NET reduces average EER under neural codec compression from 28.67% to 12.77%, while preserving competitive CoSG-based deepfake detection performance. Systems trained on Codec Resynthesized data proved most vulnerable.

Conclusion: The study reveals a significant vulnerability in SOTA audio deepfake detection systems to neural codec compression artifacts. PCL-NET provides an effective baseline mitigation through pairwise consistency learning, and the Audio Neural Codec-Spoof dataset will be publicly released to advance research in this direction.

Abstract: Existing audio deepfake detection (ADD) datasets and detectors are primarily built for vocoder-based synthesis, evaluated against traditional post-hoc perturbations such as MP3/AAC compression or additive noise, applied independently of generation. However, recent speech synthesizers, particularly ALM-based systems, use neural audio codecs both for compression and as the resynthesis reconstructing waveforms from generated tokens, producing artifacts distinct from post-hoc compression. Neural codecs thus play a dual role: some are designed for pure compression under low-bandwidth communication, while others serve as resynthesis components. Despite this dual role, robustness to codec-based compression, unlike post-hoc compression, remains largely unexplored. We expose this gap, showing that state-of-the-art (SOTA) ADD models degrade drastically on codec-compressed speech; in particular, systems trained on Codec Resynthesized data as a proxy for codec-based generation prove most vulnerable, with legitimately compressed bona fide speech often misclassified as fake. To investigate this, we construct the Audio Neural Codec-Spoof dataset by applying seven neural codec algorithms to existing ADD benchmarks, isolating codec-induced resynthesis artifacts as a controlled proxy for codec-based generation. As baseline mitigation, we propose PCL-NET (Pairwise Consistency Learned Network), fine-tuning a pretrained XLS-R (300M) encoder with a pairwise consistency objective that minimizes the representation distance between an utterance's uncompressed and codec-compressed versions, disentangling codec artifacts from the real-versus-fake decision. As a result, PCL-NET reduces average EER under neural codec compression from 28.67% to 12.77%, while preserving competitive CoSG-based deepfake detection performance. We will also make the dataset publicly available on Hugging Face upon acceptance.

</details>


### [214] [Adapting a Latent Audio Diffusion Model to Historical Guqin Recordings: A Listening-Driven Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07486)
*Huanchen Cai*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a small-data case study adapting a pretrained latent audio diffusion model (Stable Audio 3 Medium) to generate continuous guqin (seven-string Chinese zither) music. Using 412 solo performances (42.5h, 61 performers), the authors fine-tuned a rank-16 DoRA adapter with specialized training techniques. The final model achieved 3.9/5 for continuing unseen pieces and 4.6/5 for generating from scene descriptions. The study also documents valuable negative results and technical issues encountered.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to create an "AI radio" that plays guqin-style music continuously without end. This addresses the challenge of generating culturally-specific, continuous music using limited data (small-data case study). The guqin is a culturally significant instrument with unique timbral characteristics, making it an interesting test case for audio model adaptation.

Method: The methodology involves: (1) Curating 412 solo guqin performances (42.5h, 61 performers) from historical recordings, split by composition; (2) Fine-tuning a rank-16 DoRA adapter on Stable Audio 3 Medium using continuous latents; (3) Training techniques including masking weighted towards continuation, captions combining researched notes with mood tags and automatically estimated pentatonic mode, and random-length crops; (4) Early stopping based on held-out loss improvement; (5) Evaluation through seven blind listening studies by one expert listener guiding all decisions. The study also tested a from-scratch autoregressive model over the same latents as a comparison.

Result: Positive results: The final adapter achieved 3.9/5 for continuing unseen pieces (vs. 3.4 for the best earlier adapter) and 4.6/5 for generating from free-written scene descriptions. Negative results: (1) A from-scratch autoregressive model produced no recognizable timbre; (2) A signal-level friction-noise measure correlated with listener complaints in the wrong direction; (3) A pentatonic-fit measure tracked ratings overall but barely within candidate groups. Technical issues discovered: silent tail on every generated clip and a loudness feedback loop, both with simple fixes.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that adapting a pretrained latent audio diffusion model to a specific cultural instrument with limited data is feasible. The DoRA adapter approach proved effective, while autoregressive modeling failed. The authors emphasize that negative results are equally informative, and document what helped, what did not, and why. Limitations include having only one listener and at most ten clips per condition, meaning no paired difference is statistically significant. The work provides an exploratory record of design decisions for similar adaptation tasks.

Abstract: We report a small-data case study in adapting a pretrained latent audio diffusion model to the guqin, the seven-string Chinese zither, aiming at an "AI radio" that plays guqin-style music without end. From a library of historical recordings we curate 412 solo performances (42.5 h, 61 performers) and split them by composition. We fine-tune a rank-16 DoRA adapter on Stable Audio 3 Medium using its continuous latents, masking weighted towards continuation, captions that combine researched notes on each piece with mood tags and an automatically estimated pentatonic mode, and random-length crops, stopping when held-out loss stops improving. Seven blind listening studies by one expert listener guided every decision. The final adapter was rated highest for continuing unseen pieces (3.9/5, against 3.4 for the best earlier adapter) and 4.6/5 for generating from free-written scene descriptions. Negative results are equally informative: a from-scratch autoregressive model over the same latents produced no recognisable timbre, a signal-level friction-noise measure correlated with the listener's complaints in the wrong direction, and a pentatonic-fit measure tracked ratings overall but barely within a group of candidates. Chaining continuations for long playback exposed a silent tail on every generated clip and a loudness feedback loop, both with simple fixes. With one listener and at most ten clips per condition, no paired difference is statistically significant; we present an exploratory record of what helped, what did not, and why.

</details>


### [215] [SkillFormer: Skill-Decomposed Adaptation for Audio Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07533)
*Lee Seung-woo,Bowen Qi,Kim Min-jun,Jang Won-young*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SkillFormer is a method that addresses the interference problem in audio language models when jointly training on multiple skills (pitch comparison, speaker counting, tempo estimation, emotion recognition, etc.). It uses skill-specific low-rank adapters composed via a learned router that decides which adapters to activate based on the question, adding fewer than 4% extra parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint training on all audio understanding skills causes interference - gains on one skill come at the cost of another. This is a common problem in multi-task learning for audio language models that need to handle diverse capabilities like pitch comparison, speaker counting, musical tempo estimation, and emotion recognition.

Method: SkillFormer decomposes audio understanding into skill-specific low-rank adapters that are composed at inference time through a learned router. The router examines the question to determine which adapters to activate and their weighting. An alternating training schedule updates each adapter on its own skill cluster before jointly calibrating the router, preventing gradient conflicts. No changes to the audio encoder or language backbone are required.

Result: Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR benchmarks, SkillFormer raises average accuracy by 2.5 to 4.1 points with balanced gains across perception, reasoning, and semantic subcategories. The method adds fewer than 4% of the base model's parameters.

Conclusion: SkillFormer successfully addresses the multi-task interference problem in audio language models through adapter-based architecture and learned routing, achieving significant accuracy improvements while maintaining parameter efficiency. The approach is model-agnostic and preserves the original encoder and language backbone.

Abstract: Audio language models must handle dozens of distinct skills, from pitch comparison and speaker counting to musical tempo estimation and emotion recognition. Joint training on all skills at once causes interference: gains on one skill often come at the cost of another. We propose \textbf{SkillFormer}, which decomposes audio understanding into skill-specific low-rank adapters and composes them at inference time through a learned router. The router examines the question to decide which adapters to activate and how much weight each should carry, so that a pitch query engages different parameters than a genre classification query. An alternating training schedule updates each adapter on its own skill cluster before jointly calibrating the router, preventing the gradient conflicts that arise in standard multi-task optimization. SkillFormer adds fewer than 4\% of the base model's parameters and requires no changes to the audio encoder or language backbone. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, it raises the average accuracy by 2.5 to 4.1 points, with balanced gains across perception, reasoning, and semantic subcategories.

</details>


### [216] [Pronunciation-Oriented Reinforcement Learning for Japanese Text-to-Speech with Kana-Domain ASR Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07575)
*Shiao Zhu,Lianbo Liu,Kai Washizaki,Koki Nikaido,Yui Sudo*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses a representation mismatch problem in using orthographic CER (Character Error Rate) for reinforcement learning post-training of Japanese TTS systems. The authors propose using Kana-CER instead, computed in the kana domain using a kana-transcribing ASR model, which reduces target-kanji reading errors by ~26% while maintaining comparable performance metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: For Japanese TTS post-training, orthographic CER has a fundamental problem: distinct kanji readings can map to the same written form, and equivalent pronunciations can have different orthographic representations. This creates a mismatch when optimizing for pronunciation-oriented intelligibility.

Method: The authors compute CER in the kana domain using a kana-transcribing ASR model and reference readings (Kana-CER). They compare this against orthographic CER under matched group relative policy optimization (GRPO) conditions, with KL regularization to control output elongation.

Result: Kana-CER reduces target-kanji reading error by approximately 26% relative to orthographic CER reward, while maintaining comparable orthographic CER, speaker similarity, and objective speech quality. It achieves best validation performance in substantially fewer optimization steps (4k vs 18k). Unregularized Kana-CER causes severe output elongation, which is substantially suppressed by KL regularization.

Conclusion: Kana-CER is a more suitable reward signal for Japanese TTS reinforcement learning post-training than orthographic CER, as it better aligns with pronunciation-oriented optimization goals and converges faster, though KL regularization is essential to prevent output elongation.

Abstract: Character error rate (CER) computed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) is widely used as an intelligibility reward for reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of text-to-speech (TTS) systems. For Japanese, however, orthographic CER introduces a representation mismatch for pronunciation-oriented optimization: distinct kanji readings may collapse to the same orthographic representation, while equivalent pronunciations may admit different orthographic forms. We instead compute CER in the kana domain using a kana-transcribing ASR model and reference readings (Kana-CER). Under matched group relative policy optimization (GRPO) conditions, Kana-CER reduces target-kanji reading error by approximately 26% relative to the orthographic CER reward, while maintaining comparable orthographic CER and similar speaker similarity and objective speech quality. It also reaches its best validation performance in substantially fewer optimization steps (4k vs. 18k). We further observe severe output elongation under unregularized Kana-CER optimization, which is substantially suppressed by KL regularization.

</details>


### [217] [Hiding Tool Latency in On-Device Cascaded Voice Agent through Speculative Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07641)
*Kyudan Jung,Hyunsin Park,Yoonhyung Lee,Jinhwan Park,Jinhyeok Yang,KiHyun Nam,Jaegul Choo,Jinkyu Lee*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents "speculative tool execution" for on-device voice assistants, which predicts tool requests from partial ASR hypotheses and initiates tool execution while the user is still speaking, thereby reducing end-to-end response latency. The approach uses a Predictor module, rule-based validation for self-corrections, and maintains baseline LLM tool-calling as a safety net.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current tool-augmented speech assistants suffer from high latency because tool execution only begins after the user finishes speaking and the LLM identifies required tool calls. This creates delays in receiving responses.

Method: The approach introduces a Predictor module that anticipates tool calls during speech recognition from partial ASR hypotheses, executes tools speculatively, and caches results. A rule-based validation mechanism handles user self-corrections during speech. The LLM retains direct tool-calling capability as a worst-case safety net.

Result: Live measurements on Android show: median time-to-first-audio reduced from 5.79s to 4.60s; standard deviation reduced from 3.49s to 2.81s, resulting in more predictable response latency.

Conclusion: Speculative tool execution effectively reduces voice assistant response latency while maintaining reliability through validation mechanisms and fallback to baseline execution.

Abstract: Tool-augmented speech assistants typically serialize automatic speech recognition, large language model inference, and external tool execution. As a result, tool latency is incurred only after the user has finished speaking and the LLM has identified the required tool calls. We present speculative tool execution for on-device cascaded voice agents, which predicts tool requests from partial ASR hypotheses and initiates tool execution while speech is still being received, thereby reducing end-to-end response latency. Our approach introduces a Predictor module that anticipates tool calls during speech recognition, executes them speculatively, and caches the results. The cached outputs are then injected into the LLM prompt, enabling faster responses. Additionally, to mitigate errors caused by user self-corrections during speech, we employ a rule-based validation mechanism that selectively injects only valid cached results. As a final safeguard, the LLM retains the ability to issue tool calls directly, ensuring that the latency of our framework is upper-bounded by the baseline serial execution pipeline in the worst case. We evaluate our method using live measurements from a fully implemented Android voice assistant. Our approach reduces the median time-to-first-audio from 5.79,s to 4.60,s and decreases the standard deviation from 3.49,s to 2.81,s, resulting in more predictable response latency.

</details>


### [218] [Loud and Clear: Dynamic Activation Steering for Improving Speech Intelligibility in Noisy Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07647)
*Seymanur Akti,Alexander Waibel*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A method to make text-to-speech models generate more intelligible speech in noisy environments by using activation steering, without requiring retraining. The approach mimics the Lombard effect in humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans naturally adapt their voice (Lombard effect) to compensate for noisy environments, increasing vocal effort and hyper-articulation. This paper investigates whether TTS models can be similarly guided to produce more intelligible speech without retraining.

Method: Introduced a prompt-relative steering mechanism that: 1) prevents steering effects from accumulating during generation, 2) allows dynamic strength adjustment. Focused on two Lombard effect characteristics: increased vocal effort and hyper-articulation. Evaluated across seen/unseen speakers and multiple languages.

Result: Systematic changes in Lombard-related acoustic features were produced. Speaker similarity was preserved (89-95%). Word Error Rate (WER) under background noise reduced by 7-22% at 1 dB SNR.

Conclusion: Pretrained TTS models can be dynamically controlled to generate more intelligible speech without retraining, demonstrating the viability of activation steering for improving speech intelligibility in noisy environments.

Abstract: Speech becomes less intelligible in noisy environments, and humans naturally adapt their voice to compensate. Inspired by this behavior, we investigate whether a text-to-speech (TTS) model can be guided to produce more intelligible speech using activation steering, without retraining. We focus on two characteristics of the Lombard effect: increased vocal effort and hyper-articulation. We introduce a prompt-relative steering mechanism that prevents steering effects from accumulating during generation while allowing their strength to be adjusted dynamically. Across seen and unseen speakers and multiple languages, our method produces systematic changes in Lombard-related acoustic features, preserves speaker similarity (89-95%), and reduces WER under background noise by 7-22% at 1 dB SNR. These results show that pretrained TTS models can be dynamically controlled to generate more intelligible speech without retraining.

</details>


### [219] [HiPLEX: Hierarchical Policy Factorization for Full Duplex Speech Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07727)
*Kyudan Jung,Hyunsin Park,Yoonhyung Lee,Jinhwan Park,Jinhyeok Yang,KiHyun Nam,Jaegul Choo,Jinkyu Lee*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: HiPLEX is a reinforcement learning framework for full-duplex speech dialogue systems that jointly optimizes timing and semantic content by factorizing the policy into a control policy (deciding when to speak) and a conditional content policy (deciding what to say).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for dialogue systems either optimize timing or semantic content separately, but not both jointly. Full-duplex speech models need to coordinate turn-taking, backchanneling, and floor management in real time, requiring a unified approach to optimize both when and what to emit.

Method: HiPLEX factorizes a pretrained full-duplex text policy into two components: (1) a control policy selecting among 'pad' (silence), 'epad' (early pause), and 'con' (content) actions; and (2) a conditional content policy that generates tokens only when 'con' is chosen. Timing feedback is routed via event-causal masks derived from speech episodes, while semantic feedback from an LLM-judge is routed to the content factor.

Result: On Full-Duplex-Bench v1, HiPLEX reduces takeover rates during natural user pauses and backchannel opportunities, shortens post-interruption response latency compared to GRPO, while maintaining comparable interruption-response quality. On Moshi and PersonaPlex, HiPLEX better matches human turn-timing and backchannel-rate marginals than GRPO.

Conclusion: HiPLEX successfully enables joint optimization of timing and content in full-duplex dialogue systems through hierarchical policy factorization, achieving better human-like timing behaviors while preserving response quality.

Abstract: As human--AI interactions become more conversational, full-duplex speech language models capable of natural real-time dialogue are growing in importance. Beyond generating appropriate responses, these models must coordinate turn-taking, backchanneling, and floor management in real time. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a way to refine these behaviors through direct feedback on interaction outcomes. However, existing RL methods either apply timing feedback to a token policy or optimize semantic content, leaving the joint improvement of timing and content unresolved. We introduce HiPLEX, an RL framework that factorizes a pretrained full-duplex text policy into a control policy that decides when to emit content and a conditional content policy that decides what to emit. The first factor selects among 'pad', 'epad', and 'con'. The second selects a token only when 'con' is chosen. This hierarchy describes conditional actions within each frame and uses the model's existing text head. We route timing advantages to the token-group factor through event-causal masks derived from generated speech episodes, and route an LLM-judge semantic advantage to the conditional content factor. Across three Moshi seeds on Full-Duplex-Bench v1, HiPLEX reduces takeover rates during natural user pauses and backchannel opportunities, and shortens post-interruption response latency relative to GRPO, while maintaining comparable judged interruption-response quality. On Moshi and PersonaPlex, HiPLEX better matches pooled human turn-timing and backchannel-rate marginals than GRPO.

</details>


### [220] [Feature Encoding in VAE-based Audio Decoders: Effects of Input, Depth and Distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07966)
*Louis McCallum,Mick Grierson*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study investigates how neural audio synthesis models (RAVE and EnCodec) encode musical features in their internal representations through systematic layer-wise and cross-layer cluster analysis of decoder activations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio synthesis models like RAVE achieve impressive generation quality, but how their internal representations encode musical features remains poorly understood. This research aims to advance the interpretability of neural audio models and inform targeted control strategies for neural synthesis.

Method: The researchers performed layer-wise and cross-layer cluster analysis of RAVE decoder activations across three models trained on different musical domains, tested with four stimulus types. They also evaluated architectural generalization using a general-purpose EnCodec model. Both linear and nonlinear probes were used to assess encoding strength.

Result: Synthetic stimuli showed strong encoding across models and audio features (pitch: ρ=0.45, 5.1× null; BPM: ρ=0.76, 8.6× null). Natural audio showed reduced but still apparent encoding (mean ρ=0.25, 2.8× null). Nonlinear probes significantly improved natural audio encoding (R²=0.56, 18× null, +0.152 gain over linear). Middle layers showed increased joint-encoding ability across all audio features (η² all negative, p<0.05). EnCodec showed similar patterns. Cross-layer clusters improved BPM encoding strength (r=0.65, p=0.006) and prevalence (r=0.75, p=0.001) compared to best whole layers.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that neural audio models encode musical features (pitch, BPM) in their representations, with middle layers showing enhanced joint-encoding capabilities. Cross-layer cluster analysis can improve feature encoding. These results advance interpretability of neural audio models and provide insights for developing targeted control strategies in neural synthesis applications.

Abstract: Neural audio synthesis models like the Realtime Audio Variational autoEncoder (RAVE) achieve impressive genera tion quality, yet how their internal representations encode musical features remains poorly understood. We present a systematic layer-wise and cross-layer cluster analysis of RAVE decoder activations across three models trained on different musical domains, tested with four stimulus types. We then evaluate architectural generalization with a general purpose EnCodec model. For RAVE, we find that synthetic stimuli are encoded well across models and audio features (pitch |\r{ho}|=0.45, 5.1x the null, BPM |\r{ho}| = 0.76, 8.6x the null). These results are reduced but still substantively apparent when using natural audio (mean across features |\r{ho}|=0.25, 2.8x the null). Natural audio sees a stronger encoding when nonlinear probes are used (mean across features R2=0.56, 18x the null, +0.152 nonlinear gain over the linear probe R2). Encoding strength varies throughout the layers of the decoder and an increased ability to joint-encode in the middle layers is seen across all audio features (\b{eta}2 all negative, p < 0.05). The general purpose EnCodec decoder also sees similar strong synthetic responses across audio features, similar nonlinear gains for natural audio joint encoding and similar depth profiles. We find the best cross-layer cluster improves the strength (r = 0.65, p = 0.006) and prevalence (r = 0.75, p = 0.001) of BPM encoding when compared against the best whole layers within the same section, with no effect for joint encoding. These findings advance the interpretability of neural audio models and inform targeted control strategies for neural synthesis.

</details>


### [221] [Exploiting Acoustic and Content-Oriented Speaker Verification Attacks Against Multilingual Voice Anonymization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08107)
*Ridwan Arefeen,Ze Li,Rong Tong,Ming Li,Xiaoxiao Miao*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates attacker Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) systems for voice anonymization in multilingual settings, a previously underexplored area. The study evaluates both acoustic- and content-oriented attackers on multilingual anonymized speech and creates a multilingual voice-converted dataset to improve cross-lingual generalization. Key findings show that attacker effectiveness depends on linguistic utility, with acoustic-oriented attackers generally performing better, though the performance gap narrows when linguistic information is well preserved. The multilingual dataset helps reduce cross-lingual gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous research on attacker ASV systems for voice anonymization has focused primarily on English, leaving their behavior in multilingual settings unexplored. This gap is significant because conventional ASV research has demonstrated that both acoustic and contextual information are important for multilingual speaker verification, raising the question of whether the same applies to attacker ASV systems.

Method: The study evaluated both acoustic-oriented and content-oriented attackers on multilingual anonymized speech. Additionally, a multilingual voice-converted dataset was constructed to improve cross-lingual generalization. The research examined how attacker effectiveness relates to the linguistic utility of anonymized speech.

Result: Acoustic-oriented attackers generally achieve better performance than content-oriented attackers. However, when linguistic information is well preserved in the anonymized speech, the performance gap between content- and acoustic-oriented attackers narrows compared to conditions with stronger speech distortion. The multilingual voice-converted dataset further improves performance and partially reduces the cross-lingual gap.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the need for more comprehensive attacker modeling and evaluation protocols that consider both privacy and utility, rather than relying on a single attacker strategy. Future systems should account for multilingual scenarios and balance privacy protection with linguistic utility preservation.

Abstract: Attacker ASV systems for voice anonymization have been studied primarily in English, leaving their behavior in multilingual settings largely unexplored. Conventional ASV has shown that both acoustic and contextual information are important for multilingual speaker verification. Inspired by this, we investigate whether the same holds for attacker ASV on anonymized speech. We evaluate both acoustic- and content-oriented attackers on multilingual anonymized speech and construct a multilingual voice-converted dataset to improve cross-lingual generalization. Our results show that attacker effectiveness depends on the linguistic utility of the anonymized speech. Overall, acoustic-oriented attackers achieve better performance. However, when linguistic information is well preserved, the performance gap between content- and acoustic-oriented attackers narrows compared with conditions involving stronger speech distortion. The multilingual voice-converted dataset further improves performance and partially reduces the cross-lingual gap. These findings highlight the need for more comprehensive attacker modeling and evaluation protocols that consider both privacy and utility, rather than relying on a attacker strategy\footnote{Full code and pretrained models and MultiVC Dataset link are available at: https://github.com/monkeyDarefeen/DAST

</details>


### [222] [Geometric Representations for Transformed Pattern Matching in Music](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08236)
*David Meredith*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes using point set representations (geometric pitch-time coordinates) for pattern matching in polyphonic music, rather than traditional sequential representations. The authors show how musical transformations (transposition, inversion, augmentation, etc.) can be modeled as geometric transformations, and apply this to analyze Ravel's Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional sequential representations are inadequate for matching patterns in unvoiced, polyphonic keyboard music. The authors argue that point set representations are better adapted for this purpose, as they can capture geometric relationships between notes that remain invariant under various musical transformations.

Method: The authors identify eight types of geometric pitch-time representations by combining four pitch representations (chromatic pitch, morphetic pitch, morph, chroma) with two time representations (onset time, midtime). They model musical transformations as geometric transformations (translation, scaling, reflection). They introduce the concept of an inter-pattern transformation graph to visualize relationships between patterns within a transformation class.

Result: The authors demonstrate that different representations characterize different transformations differently. Using midtime instead of onset time allows precise characterization of retrograde relationships. Using morph and chroma pitch representations enables characterization of transformations involving octave displacements and duplications. They show that the musical relationships in Ravel's Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn can be precisely described using transformation classes F_2STR, F_2STRMod7, and F_2STRMod12.

Conclusion: Geometric pitch-time representations provide a powerful framework for analyzing pattern relationships in polyphonic music. The choice of representation significantly affects which transformations can be characterized, and the inter-pattern transformation graph is an effective tool for visualizing musical relationships across a set of patterns.

Abstract: We review the notion of representing music using point sets and argue that such representations are better adapted than sequential representations for matching patterns in unvoiced, polyphonic music, such as keyboard music. Musical transformations such as transposition, inversion, diminution, augmentation and retrograde can be modelled by geometric transformations in pitch-time representations that combine translation with scaling parallel to and reflection in the time axis. We identify eight types of geometric pitch-time representation that use chromatic pitch, morphetic pitch, morph or chroma to represent pitch and either onset time or midtime to represent time. We illustrate how these types of representation allow us to characterise different types of musical transformation. For example, by using midtime instead of onset time, we can precisely characterise certain retrograde relationships; and by using morph and chroma pitch representations we can characterise transformations involving octave displacements and duplications. We present the concept of a transformation class and consider the three specific classes, $F_{\mathrm{2STR}}$, $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod7}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod12}}$. We introduce the notion of an inter-pattern transformation graph for a set of patterns, $S$, and a transformation class, $F$. Each vertex in such a graph represents a pattern in $S$ and there is an edge in the graph from pattern $P_1$ to pattern $P_2$ if and only if $P_1$ can be mapped onto $P_2$ by a transformation in $F$. We show, with the aid of such graphs, that the musical relationships between the occurrences of the HAYDN theme in Ravel's Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn can be precisely described in terms of transformations in $F_{\mathrm{2STR}}$, $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod7}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod12}}$ within the pitch-time representations considered.

</details>


### [223] [Restore, Separate, Restore: A Modular Framework for Music Source Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08284)
*Tobias Morocutti,Emmanouil Karystinaios,Gerhard Widmer*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A three-stage framework for Music Source Restoration (MSR) that addresses nonlinear production effects and transmission degradations, achieving progressive improvement through mixture restoration, 8-stem separation, and stem-specific expert refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional source separation assumes linear mixtures of clean sources, but real-world recordings involve nonlinear processing (EQ, compression) and degradations (codec artifacts). MSR aims to recover original unprocessed instrument stems from mixed, mastered, and degraded recordings, requiring inversion of these nonlinear effects.

Method: Three-stage framework: (1) Mixture restoration model to address degradation before separation; (2) Single separator model for 8 target stems (vocals, guitars, keyboards, synthesizers, bass, drums, percussion, orchestra); (3) Stem-specific restoration experts fine-tuned on the separator's residual artifacts.

Result: Each stage improves restoration quality over the previous one on the MSR Challenge test set. Code and models are released publicly.

Conclusion: The proposed three-stage approach effectively handles the unique challenges of MSR by progressively improving restoration quality through dedicated restoration, separation, and expert refinement stages.

Abstract: Music Source Restoration (MSR) seeks to recover original, unprocessed instrument stems from mixed, mastered, and possibly degraded recordings. Unlike conventional source separation, which treats the mixture as a linear sum of clean sources, MSR must additionally invert nonlinear production effects, such as equalization and compression, and transmission-related degradations, such as codec artifacts. We propose a three-stage framework built around this distinction: (1) a mixture restoration model that addresses degradation before separation, (2) a single model that separates the restored mixture into eight target stems (vocals, guitars, keyboards, synthesizers, bass, drums, percussion, and orchestra), and (3) stem-specific restoration experts fine-tuned on the separator's own residual artifacts. Each stage improves restoration quality over the previous one on the MSR Challenge test set. We release code and models to support future research in MSR at https://github.com/theMoro/music_source_restoration.

</details>


### [224] [Sobolev Norms in Neural Embeddings Measure Audio Morphing Regularity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08295)
*Théo Chasle Cauchy,Modan Tailleur,Barbara Pascal,Fanny Roche,Mathieu Lagrange*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces Sobolev Distances to Ideal Morphing (SDIM), a novel objective metric for evaluating the regularity of audio morphing trajectories in perceptually relevant audio embedding spaces, addressing the challenge of evaluating perceptual morphing quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Morphing has gained renewed interest with generative models in audio and image generation, but evaluating this perceptually-defined task is challenging. Existing metrics fail to reliably discriminate between desirable and undesirable morphing trajectories.

Method: The authors propose SDIM, a novel objective metric leveraging Sobolev distances in perceptually relevant audio embedding spaces. They evaluate its discriminative power on controlled morphing trajectories with varying regularity degrees using a physics-based sound synthesizer, comparing with existing audio morphing metrics.

Result: The proposed SDIM metric reliably discriminates desirable morphing trajectories from adversarial ones, whereas state-of-the-art metrics fail to do so.

Conclusion: SDIM provides a reliable objective metric for evaluating audio morphing quality in perceptually meaningful terms, outperforming existing approaches.

Abstract: Morphing has recently gained renewed interest with the emergence of generative models, particularly in audio and image generation. In musical sound synthesis, morphing can generate intermediate sounds between two targets, helping musicians and sound engineers explore new sounds with interesting perceptual properties. As morphing is inherently defined in perceptual terms, evaluating this task is challenging. In this work, we introduce Sobolev Distances to Ideal Morphing (SDIM), a novel objective metric to quantify the regularity of audio morphing trajectories in perceptually relevant audio embedding spaces. Leveraging a physics-based sound synthesizer, we evaluate the discriminative power of SDIM on controlled morphing trajectories with varying degrees of regularity and compare it with that of existing audio morphing metrics. Results show that, contrary to state-of-the-art metrics, the proposed metric reliably discriminates desirable trajectories from adversarial ones.

</details>


### [225] [WorldSonus: Bringing Sound to Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08760)
*Pengjun Fang,Jingyi Fa,Kam Man Wu,Jiaming Wang,Haoyuan Huang,Yaguang Wu,Xiangjun Huang,Ziyang Ma,Weijia Chen,Hongyu Liu,Zeyue Tian,Qifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: WorldSonus is an interactive video-to-audio framework for real-time spatial sound synthesis in world models. It addresses three core challenges: real-time generation (RTF 0.41), interactive control via audio-centric captioning with chunk-indexed prompt scheduling, and spatial alignment using high-quality stereo supervision. The method generalizes to open-domain benchmarks, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art bidirectional models in acoustic quality and spatial alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent advances in world models enable realistic visual synthesis, but generated environments remain largely silent. Bringing sound to world models poses three core challenges: (1) real-time generation to keep pace with interactive video streams, (2) interactive control to respond to mid-stream sound instructions, and (3) spatially aligned stereo to reflect scene geometry and camera motion.

Method: WorldSonus employs three key technical components: (1) A streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture for real-time audio synthesis at RTF 0.41; (2) An audio-centric captioning pipeline with chunk-indexed prompt scheduling for dynamic sound event manipulation during generation; (3) High-quality stereo supervision curated from diverse stereo and ambisonic data for spatial alignment.

Result: WorldSonus achieves real-time audio synthesis with low latency (RTF 0.41). While tailored for world models, it generalizes effectively to open-domain video-to-audio benchmarks, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art bidirectional models in both acoustic quality and spatial alignment.

Conclusion: WorldSonus successfully brings interactive, spatially-aware audio to world models in real-time, demonstrating that the approach can generalize beyond its original design to compete with or surpass existing state-of-the-art video-to-audio methods in acoustic quality and spatial alignment.

Abstract: Recent advances in world models have enabled increasingly realistic visual synthesis. However, these generated environments remain largely silent. Bringing sound to world models poses three core challenges: real-time generation to keep pace with interactive video streams, interactive control to respond to mid-stream sound instructions, and spatially aligned stereo to reflect scene geometry and camera motion. To address these demands, we introduce WorldSonus, an interactive video-to-audio framework designed for real-time spatial sound synthesis in world models. For real-time generation, WorldSonus employs a streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that synthesizes audio chunks at a low real-time factor (RTF) of 0.41. For interactive control, we incorporate an audio-centric captioning pipeline with chunk-indexed prompt scheduling, enabling dynamic manipulation of sound events during generation. For spatial alignment, we leverage high-quality stereo supervision curated from diverse stereo and ambisonic data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while tailored for world models, WorldSonus generalizes effectively to open-domain video-to-audio benchmarks, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art bidirectional models in both acoustic quality and spatial alignment. Project page: https://noizai.github.io/WorldSonus/

</details>

### [226] [UltraDiff: Differentiable Ray Tracing in Ultrasound for Shape Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07941)
*Felix Duelmer,Magdalena Wysocki,Nassir Navab,Mohammad Farid Azampour*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: UltraDiff is a modular framework for differentiable ultrasound ray tracing that extends physically-based differentiable rendering to medical ultrasound imaging. It formulates ultrasound image formation as a path-space integral and derives Monte Carlo estimators for both forward modeling and gradient computation, enabling analysis-by-synthesis optimization of scene parameters (SDF) to reconstruct tissue interfaces from B-mode images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physically-based differentiable rendering has been successful for light transport but has not been applied to medical ultrasound. Ultrasound image formation resembles transient rendering (echoes binned by time-of-flight), presenting an opportunity to apply this paradigm. Current state-of-the-art ultrasound shape reconstruction methods rely on pre-segmented images, requiring supervision, whereas an unsupervised approach through analysis-by-synthesis would be more flexible and robust.

Method: UltraDiff formulates ultrasound image formation as a path-space integral gated by travel time between transducer and tissue interfaces. It derives a Monte Carlo estimator for both the forward model and its gradients with respect to scene parameters. The framework is implemented on top of Mitsuba 3 and uses an SDF (Signed Distance Function) representation that is optimized until simulated echoes match measured ones. The approach operates unsupervised on B-mode images through analysis-by-synthesis.

Result: The method successfully recovers vertebral surfaces from both simulated B-mode sweeps and real robotic acquisition of a spine phantom. It achieves competitive geometric accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, but operates unsupervised on B-mode images rather than relying on pre-segmented images. UltraDiff brings differentiable path tracing to the acoustic imaging domain.

Conclusion: UltraDiff demonstrates that physically-based differentiable rendering principles can be successfully applied to medical ultrasound, enabling unsupervised analysis-by-synthesis for tissue interface reconstruction. This provides a foundation for inverse problems in acoustic imaging and opens new possibilities for inverse geometry estimation in medical ultrasound applications.

Abstract: Physically-based differentiable rendering enables gradient-based optimization of scene parameters by matching rendered images to measurements, but has so far mainly focused on light transport. We extend this paradigm to medical ultrasound, where image formation resembles transient rendering: echoes are binned by time-of-flight rather than projected onto an image plane. We present UltraDiff, a modular framework for differentiable ultrasound ray tracing. UltraDiff formulates ultrasound image formation as a path-space integral, gated by travel time between the transducer and tissue interfaces, and derives a Monte Carlo estimator of both the forward model and its gradients with respect to scene parameters. We demonstrate this on an inverse geometry estimation: starting from a sphere, an SDF is optimized until simulated echoes match measured ones, recovering vertebral surfaces from simulated B-mode sweeps and from a real robotic acquisition of a spine phantom. Unlike state-of-the-art ultrasound shape reconstruction methods, which rely on pre-segmented images, our approach operates unsupervised on B-mode images through analysis-by-synthesis, while achieving competitive geometric accuracy. Implemented on top of Mitsuba 3, UltraDiff brings differentiable path tracing to a new sensing modality and provides a foundation for inverse problems in acoustic imaging.

</details>


### [227] [PrimitiveCAD: An LLM-Based Point-to-CAD Reconstruction with Primitive-Aware Tokenization and Operation Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08698)
*Jian Gao,Kailin Bi,Jiamin Xu,Jinlan Xu,Gang Xu*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: PrimitiveCAD is a novel multi-stage framework for point-to-CAD reconstruction that uses large language models to generate CAD models from point clouds. It addresses the limitation of existing methods that treat this as general point-cloud encoding without CAD-specific primitives, resulting in poor reconstruction of intricate primitive structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods approach point-to-CAD generation as a general point-cloud encoding and token prediction task, neglecting tokenization and supervision specifically for CAD-related primitives. This leads to inaccurate reconstruction of intricate primitive structures and poor preservation of geometric features in generated CAD models.

Method: The proposed method has three main components: (1) A primitive-aware point cloud tokenization model that learns robust geometric representations from CAD point clouds; (2) Supervised fine-tuning on an LLM with operation alignment loss to align key CAD operation frequencies and preserve global shape features; (3) Reinforcement learning with feature-line alignment reward to reduce stochasticity and enhance fine-grained preservation of geometric features.

Result: Experiments on DeepCAD and Fusion360 datasets show that PrimitiveCAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in code validity, geometric accuracy, and geometric feature preservation.

Conclusion: The multi-stage paradigm combining primitive-aware tokenization, supervised fine-tuning with operation alignment, and reinforcement learning with feature-line alignment effectively addresses the limitations of prior approaches, significantly improving CAD reconstruction quality from point clouds.

Abstract: Large-model-based point-to-CAD generation holds immense potential for advancing industrial design and enhancing 3D modeling efficiency. However, most existing methods approach the problem as a general point-cloud encoding and token prediction task, neglecting the tokenization and supervision specifically for CAD-related primitives. As a result, these methods often struggle to accurately reconstruct the intricate primitive structures. To address this limitation, we propose PrimitiveCAD, a novel multi-stage paradigm for point-to-CAD reconstruction that enhances the geometric accuracy of generated CAD models while better preserving critical geometric features. First, we introduce a primitive-aware point cloud tokenization model, enabling the system to learn more robust geometric representations from CAD point clouds. Next, we perform supervised finetuning on a large language model (LLM) and introduce an operation alignment loss to align key CAD operation frequencies, thereby improving the preservation of global shape features. Finally, we incorporate reinforcement learning (RL) and introduce a feature-line alignment reward to further reduce stochasticity and enhance the fine-grained preservation of geometric features. Experiments on the DeepCAD and Fusion360 datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in code validity, geometric accuracy, and geometric feature preservation.

</details>


### [228] [Local Content-Style Control for Diffusion-based Image Stylization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08704)
*Amir Semmo*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a method to enable region-specific control in image stylization pipelines using latent-diffusion models, by lifting global conditioning weights to per-location spatial maps for independent control of content and style axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current image stylization pipelines with latent-diffusion models (like ControlNet + IP-Adapter) only provide global controls, but professional retouching requires deliberate, region-specific control over both what a region depicts (content) and how it is depicted (style).

Method: The method lifts two conditioning weights from a ControlNet + IP-Adapter stylization pipeline from global scalars to per-location spatial maps. Since the two weights act on disjoint pathways in the pipeline, they can be adjusted independently to achieve local control of content and style in a single generative pass.

Result: The approach enables a 2x2 retouching vocabulary - from free regeneration to identity preservation - by independently adjusting the two weights. Edits stay confined to the retouched region, and each weight predominantly steers its own axis (content or style). The method requires no retraining and can be integrated into any such pipeline.

Conclusion: This work provides fine-grained, region-specific control for image stylization without retraining, addressing the gap between global-only controls and professional retouching needs. The approach is plug-and-play and maintains the independence of content and style axes.

Abstract: Image stylization with latent-diffusion models entangles two independently refined axes: what a region depicts and how it is depicted. Such pipelines expose only global controls, yet professional retouching demands deliberate, region-specific control. We lift two conditioning weights already present in a ControlNet + IP-Adapter stylization pipeline from global scalars to per-location spatial maps, yielding local, per-axis control of content and style in a single generative pass. Because the two weights act on disjoint pathways, adjusting them independently spans a 2x2 retouching vocabulary, from free regeneration to identity preservation. We validate that edits stay confined to the retouched region and that each weight predominantly steers its own axis. Our approach requires no retraining and drops unchanged into any such pipeline.

</details>
