### [229] [SAFESHIELD: A Decision-Organization Framework for Deployment-Time Safety of Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07276)
*Xingru Zhou,Luis Sentis,Aarti Choudhary*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents SAFESHIELD, a deployment-time safety system for small language models that organizes safety decisions into four responsibilities (admission, routing, evidence, release) and uses auditable Decision Traces. The key insight is that deployment-time safety depends not only on individual guardrail capabilities but also on how decisions are organized and coordinated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deployment frameworks provide capable mechanisms for runtime guardrails (input moderation, routing, retrieval verification, output filtering) but offer limited guidance on explicitly organizing, coordinating, and auditing the safety decisions these mechanisms produce. The authors frame deployment-time safety as a decision-organization problem.

Method: The authors formulate deployment-time safety as a decision-organization problem with two elements: (1) responsibility-oriented decomposition of safety decisions, and (2) explicit coordination among them. They instantiate this formulation in SAFESHIELD, which organizes four recurring decision responsibilities (admission, routing, evidence, and release) and records decisions in auditable Decision Traces. Evaluation includes: mechanism-level experiments, aggregate stage ablations, controlled coordination ablations (preserving safeguard mechanisms while severing their dependencies), and a deployment-oriented stress suite.

Result: Mechanism-level results show the instantiated safeguards provide required capabilities. Aggregate ablations show substantial degradation in end-to-end safety as surrounding safety organization is removed. Coordination ablations reveal: removing admission gating substantially increases false release; withholding upstream evidence from release decision reduces release accuracy from 96.0% to 69.5%.

Conclusion: Deployment-time safety depends not only on the capability of individual guardrails but also on how their decisions are organized and coordinated. This provides system-level evidence for the importance of decision organization in safety-critical LLM deployments.

Abstract: Deployment-time safety of language models is commonly implemented through runtime guardrails such as input moderation, routing, retrieval verification, and output filtering. Existing deployment frameworks provide increasingly capable mechanisms for these functions, but offer limited guidance on how the safety decisions they produce should be explicitly organized, coordinated, and audited. We formulate deployment-time safety as a decision-organization problem with two elements: responsibility-oriented decomposition of safety decisions and explicit coordination among them. We instantiate this formulation in SAFESHIELD, a deployment-time safety system for small language models that organizes four recurring decision responsibilities (admission, routing, evidence, and release) and records committed decisions in auditable Decision Traces. We evaluate SAFESHIELD through mechanism-level experiments, aggregate stage ablations, controlled coordination ablations, and a deployment-oriented stress suite. Mechanism-level results show that the instantiated safeguards provide the capabilities required by the decision process, while aggregate ablations show substantial degradation in end-to-end safety as the surrounding safety organization is removed. More importantly, dedicated coordination ablations preserve the participating safeguard mechanisms while selectively severing their dependencies: removing admission gating substantially increases false release, and withholding upstream evidence from the release decision reduces release accuracy from 96.0% to 69.5%. These results provide system-level evidence that deployment-time safety depends not only on the capability of individual guardrails, but also on how their decisions are organized and coordinated.

</details>


### [230] [Catching Developers in the Flow: Low-Latency Agentic Program Repair at Google Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07289)
*Celal Ziftci,Spencer Greene,Ray Liu,Livio Dalloro,Lorenzo Dini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FlowAgent is an AI agent deployed at Google for automatically repairing test failures in pre-submit continuous integration workflows. It uses a ReAct-style generate-and-validate loop with abstention filters to provide high-quality fixes under latency constraints. Achieved 67.18% accuracy on 195 real-world test failures and has been applied to 28,554 changes Google-wide.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual repair of program failures is time-consuming and disruptive for developers, especially during pre-submit phase in CI systems. Existing LLM-based automated repair techniques focus on post-submit workflows and don't meet low-latency requirements for real-time developer assistance.

Method: FlowAgent uses a ReAct-style generate-and-validate loop with pre-execution and post-execution abstention filters to ensure high-quality suggestions under strict latency constraints. Integrated into Google's internal developer tools (Critique and Cider).

Result: Manual evaluation on 195 real-world test failures showed 67.18% accuracy. Following deployment, FlowAgent suggested fixes on 295,508 changes; developers previewed 65,069 and applied 28,554. Developer feedback indicates the agent is useful and well-received.

Conclusion: FlowAgent demonstrates high effectiveness in automated program repair for pre-submit workflows. The integration of autonomous repair agents into industrial software engineering workflows is viable and well-received, though challenges and opportunities remain.

Abstract: Manual repair of program failures is time-consuming and disruptive for software developers, particularly during the pre-submit phase where test failures occur within continuous integration systems. While Automated Program Repair has seen significant advancement through Large Language Models, existing state-of-the-art techniques primarily focus on post-submit workflows, operating offline without the low-latency requirements necessary to assist developers in real-time within their flow before they switch context.
  In this paper, we introduce FlowAgent, an AI agent deployed at Google to automatically repair test failures in the pre-submit outer-loop workflow inside continuous integration systems. Integrated into Google's internal developer tools, Critique and Cider,FlowAgent utilizes a ReAct-style generate-and-validate loop, as well as rigorous pre-execution and post-execution abstention filters to ensure high-quality suggestions under strict latency constraints.
  Based on our case studies, FlowAgent is highly effective. First, a manual evaluation conducted on 195 real-world test failures demonstrated 67.18% accuracy in suggesting correct fixes. Following its Google-wide deployment, FlowAgent suggested fixes on 295,508changes, of which developers previewed 65,069 and applied 28,554. Developer feedback from interviews indicate that the agent is useful in suggesting correct fixes, integration of autonomous repair agents into industrial software engineering workflows is received well, while interesting challenges and opportunities still remain.

</details>


### [231] [A Validated Dataset and Benchmark for Coherent Multi-Diagram SysML Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07356)
*Ardalan Aryashad,Yan Jin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SEMAADB is a dataset of 3,000 engineering contexts with 15,000 SysML diagrams (5 views per context: Requirement, Block Definition, Activity, State Machine, Sequence) designed to evaluate language models' ability to generate coherent multi-diagram system engineering models. The benchmark includes 100 human-verified contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can generate diagrams, but their ability to create coherent sets of diagrams at scale is not well understood. Existing datasets and benchmarks do not directly measure this ability, creating a need for comprehensive evaluation resources.

Method: Created a dataset of 3,000 engineering contexts with 15,000 connected SysML views (Requirement, Block Definition, Activity, State Machine, Sequence). Validated diagram consistency and rendering. Used 100 human-verified contexts as benchmark test set. Evaluated three language models on two tasks: (1) diagram repair (semantic error correction) and (2) cross-diagram update (propagating changes across related diagrams).

Result: In diagram repair task, the strongest model repaired 64.3% of semantic errors. In cross-diagram update task, the best propagation F1 was 80.7% when applying one change across related diagrams. Syntax repair is nearly solved, but semantic repair and cross-diagram consistency remain challenging.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that while syntax repair in SysML diagram generation is nearly solved, semantic repair and maintaining consistency across multiple diagrams are still significant challenges for language models. SEMAADB provides both a large diagram resource and benchmark for measuring coherent multi-diagram SysML generation.

Abstract: Systems engineers use several diagrams to describe the structure and behavior of systems. Engineers create these diagrams together to make sure that they use the same elements and remain consistent with one another. Large language models can generate diagrams as text or code, which makes it possible to create system diagrams automatically. However, their ability to generate coherent sets of diagrams is not well understood, and existing datasets and benchmarks do not directly measure this ability at scale. We introduce SEMAADB (Systems Engineering Modeling Assistant with AI Dataset and Benchmark), a dataset of 3,000 engineering contexts and 15,000 diagrams. Each context contains five connected SysML views: Requirement, Block Definition, Activity, State Machine, and Sequence. Here, a view is a diagram that presents one aspect of a system. We checked the diagram sets for consistency and valid rendering. A set of 100 contexts is also human-verified and forms the benchmark test set. We evaluate three language models on two tasks. In diagram repair, the strongest model repairs 64.3% of semantic errors . In cross-diagram update the best propagation F1 is 80.7% when a model applies one change across related diagrams. The results show that syntax repair is nearly solved, but semantic repair and consistency across diagrams are still challenging tasks for models. SEMAADB therefore provides both a large diagram resource and a set of benchmarks for measuring coherent multi-diagram SysML generation.

</details>


### [232] [CogAdapt: Cognition-informed Sparse Adaptation of Code LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07446)
*Yueke Zhang,Zihan Fang,Kevin Leach,Yu Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CogAdapt is a cognition-informed framework that uses human EEG and attention data to guide task-dependent sparse adaptation of code models, achieving state-of-the-art pass@1 on LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench while reducing gradient-eligible adaptation parameters by 86.21-87.21%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Achieving stronger code-generation performance relies on costly model adaptation (fine-tuning). Human cognitive signals during code reading may indicate not only what to learn but also where adaptation is most useful, potentially reducing training costs while maintaining performance.

Method: CogAdapt learns transferable program-level and token-level priors from human EEG and attention data, then combines these priors with the frozen model's response to each coding task to determine adaptation allocation and which transformer blocks should receive updates. Only selected blocks are updated during fine-tuning.

Result: CogAdapt achieves the best pass@1 across both LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench, including gains of 10.86 and 6.29 percentage points over matched regular fine-tuning on LiveCodeBench, while reducing gradient-eligible adaptation parameters by 86.21-87.21%. Consistent correspondence between human reading behavior and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) computation was found across Qwen and GLM models.

Conclusion: Human comprehension signals can provide useful guidance for making code-model adaptation both more selective and more effective, enabling significant parameter reduction without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable of generating code. However, achieving stronger code-generation performance still often relies on costly model adaptation, i.e., fine-tuning pretrained model parameters. Prior studies have shown correspondence between human code processing and neural models' attention or internal computation. Human-aligned learning approaches use cognitive signals to guide training, but typically adapt a large portion of the model, leaving training costs largely unchanged. Human cognitive signals may indicate not only what the model must learn from, but also where adaptation is most useful. We investigate whether human responses during code reading correspond to code-model behavior and can guide selective adaptation without sacrificing performance.
  We present CogAdapt, a cognition-informed framework for task-dependent sparse adaptation of code models. CogAdapt first learns transferable program-level and token-level priors from human Electroencephalography (EEG) and attention data, then combines these priors with the frozen model's response to each coding task to determine how much adaptation to allocate and which transformer blocks should receive updates. During fine-tuning, only the selected blocks are updated, while no new human recordings are required for inference. Across Qwen and GLM, we find consistent correspondence between human reading behavior and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) computation. CogAdapt achieves the best pass@1 across both LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench, including gains of 10.86 and 6.29 percentage points over matched regular fine-tuning on LiveCodeBench, while reducing gradient-eligible adaptation parameters by 86.21-87.21%. These results suggest that human comprehension signals can provide useful guidance for making code-model adaptation both more selective and more effective.

</details>


### [233] [The EPIC Framework for Spec-Driven Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07534)
*Bruno Claudino,Ruizhe Xing,Yuanhao Zuo,Tyler Menezes,Anita Sarma,Kostadin Damevski,Zixuan Feng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents EPIC, a framework of 40 practices in 10 quality dimensions to help developers write complete specifications for coding agents. The framework was derived from analyzing 114 open-source SDD repositories against ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards, and shows that higher-quality specifications correlate with fewer bug fixes (11.8% vs 20.4%) and more contributors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the observation that coding agents often fill gaps in their instructions with their own assumptions, and that small wording choices (like "must" vs "should") significantly impact agent behavior. Existing SDD templates do not help developers judge whether their specifications are complete or clear enough.

Method: The researchers scored artifacts from 114 open-source SDD repositories against the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standard, derived practices from the highest-scoring repositories, and validated the resulting framework with 15 SDD practitioners.

Result: The EPIC framework contains 40 practices across 10 quality dimensions that guide developers in making expectations and decisions explicit. All 15 practitioners endorsed every practice. Repositories in the top third of specification quality had 11.8% bug fix commits vs 20.4% in the bottom third, and had 4x as many contributors.

Conclusion: Developers can use EPIC to identify and fill gaps in their specifications before coding agents do, leading to better code quality (fewer bug fixes) and increased collaboration (more contributors).

Abstract: One practitioner we interviewed said their team writes "must" instead of "should" when instructing a coding agent, because the agent may treat "should" as optional. Small wording choices matter because agents often fill gaps in their instructions with their own assumptions. Spec-driven development (SDD) asks developers to write a specification, plan, and tasks before the agent writes code. SDD frameworks provide templates for these artifacts, but the templates do not help developers judge whether they have written enough or clearly enough. We studied what good SDD specifications contain. We scored the artifacts of 114 open-source SDD repositories against ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and derived practices from the highest-scoring ones. The resulting framework, EPIC, has 40 practices in 10 quality dimensions that guide developers in making expectations and decisions explicit in specifications, plans, and tasks for coding agents. The majority of SDD practitioners (N=15) endorsed every practice. Repositories in the top third of specification quality spent 11.8% of their commits on bug fixes, compared with 20.4% in the bottom third, and had a median of 4x as many contributors. Developers can use EPIC to find and fill the gaps in a specification before the agent does.

</details>


### [234] [CheckerBench: Can Long-Horizon Agents Synthesize Static-Analysis Checkers?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07557)
*Hang He,Li Wang,Hao Chen,Yuchen Shao,Yuling Shi,Lisheng Wang,Peiyang Liu,Goose Lin,Zaiyuan Wang,Haiying Sun,Ting Su,Chengcheng Wan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CheckerBench is a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop working static-analysis checkers from CVE specifications. The benchmark contains 300 tasks from 297 CVEs across 167 repositories. Evaluation using CheckerLab shows that current coding agents achieve only 32.30% mean Pass@1 (best: 45.33%), indicating that reliable checker development remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding-agent benchmarks focus on patch generation or vulnerability detection, but rarely assess whether agents can develop a complete working checker in a repository from start to finish. This includes interpreting defect specifications, inspecting repositories, implementing analyzer-specific logic, and refining the checker through feedback.

Method: The researchers created CheckerBench with 300 tasks derived from 297 CVEs across 167 repositories, 85 CWEs, and five language ecosystems. Each task includes vulnerable and fixed revisions, a pinned analysis environment, and a checker scaffold. They introduced CheckerLab as an evaluation framework that rebuilds submitted checkers and measures diagnostic contrast, patch localization, false positives, and tool use. They tested 21 model-harness configurations with three independent repeats each.

Result: Across 21 model-harness configurations and three independent repeats per configuration, mean Pass@1 is 32.30%, while the best configuration reaches 45.33%. These results demonstrate that reliable, reusable checker development remains challenging for current coding agents.

Conclusion: Developing reliable, reusable static-analysis checkers from CVE specifications remains a significant challenge for current coding agents. The benchmark and evaluation framework (CheckerBench and CheckerLab) provide a standardized way to assess this capability in future agent development.

Abstract: Static-analysis checker synthesis requires agents to interpret a defect specification, inspect a repository, implement analyzer-specific logic, and refine the checker through repeated compilation and analysis feedback. Existing coding-agent benchmarks focus on tasks such as patch generation or vulnerability detection and rarely assess whether an agent can develop a working checker in a repository from start to finish. We introduce CheckerBench, an executable benchmark of 300 tasks derived from 297 CVEs across 167 repositories, 85 CWEs, and five language ecosystems. Each task includes vulnerable and fixed revisions, a pinned analysis environment, and a checker scaffold. We further introduce CheckerLab, a common evaluation framework that independently rebuilds submitted checkers and measures vulnerable-fixed diagnostic contrast, patch localization, false positives, and tool use. Across 21 model-harness configurations and three independent repeats per configuration, mean Pass@1 is 32.30%, while the best reaches 45.33%. These results show that reliable, reusable checker development remains challenging for current coding agents.

</details>


### [235] [When Old Facts Return: Re-Reads, Reverts, and the Limits of Temporal Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07715)
*Neeraj Yadav*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses ambiguity in memory systems between restoring obsolete values (stale values) and genuine reverts to previous states. Using 130 atomic transitions from software fixes, the study shows identity-based temporal memory achieves 98.5% accuracy under normal conditions but drops to 10.8% when old statements are re-read verbatim. A guard mechanism restores accuracy to 97.7% but cannot distinguish legitimate reverts without change provenance. The key design implication is distinguishing observation of a value from evidence of change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that memory systems cannot distinguish between a stale value (restored because the same old statement appears again) and a genuine revert (actual restoration of a previous value). This ambiguity causes significant accuracy degradation in certain conditions, specifically when old source statements are re-read verbatim.

Method: The study analyzed 130 extractor-selected atomic transitions derived from software fixes, with two supporting studies examining: (1) exposing retired history to the answer model, and (2) supplying current source for changed behavior. An exploratory extraction study over 707 software fixes provided scope context.

Result: Under ordinary transition conditions, identity-based temporal memory achieved 98.5% model-judged accuracy with zero observed errors. When appending a verbatim re-read of the old statement, accuracy dropped to 10.8% with 88.5% stale-value rate. Adding a guard that refuses to reactivate retired values restored accuracy to 97.7% and reduced stale-value rate to 0.8%, but the guard cannot recognize legitimate reverts without additional change provenance.

Conclusion: The design implication is that systems must distinguish observation of a value from evidence that the value changed. The guard mechanism effectively prevents stale value reactivation but cannot identify legitimate reverts without additional change provenance information. Limitations include selected inputs, aggregate-only answer records, related-family judges, and post-failure guard evaluation.

Abstract: A memory system can retire an obsolete value and later restore it merely because the same old statement appears again. A re-read of an old source and a genuine revert can produce the same observed sequence of values while requiring opposite current answers. We study this ambiguity on 130 extractor-selected atomic transitions derived from software fixes. In the ordinary transition condition, identity-based temporal memory reaches 98.5% model-judged accuracy with zero observed errors under a literal stale-value proxy. Appending a verbatim re-read of the old statement reduces accuracy to 10.8% and raises the stale-value rate to 88.5%. A guard that refuses to reactivate a previously retired value restores accuracy to 97.7% and reduces that rate to 0.8% in this constructed re-read condition. The guard cannot also recognize a legitimate revert without additional change provenance. Two supporting studies examine exposing retired history to the answer model and supplying current source for changed behavior. An exploratory extraction study over 707 software fixes provides scope context, not a universal coverage estimate. The design implication is to distinguish an observation of a value from evidence that the value changed. Selected inputs, aggregate-only answer records, related-family judges and a post-failure guard evaluation limit the conclusions to the retained experiments.

</details>


### [236] [Acquiring and Verifying Repository Norms for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07757)
*Kaifeng He,Xiaojun Zhang,Zhenxi Chen,Christoph Treude,Mingwei Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RepoNorm is a system that acquires repository-specific norms (both explicit and implicit) and delivers them to coding agents to improve norm compliance. It checks norm content/applicability using repository evidence and Git history. Evaluation on 121 tasks with 3 coding models shows 7-46% relative improvements in norm compliance rates, with 86% precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can pass functional tests but fail to meet repository contribution requirements (e.g., coding standards, documentation norms). Existing retrieval approaches provide general context but agents must still determine which norms apply. The problem is that repository-specific norms are dispersed across multiple sources and require interpretation of conditions and exceptions.

Method: RepoNorm acquires explicit and implicit repository norms independently of coding tasks. It checks norm content and applicability using repository evidence, consults Git history when needed, and delivers norm packages to existing coding agents. Evaluation was conducted using three coding models and 121 tasks from RepoNormBench.

Result: Against baseline (Raw - no additional guidance): 7.42-10.77% improvement for Overall Norm Compliance Rate (NCR), 31.64-45.44% for Contribution NCR, and 11.34-17.69% for Prompt-omitted NCR. All three models also outperform CodeWiki documentation. Functional success rates show 5.79-9.09 percentage point gains over Raw (not statistically significant). Sampled precision is 86% with default configuration.

Conclusion: RepoNorm effectively improves coding agents' compliance with repository-specific norms across multiple metrics. The system successfully delivers relevant norm packages, though the functional success gains did not reach statistical significance. The 86% precision indicates high reliability of the norm extraction process.

Abstract: Changes produced by coding agents can pass functional tests while leaving repository contribution requirements unmet. Following repository-specific norms requires identifying guidance dispersed across repository sources and interpreting its conditions and exceptions. Retrieval and documentation approaches supply general context, but agents must still determine which norms apply. We introduce RepoNorm to acquire explicit and implicit repository norms independently of coding tasks. It checks norm content and applicability using repository evidence, consults Git history when needed, and delivers norm packages to existing coding agents. Our evaluation uses three coding models and 121 tasks from RepoNormBench. Against the baseline with no additional generated guidance (Raw), relative improvements are 7.42-10.77% for Overall Norm Compliance Rate (NCR), 31.64-45.44% for Contribution NCR, and 11.34-17.69% for Prompt-omitted NCR. All three coding models also obtain higher values on these NCR measures with RepoNorm than with CodeWiki documentation. Functional success rates show observed gains of 5.79-9.09 percentage points over Raw; the paired comparisons do not reach the significance threshold. Sampled precision is 86% with RepoNorm's default configuration.

</details>


### [237] [ES-Trace: Auditing Ethical-Sourcing Disclosure of Code Generation Models Beyond Model Cards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07762)
*Zhuolin Xu,Haibo Wang,Shin Hwei Tan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ES-Trace is a framework for auditing ethical-sourcing disclosure in code generation models, using a Model Documentation Traceability Graph (MDTG) to trace evidence beyond model cards. The study analyzes 26 models from 10 publishers across 77 documents and 20 ethical-sourcing aspects, finding that model-card-only audits yield 1.77/5 but increase to 2.82/5 when resolving documentation references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code generation models raise ethical-sourcing concerns (IP, privacy, fairness, labor, environment), but it's unclear how much evidence existing models disclose and where that evidence can be found. Prior work defined ethical-sourcing criteria, but no framework exists to trace disclosed evidence across documentation artifacts.

Method: The researchers introduced ES-Trace framework with MDTG (Model Documentation Traceability Graph) to represent relationships among models, versions, and documentation artifacts. They applied ES-Trace to audit 26 models from 10 publishers across 77 documents, evaluating 20 ES-CodeGen aspects. They compared model-card-only auditing with full documentation scope auditing.

Result: Model-card-only auditing yields mean score 1.77/5, while resolving declared references increases it to 2.82/5. Most increase comes from documents declared in structured metadata. Key findings: (1) social and labor-related aspects remain poorly documented even with expanded audit, (2) resolving documentation references substantially increases disclosure (1.77→2.82), (3) model-card-only audits can mischaracterize release-level disclosure changes, (4) documentation mismatches can associate evidence with wrong model/version.

Conclusion: The study calls for: (1) reference-aware ethical-sourcing disclosure audits, (2) explicit model-version binding and consistency across documentation artifacts, and (3) stronger documentation of currently underreported social and labor-related aspects.

Abstract: Code generation models have been increasingly used in software development, but their development raises ethical-sourcing concerns involving intellectual property, privacy, fairness, labour practices, and environmental impact. Although prior work has defined ethical-sourcing criteria for code generation, it remains unclear how much evidence existing models disclose and where that evidence can be found. We introduce ES-Trace, a framework for ethical-sourcing disclosure audits that traces disclosed evidence beyond model cards using the Model Documentation Traceability Graph (MDTG), which represents relationships among models, versions, and documentation artifacts. We apply ES-Trace to 26 models from 10 publishers across 77 documents and 20 ES-CodeGen aspects. Model-card-only auditing yields a mean score of 1.77/5, while resolving the declared references increases it to 2.82/5, with most of the increase arising from documents that the publisher declares in structured metadata. The key findings of our study include: (1) social and labour-related aspects remain poorly documented, even when expanding the audit to the full documentation scope, (2) resolving documentation references substantially increases observed disclosure, raising the mean score from 1.77/5 to 2.82/5, (3) model-card-only audits can mischaracterize release-level disclosure changes, and (4) documentation mismatches can associate evidence with the wrong model or version, highlighting the need for explicit model--version binding and consistency across documentation artifacts. Our study calls for reference-aware ethical-sourcing disclosure audits, explicit model--version binding and consistency across documentation artifacts, and stronger documentation of currently underreported social and labour-related aspects.

</details>


### [238] [Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07832)
*Haibo Jin,Xinjie Li,Peng Kuang,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces Dev-Primitives, a modular abstraction that pairs repository artifacts with resident LLMs to enable active participation in software engineering tasks. Building on this, the authors propose HERMES, a Harness Engineering framework that uses dependency-aware dynamic activation and bug diagnosis mechanisms. Experiments on four benchmarks show HERMES outperforms baselines by 12.4% on average and achieves comparable performance to GPT-5.6 Sol while reducing inference costs by 26.2%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents with terminal access are brittle on long-horizon workflows due to: 1) need to repeatedly reconstruct program state scattered across source files, configurations, tests, dependencies, and runtime behavior; 2) increasingly long interaction histories causing context explosion; 3) semantic drift; and 4) difficulty identifying task-relevant components in large repositories.

Method: The paper proposes two key innovations: 1) Dev-Primitives - a modular abstraction that transforms repository artifacts into active participants by pairing each artifact with a resident LLM, giving it an agent-native interface grounded in its own implementation and dependencies, enabling natural-language reasoning, inter-component communication, and localized self-modification; 2) HERMES framework that instantiates Dev-Primitives at repository scale through a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to components needing revision.

Result: HERMES outperforms matched baseline harnesses by 12.4% on average across four software engineering benchmarks. With Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, HERMES remains within 4.5% of the homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol configuration across all four benchmarks while reducing inference cost by 26.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates the importance of harness design in software engineering agents. Dev-Primities enable repository artifacts to become active participants in software engineering, and HERMES provides an effective framework for scaling this approach. The significant cost reduction while maintaining competitive performance highlights that thoughtful harness architecture can substantially improve agent efficiency without sacrificing capability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) equipped with terminal access have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating software engineering tasks. However, existing agents remain brittle on long-horizon workflows, where they must repeatedly reconstruct program state scattered across source files, configurations, tests, dependencies, and runtime behavior, leading to increasingly long interaction histories, context explosion, and semantic drift. Large repositories further complicate the identification of task-relevant components. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{Dev-Primitives} (\emph{Development Primitives}), a modular and executable abstraction that transforms repository components from passive software artifacts into active participants in software engineering. Each Dev-Primitive pairs a repository artifact with a resident LLM, which gives the artifact an agent-native interface grounded in its own implementation and dependencies, enabling natural-language reasoning, inter-component communication, and localized self-modification. Building on Dev-Primitives, we propose \textbf{HERMES}, a Harness Engineering framework for software engineeRing via Modular Executable Dev-PrimitiveS, which instantiates these primitives at repository scale through a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to the components that must be revised. Extensive experiments on four software engineering benchmarks demonstrate that HERMES outperforms matched baseline harnesses by 12.4\% on average. Moreover, when paired with strong activation and diagnosis models, HERMES, even with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, remains within 4.5\% of the homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol configuration across all four benchmarks, while reducing inference cost by 26.2\% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, highlighting the importance of harness design in software engineering agents.

</details>


### [239] [Beyond the Leaderboard: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Dense and Mixture-of-Experts Models for Automated Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08173)
*Anvi Kalpesh Shah,Umamaheswara Sharma B*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Weighted Quality Index (QI) for evaluating Automated Program Repair (APR) models, combining functional correctness, maintainability, security, and generation efficiency based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model. The authors evaluate three dense Qwen2.5-Coder models (3B, 7B, 14B parameters) and one MoE model (DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite with 16B total but 2.4B active parameters) on 40 QuixBugs and 90 Defects4J bugs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current APR evaluation relies solely on test pass rates, which fails to capture important dimensions like patch maintainability, security, and computational cost. This narrow evaluation can hide critical trade-offs between different model approaches.

Method: The authors evaluated four models (three dense Qwen2.5-Coder variants at 3B, 7B, and 14B parameters, plus DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite MoE with 2.4B active parameters) on 130 bugs (40 QuixBugs + 90 Defects4J) using identical local hardware to control infrastructure effects. They applied configurable weighting schemes to combine multiple quality dimensions and used McNemar's exact test for statistical significance.

Result: Model rankings change depending on the weighting scheme used. The MoE model achieves nearly identical correctness to the 7B and 14B dense models (no statistically significant difference) while using 3-6x fewer active parameters. However, correctness increases significantly across the three dense model scales.

Conclusion: Active parameter count is a more informative metric than total parameter count for evaluating sparse code models. The proposed Weighted Quality Index reveals trade-offs that single-metric evaluation hides, suggesting that future APR evaluation should adopt multi-dimensional quality assessment.

Abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) with language models is usually evaluated by whether a generated patch passes the test suite, which can hide differences in maintainability, security, and computational cost. We propose a Weighted Quality Index (QI), inspired by the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, that combines functional correctness, maintainability, security, and generation efficiency under configurable weighting schemes. We evaluate three dense Qwen2.5-Coder models (3B, 7B, 14B) and the 16B-parameter DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model (2.4B active parameters) on 40 QuixBugs and 90 Defects4J bugs, all run locally on identical hardware to control for infrastructure effects. Model rankings change with the weighting scheme, showing that single-metric evaluation can hide trade-offs. The MoE model shows almost no statistically significant difference in correctness from the 7B and 14B dense models (McNemar's exact test) while using 3-6 times fewer active parameters, whereas correctness increases significantly across the three dense scales. These results suggest that active parameter count can be a more informative lens than total parameter count for sparse code models.

</details>


### [240] [Newer and Bigger, but Safer? A Longitudinal Study of the Functionality-Security Gap in LLM-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08240)
*Thiago Santos de Moura,Fynn Matuschek,Flavio Toffalini,Yannic Noller*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A longitudinal study of 32 LLMs from 7 families (5 open-weight) across 3 releases finds that newer models are safer in absolute terms but no family closes the functionality-security gap. Openness does not separate families—all open-weight families narrow the gap significantly. Compact models generally produce less secure code than flagship counterparts, with persistent weaknesses like CWE-117 and CWE-113, and regressions in proprietary models on memory/integer weaknesses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work concluded LLMs become smarter but not safer, with only considered open-weight family stagnating. This study investigates whether this holds for other open-weight families and compact models, addressing gaps in understanding LLM security trajectories across different model architectures and sizes.

Method: CWEval benchmark with 119 tasks across 5 programming languages and 31 CWEs, comparing 32 LLMs from 7 families (5 open-weight) across 3 successive releases in both flagship and compact variants.

Result: Newer models are safer in absolute terms but no family closes the gap. Openness does not separate families—all open-weight families narrow the gap significantly, while Gemini 3.1 Pro maintains a wide gap. Compact models usually produce less secure code than flagship counterparts (except Gemini 3.7 Flash). Persistent weaknesses include CWE-117 (log injection) and CWE-113 (HTTP response splitting). Newest proprietary models show regressions on memory and integer weaknesses. Same CWE carries different risk across languages.

Conclusion: Developers should not assume model upgrades improve security or that proprietary models are more secure. Security checks must be rerun after each model change, and secure APIs should be provided in the model's context. The functionality-security gap persists across all model families, requiring continued vigilance.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used to generate code. Although their functional plausibility keeps improving, the generated code often contains security vulnerabilities. The functionality-security gap captures code that passes functional tests but fails security tests. A recent longitudinal study of three model families concluded that LLMs become smarter but not safer, with the only considered open-weight family stagnating. Whether this holds for other (open-weight) families and particularly for compact models remains open. We present a longitudinal study of the gap across 32 LLMs from seven model families (five open-weight), covering three successive releases per family in flagship and compact variants. Using CWEval with 119 tasks in five programming languages and 31 CWEs, we compare trajectories across families, model sizes, and languages. Newer models do become safer in absolute terms, although no family closes the gap. Unlike prior work, we find that openness does not separate the families: every considered open-weight family narrows the gap significantly, while Gemini 3.1 Pro keeps a gap as wide as the one reported for Llama. Compact models usually produce less secure code than their flagship counterparts, with notable exceptions (e.g., Gemini 3.7 Flash). At the CWE level, we confirm persistent weaknesses such as log injection (CWE-117) and HTTP response splitting (CWE-113) and regressions in the newest proprietary models on memory and integer weaknesses, and show that the same CWE carries very different risk across languages. From these results, we derive implications for LLM vendors, researchers, and developers. In particular, developers should assume neither that upgrades improve security nor that proprietary models are more secure; they should rerun security checks after each model change and provide secure APIs in the model's context.

</details>


### [241] [Learning from Failures: A Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement for LLM-Based Vulnerability Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08405)
*Mandana Ghadamian,David Mohaisen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement (FDPR), a methodology that analyzes recurring LLM failure modes (false positives, false negatives, unsupported reasoning, CWE misclassification) to guide evidence-based prompt engineering for software vulnerability analysis. Evaluation on DVJA and Juliet Test Suite shows improved reliability and reusable prompt design principles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM vulnerability analysis research relies on aggregate performance metrics without understanding why models fail, limiting the ability to systematically improve prompts.

Method: FDPR methodology: (1) Identify recurring failure modes using DVJA, (2) Translate failures into targeted prompt refinements, (3) Evaluate on Juliet Test Suite, (4) Cross-model validation for generalizability.

Result: Failure-driven refinement improves reliability of LLM-based vulnerability analysis and yields reusable prompt design principles. Cross-model validation demonstrates generalizability.

Conclusion: Recurring model failures provide a principled foundation for prompt engineering, enabling systematic development of more reliable LLM-based vulnerability analysis systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models have emerged as promising tools for software vulnerability analysis, but their effectiveness depends heavily on prompt design. Existing research primarily compares prompting strategies using aggregate performance metrics, providing limited insight into why models fail or how prompts can be improved systematically. We propose Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement (FDPR), a methodology that analyzes recurring model failures to guide evidence-based prompt refinement. Using the Damn Vulnerable Java Application (DVJA), we identify recurring failure modes, including false positives, false negatives, unsupported reasoning, and CWE misclassification, and translate them into targeted prompt refinements. We then evaluate the resulting prompt on the Juliet Test Suite and perform cross-model validation to assess generalizability. The results show that failure-driven refinement improves the reliability of LLM-based vulnerability analysis while yielding reusable prompt design principles. More broadly, this work demonstrates that recurring model failures provide a principled foundation for prompt engineering, enabling the systematic development of more reliable LLM-based vulnerability analysis systems.

</details>


### [242] [RAPO-Sol: Retrieval-Augmented Preference Optimization for Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08429)
*Rongcun Wang,Shi Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RAPO-Sol is a two-stage training framework for repository-level Solidity smart contract code generation, combining Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (RAFT) with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) using Solidity Semantic-Anchor Perturbation (SAP) to create rejection samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Smart contracts written in Solidity manage assets, permissions, and irreversible state changes, making code generation both useful and security-critical. Repository-level generation is challenging due to the need to preserve consistency across multiple complex components (state variables, modifiers, events, inheritance, external calls, and access-control logic).

Method: The framework has two stages: (1) RAFT augments training inputs with similar Solidity examples to learn contract-level patterns while remaining retrieval-free at inference; (2) DPO trains the model to prefer reference contracts over flawed alternatives using SAP, which perturbs validation statements, visibility modifiers, data-location keywords, context variables, payment operations, and low-level calls.

Result: Experiments on SolidityBench with CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct show that RAFT consistently improves over supervised fine-tuning, while SAP-based DPO provides further gains in BLEU and SolidityScore. The full RAFT+DPO pipeline achieves the best performance across all three models.

Conclusion: The two-stage approach demonstrates complementary benefits: retrieval during training helps learn recurring patterns, while Solidity-aware preference optimization further improves quality without adding retrieval cost at inference time.

Abstract: Smart contracts written in Solidity manage assets, permissions, and irreversible state changes, making code generation both useful and security-critical. Repository-level Solidity generation is challenging because models must synthesize complete contracts or libraries while preserving consistency across state variables, modifiers, events, inheritance, external calls, and access-control logic. We present RAPO-Sol, a two-stage training framework for repository-level Solidity code generation. First, Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (RAFT) augments each training input with similar Solidity examples, helping the model learn recurring contract-level patterns while remaining retrieval-free at inference time. Second, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) trains the model to prefer reference contracts over close but semantically flawed alternatives. We construct rejected samples using Solidity Semantic-Anchor Perturbation (SAP), which perturbs validation statements, visibility modifiers, data-location keywords, context variables, payment operations, and low-level calls. Experiments on SolidityBench with CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct show that RAFT consistently improves over supervised fine-tuning, while SAP-based DPO provides further gains in BLEU and SolidityScore. The full RAFT+DPO pipeline achieves the best performance across all three models, demonstrating complementary benefits from retrieval during training and Solidity-aware preference optimization without adding retrieval cost at inference.

</details>


### [243] [A Case Study in Assuring AI-Written Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08651)
*Lindsey Ferris,Sierra Bonilla*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A case study of a production healthcare platform built by coding agents under the supervision of an operator without formal software-engineering training. The system evolved into a human-led meta-agent system where agents wrote, reviewed, and supervised code. The study finds that tests, monitors, and reviewing agents are fallible, and human control requires tying intended outcomes, evidence, agent permissions, and human decisions to the same underlying objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate how human control can be maintained over software systems built by AI coding agents, particularly when operators lack formal software engineering training, given that exhaustive code review is unreliable for such systems.

Method: Case study of a production healthcare platform built through coding agents over time, governed by an operator without formal software-engineering training. The system evolved into a human-led meta-agent system with agents writing code, supervising, and reviewing, while project rules carried lessons forward.

Result: Tests, monitors, and reviewing agents used to supervise the system were fallible: (1) some monitors measured proxies rather than outcomes, (2) some audits failed silently, (3) missing checks disappeared from reported results, and (4) one automated repair caused operational disruption.

Conclusion: Human control depends on keeping the intended outcome, the evidence used to judge it, the agents' permissions, and the final human decision all tied to the same underlying objective.

Abstract: Software-engineering agents can enable people without formal software training to build systems they could not otherwise implement and simultaneously can produce more code than even experts can meaningfully inspect. In both cases, exhaustive code review is not reliable as the sole basis for human control. We report a case study of a production healthcare platform built through coding agents and governed by an operator without formal software-engineering training. Over time, its workflow grew into a human-led meta-agent system where one agent wrote code, other agents supervised and reviewed it, and project rules carried lessons forward. The operator found that tests, monitors and reviewing agents used to supervise the system were fallible. Some monitors measured proxies rather than outcomes, some audits failed silently, missing checks disappeared from reported results and one automated repair caused operational disruption. In this case, human control depended on keeping the intended outcome, the evidence used to judge it, the agents' permissions and the final human decision were all tied to the same underlying objective.

</details>

### [244] [TEMPEST: Temporal Embeddings for Scalable Driver Identification via Angular Margin Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06855)
*Kyle Musgrove,Dylan B. Lewis,Sarah Powers,Emma J. Reid,Hector Santos-Villalobos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TEMPEST is a Temporal Convolutional Network embedding model with ArcFace loss for scalable driver identification. It achieves 91.71% Rank-1 accuracy on a 45-driver dataset, with only 4.3 pp degradation when scaling from 10 to 45 drivers, using 96-dimensional embeddings from 60-second multimodal driving windows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing triplet-loss embedding models for driver identification degrade rapidly with increasing driver pool size and overfit to session-specific patterns under temporal evaluation. Scalable driver identification requires embeddings that maintain discriminative performance as fleet size grows.

Method: TEMPEST uses a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) trained with additive angular margin (ArcFace) loss in a normalized angular space to enforce global class-level separation. It maps 60-second multimodal driving windows to compact 96-dimensional embeddings, enabling dynamic enrollment without retraining or classifier refitting.

Result: On a 45-driver dataset, TEMPEST achieves 91.71% Rank-1 accuracy, outperforming the best classical model by 17.9 percentage points (pp) and the strongest triplet-loss baseline by 58.4 pp. It degrades by only 4.3 pp when scaling from 10 to 45 drivers (vs. 22 pp and 32.5 pp for supervised and unsupervised triplet baselines). On the KIA Soul dataset, it outperforms the best classical model by 7.3 pp within-session and 14.3 pp cross-session.

Conclusion: TEMPEST provides a rigorous, reproducible baseline for scalable behavioral driver biometric identification with 720K parameters, 2.80 MB footprint, and 50-epoch convergence. Its global class-level separation approach successfully addresses scalability and cross-session generalization challenges.

Abstract: Scalable driver identification requires embedding models that maintain discriminative performance as fleet size grows, yet existing triplet-loss formulations degrade rapidly with driver pool size and overfit to session-specific patterns under rigorous temporal evaluation. We introduce TEMPEST, a Temporal Convolutional Network embedding model trained with an additive angular margin (ArcFace) loss that enforces global class-level separation in a normalized angular space. TEMPEST maps 60-second multimodal driving windows to compact 96-dimensional embeddings, supporting truly dynamic enrollment without any retraining or classifier refitting. Under rigorous temporal evaluation on a 45-driver dataset, TEMPEST achieves 91.71% Rank-1 accuracy, outperforming the best classical model by 17.9 pp and the strongest triplet-loss baseline by 58.4 pp. TEMPEST degrades by only 4.3 pp when growing the subject pool from 10 to 45 drivers, compared to 22 pp and 32.5 pp for supervised and unsupervised triplet-loss baselines, and its cross-session advantage is corroborated on the public KIA Soul dataset, where it outperforms the best classical model by 7.3 pp within-session and 14.3 pp cross-session. With 720K parameters, a 2.80 MB footprint, and 50-epoch convergence, TEMPEST establishes a rigorous, reproducible baseline for scalable behavioral driver biometric identification.

</details>


### [245] [When Does External Guidance Help LLM Reasoning? A Bias-Variance Theory of Guidance-Augmented GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06861)
*Sofia Torres,Gabriel Almeida,Carter Adams,Camila Rocha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Guidance-Augmented GRPO (GA-GRPO), a unified theoretical framework for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that addresses the lack of theoretical guarantees in existing methods (LUFFY, ExPO, PAPO, TAPO). The framework treats external guidance as a stochastic guidance operator and provides convergence rates, bias bounds, and MSE-optimal guidance weights. Experiments show the method matches or surpasses prior approaches while using 31% less GPU time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RLVR has become the dominant paradigm for eliciting multi-step reasoning in LLMs, and methods like LUFFY, ExPO, PAPO, and TAPO use external guidance (expert traces, self-explanations, retrieved thought patterns), none of these methods provide theoretical guarantees: convergence rates, bias bounds, or optimal weighting rules for the guidance signal. This gap motivates the development of a unified theoretical framework.

Method: The paper casts external guidance as a stochastic guidance operator G that re-writes the question distribution. The resulting policy-gradient estimator is analyzed as a biased on-policy estimator whose bias is bounded by the total-variation guidance divergence δ_G between the guidance-augmented sampling distribution and the policy's own distribution. Under smoothness and bounded-divergence assumptions, the framework derives: (1) O(1/√T) convergence rate to an O(δ√T)-neighborhood of the GRPO stationary point, (2) closed-form MSE-optimal guidance weight λ*(T, δ, σ₀²) = σ₀² / (σ₀² + R_max²δ²T), and (3) a matching minimax lower bound showing the Ω(δ²T) bias term is unavoidable.

Result: Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base across nine math and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks show that optimal-weight GA-GRPO matches or surpasses TAPO, LUFFY, ExPO, and vanilla GRPO while requiring 31% fewer GPU-hours. Eight analysis experiments validate each theoretical prediction.

Conclusion: GA-GRPO provides a unified theoretical framework that subsumes vanilla GRPO, LUFFY, ExPO, PAPO, and TAPO as special cases. The framework establishes theoretical guarantees (convergence rates, bias bounds, optimal guidance weights) that were previously absent in the literature, while demonstrating superior empirical performance and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant paradigm for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models, and a recent wave of methods (LUFFY, ExPO, PAPO, TAPO) further augments RL with \emph{external guidance} - expert traces, self-explanations, or retrieved thought patterns. Although each method reports empirical gains, none provides convergence rates, bias bounds, or an optimal weighting rule for the guidance signal. We close this gap with \emph{Guidance-Augmented GRPO} (GA-GRPO), a unified theoretical framework that casts external guidance as a stochastic guidance operator G re-writing the question distribution, and analyses the resulting policy-gradient estimator as a biased on-policy estimator whose bias is bounded by the total-variation guidance divergence delta\_G between the guidance-augmented sampling distribution and the policy's own distribution. The framework subsumes vanilla GRPO, LUFFY, ExPO, PAPO, and TAPO as special cases obtained by particular choices of G. Under smoothness and bounded-divergence assumptions we prove that GA-GRPO converges at rate O(1/sqrt(T)) to an O(delta sqrt(T))-neighbourhood of the GRPO stationary point, derive the closed-form MSE-optimal guidance weight lambda-star(T, delta, sigma\_0 squared) = sigma\_0 squared / (sigma\_0 squared + R\_max squared delta squared T), and prove a matching minimax lower bound showing the Omega(delta squared T) bias term is unavoidable. Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base across nine math and OOD benchmarks confirm that optimal-weight GA-GRPO matches or surpasses TAPO, LUFFY, ExPO, and vanilla GRPO while requiring 31\% fewer GPU-hours, and eight analysis experiments validate each theoretical prediction.

</details>


### [246] [Neutrosophic Ensemble Classification for Uncertainty-Aware Bearing Fault Detection: Evidence from Laboratory and Variable-Speed Industrial Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06880)
*Maikel Leyva-Vazquez,Dayron Rumbaut Rangel,Lorenzo Cevallos-Torres,Alexis Matheu Perez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses uncertainty quantification in bearing fault detection by proposing a refined neutrosophic decomposition of ensemble classifier outputs into four indicators. The method is evaluated on CWRU and JNU benchmarks under leave-one-condition-out protocol, with mixed results: high accuracy on CWRU but poor generalization on JNU (40.64%). Key findings include I1-hat (predictive entropy) being the most useful uncertainty indicator, and that ensemble approaches may not always outperform simpler models like Logistic Regression in distribution shift scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that conventional machine learning classifiers produce scalar confidence scores that fail to distinguish between confident errors and genuinely ambiguous predictions. Additionally, the standard truth/falsity pair (F = 1 - T) is algebraically redundant by construction. The authors aim to develop a more nuanced uncertainty quantification approach for bearing fault detection in industrial contexts.

Method: The authors operationalize a refined neutrosophic decomposition of an ensemble (Random Forest + XGBoost + Logistic Regression) into four indicators: T-hat (top-class evidence), F-hat (best-competitor evidence), predictive entropy I1-hat, and decision disagreement I2-hat. Experiments were conducted on two bearing benchmarks (CWRU and JNU) at 600-1000 rpm using a leave-one-condition-out protocol. Additional experiments included fusing time-domain and frequency-domain models using Jensen-Shannon divergence, and using literature-verified bearing fault frequencies via envelope spectrum analysis.

Result: On CWRU, after correcting a file-to-class mapping error, the ensemble achieved 100% accuracy on three of four held-out loads (92.27% on the fourth). On JNU with 1000 rpm held out, accuracy collapsed to 40.64% (below majority-class baseline), while Logistic Regression achieved 57.91%. I1-hat showed robust association with error beyond T-hat/F-hat, while I2-hat contributed little. Standalone Logistic Regression confidence outperformed the full decomposition. Fusing time-domain and frequency-domain models with Jensen-Shannon divergence achieved AURC 0.29 vs 0.36 (standard split) and 0.54 vs 0.73 (harder single-condition reproduction). Using literature-verified bearing fault frequencies from envelope spectrum achieved 99.57% accuracy with three interpretable features on CWRU.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that uncertainty quantification in bearing fault detection is complex. The neutrosophic decomposition provides useful signals (particularly I1-hat), but ensemble approaches may not always outperform simpler models under distribution shift. The Jensen-Shannon divergence between model predictions shows promise for uncertainty quantification. Additionally, domain-informed features (bearing fault frequencies from envelope spectrum) can achieve near-perfect classification with high interpretability. The authors honestly report boundary conditions and release code/data for verification.

Abstract: Machine learning classifiers for bearing fault detection produce scalar confidence scores that conflate confident errors with genuinely ambiguous predictions, and the conventional truth/falsity pair (F = 1 - T) is algebraically redundant by construction. We operationalize a refined neutrosophic decomposition of a Random Forest + XGBoost + Logistic Regression ensemble into four indicators -- T-hat (top-class evidence), F-hat (best-competitor evidence), predictive entropy I1-hat, and decision disagreement I2-hat -- evaluated on two bearing benchmarks (CWRU and JNU, 600-1000 rpm) under a leave-one-condition-out protocol. On CWRU, after correcting a file-to-class mapping error, the ensemble reaches 100.00 percent accuracy on three of four held-out loads (92.27 percent on the fourth), leaving too few errors for uncertainty analysis. On JNU, holding out 1000 rpm, accuracy collapses to 40.64 percent, below a majority-class baseline; Logistic Regression (57.91 percent) generalizes far better than the tree ensembles. I1-hat shows a robust association with error beyond T-hat/F-hat, while I2-hat contributes little; standalone Logistic Regression confidence outperforms the full decomposition, a boundary condition we report honestly. Two further results extend this: fusing a time-domain and a frequency-domain model of the same signal and scoring their Jensen-Shannon divergence beats that model own entropy (AURC 0.29 vs. 0.36 on the standard split; 0.54 vs. 0.73 under a harder single-condition reproduction), the only indicator moving correctly under a CWRU-versus-JNU distributional-shift contrast; and, on CWRU alone, literature-verified bearing fault frequencies, correctly demodulated via the envelope spectrum, separate most fault classes almost perfectly (99.57 percent) using three interpretable features. Code, logs, and figures are released for independent verification.

</details>


### [247] [Comparative review of hybrid forecasting models for short-term prediction of building thermal load](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06881)
*Nikolaos A. Efkarpidis,Despoina Kothona,Georgios C. Christoforidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a comparative review of 13 hybrid models for short-term forecasting of building thermal demand, evaluating data-driven models enhanced with metaheuristics and other techniques using Scottish household data and weather forecasts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve short-term forecasting accuracy of building thermal demand (heating and domestic hot water) by identifying and comparing the most effective hybrid modeling approaches that combine data-driven methods with optimization techniques.

Method: Literature review of existing hybrid techniques with qualitative evaluation (input/output features, advantages, drawbacks); empirical assessment using Scottish household thermal demand dataset and historical weather forecasts to compare 13 hybrid methods including EMD-LSTM-Markov, SVM-SA, and RF-ISSA-LSTM.

Result: EMD-LSTM-Markov achieves highest accuracy for day-ahead power pattern prediction of heating and DHW demands, though it underestimates high power swells and spikes. SVM-SA and RF-ISSA-LSTM predict smooth patterns but underestimate most power peaks during rapid changes.

Conclusion: The EMD-LSTM-Markov model is recommended for short-term thermal demand forecasting, but limitations remain in capturing extreme power events; further improvement is needed for high power swells and spike predictions.

Abstract: In this paper, a comparative review of different hybrid models for short-term forecasting of building thermal demand is carried out. Particularly, the assessment tackles the comparison of data-driven models enhanced with other state-of-the-art techniques. At the first step, the existing techniques reported in the literature are analysed. It is concluded that Metaheuristics or a data-driven model are used to identify the parameters of the basic model. The qualitative evaluation includes for each method the input and output features, main advantages and drawbacks. At the second step, an existing dataset of historical thermal demand from Scottish households, as well as historical weather forecasts are utilized to assess additionally the performance of existing hybrid methods. From the assessment of 13 hybrid methods, the Empirical Modal Decomposition - long short-term memory - Markov (EMD-LSTM-Markov) model can predict with the highest accuracy the day-ahead power pattern of heating and domestic hot water (DHW) demands. Though local power peaks are also accurately predicted, high power swells and spikes are underestimated. Other methods, such as Support Vector Machine - Simulated Annealing (SVM-SA) and Random Forest - Improved Sparrow Search Algorithm - LSTM (RF-ISSA-LSTM) predict a smooth pattern of heating and DHW demand profiles with rapid changes underestimating most power peaks.

</details>


### [248] [Learning When to Refine: Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning for Budgeted Neural-Operator PDE Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06883)
*Ange Tong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses a budget allocation problem in autoregressive neural operator deployment for time-dependent PDEs. The authors propose a budgeted adaptive neural-operator solver with a global Fourier neural operator, local residual correction operator, set-aware selector, and macro policy. They introduce rollout-verified policy improvement (RV-PI) which uses actual continuation rollouts to evaluate refinement decisions and converts long-horizon advantages into conservative policy targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural operators provide fast surrogates for PDEs but autoregressive deployment creates a refinement-allocation problem: prediction errors vary over space and time, while only finite local corrections can be committed along a trajectory. The key insight is that the value of a local correction depends on its downstream effect on the trajectory, not just immediate error reduction.

Method: The proposed framework combines: (1) a global Fourier neural operator for full field advancement, (2) a local operator proposing patch-wise residual corrections, (3) a set-aware selector for choosing refinement locations, and (4) a macro policy for budget allocation. The core contribution is Rollout-Verified Policy Improvement (RV-PI), which evaluates feasible refinement counts through actual continuation rollouts, converts long-horizon advantages into conservative policy targets, and accepts updates only when held-out trajectory error improves.

Result: On shallow-water benchmark (32-intervention budget): RV-PI achieves 0.6910 mean trajectory relative L2 error, improving 5.37% over immediate-only policy improvement and 2.41% over RandomMacro. On forcing-driven Brusselator benchmark (76-intervention budget): RV-PI achieves 0.09954, improving 2.31% over immediate-only policy improvement and 5.32% over RandomMacro.

Conclusion: Under a fixed refinement budget, the value of a local correction depends on its downstream effect on the autoregressive trajectory, not only on its immediate error reduction. RV-PI successfully leverages long-horizon rollout information to make better budget allocation decisions, outperforming methods that only consider immediate error reduction.

Abstract: Neural operators provide fast surrogates for time-dependent PDEs, but autoregressive deployment creates a refinement-allocation problem: prediction errors vary over space and time, while only a finite number of local corrections can be committed along a trajectory. We formulate this as budgeted adaptive neural-operator solving. A global Fourier neural operator advances the full field, a local operator proposes patch-wise residual corrections, and a set-aware selector chooses where to refine. A macro policy decides when and how much of the remaining refinement budget to spend. We introduce rollout-verified policy improvement (RV-PI), which evaluates feasible refinement counts through actual continuation rollouts of the learned PDE solver, converts long-horizon advantages into conservative policy targets, and accepts an update only when held-out trajectory error improves. On the shallow-water benchmark with a 32-intervention budget, RV-PI achieves a three-seed mean trajectory relative L2 error of 0.6910, improving over immediate-only policy improvement by 5.37% and RandomMacro by 2.41%. On the forcing-driven Brusselator benchmark with a 76-intervention budget, RV-PI attains 0.09954, improving over immediate-only policy improvement by 2.31% and RandomMacro by 5.32%. These results show that, under a fixed refinement budget, the value of a local correction depends on its downstream effect on the autoregressive trajectory, not only on its immediate error reduction.

</details>


### [249] [Event-Driven ML Pipeline Orchestration for Manufacturing: An AWS Industry Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06890)
*Zhengyang,Gu,Thomas Cook,Fredaljohn Rohrbaugh,Joseph E. Hernandez,Chris Couch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An industry experience report detailing three years of operating an event-driven cloud infrastructure for continuous ML training in automotive manufacturing. The system uses AWS ECS, EC2 GPU, SQS, Lambda, and Terraform to orchestrate GPU-accelerated training jobs across multiple plants, achieving 72-78% cost reduction compared to always-on GPU infrastructure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the challenge of running continuous machine learning training in automotive manufacturing at scale, coordinating long-running GPU workloads triggered by manufacturing events while managing costs and ensuring reliability.

Method: The architecture combines Amazon ECS with EC2 GPU capacity providers, SQS-based messaging with dead-letter queues, and an admission-controlled Lambda dispatcher for cluster concurrency limits. A Conductor orchestrator on ECS Fargate manages dependency-aware retraining chains on a weekly schedule. The infrastructure is codified in modular Terraform with multi-account separation.

Result: From 40,000+ production training jobs, the system achieved 72-78% cost reduction versus always-on GPU infrastructure. Discrete-event simulation confirmed that admission control is necessary (naive dispatch loses 65% of jobs) and that queue-draining matches AWS Step Functions latency while eliminating per-job startup overhead.

Conclusion: The paper provides lessons learned from three years of production operation and releases the simulator and Terraform module skeletons as open-source artifacts, offering a practical reference for similar event-driven ML training infrastructure deployments.

Abstract: We present an industry experience report on three years of operating an event-driven cloud infrastructure for continuous machine learning training in automotive manufacturing. Our system orchestrates GPU-accelerated training of product-specialized model pairs, a physics prediction model and a reinforcement-learning control policy, across multiple plants, coordinating long-running GPU workloads triggered by manufacturing events. The architecture combines Amazon ECS with EC2 GPU capacity providers, SQS-based messaging with dead-letter queues, and an admission-controlled Lambda dispatcher that enforces cluster concurrency limits. A Conductor orchestrator on ECS Fargate initiates dependency-aware retraining chains on a weekly schedule. The entire infrastructure is codified in modular Terraform with multi-account separation. From 40000+ production training jobs we report a 72-78% cost reduction versus always-on GPU infrastructure. A discrete-event simulation confirms that admission control is necessary (naive dispatch loses 65% of jobs) and that queue-draining matches AWS Step Functions latency while eliminating per-job startup overhead. We provide lessons learned and release the simulator and Terraform module skeletons as open-source artifacts.

</details>


### [250] [Learning from Unreliable Trajectories: Adversarially-Robust Federated Q-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06918)
*Sreejeet Maity,Aritra Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses robust federated reinforcement learning where multiple agents collaborate to learn the optimal Q-function while tolerating a fraction of adversarial agents that transmit corrupted information. The authors propose Robust Async-Fed-Q, an algorithm combining variance-reduced Bellman operator estimation with robust aggregation, and provide the first nearly matching upper and lower bounds for this setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand whether the sample-efficiency benefits of federated learning can be preserved when some agents behave adversarially and send corrupted information to the central server. This is important for practical deployments where network participants may be unreliable or malicious.

Method: The paper proposes Robust Async-Fed-Q, an epoch-based federated learning algorithm that: (1) uses variance-reduced estimation of the Bellman optimality operator at individual agents, and (2) employs robust aggregation at the server to handle adversarial corruption. The method accommodates asynchronous sampling and is extended to handle single-trajectory Markovian sampling and heterogeneous partial coverage where different agents explore different state-action regions.

Result: The main results include: (1) High-probability finite-time guarantees showing the method preserves statistical gains of collaboration among honest agents while tolerating adversarial corruption; (2) The effect of adversarial agents diminishes as honest agents collect more data and vanishes in the infinite-sample limit; (3) Information-theoretic lower bounds characterizing the unavoidable statistical cost of corruption; (4) The first nearly matching upper and lower bounds for adversarially robust federated RL; (5) Improved communication complexity compared to prior work.

Conclusion: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for robust federated reinforcement learning, demonstrating that collaboration benefits can be retained even in the presence of adversarial agents. The effect of corruption becomes negligible with sufficient data, and the nearly matching bounds provide a complete characterization of the statistical costs of adversarial behavior.

Abstract: We study federated reinforcement learning in which multiple agents interact with a common Markov decision process and communicate through a central server to collaboratively learn the optimal state-action value function. Our goal is to understand whether the sample-efficiency benefits of collaboration can be retained when a fraction of the agents behave adversarially and transmit arbitrarily corrupted information. To address this problem, we introduce Robust Async-Fed-Q, an epoch-based federated learning algorithm that combines variance-reduced estimation of the Bellman optimality operator at the agents with robust aggregation at the server. We establish high-probability finite-time guarantees showing that the proposed method preserves the statistical gains of collaboration among the honest agents while tolerating adversarial corruption. In particular, the effect of the adversarial agents decreases as the amount of data collected by each honest agent grows and eventually vanishes in the infinite-sample limit. We complement these guarantees with information-theoretic lower bounds that characterize the unavoidable statistical cost of adversarial corruption, leading to the first nearly matching upper and lower bounds for adversarially robust federated reinforcement learning.
