We further extend our framework to accommodate single-trajectory Markovian sampling and heterogeneous partial coverage, where different agents may explore different regions of the state-action space and learning relies on their collective coverage. Finally, our epoch-based design substantially improves the best known communication complexity for federated Q-learning under asynchronous sampling.

</details>


### [251] [AttSVD:Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Attention-Guided SVD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06927)
*Sara Abdali,Jongwoo Ko,Pashmina Cameron*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AttSVD is a training-free KV cache compression method that uses per-prompt truncated SVD to reduce memory by 50% while maintaining performance. Instead of evicting tokens (irreversible sequence-axis reduction), it compresses along the feature axis by keeping only the directions attention actually reads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The KV cache in autoregressive transformers grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context. Existing training-free methods evict low-importance tokens irreversibly along the sequence axis. This paper proposes a different approach: keep every token but store it more cheaply along the feature axis.

Method: AttSVD uses an online, per-prompt truncated SVD compression where the basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry. It keeps only the directions attention actually reads, reducing persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to retained rank. Two decoding strategies are proposed: accumulating (for short generation) and streaming (for long generation). Two refinements make compression adaptive: (1) per-matrix energy rule sizes logit space and attention mass independently, (2) attention-aware basis truncates only in spaces attention actually reads, preserving both attention logits and output.

Result: AttSVD achieves up to 50% KV-cache memory reduction while staying on par with dense cache on both an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite across multiple models. The method also provides free, per-head interpretability insights into effective rank and geometry attention consumes.

Conclusion: AttSVD offers a training-free, interpretable low-rank compression that significantly reduces KV cache memory usage without sacrificing performance. By compressing along the feature axis instead of evicting tokens, it preserves all contextual information while achieving substantial memory savings.

Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache of autoregressive transformers grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context. Most training-free remedies evict low-importance tokens, an irreversible choice along the sequence axis. We instead keep every token and store it more cheaply along the "feature" axis. We therefore propose AttSVD, a new "interpretable" low-rank compression whose basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry: an online, per-prompt truncated SVD that keeps only the directions attention actually reads, cutting persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to the retained rank. We propose two decode-time caching strategies, accumulating and streaming, for short and long generation regimes. Furthermore, we propose two refinements that make compression adaptive. A per-matrix energy rule sizes the logit space and the attention mass independently. An attention-aware basis truncates only in the spaces attention actually reads, preserving both the attention logits and the attention output. The same factors also provide free, per-head interpretability insights into the effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. Across multiple models, on both an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite AttSVD stays on par with the dense cache while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory.

</details>


### [252] [Near-Optimal Sample Complexity for Recursive Entropic Risk Reinforcement Learning with a Generative Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06931)
*Amirparsa Bahrami,Oliver Mortensen,Mohammad Sadegh Talebi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies sample complexities of value and policy learning in finite discounted MDPs under recursive entropic risk preferences with risk parameter β ≠ 0, using a generative model. It provides refined analysis of MB-RS-QVI method and derives (ε,δ)-PAC guarantees that improve upon previous bounds by removing exponential dependence on effective horizon, matching lower bounds up to polynomial gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the sample complexity of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning under recursive entropic risk preferences. Previous work had an exponential gap between upper and lower bounds, and this paper aims to close this gap by providing improved (ε,δ)-PAC guarantees for learning optimal Q-value functions and ε-optimal policies.

Method: The method used is model-based risk-sensitive Q-value iteration (MB-RS-QVI), a plug-in model-based approach. The analysis provides refined theoretical guarantees for this method under the recursive entropic risk measure with parameter β ≠ 0 in finite discounted MDPs with access to a generative model.

Result: The results show improved (ε,δ)-PAC guarantees that eliminate the exponential dependence on effective horizon 1/(1-γ) compared to prior work. The bounds match existing lower bounds in exponential dependence on |β|/(1-γ), S, A, ε, and |β|, up to logarithmic factors. This removes the exponential gap between previously known upper and lower bounds, leaving only a polynomial gap in the effective horizon.

Conclusion: The conclusion demonstrates that the analysis successfully removes the exponential gap between upper and lower bounds for risk-sensitive MDP learning under recursive entropic risk preferences, achieving near-optimal sample complexity bounds that match the lower bounds in their exponential dependence on key parameters.

Abstract: In this paper, we study the sample complexities of value and policy learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs) under recursive entropic risk preferences with risk parameter \(β\neq 0\), assuming access to a generative model of the MDP. We provide a refined analysis of model-based risk-sensitive Q-value iteration (MB-RS-QVI), a plug-in model-based method introduced in prior work, and derive \((\varepsilon,δ)\)-PAC guarantees for both learning the optimal \(Q\)-value function and an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal policy. Our bounds improve the exponential dependence on the effective horizon \(1/(1-γ)\) compared with the best existing guarantees for this setting. In particular, they match the existing lower bounds in their exponential dependence on \(|β|/(1-γ)\), as well as in \(S\), \(A\), \(\varepsilon\), and \(|β|\), up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our analysis removes the exponential gap between the previously known upper and lower bounds, leaving only a polynomial gap in the effective horizon.

</details>


### [253] [QiYao-I: A Manifold Based Foundation Model for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06936)
*Linfeng Wang,Ruitong Zhang,Kai Zhao,Yang Shu,Zhongwen Rao,Meng Wang,Yijie Li,Bin Yang,Chenjun Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QiYao-I is a manifold-based foundation model for irregular multivariate time series forecasting. It addresses challenges of irregular sampling and asynchronous cross-variable dependencies through a sampling-conditioned temporal manifold attention mechanism and a dynamic variable interaction mechanism with frequency awareness. The model achieves superior performance on real-world benchmarks with strong zero-shot and few-shot generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time series foundation models are built on regularly sampled sequences and cannot effectively handle irregular time intervals and asynchronous cross-variable dependencies, which are common in real-world applications where observations are irregularly sampled and asynchronously recorded across variables.

Method: QiYao-I introduces two novel mechanisms: (1) A sampling-conditioned temporal manifold attention that maps real timestamps into a learnable temporal manifold feature space and injects temporal manifold biases into attention layers, enabling capture of irregular time intervals and local sampling structures; (2) A dynamic variable interaction mechanism with frequency awareness that selectively performs cross-variable message passing under asynchronous observations.

Result: Extensive experiments on real-world irregular multivariate forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that QiYao-I achieves superior performance compared with both time series foundation models and end-to-end irregular forecasting models, showing strong generalization ability in zero-shot and few-shot settings.

Conclusion: QiYao-I successfully addresses the challenges of irregular multivariate time series forecasting by leveraging manifold-based learning and frequency-aware dynamic interactions, providing a foundation model that generalizes well across different sampling patterns and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting is a challenging yet important problem in real-world applications, where observations are often irregularly sampled and asynchronously recorded across variables. Existing time series foundation models are mostly built on regularly sampled sequences, making them difficult to generalize to irregular time intervals and asynchronous cross-variable dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose QiYao-I, a manifold based foundation model for irregular multivariate time series forecasting. Specifically, we introduce a novel sampling-conditioned temporal manifold attention mechanism that maps real timestamps into a learnable temporal manifold feature space and injects temporal manifold biases into attention layers, enabling the model to capture both irregular time intervals and local sampling structures. Further, we propose a dynamic variable interaction mechanism with frequency awareness. It selectively performs cross-variable message passing under asynchronous observations. Extensive experiments on real-world irregular multivariate forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that QiYao-I achieves superior performance compared with both time series foundation models and end-to-end irregular forecasting models, showing strong generalization ability in zero-shot and few-shot settings.

</details>


### [254] [Learning to Remember: Distilling Memory Retention for Compact Recurrent Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06942)
*Nilushika Udayangania,Kishor Nandakishora,Marimuthu Palaniswami*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Memory-Discrepancy Knowledge Distillation (MemKD), a novel knowledge distillation framework specifically designed for compressing recurrent neural networks (RNNs/LSTMs) for time series analysis. The method addresses the limitation that existing KD methods, originally designed for computer vision, fail to capture temporal dependencies and memory retention characteristics unique to time series models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models like RNNs and LSTMs have advanced time series analysis but face deployment challenges in resource-constrained environments (wearable devices, edge computing) due to high computational complexity and large model sizes. While Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers a solution by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, existing KD methods neglect the unique temporal dependencies and memory retention characteristics of time series models.

Method: MemKD leverages a specialized loss function that captures memory retention discrepancies between teacher and student models across subsequences within time series data. This ensures the student model effectively mimics the teacher's behavior while maintaining compactness for real-time deployment.

Result: MemKD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KD methods. It can match the teacher model's performance across various compression levels, achieving notable reductions in parameter count and memory usage without significant accuracy loss.

Conclusion: MemKD successfully enables the development of compact, high-performing recurrent neural networks suitable for real-time time series analysis tasks. It addresses the gap between model performance and deployment constraints in resource-limited environments, providing an effective solution for time series model compression.

Abstract: Deep learning models, particularly recurrent neural networks and their variants, such as long short-term memory, have significantly advanced time series analysis. These models capture complex, sequential patterns in time series, enabling real-time assessments. However, their high computational complexity and large model sizes pose challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments, such as wearable devices and edge computing platforms. Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers a solution by transferring knowledge from a large, complex model (teacher) to a smaller, more efficient model (student), thereby retaining high performance while reducing computational demands. Current KD methods, originally designed for computer vision tasks, neglect the unique temporal dependencies and memory retention characteristics of time series models. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel KD framework termed Memory-Discrepancy Knowledge Distillation (MemKD). MemKD leverages a specialized loss function to capture memory retention discrepancies between the teacher and student models across subsequences within time series data, ensuring that the student model effectively mimics the teacher's behaviour. This approach facilitates the development of compact, high-performing recurrent neural networks suitable for real-time, time series analysis tasks. We provide additional experiments, in-depth theoretical analysis, and insights into the proposed framework across extended time series benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that MemKD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KD methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that it can match the teacher model's performance across a wide range of compression levels, achieving notable reductions in parameter count and memory usage without a significant loss in accuracy.

</details>


### [255] [Learning to Decide, Not to Reason: Parameter-Efficient Decision Operators via Low-Rank Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06950)
*Ran Li,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DecisionSteer introduces a parameter-efficient method for injecting skills into frozen language models, using a 330K-parameter System-1 decision operator trained by behavior cloning that matches a 1.33M-parameter RL-trained operator, with a 23K parameter rank-4 variant sufficient for many tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for injecting skills into frozen language models require approximately one million parameters and a reinforcement-learning pipeline, which is computationally expensive. The authors aim to reduce this cost by roughly two orders of magnitude while maintaining or exceeding performance.

Method: The method uses a zero-initialized output projection inside a shared low-rank backbone, trained by behavior cloning. This addresses the trainability issue caused by initialization that zeroes gradients in prior operators. The approach functions as a System-1 decision operator, collapsing 3,685-token deliberation into 6-token decisions.

Result: The default 330K-parameter operator matches a 1.33M-parameter RL-trained operator while collapsing deliberation length significantly. A rank-4 variant with 23K parameters (1/58 of the strongest prior operator) suffices for SearchQA and nearly suffices for LiveMath. The method transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains persisting on newly released problems. The operator amplifies answers along the model's existing late-layer pathway, and skills compose as approximately linear operators.

Conclusion: The key to the method is trainability set jointly by initialization and architecture. Prior operators' initialization zeroes gradients at the first optimization step, whereas the zero-initialized output projection receives gradients immediately. This enables efficient skill injection without chain-of-thought compression, with gains tracking the base model's headroom across 13 base-task pairs. Skills can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped at inference time.

Abstract: Injecting skills into a frozen language model currently costs a million parameters and a reinforcement-learning pipeline. We introduce \method{}, a System-1 decision operator trained by behavior cloning that lowers this cost by roughly two orders of magnitude. The default operator uses 330K parameters to match a 1.33M-parameter operator trained with reinforcement learning, exceeds or achieve comparable performance, while collapsing 3,685-token deliberation into a 6-token decision with no loss in accuracy. A rank-4 variant with 23K parameters, 1/58 of the strongest published skill operator, suffices for SearchQA and near-suffices for LiveMath, where higher rank still helps; the same recipe transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains persisting on LiveMath problems released months after training. The gap to prior work is trainability, and it is set jointly by initialization and architecture: the initialization of prior operators zeroes the gradient of both large factor matrices at the first optimization step, whereas our zero-initialized output projection inside a shared low-rank backbone receives a gradient immediately, which a gradient-flow probe confirms directly. The gain isn't chain-of-thought compression: 23 of 57 LiveMath points beat the base model's best-of-8 sampling, and a logit-lens probe shows the operator amplifies the answer along the model's existing late-layer pathway, not writing it earlier. Gains track the base model's headroom across 13 base--task pairs, and skills compose as approximately linear operators that can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped at inference time. Code on https://github.com/rlisml/decisionsteer.

</details>


### [256] [Do Neural PDE Solvers Learn the Right Dynamics?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06952)
*Haonan Li,Yue Song,Bin Yang,Kaihong Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an evaluation framework for neural PDE solvers that goes beyond prediction accuracy to assess dynamical fidelity through three aspects: error formation, ensemble geometry, and extreme events. Using 2D Kolmogorov flow experiments, the authors demonstrate that conventional metrics can obscure significant limitations in learned dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current neural PDE solvers are evaluated primarily by prediction errors, which fail to capture how errors accumulate, how nearby states diverge, or how extreme events arise. This provides an incomplete picture of whether these models truly capture the underlying dynamics of the systems they model.

Method: The authors propose an evaluation framework that evolves ensembles of nearby initial states and compares them with direct numerical simulation. They assess three complementary aspects: error formation (how errors accumulate over time), ensemble geometry (the spatial directions where nearby states diverge), and extreme events (prediction of persistent extreme events).

Result: Experiments on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow reveal that: (1) smaller trajectory errors can reflect weaker error amplification despite less accurate local updates; (2) models can match ensemble spread and effective dimension while failing to capture spatial directions of divergence; (3) matching overall event frequencies can conceal failures to predict persistent extreme events.

Conclusion: Improved prediction accuracy does not necessarily imply greater dynamical fidelity. The proposed framework makes this distinction measurable and provides concrete criteria for evaluating whether advances in neural PDE solvers better capture the underlying dynamics.

Abstract: Neural PDE solvers can achieve low prediction errors, but do they reproduce the dynamics of the systems they model? Prediction scores alone offer an incomplete answer: they measure agreement with reference solutions but provide limited insight into how errors accumulate, nearby states diverge, or extreme events arise. We propose an evaluation framework that directly examines these behaviors in deterministic and stochastic neural solvers. By evolving ensembles of nearby initial states and comparing them with direct numerical simulation, we assess three complementary aspects of learned dynamics: error formation, ensemble geometry, and extreme events. Experiments on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow reveal limitations that conventional scores can obscure. Smaller trajectory errors can reflect weaker error amplification despite less accurate local updates. Models can match an ensemble's overall spread and effective dimension while failing to capture the spatial directions where nearby states diverge. Similarly, matching overall event frequencies can conceal failures to predict persistent extreme events. These findings show that improved prediction accuracy does not necessarily imply greater dynamical fidelity. Our framework makes this distinction measurable, providing concrete criteria for evaluating whether advances in neural PDE solvers better capture the underlying dynamics.

</details>


### [257] [EVFormer: An Egocentric Vision-EMG Bidirectional Attention Model for Bimanual Hand Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06970)
*JiaCheng Ge,SiYu Zhang,ShengJie Li,XinTong Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EVFormer is a multimodal framework that combines egocentric RGB vision with bilateral wrist sEMG data to estimate 44 finger and wrist joint angles, achieving 11.482° MAE (13.20% better than vision-only, 14.23% better than late fusion) in a single-participant feasibility study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Egocentric bimanual hand pose estimation is important for virtual interaction, wearable control, and rehabilitation, but visual observations suffer from self-occlusion, hand-hand contact, and object manipulation. This work aims to address these limitations by integrating sEMG signals that can capture muscle activity independent of visual occlusion.

Method: EVFormer uses a dual-branch architecture: (1) encodes visual spatial features from current RGB frame, (2) encodes sEMG temporal features from preceding 200ms of bilateral wrist sEMG. Cross-modal interaction occurs through sequential bidirectional cross-attention, followed by feature-wise gated fusion to integrate the two modalities.

Result: On 296 test samples, EVFormer achieves 11.482° mean absolute error, compared to 13.228-13.610° for vision-only, sEMG-only, late-fusion, and training-mean baselines. This represents 13.20% relative error reduction vs. vision-only and 14.23% vs. late fusion. EVFormer also achieved lowest error in 4 of 5 gesture classes.

Conclusion: Feature-level interaction between egocentric vision and sEMG can improve bimanual hand pose estimation. However, generalizability requires further evaluation across multiple participants, recording sessions, sensor placements, and real-world conditions.

Abstract: Egocentric bimanual hand pose estimation is important for virtual interaction, wearable control, and rehabilitation, but visual observations are often degraded by self-occlusion, hand-hand contact, and object manipulation. We propose EVFormer, a multimodal framework that combines the current RGB frame with the preceding 200 ms of bilateral wrist surface electromyography (sEMG) to estimate 44 finger and wrist joint angles. EVFormer separately encodes visual spatial features and sEMG temporal features, enables cross-modal information exchange through sequential bidirectional cross-attention, and integrates the two modalities using feature-wise gated fusion. We evaluate EVFormer in a single-participant feasibility study using one synchronized public EgoEMG recording with chronologically separated training, validation, and test splits. On 296 test samples, EVFormer achieves a mean absolute error of 11.482 degrees, compared with 13.228-13.610 degrees for vision-only, sEMG-only, late-fusion, and training-mean baselines. This corresponds to relative error reductions of 13.20% compared with the vision-only model and 14.23% compared with late fusion. EVFormer also achieves the lowest error in four of the five evaluated gesture classes. These results provide preliminary evidence that feature-level interaction between egocentric vision and sEMG can improve bimanual hand pose estimation. Further evaluation across participants, recording sessions, sensor placements, and real-world interaction conditions is required to establish the generalizability of the approach.

</details>


### [258] [Uncertainty in Representation Learning on Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06974)
*Yuqicheng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This thesis addresses three sources of uncertainty in knowledge graph embedding (KGE): knowledge uncertainty (incomplete/noisy input), algorithmic uncertainty (training randomness), and predictive uncertainty (output reliability). It proposes model-agnostic solutions including a voting-based aggregation framework, conformal prediction adaptation for distribution-free coverage guarantees, and embedding-based approaches for probabilistic reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current KGE methods achieve strong benchmark performance but lack principled reliability guarantees, making them unsuitable for high-stakes applications. Uncertainty exists throughout the KGE pipeline (input, training, prediction), requiring systematic investigation.

Method: The thesis develops three complementary approaches: (1) Voting-based aggregation to mitigate training instability; (2) Conformal prediction adaptation to provide distribution-free coverage guarantees and predicate-conditional reliability; (3) Statistically valid prediction intervals and embedding-based probabilistic reasoning with formal soundness guarantees.

Result: The work demonstrates that models under identical settings produce substantially different predictions, and provides theoretically grounded uncertainty quantification methods that are model-agnostic and practically applicable.

Conclusion: The proposed methods advance KGE beyond predictive accuracy toward reliable, uncertainty-aware knowledge graph reasoning, offering practical solutions with theoretical guarantees for high-stakes applications.

Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) methods represent entities and predicates in continuous vector spaces to infer missing knowledge. Despite strong benchmark performance, their predictions often lack principled reliability guarantees, limiting their use in high-stakes applications. Moreover, uncertainty arises throughout the KGE pipeline, from incomplete or probabilistic input knowledge to stochastic training and prediction. This thesis systematically investigates three sources of uncertainty in KGE: knowledge uncertainty, arising from incomplete, noisy, or probabilistic input knowledge; algorithmic uncertainty, induced by randomness in model training; and predictive uncertainty, concerning the reliability of model outputs. To address algorithmic uncertainty, the thesis demonstrates that models trained under identical settings can produce substantially different predictions and introduces a voting-based aggregation framework to mitigate this instability. To quantify predictive uncertainty, it adapts conformal prediction to KGE, constructing answer sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees and extending them to provide predicate-conditional reliability guarantees. To support reasoning under knowledge uncertainty, it develops statistically valid prediction intervals for confidence-scored triples and an embedding-based approach to approximate probabilistic reasoning over statistical ontologies with formal soundness guarantees. Together, these complementary, model-agnostic methods provide a practical and theoretically grounded approach to uncertainty in KGE, advancing beyond predictive accuracy toward reliable and uncertainty-aware knowledge graph reasoning.

</details>


### [259] [FC-SWE: Failure-Conditioned RL for Long-Horizon Software Engineering Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07898)
*Jia Liufu,Bin Hu,Linglin Jing,Terry Kong,Yuki Huang,Ashwath Aithal,Wenming Yang,Jun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FC-SWE introduces a failure-conditioned reinforcement learning framework for software engineering agents that incorporates recovery attempts into training by using failed patches and verifier feedback as context for subsequent recovery trajectories, achieving 41.7% Resolved@1 on SWE-bench Verified compared to GRPO's 38.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SWE agent training with GRPO independently samples multiple trajectories per issue but does not reuse verifier feedback from failed patches as context for subsequent attempts, despite this feedback containing valuable diagnostic information about what went wrong.

Method: FC-SWE restores the repository to its original task state after a patch fails, then uses the failed patch and verifier feedback as context for a recovery trajectory. Two key mechanisms: (1) Trajectory-local rewards preserve each attempt's verifier outcome, preventing recovery success from rewarding earlier failed patches; (2) Active-set advantage estimation forms comparison groups from all actually executed trajectories for the same issue.

Result: On all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a verifier-assisted protocol with Qwen3.5-4B and SWE-agent: FC-SWE achieves 41.7% Resolved@1 and 52.8% Resolved@2, compared to GRPO's 38.9% and 48.5%. With 11 attempts at test time, FC-SWE reaches 70.7% Resolved@11.

Conclusion: FC-SWE effectively leverages failure feedback by conditioning recovery attempts on failed patches and verifier output, significantly improving SWE agent performance over GRPO, with substantial gains when allowed multiple attempts at test time.

Abstract: Repository-level software engineering (SWE) is a challenging long-horizon setting: agents must reason over extended interactions, use tools, and adapt to stateful environments. Recent work trains SWE agents with reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which independently sample multiple trajectories per issue, test the resulting patches, and compare terminal rewards within a fixed group. However, this training setup does not reuse verifier feedback from failed patches as context for subsequent attempts, even though this feedback contains valuable diagnostic information about what went wrong. Training on recovery trajectories is challenging because the preceding outcome determines whether the next trajectory is generated, while the failed execution determines its conditioning context. We introduce FC-SWE, a failure-conditioned RL framework that incorporates recovery attempts into policy training. After a patch fails verification, FC-SWE restores the repository to its original task state and uses the failed patch and verifier feedback as context for a recovery trajectory. FC-SWE adapts GRPO to these chains of complete, multi-turn tool-use trajectories through two mechanisms. Trajectory-local rewards preserve each attempt's verifier outcome, preventing recovery success from rewarding an earlier failed patch. Active-set advantage estimation forms a comparison group from all initial and recovery trajectories actually executed for the same issue, so failed attempts remain in the group while unexecuted attempts are excluded. On all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a verifier-assisted protocol, FC-SWE with Qwen3.5-4B and SWE-agent achieves 41.7% Resolved@1 and 52.8% Resolved@2, compared with 38.9% and 48.5% for GRPO. Although trained with at most two attempts per chain, FC-SWE reaches 70.7% Resolved@11 under an eleven-attempt test-time budget.

</details>


### [260] [A Data-Driven Framework for Unsupervised Monitoring of Transmission Systems Using End-of-Line Testing Data: A Case Study at Ford Motor Company](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06980)
*Mohammad N. Bisheh,Mehrdad Moradi,Parinaz Farajiparvar,Colin Brady,Rajesh Gupta,Xueling Li,Javad Navaei,Milad Parvaneh,Kamran Paynabar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An advanced multivariate monitoring framework for high-dimensional temporal data in manufacturing, using nonlinear dimensionality reduction and control chart-based phase I monitoring, achieving superior accuracy, recall, and F1 score over existing models at Ford Motor Company.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional statistical monitoring methods struggle with nonlinear structure in HD temporal data, while deep learning models are unsuitable when data collection is costly and interpretability, low-latency, computational efficiency, and usability by non-technical practitioners are required.

Method: Two-stage framework: (1) preprocessing to remove incomplete/non-informative samples and temporally align time series; (2) nonlinear dimensionality reduction followed by anomaly detection through control chart-based phase I monitoring. Supports both unsupervised and supervised settings.

Result: On Ford automotive manufacturing production data, the method improved accuracy from 0.50 to 0.625, recall from 0.30 to 1.00, and F1 score from 0.429 to 0.769.

Conclusion: The proposed framework outperforms the existing Ford model with flexible, modular components adaptable to different domains, offering a practical balance between predictive performance and industrial usability requirements.

Abstract: Sensing technologies have advanced rapidly across industries ranging from energy to automotive manufacturing. These systems generate high-dimensional (HD) data characterized by complex nonlinear patterns and strong temporal dependencies. Traditional statistical monitoring methods are often limited in their ability to capture such nonlinear structure. Likewise, many analytical approaches used in End-of-Line testing rely on predefined thresholds and heuristic rules, which restrict their ability to detect informative anomaly signatures in HD temporal data. In contrast, while modern deep learning and generative AI models offer strong predictive capabilities, they are often unsuitable in applications where data are costly to collect and where the monitoring system must remain interpretable, low-latency, computationally efficient, and usable by non-technical practitioners. To overcome these limitations, we propose an advanced multivariate monitoring framework for HD data. The framework operates in two stages. In the first stage, the data are preprocessed to remove incomplete and non-informative samples and to temporally align time series data. In the second stage, nonlinear dimensionality reduction is performed, followed by anomaly detection through a control chart based phase I monitoring procedure. The framework can be used in both unsupervised and supervised settings, depending on the availability of ground truth labels during training. Moreover, its flexible and modular structure allows practitioners to adapt its components to different domains and operational requirements. We evaluate the proposed framework on real production data from an automotive manufacturing environment at Ford Motor Company. The proposed method achieves higher accuracy, recall, and F1 score than the company's existing model, improving these metrics from 0.50, 0.30, and 0.429 to 0.625, 1.00, and 0.769, respectively.

</details>


### [261] [An Information-Theoretic Evaluation Framework for Benchmark and Model Diagnosis in Knowledge Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06988)
*Houru Jiang,Zixi Wang,Tengteng Cheng,Xueyi Li,Mingliang Hou,Jiaqi Zheng,Renqiang Luo,Teng Guo,Zitao Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an information-theoretic evaluation framework for knowledge tracing (KT) benchmark diagnosis using Context Tree Weighting (CTW). Instead of relying solely on global aggregate metrics like AUC and accuracy, the framework evaluates model performance across distinct entropy bands to identify where errors originate and whether benchmarks are approaching saturation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current KT models are predominantly evaluated using aggregate metrics (AUC, accuracy) which obscure the source of remaining errors and fail to indicate whether benchmarks are approaching saturation. While estimating global theoretical performance limits is challenging, quantifying local predictability is feasible.

Method: The framework uses Context Tree Weighting (CTW) on item-response histories and current-item queries as an operational causal uncertainty coordinate. It distinguishes this from unobserved Local Irreducible Uncertainty (LIU) under the full KT information set. Predictions are projected onto this shared uncertainty coordinate to evaluate performance gains across distinct entropy bands. Additional analyses include item-aware references, log-loss, and equal-frequency analyses.

Result: Comprehensive evaluations on NIPS Task 3/4 and Algebra 2005 reveal that model improvements are highly non-uniform. Modern KT models show substantial gains in high-entropy regions. The framework also flags regions where apparent gains require checks for noise-sensitive behavior.

Conclusion: This approach provides a diagnostic tool for studying both residual predictive structure and the limitations of current KT benchmarks and models by surfacing local modeling failures alongside genuine gains.

Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) models are predominantly evaluated using aggregate metrics such as area under the curve (AUC) and accuracy. However, these global scores obscure where the remaining errors originate and fail to indicate whether a benchmark is approaching saturation. While estimating a global theoretical performance limit is challenging in realistic KT settings, it is possible to quantify local predictability. To address this, we propose an information-theoretic evaluation framework for KT benchmark diagnosis. We use Context Tree Weighting (CTW) on item-response histories and current-item queries as an operational causal uncertainty coordinate, while distinguishing it from the unobserved Local Irreducible Uncertainty (LIU) under the full KT information set. By projecting predictions onto this shared uncertainty coordinate, we evaluate model performance gains across distinct entropy bands rather than only at the global level. Comprehensive evaluations on NIPS Task 3/4 and Algebra 2005 reveal that model improvements are highly non-uniform. Modern KT models show substantial gains in high-entropy regions, and additional item-aware references, log-loss, and equal-frequency analyses support this localization. The framework also flags regions where apparent gains require checks for noise-sensitive behavior. By surfacing these local modeling failures alongside genuine gains, this approach provides a diagnostic tool for studying both residual predictive structure and the limitations of current KT benchmarks and models.

</details>


### [262] [Repair Lot Skyline: A Weighted Constraint Satisfaction Approach to Pavement Repair Optimization from Geospatial Hazard Density](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06989)
*Takato Yasuno,Keita Kobayashi,Ryuta Sakaguchi,Takuya Okamoto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes pavement repair planning as a Repair Lot Skyline problem using Weighted Constraint Satisfaction Problem (WCSP). The approach identifies 143 hazard clusters and produces an optimal repair plan covering 100% of potholes and 91.6% of cracks while achieving 83.7% efficiency in repair length. Hyperparameter tuning further reduces crew mobilizations by 7.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pavement agencies need to convert spatial distress data into actionable repair plans. The challenge is balancing accident-critical defects (potholes) that must be addressed, lower-risk defects (cracks) that should be included only when benefit justifies cost, and historical patch locations that signal re-degradation risk without triggering repair.

Method: The problem is formalized as a WCSP defined over chainage (distance along the road) rather than over time, requiring only a single-epoch distress survey. The approach involves: 1) Identifying candidate hazard clusters (hard and soft), 2) Merging candidates into repair lots using minimum-lot-length L_min and historical-context radius κ hyperparameters, 3) Generating a skyline frontier to identify optimal trade-offs, 4) Four-objective hyperparameter search over L_min and κ.

Result: The WCSP identified 143 candidate hazard clusters (61 hard, 82 soft), with 106 merged into a final repair plan totaling 1,997.4 m—83.7% of the 2,385.9 m required if all soft candidates were included. The plan covers 100% of potholes (138/138) and 91.6% of cracks (404/441), capturing 93.6% of total hazard benefit. The skyline frontier shows pronounced diminishing returns: the remaining 37 excluded soft candidates would add only 6.8% additional benefit for a 19.4% increase in repair length. Recommended configuration (L_min = 14.7 m, κ = 10 m) reduces repair-crew mobilizations by 7.1% relative to untuned default, at the cost of a 12.9% larger budget and a 1.1-percentage-point lower crack coverage.

Conclusion: The Repair Lot Skyline framework using WCSP effectively optimizes pavement repair planning by balancing multiple objectives. The approach achieves high coverage of critical hazards (100% potholes) while maintaining efficiency. Hyperparameter tuning provides additional operational benefits, though with slight trade-offs in budget and crack coverage. The method requires only single-epoch distress data and makes no assumptions about future deterioration.

Abstract: Pavement agencies must translate a spatially distributed distress inventory into a bounded, actionable repair-lot plan: accident-critical defects (potholes) must always be addressed, lower-risk defects (cracks) should be included only when their benefit justifies the repair cost, and historical patch locations signal re-degradation risk without themselves triggering repair. We formalize this as a Repair Lot Skyline problem: a Weighted Constraint Satisfaction Problem (WCSP) defined over chainage (distance along the road) rather than over time, so that it requires only a single-epoch distress survey and makes no claim about future deterioration. The WCSP identifies 143 candidate hazard clusters (61 hard, 82 soft), of which 106 are merged into a final repair plan totaling 1,997.4 m---83.7% of the 2,385.9 m that would be required if every soft candidate were included regardless of cost. This plan covers 100% of observed potholes (138/138) and 91.6% of observed cracks (404/441), capturing 93.6% (542/579) of the total hazard benefit available in the full candidate set. The skyline frontier shows pronounced diminishing returns beyond this point: the remaining 37 excluded soft candidates would add only 6.8% additional benefit for a 19.4% increase in repair length. We further formalize the minimum-lot-length $L_{\min}$ and historical-context radius $κ$ as a joint, four-objective hyperparameter search over this WCSP; on the same case study, the recommended configuration ($L_{\min} = 14.7$ m, $κ= 10$ m) reduces repair-crew mobilizations by 7.1% relative to an untuned default, at the cost of a 12.9% larger budget and a 1.1-percentage-point lower crack coverage.

</details>


### [263] [DART-ES: Difficulty-Aware Reweighting and Targeted Replay for Fine-Tuning LLMs with Evolution Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06993)
*Zhishen Sun,Hongzhan Wang,Sizhe Dang,Guang Dai,Haishan Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DART-ES improves Evolution Strategies for LLM fine-tuning by dynamically reweighting problems based on estimated difficulty and replaying rare solvable samples, achieving better accuracy than ES and GRPO while being more memory and time efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Evolution Strategies uniformly average rewards across problems and compress problem-level feedback into a single scalar, making it difficult to capture how the learning value of each problem changes with model capability.

Method: DART-ES estimates local solvability of each problem from pass rate across perturbation population and aggregates historical observations to construct a dynamic difficulty state. This shared state jointly guides continuous difficulty reweighting and rare solvable sample replay, without introducing an additional difficulty model or backpropagation.

Result: DART-ES outperforms ES on all five base models, improving average accuracy from 72.07% to 73.53%, exceeding GRPO's 73.26% on GSM8K. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, DART-ES achieves 49.20% vs 48.34% for ES. It also shows gains in instruction tuning, code generation, and Countdown task with 14B model.

Conclusion: DART-ES provides a simple yet effective approach to improve ES for LLM fine-tuning, achieving competitive performance with strong 7B RL-trained models while offering significant efficiency advantages: 15.2%--50.2% runtime reduction and 21.1%--51.1% memory reduction compared with GRPO, even outperforming GRPO+LoRA in efficiency despite full parameter fine-tuning.

Abstract: Evolution Strategies (ES) enable memory efficient full parameter fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) using only forward computation. However, standard ES uniformly averages rewards across problems and compresses problem level population feedback into a single scalar, making it difficult to capture how the learning value of each problem changes with model capability. To address this limitation, we propose Difficulty-Aware Reweighting and Targeted Replay for Evolution Strategies (DART-ES). DART-ES estimates the local solvability of each problem from its pass rate across the perturbation population and aggregates historical observations to construct a dynamic difficulty state. This shared state jointly guides continuous difficulty reweighting and rare solvable sample replay, thereby improving perturbation direction evaluation and training data allocation without introducing an additional difficulty model or backpropagation. Extensive experiments show that DART-ES achieves good fine-tuning performance. DART-ES outperforms ES on all five base models and improves the average accuracy from 72.07\% to 73.53\%, exceeding the 73.26\% achieved by GRPO on GSM8K. Across five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, DART-ES achieves an average accuracy of 49.20\%, compared with 48.34\% for ES and remains competitive with strong 7B models trained with RL. Further experiments show consistent gains in instruction tuning, code generation and the Countdown task with a 14B model, demonstrating strong generalization across tasks and scalability to larger models. Beyond performance gains, DART-ES also shows clear advantages in system efficiency. It reduces runtime per step by 15.2\%--50.2\% and peak memory usage per GPU by 21.1\%--51.1\% compared with GRPO. Despite performing full parameter fine-tuning, DART-ES also requires less runtime and GPU memory than GRPO+LoRA.

</details>


### [264] [Mask-Guided KV Cache Eviction in Block Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06996)
*Gleb Molodtsov,Ekaterina Alimaskina,Evgeny Uskov,Artur Zagitov,Aleksandr Beznosikov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MaskAhead is a training-free method that reduces KV cache memory and improves generation speed in block diffusion language models by using a mask-query-based ranking mechanism to jointly solve token selection and eviction problems. Q-MaskAhead further extends this to 20.1x KV memory reduction with minimal quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Block diffusion language models maintain a large KV cache throughout generation and attend to it at every denoising step, which limits both memory capacity and generation speed. Current methods require separate solutions for token selection (denoising current block) and eviction (keeping for future blocks), and these are often tackled independently.

Method: MaskAhead uses a single mask-query-based ranking mechanism to solve both selection and eviction tasks. Selection is guided by current-block masks, while eviction is guided by probes of upcoming masked blocks. Both rank KV entries by their estimated contribution to attention output. Q-MaskAhead computes selection and attention directly from low-bit quantized KV, preserving selected entries.

Result: On long-prompt QA tasks, MaskAhead reduces KV memory by 9.5x on average with only 1.2-point mean F1 loss. Q-MaskAhead increases reduction to 20.1x with 2.3-point mean F1 loss. In batch-32 systems profiling, MaskAhead achieves 1.23x end-to-end and 1.68x decode-stage speedups over dense inference.

Conclusion: MaskAhead effectively reduces KV cache memory and improves generation speed in block diffusion language models with minimal quality degradation. The quantized variant Q-MaskAhead achieves even greater memory reduction. The method is training-free and works across various long-generation reasoning, long-prompt QA, and retrieval tasks.

Abstract: Block diffusion language models keep a large key-value (KV) cache throughout generation and attend to it at every denoising step, limiting both memory capacity and generation speed. Reducing these costs requires deciding which past tokens to use for denoising the current block (selection) and which to keep in memory for future blocks (eviction). We propose MaskAhead, a training-free method that solves both tasks with a single mask-query-based ranking mechanism. Current-block masks guide selection, while probes of upcoming masked blocks guide eviction. Both rank KV entries by their estimated contribution to the attention output. Our quantized variant, Q-MaskAhead, computes selection and attention directly from low-bit KV, largely preserving the selected entries. Experiments on Fast-dLLM-v2, DreamReasoner, and LLaDA2.0-mini cover long-generation reasoning, long-prompt question answering, and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. On long-prompt QA, MaskAhead reduces KV memory by $9.5\times$ on average with a 1.2-point mean F1 loss relative to dense inference. Q-MaskAhead increases the reduction to $20.1\times$ with a 2.3-point mean F1 loss. In a batch-32 systems profile, MaskAhead achieves $1.23\times$ end-to-end and $1.68\times$ decode-stage speedups over dense inference.

</details>


### [265] [Should We Skip Diffusion?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07002)
*Yiping Ji,James Martens,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DDT-RFE removes residual connections in the diffusion transformer's condition encoder while fusing multi-depth features to improve both image generation quality (lower FID on ImageNet) and visual understanding tasks (classification, segmentation, object discovery, semantic correspondence).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Skip/residual connections in the encoder allow shallow features to bypass successive transformations, limiting progressive abstraction and making it difficult to disentangle different levels of abstraction. The decoder needs both high-level abstract structures and low-level details for effective denoising at all noise levels.

Method: DDT-RFE removes residual connections around Self-Attention and MLP operations in each encoder block while maintaining stable training. It fuses the input patch embedding with intermediate and final encoder features to form the encoder output, giving the decoder access to information from multiple encoder depths while enabling each block to learn more abstract representations.

Result: DDT-RFE achieves overall improvements over DDT across visual understanding tasks (image classification, semantic segmentation, object discovery, and semantic correspondence) with fewer encoder blocks, and achieves a lower FID for image generation on ImageNet.

Conclusion: Removing residual connections in diffusion transformer encoders and fusing multi-depth features enables better abstraction learning, improving both generative and discriminative visual tasks while being more parameter-efficient.

Abstract: Diffusion models learn semantic representations while generating images. In the Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (DDT), a condition encoder provides features that guide a velocity decoder in denoising. To enable effective denoising at all noise levels, these features must capture both high-level abstract structures and low-level details. However, skip/residual connections in the encoder allow shallow features to bypass successive transformations, which may limit progressive abstraction, or at least make it difficult to disentangle different levels of abstraction. We propose DDT-RFE, which removes the residual connections around the Self-Attention and MLP operations in each encoder block while maintaining stable training. To retain the information that abstraction discards but that the decoder still needs, we fuse the input patch embedding with intermediate and final encoder features to form the encoder output. The decoder thus has access to information from multiple encoder depths, while each encoder block is able to learn more abstract representations. DDT-RFE achieves overall improvements over DDT across visual understanding tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, object discovery, and semantic correspondence, while using fewer encoder blocks. It also achieves a lower FID for image generation on ImageNet.

</details>


### [266] [STOCK-JEPA: Prior-Anchored Latent Revision Representation Learning in Equity Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07006)
*Yizhi Luo,Jiahe Yi,Jianhui Zhang,Shuo Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Stock-JEPA is a joint-embedding predictive architecture that combines interpretable financial priors with deep learning to learn equity representations. It uses a low-complexity financial model as a fixed anchor and learns predictable revisions from historical context, achieving state-of-the-art performance across China and U.S. equity markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the tension between interpretable linear financial models (which oversimplify and miss non-linear signals) and black-box deep learning models (which overfit noise and lack economic structure). The goal is to combine the strengths of both approaches for better equity market representation learning.

Method: The method has three components: (1) A prior branch using a low-complexity financial model to generate multi-horizon return/risk statistics, projected into latent space as an anchor; (2) A revision branch using a context-conditioned predictor to estimate predictable displacement from the anchor; (3) Separate loss functions for both branches. The representation modules are frozen for downstream forecasting evaluation.

Result: Stock-JEPA outperforms 13 strong baselines across large-scale China and U.S. equity universes on 5 key evaluation metrics. Theoretically, the optimal revision reduces the prior anchor's expected squared error by exactly E[||Δ||²], representing the expected squared magnitude of predictable signal from historical context.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully bridges classic financial models and deep learning by learning incremental revisions to financial priors. This approach provides both interpretability (through the prior) and enhanced predictive power (through revision learning), demonstrating practical value for equity market representation learning.

Abstract: Learning effective representations helps characterize the structure and dynamics of equity markets from financial data with a low signal-to-noise ratio. Black-box deep models can capture complex patterns but may overfit sample noise and lack explicit economic structure. Meanwhile, classic linear financial models provide interpretable references, but their oversimplified assumptions leave non-linear signals uncaptured. To combine the strengths of these two directions, we propose Stock-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive framework that learns predictable incremental revisions relative to a point-in-time financial prior. First, we leverage a low-complexity financial model to produce fixed statistics summarizing multi-horizon return and risk. A prior projector then maps these statistics into the target encoder's latent space as an anchor. Second, we design a context-conditioned revision predictor to estimate the future representation's predictable displacement from the anchor. Separate losses update the two branches: the anchor learns from prior statistics, while the revision captures additional predictable information from historical context. Third, we freeze all representation modules and train a downstream readout, evaluating its forecasts through cross-sectional ranking and portfolio performance. Theoretically, we prove that optimal revision reduces the prior anchor's expected squared error for the same future representation by exactly $\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbolΔ\|_2^2]$. This non-negative gain is the expected squared magnitude of the additional signal predictable from historical context. Experimentally, Stock-JEPA outperforms 13 strong baselines across large-scale China and U.S. equity universes on 5 key evaluation metrics. Ablation studies and representation analysis further demonstrate the value of the learned revisions for representation learning in equity markets.

</details>


### [267] [Identifiable World Models from Pretrained Diffusion Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07028)
*Ruchi Sandilya,Conor Liston,Logan Grosenick*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes ConDA (Contrastive Diffusion Alignment), a method that equips frozen pretrained diffusion models with identifiable latent coordinates without retraining, using auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees and a lightweight alignment map.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based world models can generate trajectories but their latent coordinates don't necessarily recover underlying state variables or causal interactions. The authors ask whether identifiable coordinates can be added to a frozen diffusion model without retraining.

Method: The method uses auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees transferred to ConDA, which learns only a lightweight alignment map on top of frozen diffusion latents. Under TCL/GCL assumptions, the approach identifies latent states up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, preserves the latent dynamic SCM, and reduces lagged graph recovery to transition-Jacobian sparsity. Evaluation compares TCL-, GCL-, and CEBRA-based ConDA against TDRL, CaRiNG, IDOL, temporal SuaVE, and iVAE across physical and robotic video systems.

Result: TCL and GCL achieve near-perfect blockwise state recovery and competitive lagged graph recovery, including exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system. In a simulated bipedal robot, learned dynamics recover the sign and temporal structure of responses to held-out control perturbations.

Conclusion: A frozen generative diffusion model can be equipped with coordinates that are identifiable, structurally interpretable, and useful for analyzing intervention-relevant dynamics.

Abstract: Diffusion-based world models can generate and predict trajectories in high-dimensional dynamical systems, but predictive accuracy does not imply that their latent coordinates recover the underlying state variables or causal interactions. We ask whether a frozen pretrained diffusion model can be equipped with identifiable coordinates without retraining its generative backbone. We show that auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees can be transferred to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA), which learns only a lightweight alignment map on top of frozen diffusion latents. Under standard TCL/GCL assumptions, the aligned representation identifies latent dynamical states up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, preserves the latent dynamic structural causal model, and reduces lagged graph recovery to transition-Jacobian sparsity. We evaluate TCL-, GCL-, and CEBRA-based ConDA against TDRL, CaRiNG, IDOL, temporal SuaVE, and iVAE across physical and robotic video systems. TCL and GCL achieve near-perfect blockwise state recovery and competitive lagged graph recovery, including exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system. In a simulated bipedal robot, learned dynamics recover the sign and temporal structure of responses to held-out control perturbations. These results show that a frozen generative diffusion model can be equipped with coordinates that are identifiable, structurally interpretable, and useful for analyzing intervention-relevant dynamics.

</details>


### [268] [Shaping the Wind: Nested Potentials for Kinematically Admissible Urban Wind Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07033)
*Yidi Wang,Yunhe Zhang,Jiawei Gu,Ziyue Qiao,Pengyang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents Sculpt, a neural network framework for predicting urban wind fields that enforces kinematic admissibility (mass conservation and wall impermeability) through a nested potential formulation on staggered grids, eliminating the need for post-hoc correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building-resolving large-eddy simulation is computationally expensive for urban wind prediction. While neural surrogates offer faster alternatives, they fail to guarantee kinematic admissibility (local mass conservation and wall impermeability), leading to physically inconsistent predictions that require correction potentially compromising conservation.

Method: The proposed Sculpt framework uses a nested potential parameterization: (1) volume vector potential defined on a 3D staggered grid, where velocity is generated via discrete curl operation ensuring divergence-free flow; (2) shared scalar potential constraining boundary values to enforce wall impermeability without pressure projection; (3) multi-resolution parameterization of the volume potential to preserve large-scale gradient signals during backpropagation. The method is evaluated on UrbanWindFlow, a new LES dataset covering various urban morphologies and inflow conditions.

Result: The method generates divergence-free velocity updates that automatically satisfy both mass conservation and wall impermeability constraints through the mathematical structure of the framework itself, rather than requiring post-hoc correction.

Conclusion: Sculpt demonstrates that embedding physical constraints directly into neural network architecture (physics-informed by design) can produce kinematically admissible predictions without sacrificing computational efficiency or requiring iterative correction schemes.

Abstract: Predicting transient urban winds is fundamental to understanding urban microclimates and designing climate-resilient cities. Building-resolving large-eddy simulation produces detailed incompressible urban wind fields at substantial computational cost for each layout. Neural surrogates offer a faster alternative by learning to predict the evolution of velocity fields. However, minimizing velocity prediction error does not guarantee local mass conservation and wall impermeability, which together define kinematic admissibility. This limitation stems from an unconstrained output representation: geometry conditioning guides predictions but does not restrict them to admissible velocity fields. Correcting boundary violations in these outputs changes the flux balance in adjacent fluid cells and may consequently compromise local mass conservation. To address the challenge, we propose Sculpt, a nested potential framework that builds the coupled, geometry-dependent constraints directly into its parameterization. This nested parameterization generates divergence-free velocity updates through the discrete curl of a volume vector potential on the native three-dimensional staggered grid. A shared scalar potential constrains the vector potential's boundary values so that the same operator also enforces impermeability, without a per-step pressure projection. Because backpropagation through this curl attenuates large-scale gradient signals, we parameterize the volume potential at multiple resolutions to better capture large-scale flow structures. We introduce UrbanWindFlow, an LES dataset spanning urban morphologies and inflow conditions, to evaluate accuracy and kinematic admissibility together.

</details>


### [269] [The Premise Is the Problem: Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07038)
*Weijia Han,Lisha Qu,Zhenda Li,Liying Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the reliability of self-monitored adaptation in forecasting models. The authors examine whether statistical guarantees remain valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same prediction error feedback. In multi-step time-series forecasting, they demonstrate that overlapping targets and forecast error dependence can break key assumptions required by the guarantee, leading to false alarms and degraded prediction quality. Adaptation can also hide sustained changes from its own monitor while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern forecasting models are updated after deployment to respond to changing data. However, these updates can worsen predictions, creating a need for reliable monitors that detect harmful changes and trigger protection. The natural design uses the same prediction errors that guide updates to monitor the system. The motivation is to determine whether this self-monitoring approach maintains its statistical guarantees.

Method: The authors study this problem in the context of multi-step time-series forecasting. They analyze the statistical properties of monitors that share feedback with adaptation mechanisms, examining how overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors affect the key assumptions required for valid statistical guarantees.

Result: The study reveals that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the monitor's statistical guarantee. This leads to: (1) false alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, (2) protective responses that further damage prediction quality, (3) adaptation hiding sustained changes from its own monitor, while (4) the original frozen model retains a clearer signal of the changes.

Conclusion: The results expose a fundamental failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. The paper demonstrates why reliable deployment requires: checking the monitor's assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response. This work highlights a critical limitation in current adaptive forecasting systems and provides guidance for more robust deployment practices.

Abstract: Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data. These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor's assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response.

</details>


### [270] [TRIAGE: Direction-Aware Mismatch Stabilization of Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07043)
*Zhen Li,Shuai Zhang,Yanggan Gu,Yiming Zhang,Yang Yu,Mingfa Feng,Congkai Xie,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai,Hongxia Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRIAGE is a direction-aware stabilization method for low-precision (NVFP4) reinforcement learning that addresses the destabilizing interaction between learner-sampler mismatch and policy-gradient updates. It selectively rebalances policy-gradient contributions and applies bounded repair to severe mismatch, achieving full precision-level performance while delivering 2.3x higher rollout throughput than BF16.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-precision execution can accelerate RL for LLMs, but discrepancies between learner and sampler execution destabilize policy optimization. The mismatch magnitude alone cannot identify whether its effect amplifies or contracts the policy-gradient direction.

Method: TRIAGE introduces segment-level diagnosis to distinguish locally amplifying from contracting update contributions caused by mismatch. It selectively rebalances policy-gradient updates and applies bounded repair to residual severe mismatch. The method retains native NVFP4 weight-and-activation 4-bit (W4A4) forward execution on both sampler and learner.

Result: TRIAGE achieves stable optimization throughout the training horizon and attains full precision-level performance across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Native NVFP4 with TRIAGE provides up to 2.3x higher rollout throughput than BF16. Experiments conducted on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B.

Conclusion: TRIAGE effectively stabilizes low-precision RL training by addressing direction-aware mismatch effects, enabling practical deployment of 4-bit execution while maintaining performance and significantly improving throughput.

Abstract: Low-precision execution can substantially accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models, but discrepancies between learner and sampler execution can destabilize policy optimization. In this paper, we characterize the interaction between mismatch and the policy-gradient direction, distinguishing locally amplifying from contracting update contributions that mismatch magnitude alone cannot identify. In native NVFP4 runs, we observe an early imbalance between the two amplifying regions, favoring negative-advantage, negative-gap updates. Their tail tokens become concentrated in a small fraction of response segments before mismatch spreads globally. Motivated by these findings, we introduce TRIAGE, a direction-aware stabilization method that uses segment-level diagnosis to selectively rebalance policy-gradient updates and applies bounded repair to residual severe mismatch. TRIAGE modifies the optimization objective while retaining native NVFP4 weight-and activation 4-bit (W4A4) forward execution on both the sampler and learner. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B show stable optimization throughout the evaluated training horizon and achieve full precision level performance across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, while native NVFP4 with TRIAGE provides up to 2.3x higher rollout throughput than BF16.

</details>


### [271] [Skillful Data-Driven Subseasonal Soil Moisture Forecasting: Prospects and Limits for Flash Drought Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07060)
*Noelia Otero,Atahan Özer,Miguel-Ángel Fernández-Torres,Jackie Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a Vision Transformer-based model for subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) soil-moisture forecasting over Europe. The key finding is that forecast skill depends heavily on problem formulation—specifically, forecasting root-zone soil moisture in physical units rather than standardized anomalies significantly improves predictability. The model outperforms deep-learning and operational ECMWF baselines but struggles with flash drought onset detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite progress in weather forecasting, predicting high-impact events like flash droughts remains challenging for both early warning systems and S2S prediction models. The research aims to improve S2S soil-moisture forecasting over Europe using deep learning approaches.

Method: The study uses a Vision Transformer-based architecture with dual-pathway temporal and spatial attention, incorporating residual learning. They compare forecasting in physical units vs. standardized anomalies and apply quantile-head fine-tuning for probabilistic predictions. The model is benchmarked against deep-learning and operational ECMWF S2S baselines over 2021-2022.

Result: The model achieves highest deterministic and probabilistic skill at all lead times when forecasting root-zone soil moisture in physical units. It reliably detects anomalously dry root-zone states (below 20th percentile). However, flash drought onset prediction (defined by multi-pentad intensification criteria) remains fundamentally challenging across all current S2S systems.

Conclusion: Data-driven S2S soil-moisture forecasting can outperform operational systems when properly formulated (using physical units). However, rapid drought development (flash drought onset) remains a key challenge even for advanced deep learning models, highlighting a fundamental limitation in current S2S prediction capabilities.

Abstract: Despite substantial progress in short-to-medium-range weather forecasting, predicting high-impact events such as flash droughts remains a key challenge for both early warning operations and physically-based subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction systems. Here we demonstrate that, for S2S soil-moisture forecasting over Europe, forecast skill depends as much on how the prediction problem is formulated as on the forecasting model itself. Using a Vision Transformer-based architecture with dual-pathway temporal and spatial attention, we show that residual learning is essential to outperform persistence. This advantage is realized only when forecasting root-zone soil moisture in physical units rather than standardized anomalies, revealing that the target representation itself constrains predictability. A probabilistic extension via quantile-head fine-tuning further provides well-calibrated predictive distributions. Benchmarked against deep-learning and operational ECMWF S2S baselines over 2021-2022, our model achieves the highest deterministic and probabilistic skill at all lead times and reliably detects anomalously dry root-zone states (below the 20th percentile). Yet flash drought onset, defined by multi-pentad intensification criteria, remains a fundamental challenge shared across all current S2S systems. These findings advance data-driven S2S soil-moisture forecasting while highlighting the remaining challenge of predicting rapid drought development.

</details>


### [272] [Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07062)
*Yining Zhao,Bushi Liu,Haofei Yu,Zhengyang Qi,Shanyong Wang,Chuyue Li,Yuxiang Liu,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces macro2mind, a method to train large language models to simulate human behavioral reasoning by learning from prediction market data. It uses GRPO with market signals, incorporating social behavioral decomposition to explicitly model how different participant groups interpret news, update beliefs, and interact. A hindsight-regret curriculum focuses training on informative transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based human simulation relies on behavioral reasoning from pretraining or limited individual-level annotations, which lack diversity and provide insufficient supervision of the reasoning process. Prediction markets offer a novel solution by capturing population-level responses to real-world events through price trajectories.

Method: The method trains a language model using GRPO with market signals. Key components include: (1) Social behavioral decomposition that models explicit behavioral reasoning by inferring participant groups, predicting their individual interpretation and belief updates, reasoning about group interactions, and aggregating into price predictions; (2) A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling that focuses training on transitions where identified groups substantially improve forecasts while maintaining learnability.

Result: macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket (SWM-Bench). It transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, CAD) with competitive performance among zero-shot methods. As a data generator, it improves downstream simulator accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming its backbone by 13.2 points.

Conclusion: Learning behavioral reasoning from prediction markets is viable and effective. The model successfully transfers from market data to user simulation without further training, demonstrating that market-derived reasoning generalizes to downstream behavioral simulation tasks. This approach provides scalable supervision for behavioral reasoning in LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.

</details>
