### [273] [What Must Replay Preserve? Separating Correctable Bias from Class Correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07077)
*BoRen Deng,Xiangyue Ma,Chenglong Li,Xiaoting Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a diagnostic framework to analyze the benefits of logit replay in class-incremental learning. The authors investigate whether the accuracy cost of deleting replay matching comes from the stored scores themselves or from classifier bias toward recent classes, and find that most of the large cost (14.9→1.8 points) is correctable via an offset, while a smaller persistent cost (4.3→4.0 points) remains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logit replay methods like DER and DER++ mitigate catastrophic forgetting by matching the model's past predictions on stored examples. However, it was unclear whether the benefit comes from the stored prediction scores themselves or from the classifier's bias toward recent classes. The authors sought to diagnose this by separating classes known at storage from classes learned afterward.

Method: The authors propose a diagnostic framework that treats cached predictions as temporally heterogeneous supervision. They separate classes known when an example was stored from classes learned afterward, edit each group, and evaluate every model before and after a task-level offset that leaves within-task predictions unchanged. Experiments were conducted on CIFAR-100 using DER++.

Result: On CIFAR-100 with DER++: (1) The large cost of deleting later-class matching (14.9 points) was reduced to 1.8 points after applying the offset, showing it was mostly due to classifier bias. (2) Reassigning non-gold scores of classes known at storage (preserving their values and each task's target probability) showed persistent costs of 4.3 points before and 4.0 points after the offset. (3) This smaller cost persists in image distillation, indicating it comes from disrupting class correspondence.

Conclusion: In the fixed-head setting tested, the large cost of deleting later-class matching is mostly correctable by the task-level offset (classifier bias), whereas the smaller cost of disrupting class correspondence persists. This suggests two distinct mechanisms in replay methods: one related to classifier bias (correctable) and one related to class representation preservation (persistent).

Abstract: Class-incremental learning must recognize all classes seen so far without task labels. Logit replay methods such as DER and DER++ mitigate forgetting by matching the model's past predictions on stored examples. Deleting this matching reveals its benefit, but the resulting accuracy cost cannot show whether the stored scores themselves are needed, or whether the cost survives correction of the classifier's bias toward recent classes. We propose a diagnostic framework that treats a cached prediction as temporally heterogeneous supervision: it separates classes known when an example was stored from classes learned afterward, edits each group, and evaluates every model before and after a task-level offset that leaves within-task predictions unchanged. On CIFAR-100 with DER++, suitable fixed constants replace the unrefreshed stored scores of later-learned classes within an equivalence margin of 1 percentage point, and the offset reduces the cost of deleting their matching from 14.9 to 1.8 points. Reassigning the non-gold scores of classes known at storage, which preserves their values and each task's target probability, costs 4.3 points before and 4.0 after the offset, and a parallel cost persists in image distillation. In the tested fixed-head setting, the large cost of deleting later-class matching is thus mostly correctable by this offset, whereas the smaller cost of disrupting class correspondence persists. Code and data are available at anonymous.4open.science/r/replay-preserve-E22B.

</details>


### [274] [Few-Shot Bioactivity Prediction with Meta-Learning under Assay Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07079)
*Michal Kmicikiewicz,Tommy Rochussen,Vincent Fortuin,Ewa Szczurek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MetaHeta is a meta-learning framework that addresses assay heterogeneity in few-shot bioactivity prediction by combining linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, improving drug discovery outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Individual drug discovery assays often contain too few measurements to train reliable models independently. While meta-learning offers a principled few-shot approach, its effectiveness is limited by assay heterogeneity - meta-learning performance degrades as meta-training tasks become more heterogeneous.

Method: MetaHeta accounts for assay heterogeneity by conditioning predictions on auxiliary data from related assays, with relatedness flexibly defined from available assay information. The architecture combines linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, enabling efficient scaling without compromising exact attention over the context.

Result: Demonstrated on assays from ChEMBL and BindingDB, MetaHeta improves few-shot bioactivity prediction and downstream compound prioritization in retrospective Bayesian optimization compared to baseline approaches.

Conclusion: Accounting for assay heterogeneity in meta-learning frameworks significantly improves few-shot bioactivity prediction, enabling better compound prioritization in early-stage drug discovery pipelines.

Abstract: Accurate bioactivity prediction is a central challenge in early-stage drug discovery, as individual assays often contain too few measurements to train reliable models independently. Meta-learning offers a principled approach to this few-shot setting, but assay heterogeneity may limit its effectiveness. Here, we test this hypothesis and show that meta-learning performance degrades as meta-training tasks become more heterogeneous. To address this, we introduce MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework that accounts for assay heterogeneity by conditioning predictions on auxiliary data from related assays, with relatedness defined flexibly from available assay information. The architecture of MetaHeta combines linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, enabling efficient scaling to the former without compromising exact attention over the latter. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on assays from ChEMBL and BindingDB, improving few-shot bioactivity prediction and downstream compound prioritization in retrospective Bayesian optimization.

</details>


### [275] [When Attention Does Not Explain the Peak: Temporal Reference vs. Forecast Output in Attention-Based Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07080)
*Yuji Akamatsu,Takao Yamanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the interpretation that attention maps in load-forecasting models indicate what the model uses for predictions. Through experiments on the Panama dataset, the authors show that while attention patterns are structured, consistent, and sensitive to inputs, they do not selectively identify peak timings—suggesting attention serves an integrative rather than selective role.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether attention maps in load-forecasting models can be interpreted as evidence of what the model uses when making predictions, particularly for identifying peak timing. They challenge the common assumption that high attention weights indicate causal importance for predictions.

Method: The authors use a horizon-level attention descriptor (Ψ_out) and test its predictive power on the Panama load dataset across 31 day-aligned windows. They compare: (1) the forecast peak timing vs. observed peak timing, (2) the argmax of attention weights vs. observed peak timing, (3) attention concentration around peaks vs. uniform baseline, (4) cross-window consistency of attention patterns, and (5) the effect of replacing future weather features with training-set means.

Result: The forecast achieves a median peak-time error of 0 hours with 51.6% exact match, while the argmax of attention has a median error of 5 hours with 0% exact match. The forecast peak is closer to the observed peak in 27 out of 31 windows. Attention concentration around peaks is weak (only 1.16x, 1.11x, and 1.14x the uniform baseline for observed, predicted, and weekly-naive peaks). However, attention shows high cross-window consistency (0.83) and is sensitive to future weather variation (replacing weather features with means makes the profile nearly uniform). Results are reproducible across three random-seed runs.

Conclusion: Structured, input-sensitive, and reproducible horizon-level cross-attention does not necessarily provide a valid peak-selective explanation of forecast behavior. The attention appears to serve an internal horizon-reference role for integrating future exogenous information rather than explicitly identifying peak timing, though this functional role is not causally established.

Abstract: Attention maps are often interpreted as evidence of what a forecasting model uses when making predictions. In our load-forecasting model, a CLS representation of historical demand queries 24 future exogenous horizon tokens through cross-attention, inviting a temporal interpretation in which highly attended horizons may appear to explain forecast peak timing. We test this interpretation using a horizon-level attention descriptor, $Ψ_{\mathrm{out}}$. Across 31 day-aligned windows of the Panama load dataset, the forecast achieves a median peak-time error of 0 h and a 51.6% exact-match rate, whereas the argmax of $Ψ_{\mathrm{out}}$ has a median error of 5 h and 0% exact match. The forecast peak is closer to the observed peak in 27 of 31 windows. This dissociation is not merely an argmax artifact: within $\pm1$ h, attention reaches only $1.16\times$, $1.11\times$, and $1.14\times$ the uniform baseline around observed, predicted, and weekly-naive peaks, respectively, indicating weak and non-selective concentration. Yet the attention profile is structured, with cross-window consistency of 0.83. Replacing 12 future weather features with their training-set means makes the profile nearly uniform, showing sensitivity to future weather variation rather than fixed horizon position alone. The dissociation is also reproduced across three random-seed runs. These results show that structured, input-sensitive, and reproducible horizon-level cross-attention need not provide a valid peak-selective explanation of forecast behavior. The observed behavior is instead consistent with an internal horizon-reference role for integrating future exogenous information, although this functional role is not causally established.

</details>


### [276] [SchemaFill: Efficient LLM Tool Calling via Slot-Parallel Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07086)
*Zhi-Kai Chen,Song-Yan Li,De-Chuan Zhan,Han-Jia Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SchemaFill improves LLM tool-calling efficiency by using slot-parallel speculative decoding to generate multiple argument values concurrently, achieving up to 4.05× throughput improvement over standard autoregressive decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard autoregressive decoding generates tool calls token by token, causing substantial latency when handling multiple calls or many argument fields. There was a need to exploit parallelism across slots and calls while maintaining output correctness.

Method: SchemaFill generates future slot values concurrently as candidates without requiring advance knowledge of actual call sequence or argument values. Candidates spanning multiple fields and calls are concatenated for verification by the target model under the actual output prefix. Only verified tokens are committed, and the target supplies corrections when candidates disagree.

Result: On Glaive and BFCL datasets, SchemaFill achieves up to 4.05× improvement in end-to-end throughput over autoregressive decoding.

Conclusion: SchemaFill successfully applies target verification while exploiting parallelism across slots and calls, significantly reducing latency in LLM tool-calling scenarios.

Abstract: LLM agents interact with external systems by generating structured tool calls. Given a user request, conversational context, and a catalog of tool schemas, a tool-calling model must select tools and generate their arguments, potentially producing multiple calls in a single response. Standard autoregressive decoding generates these calls token by token, incurring substantial latency for requests involving multiple calls or many argument fields. The explicit argument structure offers opportunities for parallel generation, but later argument values may depend on preceding fields and calls, so independently generated values can differ from the target model's output. We present SchemaFill, a framework for efficient LLM tool calling through slot-parallel speculative decoding. SchemaFill generates future slot values concurrently as candidates, without requiring advance knowledge of the actual call sequence or argument values. Candidates spanning multiple fields and calls are concatenated for verification by the target model under the actual output prefix. Only verified tokens are committed, and the target supplies corrections when candidates disagree. This applies target verification while exploiting parallelism across slots and calls. On Glaive and BFCL, SchemaFill achieves up to a 4.05$\times$ improvement in end-to-end throughput over autoregressive decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/Czzzk/SchemaFill.

</details>


### [277] [Muon Is Theoretically Wrong For Convolutions, But Empirically Effective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07103)
*Thibaut Boissin,Thomas Massena,Mathieu Serrurier,Franck Mamalet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the application of Muon optimizer to convolutional neural networks. While Muon has clear theoretical interpretation for matrix-valued updates, standard implementations reshape 4D convolutional kernels into matrices, breaking theoretical alignment. The authors propose Convolutional Newton-Schulz (Conv-NS) to preserve kernel support while approximating the polar factor in convolutional operator geometry. Both methods achieve comparable accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with the unexpected finding that the theoretically superior method doesn't outperform the simpler reshape-based approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon is an efficient optimizer with clear interpretation for matrix-valued updates, but convolutional kernels are stored as 4D tensors. Standard implementations reshape these tensors into matrices, which breaks the theoretical understanding behind Muon. The authors aim to investigate this theoretical-practical gap.

Method: The authors formalize the optimization objective directly in convolutional operator geometry and introduce Convolutional Newton-Schulz (Conv-NS), which approximates the polar factor in this geometry while preserving kernel support. They compare Conv-NS with reshape-based Muon on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification tasks.

Result: Both Conv-NS and reshape-based Muon are computationally efficient and achieve comparable accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification tasks. Contrary to expectations, the theoretically aligned Conv-NS does not outperform the reshape-based Muon.

Conclusion: The mismatch between practice and theoretical understanding suggests that exact convolutional orthogonalization may overconstrain updates. These findings highlight Muon's strong practical performance while opening directions for its further development on convolutions.

Abstract: Muon, an optimizer known for its efficiency, has a clear interpretation for matrix-valued updates, but convolutional kernels are stored as four-dimensional tensors. Standard implementations reshape these tensors into matrices, a shortcut which breaks the theoretical understanding behind Muon. To investigate this, we formalize the corresponding optimization objective directly in convolutional operator geometry and introduce Convolutional Newton-Schulz (Conv-NS), which approximates the polar factor in this geometry while preserving kernel support. When applied in fast training experiments, Conv-NS and reshape-based Muon are both computationally efficient and achieve comparable accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification tasks. However, as one could expect a theoretically aligned Conv-NS to outperform reshape-based Muon, we investigate this mismatch between practice and theoretical understanding, with the hypothesis that exact convolutional orthogonalization may overconstrain updates. These findings highlight Muon's strong practical performance while opening directions for its further development on convolutions. Our code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/thib-s/muonconv-cifar10-airbench}{github conv-muon}.

</details>


### [278] [LiLib: Lifelong Air-to-Ground Path-Loss Prediction on UAVs via a Drift-Triggered Model Library](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07111)
*Minh Tran*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LiLib is a lightweight continual-learning scheme for UAVs to predict air-to-ground path-loss by maintaining a small library of recursive-least-squares experts, using windowed residual tests for drift detection and probe phases for expert reuse or creation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UAVs acting as relays or base stations need accurate path-loss predictions, but propagation conditions change as UAVs move between different environments. Existing approaches either forget previous environments (sliding-window) or average incompatible regimes (single model).

Method: LiLib maintains a small library of recursive-least-squares experts. A windowed residual test detects drift; a short probe phase then either reuses the best stored expert or creates a new one. The system identifies regimes without labels.

Result: LiLib reduces prediction RMSE from 5.89 dB to 4.03 dB (p < 0.001), lowers error after returning to known environments from 12.3 dB to 5.7 dB, and recovers 99% of throughput of a regime-aware oracle. The library stores four experts in under 0.5 KB with 92% regime identification purity. When initialized with a peer's library, error after environment changes halves.

Conclusion: For recurring drift, remembering (storing expert models) is more effective than re-adapting (forgetting and relearning). Limitations include not reaching oracle performance and potential merging of similar regimes under strong shadowing.

Abstract: UAVs that act as relays or base stations need accurate air-to-ground path-loss predictions for rate adaptation and placement, but propagation conditions change as a UAV moves between suburban, urban and high-rise areas, and the same areas are often revisited. Online regressors that adapt by forgetting must relearn each environment from scratch, whereas a single model trained on all data averages incompatible regimes. We propose LiLib, a lightweight continual-learning scheme in which a UAV maintains a small library of recursive-least-squares experts. A windowed residual test detects drift; a short probe phase then either reuses the best stored expert or creates a new one. In simulations based on four standard urbanization profiles, LiLib reduces prediction RMSE from 5.89 dB (best sliding-window baseline) to 4.03 dB (p < 0.001), lowers the error shortly after a return to a known environment from 12.3 dB to 5.7 dB, and recovers 99% of the throughput of a regime-aware oracle in rate adaptation. The library stores four experts in under 0.5 KB, and identifies regimes with 92% purity without labels. When a second UAV is initialized with the library of a peer, its error after environment changes halves. LiLib does not reach the oracle, and similar regimes may be merged when shadowing is strong. The results indicate that, for recurring drift, remembering is more effective than re-adapting.

</details>


### [279] [Sample-Optimal Estimation of the Fréchet Inception Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07114)
*Ziyun Chen,Jerry Li,Kevin Tian,Yusong Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses finite-sample bias in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) estimation for generative models. The authors establish tight statistical bounds for bias and variance, develop extrapolation methods, and introduce Relative Taylor Debiasing (RTD) achieving optimal O(d/ε²) sample complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FID is a standard metric for evaluating generative models, but its empirical plug-in estimator suffers from finite-sample bias. Understanding sample complexity and developing unbiased estimators is crucial for reliable model evaluation, especially as dimensionality increases.

Method: The authors derive finite-sample bounds for bias and variance of the empirical plug-in estimator between d-dimensional Gaussians. They generalize FID_∞ to order-k extrapolation methods and introduce Relative Taylor Debiasing (RTD) using debiasing techniques from U-statistics. They also develop VALE_2, a second-order variance-aware extrapolation estimator.

Result: Three main results: (1) Empirical plug-in has Θ(d²/n) bias and Θ(d/n + d²/n²) variance, requiring ≳ d² samples; (2) Order-k extrapolation achieves Θ(d^{k+2}/n^{k+1}) bias; (3) RTD achieves optimal O(d/ε²) sample complexity. Empirically, RTD achieves lowest error at 50K samples on ImageNet, while VALE_2 matches FID_∞ accuracy at 50K with only 10K samples.

Conclusion: The paper provides a complete statistical framework for FID estimation, demonstrating that RTD achieves optimal sample complexity. The proposed methods significantly reduce sample requirements for accurate FID estimation, making evaluation more practical for high-dimensional embeddings.

Abstract: The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) is widely used to evaluate generative models, but its empirical plug-in estimator suffers from finite-sample bias [BSAG18, CF20]. We study the sample complexity $n$ of estimating FID to error $ε$ between $d$-dimensional Gaussians with bounded mean distance and covariances, when one distribution is known. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We establish tight finite-sample $Θ(\frac{d^2}{n})$ bias and $Θ(\frac{d}{n} + \frac {d^2} {n^2})$ variance bounds for the empirical plug-in estimator, establishing a $\gtrsim d^2$ sample complexity. (2) To debias the empirical plug-in estimator, we generalize the ${\rm FID}_\infty$ estimator of [CF20] to extrapolation methods of arbitrary order $k$. We further prove tight bias and variance bounds of $Θ(\frac{d^{k + 2}}{n^{k + 1}})$ and $Θ(\frac d n + \frac{d^2}{n^2})$ for any order-$k$ extrapolation under our framework. (3) We introduce Relative Taylor Debiasing (RTD), a new, computationally efficient FID estimation algorithm using debiasing techniques inspired by U-statistics. We show that RTD achieves an $O(\frac d {ε^2})$ sample complexity, and prove that this is optimal. We provide a complementary empirical evaluation of our new estimators. Our experiments on synthetic Gaussians validate the predicted residual bias and support the tightness of our bounds. On ImageNet with Inception embeddings, RTD achieves the lowest mean estimation error at the standard 50K sample budget, while our second-order variance-aware extrapolation estimator (VALE$_2$) uses only 10K samples to achieve accuracy comparable to FID$_\infty$ at 50K samples.

</details>


### [280] [Will the Judge Flip? Predicting Position-Sensitive LLM Judgments from Residual Stream Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07115)
*Hashmath Shaik,Gnaneswar Villuri,Alex Doboli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether residual stream activations recorded before an LLM judge's initial verdict can predict whether changing the candidate response order would flip the judge's decision. Using linear probes on 534 JudgeBench pairs and validated on 1,802 MT-Bench comparisons, the study demonstrates that pre-verdict activations can effectively predict order susceptibility, outperforming traditional confidence-based and logits-based predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The order of candidate responses can influence LLM judge verdicts, but detecting this position flip conventionally requires doubling judgments by testing each pair in both orders. This study seeks a more efficient approach by predicting flip susceptibility from neural activations rather than relying on additional judgments.

Method: The researchers employed nested grouped cross-validation with regularized linear probes trained on residual stream activations captured immediately before the initial verdict. They evaluated this approach on 534 JudgeBench pairs across three Qwen3 models and Llama-3.1-8B, then tested generalization on 1,802 MT-Bench comparisons without recalibration.

Result: Linear probes achieved AUROCs ranging from .621 to .850 on JudgeBench, outperforming a combined baseline (verbalized confidence, verdict-label logits, response lengths, and initial choice) by .062 to .113 AUROC. When frozen and applied to MT-Bench, probes achieved AUROCs of .685-.853, demonstrating strong cross-dataset generalization.

Conclusion: Pre-verdict residual stream activations contain predictive information about candidate order susceptibility that exceeds the predictive power of non-activation-based indicators. This approach offers a practical solution for identifying when LLM judges are vulnerable to order effects without requiring paired reverse judgments.

Abstract: The order in which candidate responses are presented can change an LLM judge's verdict. Detecting such a position flip ordinarily requires judging each pair in both orders, which doubles the number of judgments. We investigate whether residual stream activations recorded immediately before the initial verdict can predict a flip. We use nested grouped cross-validation to evaluate regularized linear probes on 534 JudgeBench pairs for three Qwen3 judges and Llama-3.1-8B. The linear probes achieve AUROCs of .621-.850 and outperform a combined baseline that uses verbalized confidence, verdict-label logits, response lengths, and the judge's initial choice by .062-.113 AUROC. Linear probes trained on JudgeBench and then frozen achieve AUROCs of .685-.853 on 1,802 MT-Bench comparisons without MT-Bench fitting or recalibration. These results show that pre-verdict activations support prediction of susceptibility to candidate order and outperform the non-activation predictors evaluated here.

</details>


### [281] [SoloQ: Calibration-Free Quantization for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07121)
*Donghyun Lee,Arkapravo Ghosh,Varun Manjunath,Bumjoon Kyle Rhee,Hyunho Kook,Shiting Xiao,Youngeun Kim,Priyadarshini Panda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SoloQ is a calibration-free quantization framework for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with predictable marginal distribution, eliminating the need for calibration data while maintaining accuracy under 4-bit quantization and achieving 2.61X memory reduction and 2.24X inference speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion large language models face efficiency challenges due to large model sizes and high inference costs. While low-bit quantization is attractive, existing post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps, making data-independent quantization necessary.

Method: SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction to map weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with predictable marginal distribution. This enables calibration-free quantization and supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, commit-time KV-cache quantization is applied to compress persistent states.

Result: SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, it reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA, Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs (Fast-dLLM v2, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion).

Conclusion: SoloQ successfully enables calibration-free quantization for dLLMs, providing a practical solution for efficient deployment of diffusion-based language models without requiring calibration data while achieving significant memory and inference improvements.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models through bidirectional diffusion-based token generation. However, their growing model sizes and high inference costs make efficient deployment challenging: full-sequence denoising repeatedly invokes compute-intensive forward passes, while block-diffusion models additionally introduce a memory-intensive KV-cache. Low-bit weight-activation quantization is therefore attractive, yet existing dLLM post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps. We present SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction for calibration-free quantization. Its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, SoloQ further applies commit-time KV-cache quantization to compress persistent states without perturbing the actively denoised block. Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs(Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, SoloQ reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X.

</details>


### [282] [The Implicit Bias of Hyperbolic Representation Learning for Multiclass Data: A Busemann Risk Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07131)
*Xingrun Li,Sho Kuno,Yusuke Mukuta,Xin Yang,Tatsuya Harada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow in hyperbolic space for multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes, focusing on PERM losses. The study reveals two key phenomena: boundary saturation (radius dynamics determined by drift coefficient μ) and near-boundary clustering (direction convergence to Busemann risk critical points).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding implicit bias in hyperbolic representation learning is crucial because hyperbolic space naturally captures hierarchical structures. This work addresses the gap in theoretical understanding of how gradient descent behaves in hyperbolic space, particularly for multiclass classification problems where traditional Euclidean analysis fails.

Method: The authors use a decomposition approach: separating the distance to each prototype into a radial term and a direction-dependent term described by the Busemann function. They then analyze the asymptotic behavior of Riemannian gradient flow to prove a radial dichotomy based on drift coefficient μ.

Result: Two main results: (1) A radial dichotomy where the sign of drift coefficient μ determines trajectory behavior - positive drift leads to r(t)=½log t+O(1) toward the ideal boundary, while negative drift returns trajectories to the large-radius threshold in finite time. (2) The boundary direction converges to a critical point of the Busemann risk on ∂ℍⁿ.

Conclusion: This work provides a rigorous asymptotic framework for understanding boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering phenomena in hyperbolic representation learning, offering theoretical insights into why hyperbolic embeddings are effective for hierarchical data.

Abstract: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction-dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $μ$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\frac{1}{2}\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large-radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that the boundary direction converges to a critical point of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb{H}^n$. These results provide a rigorous asymptotic perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.

</details>


### [283] [Adversarial Training for Deep Hedging in Nonstationary Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07162)
*Philipp J. Schneider,Lukas Looser,Antoine Garin,Shuhan Liu,Daniel Kuhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WRAP (Wasserstein-Reweighting Adversarial Perturbation) is a drift-aware adversarial training framework for deep hedging that addresses nonstationarity in market trajectories by combining two types of distributional robustness: trajectory reweighting via φ-divergence and path perturbation via optimal transport.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep hedging learns trading policies from historical or simulated market trajectories, but under market nonstationarity, training paths may not represent future market conditions, leading to potential model failure when deployed in different market regimes.

Method: The framework derives from a two-budget distributionally robust optimization (DRO) formulation anchored to a weighted empirical reference distribution. The ambiguity set allows an adversary to (1) reweight observed trajectories subject to a φ-divergence constraint, and (2) perturb paths subject to an optimal-transport (OT) constraint. A joint first-order expansion yields a tractable finite-dimensional adversarial attack that approximates the distributional inner supremum.

Result: The first-order expansion reveals that the leading-order increase in expected loss decomposes into: (1) a reweighting contribution determined by the dispersion of hedging losses across trajectories, and (2) a transport contribution determined by the sensitivity of the loss to path perturbations. Experiments on Heston dynamics (stationary/nonstationary) and generalized affine diffusion (GAD) show complementary benefits from reweighting and transport, with joint adversarial training providing the largest gains under nonstationarity.

Conclusion: The proposed WRAP framework effectively addresses distributional misspecification in deep hedging by combining trajectory reweighting and path perturbation. The complementary nature of these two approaches provides robust hedging strategies, especially under nonstationary market conditions, demonstrating the importance of accounting for both sampling uncertainty and temporal drift in financial machine learning.

Abstract: Deep hedging learns trading policies from historical or simulated market trajectories, yet under nonstationarity these training paths may not represent future market conditions. We propose WRAP (Wasserstein-Reweighting Adversarial Perturbation), a drift-aware adversarial training framework derived from a two-budget distributionally robust optimization (DRO) formulation. The formulation is anchored to a weighted empirical reference distribution whose fixed baseline weights are chosen to balance sampling uncertainty against temporal drift. Around this reference distribution, the ambiguity set addresses two complementary forms of distributional misspecification by allowing an adversary to reweight the observed trajectories subject to a $φ$-divergence constraint and perturb their paths subject to an optimal-transport (OT) constraint. We derive a joint first-order expansion in which the leading-order increase over the nominal expected loss decomposes into a reweighting contribution determined by the dispersion of hedging losses across trajectories and a transport contribution determined by the sensitivity of the loss to path perturbations. This expansion yields an explicit finite-dimensional adversarial attack that replaces the distributional inner supremum with a tractable first-order approximation. Across stationary and nonstationary Heston dynamics and a generalized affine diffusion (GAD), the experiments show complementary benefits from reweighting and transport, with joint adversarial training providing the largest gains under nonstationarity.

</details>


### [284] [A theory of platonic representations in language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07168)
*Darshil Doshi,Wenjie Zhou,Corinna Elena Wegner,Daniel J. Korchinski,Santiago Acevedo,Matthieu Wyart*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper explains why translated sentences have similar representations in middle layers of multilingual language models, proposing that this arises from a hidden hierarchical structure where abstract levels are shared across languages while surface levels are language-specific. Using synthetic languages from probabilistic context-free grammars and belief propagation, the framework predicts and empirically confirms several phenomena including why cross-lingual similarity peaks in middle layers and how alignment occurs with code-switched data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The observation that translated sentences have similar representations in the inner layers of multilingual language models remains unexplained theoretically. This phenomenon relates to the "platonic representation hypothesis" but lacks a formal explanation. The authors aim to provide a theoretical foundation for this cross-lingual similarity pattern observed in multilingual transformers.

Method: The authors generate synthetic languages from probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) that share upper-level production rules but not lower-level ones across languages. They show that the Bayes-optimal next-token predictor corresponds to belief propagation (BP), and encoding BP messages in successive layers of a transformer yields analytical predictions that can be compared with transformers trained on the same data.

Result: The framework successfully explains multiple empirical observations: (1) cross-lingual similarity peaks in middle layers, (2) this similarity coexists with language-specific structure, (3) similarity strengthens with language proximity, model quality, and data exposure, (4) the framework distinguishes similarity (shared neighborhood geometry) from alignment (shared coordinates), with alignment occurring when code-switched data is abundant, and (5) subtracting from each layer the component linearly predictable from the preceding one increases cross-lingual similarity, which was confirmed in pretrained LLMs.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical structure hypothesis, combined with belief propagation as the optimal predictor, provides a theoretical explanation for the cross-lingual representation patterns observed in multilingual language models. This framework unifies multiple empirical findings and makes testable predictions that hold across different conditions (language proximity, model quality, data exposure) and in pretrained LLMs.

Abstract: Representations of translated sentences are similar in the inner layers of multilingual language models -- an observation connected to the platonic representation hypothesis, yet unexplained theoretically. We provide an explanation based on the assumption that data have a hidden hierarchical structure whose abstract levels are shared across languages while surface levels are modality- or language-specific. Concretely, we generate synthetic languages from probabilistic context-free grammars sharing upper-level but not lower-level production rules. In this setting the Bayes-optimal next-token predictor is belief propagation (BP); encoding its messages in successive layers yields analytical predictions that agree well with transformers trained on the same data. The framework explains why cross-lingual similarity peaks in middle layers, coexists with language-specific structure, and strengthens with language proximity, model quality and data exposure. It distinguishes similarity (shared neighborhood geometry) from alignment (shared coordinates), showing that the latter occurs when code-switched data, i.e. mixed-language sentences, are abundant enough. It further predicts that subtracting from each layer the component linearly predictable from the preceding one increases cross-lingual similarity, which we confirm in pretrained LLMs.

</details>


### [285] [CLM-as-a-Judge: Evaluating an Open Contrastive Decision Model on Public Judge Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07177)
*Gowthamkumar Nandakishore*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates an open contrastive decision model (CLM) as a judge on preference benchmarks and finds it performs near chance (0.351-0.593), indistinguishable from coin flipping. While the model shows overconfident calibration, temperature scaling can repair it. A confidence-gated cascade escalates 92.3-100% of items to a stronger judge, rendering the near-chance judge nearly useless in practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether open contrastive decision models can serve as effective judges on hard public benchmarks, comparing them against generative judges, reward models, and trivial baselines.

Method: Five public preference benchmarks and one hallucination benchmark were evaluated under preregistration. The model was compared against generative judge, reward model, and trivial always-first baselines. Statistical significance was assessed with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Temperature scaling was applied to calibrate confidence estimates.

Result: CLM-v0.1-8B scores 0.351-0.593, statistically indistinguishable from chance. Reward models (0.764-0.976) and generative judges (0.611-0.778) significantly outperform it. Raw confidences are overconfident (+0.401), but temperature scaling reduces ECE to ≤0.062. Decision order-flip rate (0.0002) and length-preference shift (-0.023) are lower than generative judge. The confidence-gated cascade escalates 0.923-1.000 of items to the strong judge at 0.97 retention threshold.

Conclusion: Contrastive decision models perform near chance as judges, though they exhibit better calibration properties than generative judges. The confidence-gated cascade fails because calibrated confidence about a near-chance judge has almost nothing to keep. The design emphasizes rigorous evaluation with preregistration, multiple benchmarks, and per-item predictions.

Abstract: An open contrastive decision model is near chance as a judge on the hard public benchmarks: Contrastive-LM/CLM-v0.1-8B scores between 0.351 (best- of-four, chance 0.250) and 0.593 (pairwise, chance 0.500), is statistically indistinguishable from coin flipping on RM-Bench and JudgeBench, and answers every HaluEval item with one constant label, matching the trivial always-first baseline at 0.581. Judges with the same parameter count score far higher everywhere: a reward model reaches 0.764 to 0.976 and a generative judge 0.611 to 0.778, and every gap to CLM is significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Two properties do work. Raw confidences are overconfident by up to +0.401, yet one pooled temperature fit on held-out calibration items repairs expected calibration error to at most 0.062, and the repaired confidence ranks the model's own errors above chance on three of six benchmarks. The decision order-flip rate is 0.0002 against 0.2188 for the generative judge, and the length-preference shift is -0.023 against -0.217. The confidence-gated cascade, however, escalates between 0.923 and 1.000 of items to the strong judge at the preregistered 0.97 retention bar: calibrated confidence about a near-chance judge has almost nothing to keep. The design: five public preference benchmarks and one hallucination benchmark with real labels, scored under a preregistration frozen before any test item was seen, against generative, reward-model, and trivial baselines, with per-item predictions released.

</details>


### [286] [Learning Scientific Exploration from Human Research Decision Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07184)
*Xuchen Gong,Shane Gu,Haokun Liu,Dixi Yao,Chenhao Tan,Tian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ResearchTrails is a dataset of human research trajectories constructed from Git repository commit histories, capturing the systematic process of scientific exploration including changes to methods, experiments, and ablations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific corpora primarily record final outcomes rather than research trajectories. A key challenge in building AI systems for scientific research is enabling scientific exploration - the systematic process of investigating unknown phenomena to gain new knowledge through sequences of research decisions and actions.

Method: Developed an automated and scalable pipeline that extracts structured research trajectories from repository commits, capturing successive changes to methods, experiments, and ablations.

Result: The dataset contains meaningful signals about intermediate research decisions beyond what final papers reveal. Demonstrated utilities include retrieving human research experience as external skills at test time and training models on research trajectories to improve generalization to new research decisions.

Conclusion: The work suggests a path toward AI systems that learn not only from the products of science, but from the evolving process of discovery itself.

Abstract: A key challenge in building AI systems for scientific research is enabling $\textit{scientific exploration}$: the systematic process of investigating unknown phenomena or ideas to gain new knowledge through sequences of research decisions and actions. Yet this process is largely missing from existing scientific corpora; for example, research papers primarily record final outcomes rather than the trajectories that produced them. In this work, we introduce $\textbf{ResearchTrails}$, a dataset of $\textbf{human research trajectories constructed from Git repositories}$, where $\textbf{commit histories}$ serve as proxies for research exploration. We develop an automated and scalable pipeline that extracts structured research trajectories from repository commits, capturing successive changes to methods, experiments, and ablations. We characterize the resulting dataset and show that these trajectories contain meaningful signals about intermediate research decisions beyond what final papers reveal. We further demonstrate utilities of ResearchTrails in multiple use cases, including retrieving human research experience as external skills at test time and training models on research trajectories to improve generalization to new research decisions. Our results suggest a path toward AI systems that learn not only from the products of science, but from the evolving process of discovery itself.

</details>


### [287] [Exact Unlearning via Quantized Sufficient Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07197)
*Ami Tavory,Shripad Gade,Tal Sarig,Noam Touitou,Ido Guy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Quantized Sufficient Statistics (QSS), a new approach to exact machine unlearning that separates a small frozen schema (learns global structure) from mutable content (stores additive corrections). It offers two variants: QSS-L (removes label only) and QSS-E (removes both input and label). Experiments on 15 datasets show QSS-L matches SISA accuracy on 11 tasks while providing 4-483x lower expected deletion latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing exact unlearning methods (like SISA) use disjoint shards but require invalidating entire model shards for each deletion request, and smaller shards reduce data available to each predictor. The authors seek a method that enables exact deletion without full model retraining while maintaining accuracy.

Method: QSS separates model parameters into: (1) a frozen schema that learns global structure from all data, and (2) mutable content storing local prediction corrections as additive statistics indexed by quantized regions. Deletion is implemented as arithmetic subtraction rather than optimization. The approach uses a probabilistic deletion mechanism where with probability 1-ρ it takes a fast arithmetic path, and with probability ρ it triggers a full rebuild.

Result: Across 15 vision, text, and tabular datasets at ρ=0.5%, QSS-L is within 2 percentage points of SISA on 11 tasks and provides 4-483× lower expected deletion latency on low-class-count tasks. QSS-E quantifies the additional accuracy cost of removing every trace of an input.

Conclusion: QSS provides an efficient exact unlearning approach that balances accuracy and deletion speed. The schema-based approach is particularly effective for tasks with fewer classes, achieving significant latency reductions while maintaining comparable accuracy to SISA. The trade-off between QSS-L and QSS-E allows practitioners to choose between retaining unlabeled inputs or complete removal.

Abstract: Exact unlearning requires a deployed predictor to match one rebuilt without the information named by a deletion request. Existing general-purpose exact methods localize retraining through disjoint shards, but every request still invalidates a model, and smaller shards reduce the data available to each constituent predictor. We introduce Quantized Sufficient Statistics (QSS), which separates a small frozen schema from mutable, sum-decomposable content. The schema learns global structure; the content stores local prediction corrections as additive statistics indexed by quantized regions. Deleting content is therefore exact subtraction rather than optimization. We distinguish two guarantees: QSS-L exactly removes a label while retaining the unlabelled input, whereas QSS-E exactly removes both input and label by learning the schema without deletable examples. A deletion takes the arithmetic fast path with probability $1-ρ$ and triggers a full rebuild with probability $ρ$; all reported expected latencies include both events. Across 15 vision, text, and tabular datasets at $ρ=0.5\%$, QSS-L is within 2 percentage points of SISA on 11 tasks and provides 4--483$\times$ lower expected deletion latency on the low-class-count tasks where a compact schema is effective. QSS-E quantifies the additional accuracy cost of removing every trace of an input.

</details>


### [288] [Distributionally Robust Mixture-of-Experts Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07207)
*Xin Teng,Muxiao Li,Hongyi Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DRMoET addresses reliability issues in sparse MoE transformers where routing imperfections can send tokens to insufficiently trained experts. It uses an entropy-regularized softmax rule on EMA-smoothed, activation-weighted expert losses to strengthen plausible non-top routing paths, improving the seven-task average from 0.6625 to 0.6767 at 10.3B parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixture-of-Experts transformers create a hidden reliability problem: when routing is imperfect, load-balanced models may send tokens to experts that are insufficiently trained for the assigned inputs. Current approaches focus on utilization balance but ignore routing robustness.

Method: DRMoET treats layer-wise experts as endogenous robustness groups and optimizes high-loss routing outcomes rather than merely equalizing traffic. It updates per-layer expert distribution using an entropy-regularized softmax rule on EMA-smoothed, activation-weighted expert losses, strengthening plausible non-top routing paths while preserving standard MoE computation.

Result: At 10.3B total parameters and 67B training tokens, DRMoET improves the seven-task average from 0.6625 to 0.6767, while the auxiliary-loss-free baseline achieves 0.6431. It shows lower expert-loss variance with nearly unchanged mean loss, 4.3% lower excess loss under forced mid-k misrouting, and improved domain-expert specialization.

Conclusion: Routing robustness—not only utilization balance—should be a practical objective for reliable sparse MoE scaling. The method is a drop-in objective that works under the FLAME-MoE recipe at both 746M-total and 10.3B-total scales.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers scale capacity by activating only a few experts per token, but this sparsity creates a hidden reliability problem: when routing is imperfect, load-balanced models may send tokens to experts that are insufficiently trained for the assigned inputs. We propose Distributionally Robust MoE Training (DRMoET), a drop-in objective that treats layer-wise experts as endogenous robustness groups and optimizes high-loss routing outcomes rather than merely equalizing traffic. DRMoET updates a per-layer expert distribution by an entropy-regularized softmax rule on EMA-smoothed, activation-weighted expert losses, strengthening plausible non-top routing paths while preserving standard MoE computation. Under the FLAME-MoE recipe at 746M-total and 10.3B-total scales, DRMoET improves downstream averages over both standard FLAME-MoE and auxiliary-loss-free balancing. At 10.3B total parameters and 67B training tokens, DRMoET improves the seven-task average from 0.6625 to 0.6767, while the auxiliary-loss-free baseline achieves 0.6431. Mechanistic analyses show lower expert-loss variance with nearly unchanged mean loss, 4.3% lower excess loss under forced mid-$k$ misrouting, and improved domain-expert specialization. These results position routing robustness-not only utilization balance-as a practical objective for reliable sparse MoE scaling. Project page and code are available at: https://drmoet.github.io/.

</details>


### [289] [Can LLM-assisted regularization increase forecast accuracy for migration flows in low data regimes?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07208)
*Nathaniel T. Hindman,Fabricio Murai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can improve migration forecasting by extracting contextual migration-related signals from news articles and incorporating them into a weighted Lasso forecasting framework through feature-specific regularization penalties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional gravity-based forecasting models rely on structured socio-economic indicators such as economic disparity, political stability, and geographic distance, but struggle to accurately predict migration flows. This work aims to improve migration forecasting by leveraging contextual signals from news articles via LLMs.

Method: The proposed framework uses hierarchical LLM inference pipelines to classify migration-related push-pull signals from news data and incorporates them into a weighted Lasso forecasting framework through feature-specific regularization penalties. The approach is evaluated across multiple migration corridors (Mexico-US, Ukraine-Poland, Syria-Turkey) between November 2021 and November 2022.

Result: Mixed performance was observed across migration corridors and modeling strategies. Best Mexico configuration (gravity-based + push-pull ratios) achieved MAPE of 17.15%; strongest Syria configuration (Direct LLM-Lasso) achieved MAPE of 29.29%; best Ukraine configuration (LLM-Assisted Regularization) achieved MAPE of 41.05%. No single regularization approach consistently outperformed others.

Conclusion: Contextual article-derived features and LLM-guided regularization can improve migration forecasting under certain conditions, although migration corridor characteristics, article volume, and hyperparameter configuration strongly influence performance.

Abstract: Predicting migration flows remains a significant challenge for traditional gravity-based forecasting models, which primarily rely on structured socio-economic indicators such as economic disparity, political stability, and geographic distance. This work investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can improve migration forecasting by extracting contextual migration-related signals from news articles and incorporating them into a weighted Lasso forecasting framework through feature-specific regularization penalties. The proposed framework uses hierarchical LLM inference pipelines to classify migration-related push--pull signals from news data and evaluates the resulting forecasting performance across multiple migration corridors between November 2021 and November 2022, including Mexico--United States, Ukraine--Poland, and Syria--Turkey. Experimental results showed mixed performance across migration corridors and modeling strategies, and no single regularization approach consistently outperformed the others across all experiments. The best-performing Mexico configuration, which consisted of a gravity-based model augmented with the proposed push--pull ratios, achieved a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 17.15%, while the strongest Syria configuration achieved a MAPE of 29.29% using Direct LLM-Lasso. For Ukraine, the best-performing configuration used LLM-Assisted Regularization (AR) and achieved a MAPE of 41.05%. Overall, the results suggest that contextual article-derived features and LLM-guided regularization can improve migration forecasting under certain conditions, although migration corridor characteristics, article volume, and hyperparameter configuration strongly influenced performance.

</details>


### [290] [Reward-Driven Learning under Prompt-Level Differential Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07212)
*Jiachen Zhao,Antonia Januszewicz,Taeho Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first differential privacy guarantee for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), protecting against revelation of training problems. The method aggregates gradients per prompt, applies single clipping, adds Gaussian noise, and achieves ε=8 privacy budget. Experiments show RLVR retains 85-90% of non-private performance gains while outperforming private supervised fine-tuning by 2.3-3.8 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training language models on confidential problems via RLVR can leak which problems were seen in training. The paper addresses this by requiring (ε,δ)-differential privacy at the prompt level, where each prompt (with its multiple responses) is treated as a single privacy record.

Method: The method aggregates gradients from all responses to one prompt, clips the prompt's contribution only once (regardless of response count), adds Gaussian noise to the clipped aggregate, and composes privacy loss across updates. This ensures the privacy budget depends neither on the number of responses per prompt nor on the clipping norm. Training uses Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with LoRA at ε=8.

Result: Compared to control (removing only reward signal), RLVR improves accuracy by 2.65 points on MATH and 3.24 on GSM8K. The improvement survives format-robust scoring (1.3 points on MATH). Against two private supervised fine-tuning recipes at same budget, the private model outperforms by 2.3-3.8 points on both MATH and GSM8K. The approach retains 85-90% of non-private GRPO gains. An eightfold tighter budget costs at most 1.2 points on MATH. Effects also transfer to CommonsenseQA.

Conclusion: Verifier feedback remains a usable learning signal under prompt-level differential privacy, achieving meaningful accuracy gains while maintaining formal privacy guarantees. The proposed DP-GRPO method successfully bridges the gap between privacy requirements and RL training effectiveness.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model on problems that may themselves be confidential, and the trained model can reveal which problems it saw. We study RLVR under prompt-level differential privacy: the released weights must be (ε,δ)-differentially private with respect to the presence of any one training problem. Taking the group of responses to one prompt as the privacy record, our method aggregates their gradients, clips the prompt's contribution once, adds Gaussian noise, and composes the privacy loss across updates, so the budget depends on neither the number of responses per prompt nor the clipping norm; to our knowledge this is the first differential privacy guarantee for RLVR training. We train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with LoRA at a per-run budget of ε=8 and compare, on the same prompts and at the same budget, a control that removes only the reward signal and two private supervised fine-tuning recipes. The reward signal improves accuracy over the control by 2.65 points on MATH and 3.24 on GSM8K, in every seed; the improvement survives a format-robust scorer, at 1.3 points on MATH, and is not explained by response length. At the same budget the private model outperforms both supervised recipes on MATH and GSM8K by 2.3 to 3.8 points, retains 85--90% of the gain of non-private GRPO on these tasks, and on MATH the noise of an eightfold tighter budget costs at most 1.2 points. The reward effect also carries to CommonsenseQA, an exploratory non-mathematical task. Verifier feedback thus remains a usable learning signal under prompt-level privacy.

</details>


### [291] [Constant-Curvature Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein for Heterogeneous Cross-Curvature Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07218)
*Shanglin Li,Wenjing Lu,Muyang Li,Nicu Sebe,Ziheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes CCSGW (constant-curvature sliced Gromov-Wasserstein), a novel divergence for aligning distributions across heterogeneous constant-curvature spaces (hyperbolic and spherical). It introduces geodesic-based 1D projections for spherical spaces and extends sliced GW to enable efficient comparison across manifolds with different curvatures, with applications in graph anomaly detection, node classification, and multimodal learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixed-curvature models typically learn each component space independently due to the inherent heterogeneity of spaces with different curvatures, lacking a unified metric and explicit mechanisms to enforce geometric consistency. Additionally, the problem of comparing probability distributions across mixed-curvature spaces remains unexplored.

Method: The authors propose CCSGW, which: 1) Introduces missing geodesic-based one-dimensional projections for spherical spaces; 2) Extends sliced Gromov-Wasserstein to constant-curvature spaces; 3) Enables efficient and principled comparison across manifolds with different curvatures while preserving intrinsic geometric relationships.

Result: CCSGW controls intrinsic geometric discrepancy across heterogeneous spaces and promotes distribution-level geometric consistency. Integration into existing mixed-curvature learning tasks (graph anomaly detection, node classification, multimodal learning) yields consistent performance gains.

Conclusion: The proposed CCSGW provides a principled framework for comparing distributions across heterogeneous constant-curvature spaces, addressing the limitations of independent component learning in mixed-curvature models and enabling effective geometric alignment across hyperbolic and spherical manifolds.

Abstract: Recent advances in representation learning have highlighted the utility of constant-curvature models, such as hyperbolic and spherical spaces, for modeling complex data. Mixed-curvature models further enhance this by integrating multiple constant-curvature components. However, these models typically learn each component space independently because spaces with different curvatures are inherently heterogeneous and lack a unified metric. Consequently, they lack explicit mechanisms to enforce geometric consistency across various spaces. Moreover, the problem of comparing probability distributions across mixed-curvature spaces remains unexplored. To compare distributions on heterogeneous spaces, Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distances provide a principled framework by aligning their intra-space geometries. Building on this, we propose constant-curvature sliced Gromov-Wasserstein (CCSGW), a novel divergence for aligning distributions supported on heterogeneous constant-curvature spaces. We first introduce the missing geodesic-based one-dimensional projections for spherical spaces, and then extend sliced GW to constant-curvature spaces, enabling efficient and principled comparison across manifolds with different curvatures. This formulation preserves intrinsic geometric relationships while avoiding the high computational cost. We provide theoretical analysis showing that CCSGW controls intrinsic geometric discrepancy across heterogeneous spaces, promoting distribution-level geometric consistency. By integrating CCSGW into existing mixed-curvature learning tasks, including graph anomaly detection, graph node classification, and multimodal learning, we observe consistent performance gains across diverse settings.

</details>


### [292] [Data, Numbers, and Geometry: Three Tutorials on Numerical Methods, Machine Learning, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07220)
*Jessica N. Howard,Yidi Qi,Tomás S. R. Silva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Three practical tutorials on numerical computation and machine learning for mathematical research, covering exterior calculus, neural network design guided by mathematical structure, and machine learning evaluation/visualization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide mathematical researchers with practical computational tools and techniques, bridging the gap between pure mathematics and applied numerical/machine learning methods.

Method: Three independent tutorials: (1) numerical exterior calculus via flux formulation of exterior derivative; (2) using mathematical structures (elliptic curves, quivers, boundary value problems) to guide neural network architecture design with interval arithmetic for residual bounds; (3) comprehensive coverage of ML evaluation metrics, statistical uncertainty, classification thresholds, ROC curves, and accessible figure design.

Result: Tutorials distinguish between numerical agreement, predictive accuracy, structural guarantees, and rigorous bounds as different forms of evidence. Includes notebooks and exercises for reproducibility.

Conclusion: These tutorials provide mathematical researchers with practical tools to integrate numerical computation and machine learning into their work, with emphasis on understanding the different types of evidence each approach provides.

Abstract: We present three practical tutorials on numerical computation and machine learning for mathematical research, developed for the DANGER: Data, Numbers, and Geometry workshop held at the Banff International Research Station in April 2026. The first develops a numerical approach to exterior calculus from pointwise evaluations of differential forms, using a flux formulation of the exterior derivative. Examples in Euclidean space and on the sphere illustrate geometric identities, topological features, and the effects of approximation and finite precision. The second examines how mathematical structure guides neural network design through examples involving elliptic curves, quivers, and a boundary value problem. It explores how architectural choices affect learning and uses interval arithmetic to bound the residual of a trained network over the full interval of the boundary value problem. The third addresses the evaluation and presentation of machine learning results, covering performance metrics, statistical uncertainty, classification thresholds, receiver operating characteristic curves, and accessible figure design. Throughout, the tutorials distinguish numerical agreement, predictive accuracy, structural guarantees, and rigorous bounds as different forms of evidence. Each contribution can be read independently, with accompanying notebooks and exercises that allow readers to reproduce the examples and adapt the methods to other problems.

</details>


### [293] [Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07226)
*T. Y. Tsui,Zihao Ye,Pengxiang Cai,Yanchao Li,Yuqiang Li,Zhehong Ai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MWRL (Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning) addresses the problem of identifying all minimal sufficient witnesses (explanations/mechanisms) that produce an outcome, rather than just finding one solution or redundant supersets. The method uses credit assignment based on set coverage to recover the entire family of witnesses from verifier feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL methods only reveal one solution or redundant ones when asked to find minimal sufficient witnesses. The authors seek to identify ALL minimal witnesses that satisfy a condition, not just a single solution or redundant set.

Method: MWRL takes the union of sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy, then credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This yields both a value iteration planner (for complete witness recovery) and a policy gradient method (that scales to LLMs).

Result: Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. The approach expands RL beyond single-solution optimization to learning witness families from verifier feedback.

Conclusion: MWRL successfully unifies minimality and alternative recovery through a principled credit assignment mechanism derived from the problem definition. It can scale to large language models and provides a framework for learning complete witness families from a simple black-box verifier.

Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

</details>


### [294] [Conditional Flow Matching for Transport Between Markov Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07229)
*Syamantak Kumar,Dheeraj Nagaraj,Saptarshi Roy,Purnamrita Sarkar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses sequence-to-sequence transport for time-series domain adaptation by formulating a flow matching algorithm that learns transport maps between trajectory distributions of Markov processes while preserving the Markov structure. The method is theoretically justified with consistency guarantees and finite-sample bounds, and demonstrates practical success in EEG-based image retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is motivated by sequence-to-sequence transport in the context of time-series domain adaptation. The authors aim to transport trajectories of Markov processes between source and target distributions while preserving the Markov structure, which is challenging due to the temporal dependencies inherent in time-series data.

Method: The authors propose a flow matching based algorithm that learns a transport map from source to target trajectory distribution while preserving the Markov structure. The theoretical analysis follows classical statistical problems (regression, PCA, matrix concentration) in the Markov setting, using mixing time assumptions.

Result: The method is consistent in the population limit. Finite-sample error bounds are derived under mixing time assumptions. A lower-bound construction shows that mixing-time dependent sample complexity is unavoidable even with regular Gaussian conditional transitions. For the EEG application (THINGS-EEG2 dataset), augmenting the ENIGMA decoder with a conditional flow improved mean top-5 retrieval accuracy from 43.87% to 49.05%, representing an 11.82% relative improvement.

Conclusion: The proposed flow matching approach provides a theoretically sound method for trajectory transportation in time-series domain adaptation, with practical effectiveness demonstrated in EEG-based image retrieval. The theoretical results establish that mixing-time dependent sample complexity is a fundamental requirement.

Abstract: Motivated by sequence-to-sequence transport in the context time-series domain adaptation, we study the problem of transportation between trajectories of Markov processes. Given a limited number of trajectories from source distribution and the target distribution, we formulate a flow matching based algorithm which learns a transport map from the source to target trajectory distribution, while preserving the Markov structure. We show that this is consistent in the population limit and derive finite-sample error bounds under mixing time assumptions, following the analysis of classical statistical problems including regression (Nagaraj et al., 2020), principal component analysis (Kumar and Sarkar, 2023), and matrix concentration (Neeman et al., 2024) in the Markov setting. We complement that with a lower-bound construction showing that a mixing-time dependent sample complexity is unavoidable even with regular Gaussian conditional transitions. We evaluate on synthetic and real-world data. For image retrieval from electroencephalography (EEG) on THINGS-EEG2 (Gifford et al., 2022), the task is to identify the viewed image from EEG signals captured from human subjects, which suffers from high inter subject variability. We augment the ENIGMA decoder (Kneeland et al., 2026) with a conditional flow before its subject-specific temporal map. This improves mean top-5 retrieval accuracy from 43.87% to 49.05%, an 11.82% relative improvement.

</details>


### [295] [Benchmarking Time Series Foundation Models for Load Forecasting Under Covariate Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07232)
*Tomas Kaljevic,Ivan Arzola,Yu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks time series foundation models (TSFMs) against traditional trained-from-scratch models for short-term load forecasting (STLF) across three real-world datasets under varying operational conditions. The study evaluates model performance under different levels of covariate availability and quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the gap in knowledge regarding the effectiveness of TSFMs for STLF under realistic operational conditions, particularly when future covariate information may be unavailable or inaccurate.

Method: The researchers conducted a comprehensive benchmark comparing four trained-from-scratch (TFS) models and four TSFMs across three real-world load forecasting datasets under various operational scenarios differing in covariate availability and quality.

Result: Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings when future covariates are available or accurately forecast. However, its performance degrades with increasing covariate noise. TimesNet demonstrates greater robustness under severe covariate uncertainty.

Conclusion: Covariate-informed TSFMs are effective for STLF, but robust covariate modeling is critical in real-world applications where covariate forecasts may be noisy or unavailable.

Abstract: Accurate short-term load forecasting (STLF) is essential for the reliable and efficient operation of modern power systems. While time series foundation models (TSFMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of forecasting tasks, their effectiveness for STLF under realistic operational conditions remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a comprehensive benchmark of four trained-from-scratch (TFS) models and four TSFMs across three real-world load forecasting datasets under operational scenarios that differ in the availability and quality of future covariate information. Our results show that Chronos-2 consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings when future covariates are available or accurately forecast. However, its performance degrades as covariate forecasts become increasingly noisy, whereas TimesNet exhibits greater robustness under severe covariate uncertainty. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of covariate-informed TSFMs for STLF while highlighting the critical role of robust covariate modeling in real-world forecasting applications.

</details>


### [296] [Learning What to Distill: Bilevel Top-K Token Selection for Self-Distillation in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07247)
*Heng Liang,Xinwen Zhang,Hongchang Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BiToK-SD is a novel bilevel-optimization-based token selection method for on-policy self-distillation that adaptively learns which token positions are most beneficial for distillation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks with minimal computational overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing knowledge distillation methods for compact language models either apply uniform distillation across all token positions or use fixed heuristic criteria for token selection, failing to adaptively identify which tokens are most beneficial for learning reasoning capabilities. There is a need for a method that can dynamically learn which positions to distill during the training process.
