Method: BiToK-SD formulates token selection as a bilevel optimization problem: (1) Lower-level uses differentiable threshold-based relaxation for Top-K token selection, allowing selected positions to adapt as the student model evolves; (2) Upper-level performs knowledge distillation only on the selected positions. This enables adaptive learning of beneficial distillation positions.

Result: BiToK-SD achieves the best average performance among all compared methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while requiring only lightweight additional computation.

Conclusion: The proposed bilevel optimization approach successfully enables adaptive token selection for self-distillation, demonstrating that learning which tokens to distill is more effective than uniform or fixed heuristic approaches. This provides a practical and efficient method for transferring reasoning capabilities to compact language models.

Abstract: Large language models have shown strong reasoning capabilities, but their high inference costs make knowledge distillation an important approach for transferring such capabilities to compact models in resource-constrained scenarios. On-policy self-distillation further reduces the reliance on external large teacher models while improving the reasoning ability of compact language models. However, existing methods typically either distill all token positions uniformly or select tokens using fixed heuristic criteria, assigning the same distillation strength to the selected positions rather than adaptively learning which tokens are most beneficial for distillation. To address these limitations, we propose BiToK-SD (Bilevel Top-K Token Selection for Self-Distillation), a bilevel-optimization-based token selection method that learns where distillation should be applied during on-policy self-distillation. Specifically, BiToK-SD is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, where the lower-level problem models Top-K token selection as a differentiable threshold-based relaxation, allowing the selected positions to adapt as the student policy evolves, while the upper-level problem performs knowledge distillation on the selected positions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that BiToK-SD achieves the best average performance among all compared methods while requiring only lightweight additional computation.

</details>


### [297] [Neural Fields Encode Adaptation Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07253)
*Prateik Sinha,Stefania Druga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "adaptation geometry" as a framework for evaluating neural fields beyond their reconstruction capability, focusing on how easily networks can adapt to new observations and what information their weights retain from training history. The authors demonstrate that tangent kernel geometry predicts both adaptation cost and weight retention in image and physical field domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of neural fields relies solely on reconstruction quality, which the authors argue misses two important properties: (1) how easily the network can adapt to new observations, and (2) what information the weights retain from earlier training. The paper aims to characterize these properties through the lens of adaptation geometry.

Method: For image tasks, the authors meta-learn class-specific initializations, adapt each to new images, and measure adaptation cost using a local linear model prediction. They replace one network's tangent kernel with another's to test kernel dependence. For physical fields, they repeatedly fit the same network to sequences of wave observations and analyze what information final weights retain about the history.

Result: For images: A local linear model closely predicts adaptation cost, while swapping tangent kernels substantially worsens predictions, confirming adaptation depends on local geometry rather than just reconstruction. For physical fields: When two wave histories end at the same observation, final weights recover wave velocity sign with 68.6% accuracy (vs. 50% baseline). Tangent-kernel eigenvalues predict both learnability of changes and overwrite speed.

Conclusion: Neural fields contain useful information beyond their current reconstruction: the geometry of how they can change (adaptation) and how they got there (weight history). This adaptation geometry, characterized by tangent kernels, provides a new dimension for evaluating and understanding neural fields.

Abstract: Neural fields are usually evaluated by how well they reconstruct an observation. We show that this misses two useful properties of a fitted network: how easily it can adapt to new observations, and what its weights retain from earlier ones. We study these properties as adaptation geometry. For images, we meta-learn class-specific initializations, adapt each one to a new image, and measure how much the network must change to fit it. A simple local linear model closely predicts this adaptation cost, while replacing one network's tangent kernel with another's substantially worsens the prediction. Adaptation thus depends on the local geometry of the fitted network, not only on its current reconstruction. For physical fields, we repeatedly fit the same network to observations from a sequence. Its weights then retain information about that history. When two wave histories end at exactly the same observation, the final weights recover the sign of the wave velocity with 68.6% accuracy, whereas the current observation alone contains no such information and gives 50%. These two phenomena are quantitatively linked: tangent-kernel eigenvalues predict both which changes are easy to learn and how quickly they are overwritten by later fitting. Together, these results show that neural fields contain useful information beyond what they currently reconstruct: in how they can change and in how they got there.

</details>


### [298] [Neural Algorithmic Reasoning for Graph Saddle Point Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07255)
*Samantha Chen,Jesse He,Coleman Clougherty,Gal Mishne,Chester Holtz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraphPDHG is a novel message-passing framework based on the Chambolle-Pock Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient method for solving general graph saddle-point problems. It can simulate PDHG efficiently and learn an accelerated version, showing stronger size generalization than non-aligned GNNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural algorithmic reasoning aims to solve polynomial-time-solvable and harder combinatorial optimization problems by aligning neural networks with algorithmic paradigms. Existing approaches lack a unified framework for general graph saddle-point problems. This work addresses the need for a systematic approach to incorporate classical optimization methods (PDHG) into graph neural network architectures.

Method: The paper proposes GraphPDHG, a message-passing framework that simulates the Chambolle-Pock Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient (PDHG) method for solving graph saddle-point problems. The method is designed to learn an accelerated PDHG algorithm, and the model is evaluated as a learned warm start for second-order optimization (SSNAL).

Result: The theoretical analysis shows GraphPDHG can efficiently solve a family of graph saddle-point problems by simulating PDHG. Experiments demonstrate that the learned accelerated PDHG improves performance as a warm start for SSNAL, and alignment with PDHG leads to stronger size generalization compared to non-aligned GNN baselines.

Conclusion: GraphPDHG provides a novel architecture for solving a general family of optimization problems on graphs. The work demonstrates that aligning neural networks with classical optimization algorithms (PDHG) improves both optimization performance and generalization across different problem sizes, establishing a promising direction for neural algorithmic reasoning.

Abstract: Neural algorithmic reasoning, or aligning a neural network with an algorithmic paradigm, has emerged as an approach to solving polynomial-time-solvable and computationally harder combinatorial optimization problems. We propose a new message-passing framework based on the Chambolle-Pock Primal--Dual Hybrid Gradient (PDHG) method called \textsc{GraphPDHG} for solving general graph saddle-point problems. Theoretically, we show that \textsc{GraphPDHG} can efficiently solve a family of graph saddle-point problems by simulating PDHG. We also show that our network can learn an accelerated PDHG algorithm. Experimentally, we support our results on accelerated PDHG by evaluating the performance of our model as a learned warm start for second-order optimization techniques (SSNAL). We also show that alignment with PDHG leads to stronger size generalization than non-aligned graph neural network (GNN) baselines. Overall, we propose a novel architecture for solving a general family of optimization problems on graphs.

</details>


### [299] [Algorithmically Aligned Neural Agglomerative Tree Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07271)
*Robert R Nerem,Pranav Singh,Cheyenne Ward,Yusu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces NN-linkage, a neural network model that learns task-specific merge rules for hierarchical clustering while retaining the efficiency of classical linkage algorithms. It aligns with the Lance-Williams framework and can approximate both local and global linkage rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to bridge the gap between classical linkage algorithms (efficient but inflexible) and neural approaches (flexible but inefficient). The goal is to learn task-specific merge rules while maintaining the recursive structure and size generalization of classical hierarchical clustering methods.

Method: NN-linkage is algorithmically aligned with the Lance-Williams (LW) recurrence framework. It uses a neural network to learn locally-dependent merge rules and can be paired with a transformer encoding to approximate globally-dependent rules. The model is theoretically shown to be a universal approximator for continuous linkage functions.

Result: NN-linkage can exactly implement any symmetric constant-coefficient LW recurrence across all input sizes. Empirically, it demonstrates effectiveness over classical algorithms and neural approaches on clock-tree routing and phylogenetic reconstruction tasks using both synthetic and real datasets.

Conclusion: NN-linkage successfully extends efficient hierarchical clustering to scientific and engineering objectives by learning merge rules directly from target trees, capturing task-specific patterns that existing hand-designed linkage rules cannot.

Abstract: Linkage algorithms for hierarchical clustering (HC) are a powerful and efficient framework for constructing clustering trees, yet it is often unclear which merge rule best suits a given dataset or task. In contrast, neural approaches can learn from data, but often fail to retain the efficiency and size generalization of classical algorithms. We introduce NN-linkage, a neural network (NN) model that can learn task-specific and locally dependent merge rules while retaining the recursive structure and efficient inference of classical linkage algorithms. In particular, our model is algorithmically aligned with the Lance-Williams (LW) recurrence, a parameterized framework for defining a broad, continuous family of linkage rules for agglomerative HC. Classical methods such as single linkage (SL), complete linkage (CL), and average linkage arise as discrete choices within this broader family. We show that NN-linkage is a universal approximator for continuous linkage functions, including LW recurrences, and, when paired with a transformer encoding, can also approximate globally dependent rules such as robust single-linkage. We further show that NN-linkage can exactly implement any symmetric constant-coefficient LW recurrence across all input sizes. On the empirical front, we evaluate NN-linkage in real-world applications, clock-tree routing and phylogenetic reconstruction, using both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness over both classical algorithms and other neural approaches. By learning merge rules directly from target trees, NN-linkage extends efficient HC to scientific and engineering objectives not adequately captured by existing hand-designed linkage rules.

</details>


### [300] [Lock-in EP: An In-Situ Training Algorithm for Oscillatory Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07283)
*Sowjanya Tammali,Wilkie Olin-Ammentorp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Lock-in Equilibrium Propagation (LIEP), a training method for oscillatory networks that provides local gradient information without separate forward/backward sweeps, enabling in-situ learning on analog hardware while handling component variability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analog hardware platforms offer energy efficiency over digital architectures, but large-scale analog systems must be able to operate with or recover from component variability. This paper aims to develop a training method that enables analog oscillatory hardware to learn and adapt.

Method: The authors derive and demonstrate LIEP, which provides local gradient information for each component in an oscillatory network without requiring separate forward and backward sweeps. This allows for potential in-situ learning capabilities on analog oscillatory hardware platforms.

Result: LIEP can be used for ab-initio training (training from scratch) as well as recovering performance when pre-trained parameters are perturbed. The method can be formulated as a three-factor update rule. However, it is currently only validated on shallow networks.

Conclusion: LIEP presents a promising approach for training analog oscillatory hardware, but its current limitation to shallow networks requires further research on alternate architectures to extend it to deep and large-scale networks capable of addressing complex tasks.

Abstract: Analog hardware platforms offer the potential to reduce energy consumption over digital architectures, but in order to succeed, large-scale analog systems must also be able to operate with or recover from the variability of their components. Towards this goal, we derive and demonstrate the lock-in equilibrium propagation (LIEP) training method. LIEP provides local gradient information for each component in an oscillatory network without separate forward and backward sweeps, potentially allowing for in-situ learning capabilities on analog oscillatory hardware platforms. We demonstrate that LIEP can be used both for ab-initio training as well as recovering performance when pre-trained parameters are perturbed. We show that LIEP can be formulated as a three-factor update rule, and suggest that although the method is currently only validated on shallow networks, alternate architectures may allow it to extend to deep and large-scale networks addressing complex tasks.

</details>


### [301] [FlexiFlow: Bandit-based Model Switching in ML Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07286)
*Abhilash Jindal,Todd Nief,Bhanu Prakash Vangala,Shankaradithyaa V,Tvisha Malik,Anshik Sahu,Aaron Schein,Amitabh Chaudhary,Tanu Malik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlexiFlow is a dataflow system that dynamically switches between alternate ML models when the current model exhibits low accuracy, using a multi-armed bandit approach that considers model runtimes, user-defined assertions, and workflow computational structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ML systems rely on a single model for inference across all data batches, which fails to maximize accuracy. Real ML workflows show that switching models can improve accuracy by up to 23%, but existing systems lack adaptive model switching capabilities, forcing manual testing.

Method: FlexiFlow uses a novel multi-armed bandit approach that learns to rank models by accounting for: (1) model runtimes, (2) probability of passing user-defined assertions, and (3) computational structure of the ML workflow. The system reuses intermediate results when switching models.

Result: Standard Thompson sampling is insufficient for switching models in ML workflows. The proposed approach achieves up to 23% accuracy improvement and 48% efficiency gain compared to sequential workflow runs by switching models at runtime while reusing intermediate results.

Conclusion: Adaptive model switching based on data characteristics is essential for maximizing ML workflow accuracy. FlexiFlow's approach effectively scales to complex real-world ML workflows and provides both higher accuracy and significant efficiency gains through intelligent model selection and result reuse.

Abstract: Model optimizations help improve inference performance and accuracy of ML workflows. However, relying on a single model to perform inference across all data batches often fails to maximize accuracy and thus overall performance. In many cases, alternate models could perform better on specific subsets of data where a primary model underperforms. Our experiments with real ML workflows indeed show that switching models improves workflow accuracy by up to 23%. Yet, current systems lack the ability to adaptively switch between models based on performance, forcing users to manually test models in sequence. We present FlexiFlow, a dataflow system that dynamically switches between alternate models when the current model exhibits low accuracy. FlexiFlow learns to rank models using a novel multi-armed bandit approach that accounts for model runtimes, probability of passing user-defined assertions, and the computational structure of the ML workflow. We show that the standard Thompson sampling approach is insufficient for switching models in ML workflows. In contrast, our proposed approaches are effective and scales to complex real-world ML workflows. Experiments show that switching models at runtime while reusing intermediate results provides higher accuracy, but also 48% efficiency gain compared to sequential workflow runs.

</details>


### [302] [ATLAS-AL: Adaptive Trust-Region for Latent Adversarial Searches via Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07323)
*Marsalis Gibson,Claire Tomlin,Shankar Sastry*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ATLAS is a query-based framework that discovers adversarial input sets for black-box learning systems by casting attack generation as active learning level set estimation, combining calibrated approximations with local-global sampling to find and sample from adversarial regions in the input space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current security evaluation of learning-based systems relies on testing against fixed attack collections, which is insufficient. There is a need for adaptive mechanisms that can efficiently discover sets of inputs that induce model failure for comprehensive robustness assessment.

Method: ATLAS combines: (1) active learning level set estimation for attack generation, (2) calibrated approximations, and (3) a local-global sampling architecture. It first identifies regions of the input space containing adversarial examples, then samples within these regions to build representative adversarial sets.

Result: On toy experiments, ATLAS recovers more adversarial region under limited query budget than previous methods. On standard and adversarially trained MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet models, ATLAS produces better representative attacks than query-based black-box baselines (NES, SignHunter, BayesOpt).

Conclusion: ATLAS serves as an automated red-teaming framework for analyzing robustness of learning-based systems during development and enables continuous auditing to track robustness changes over time.

Abstract: Security evaluation of learning-based systems requires more than just testing the system against a fixed collection of attacks. It requires adaptive mechanisms that can efficiently discover \textit{sets} of inputs that induce model failure. We introduce ATLAS (Adaptive Trust-Regions for Latent Adversarial Searches), which is a query-based framework that discovers adversarial input sets for black-box learning systems. ATLAS casts attack generation as an active learning level set estimation problem then combines calibrated approximations with a local-global sampling architecture to find regions of the input space that contain adversarial examples. Once discovered, ATLAS is designed to sample points within these adversarial regions to build adversarial sets that accurately represent the state of robustness of the target model. When applied on toy experiments, we find that ATLAS is able to recover more of the adversarial region under a limited query budget than does previous work. When applied to standard and adversarially trained MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet model targets, ATLAS produces better representative attacks than other query-based black-box attacks (NES, SignHunter, BayesOpt). ATLAS represents an automated red-teaming framework that can be used for both analyzing the robustness of learning-based systems under development and continuous auditing to see how the robustness of a system changes over time.

</details>


### [303] [Scale-Invariant Training for Time Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07324)
*Ignacy Stepka,Willa Potosnak,Kin G. Olivares,Artur Dubrawski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies and solves a fundamental problem in time series foundation models (TSFMs) called scale-contaminated training (ScaleCon), where series with different magnitudes receive unequal gradient weights during training. The authors prove that computing loss on scaled targets (ScaleIn) makes optimization trajectories fully invariant to arbitrary rescaling of training series, and demonstrate average MASE reductions of 18.8% on GIFT-Eval and 21.9% on M-competitions across four TSFM architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time series foundation models are trained on diverse datasets with vastly different scales (typical magnitudes of values). Existing affine scaling methods like Reversible Instance Normalization (ReVIN) scale inputs but then reverse the transform before computing loss, inadvertently causing high-scale series to dominate training. No consistent convention existed for how to compute training loss in TSFMs.

Method: The authors mathematically prove that for any scale-equivariant scaler and residual loss homogeneous of degree p (including MSE, MAE, and Quantile Loss), computing loss on scaled targets makes every mini-batch gradient invariant to arbitrary independent rescaling of training series. They validate this theoretically through controlled studies on synthetic and real data, then test ScaleIn across four TSFM architectures in pretraining experiments.

Result: ScaleIn lowers MASE in all 24 architecture-benchmark comparisons, with average reductions of 18.8% on GIFT-Eval and 21.9% on M-competitions. Gains extend to supervised neural forecasting (16 of 20 settings). ScaleCon is isolated as the cause of convergence disparity, and ScaleIn corrects it.

Conclusion: Scale-invariant training (ScaleIn) is a simple, provably correct solution that can be adopted with a one-line code change in most existing time series forecasting pipelines. It consistently outperforms scale-contaminated training across architectures, benchmarks, and forecasting settings.

Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are trained on large collections of time series datasets that span various morphologies and domains. This setting exposes models to series whose scales -- typical magnitudes of their values -- can differ substantially. Affine scaling methods such as Reversible Instance Normalization (ReVIN) scale model inputs and reverse the transform before computing the loss. We show that this inversion multiplies each series' gradient by $b^p$ relative to loss on scaled targets, where $b$ is the scaling denominator (e.g., standard deviation) and $p$ is the loss degree. We call this scale-contaminated training (ScaleCon), because the scale of each series consequently becomes an importance weight, causing high-scale series to dominate training. For any scale-equivariant scaler and residual loss that is homogeneous of degree $p$, including MSE, MAE, and Quantile Loss, we prove that computing loss on scaled targets makes every mini-batch gradient and, consequently, the full optimization trajectory invariant to arbitrary independent rescaling of the training series, yielding scale-invariant training (ScaleIn). Notably, existing TSFMs use both objectives, with neither consistent reporting nor a common convention on how to compute training loss. We isolate the convergence disparity induced by ScaleCon and its correction under ScaleIn in controlled studies on synthetic and real data. In pretraining across four TSFM architectures, ScaleIn lowers MASE in all 24 architecture-benchmark comparisons, with average reductions across TSFMs of 18.8% on GIFT-Eval and 21.9% on the M-competitions. The gains extend to supervised neural forecasting, where it lowers MASE in 16 of 20 matched settings. Most existing time series forecasting pipelines can adopt ScaleIn with a one-line code change.

</details>


### [304] [Structuring MoE Expert Selection for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07332)
*Bolian Li,Ting-Yao Hu,Cheng-Yu Hsieh,Sanjoy Chowdhury,Oncel Tuzel,Raviteja Vemulapalli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the co-design of agentic post-training and MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) routing in long-horizon LLM agents. The authors discover that expert selection in off-the-shelf MoE models naturally aligns with agentic trajectories, showing semantic clustering across similar operations. Since standard RL algorithms ignore this specialization, they propose a hierarchical routing control framework that encourages turn-level expert alignment with agentic operations while maintaining token-level consistency, along with an entropy-gated control mechanism for training stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents are frequently implemented using sparse MoE models, but the co-design of agentic behavior and MoE structures remains underexplored. Standard RL algorithms ignore the natural specialization in expert selection, limiting task performance and inference efficiency.

Method: The authors introduce a hierarchical routing control framework with two components: (1) encouraging turn-level expert selections to align with agentic operations (e.g., READ, UPDATE), and (2) regularizing token-level expert selections to maintain local consistency. They also propose an entropy-gated control mechanism to resolve stability issues during post-training.

Result: The routing control framework achieves over 10-point improvements in success rate on all evaluated benchmarks. Expert routing shows more overlap between turns with semantically similar operations (e.g., READ, UPDATE) than between turns with differing operations.

Conclusion: Agentic trajectory structure provides an effective signal for optimizing MoE capacity during RL post-training. The proposed hierarchical routing control framework successfully leverages this structure to improve both task performance and inference efficiency.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents are frequently implemented using sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, yet the co-design of agentic behavior and MoE structures remains underexplored. In this work, we comprehensively study the connections between agentic post-training and MoE expert selection. In off-the-shelf MoE models, we observe expert selection exhibits a specialized structure that naturally aligns with agentic trajectories. Specifically, expert routing overlaps more between turns where the agent performs semantically similar operations (e.g., READ, UPDATE) than between turns with differing operations. However, standard RL algorithms ignore this specialization, allowing the MoE routing to go uncontrolled during training, which empirically limit task performance and inference efficiency. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical routing control framework for agentic tasks. We explicitly encourage turn-level expert selections to align with agentic operations while regularizing token-level expert selections to maintain local consistency. To resolve stability issues that arise during post-training with the proposed methods, we further introduce an entropy-gated control mechanism. Overall, our routing control framework achieves over 10-point improvements in success rate on all evaluated benchmarks. These results demonstrate that agentic trajectory structure provides an effective signal for optimizing MoE capacity during RL post-training.

</details>


### [305] [Weight Oracles: Reading Neural Network Weights with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07334)
*Krishna Kabra,Constantin Venhoff,Christian Schroeder de Witt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Weight Oracles are fine-tuned language models that diagnose neural network properties by reading raw weights directly, without behavioral testing. This approach achieves 99% accuracy in simulating small transformers and AUROC 0.93 on detecting attention-routed backdoors (0.81 on diversified threats), outperforming hand-crafted statistical detectors that fail on threat-model shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current interpretability methods are reactive—they analyze activations produced during forward passes, requiring known inputs to detect hidden capabilities like backdoors. This work proposes a proactive approach that reads weights directly to diagnose network properties without behavioral testing.

Method: Phase I uses a staged curriculum and external chain-of-computation to train an explainer LLM to simulate forward passes of small transformers from weights alone, achieving 99% holdout accuracy. Phase II trains an oracle on natural language diagnostic questions about weight anomalies using benign pathologies, then evaluates zero-shot on backdoors absent from training.

Result: The oracle achieves AUROC 0.93 on attention-routed backdoors and 0.81 across a diversified threat distribution including stealth and adversarially regularized variants. Hand-crafted statistical detectors perform well on specific threat models but collapse on threat-model shift, while the oracle remains uniformly competent across attack types.

Conclusion: The Weight Oracle paradigm is feasible and promising for safety auditing. It outperforms traditional statistical detectors by maintaining uniform competence across diverse attack types. The principal open challenge is scaling to realistic model sizes.

Abstract: Interpretability methods for neural networks are predominantly reactive: they analyse activations produced during specific forward passes, requiring known inputs to find hidden capabilities such as backdoors. We propose Weight Oracles, fine-tuned language models that diagnose properties of a target network by reading its raw weights directly, without behavioural testing. We investigate this paradigm in two phases. Phase I establishes feasibility: through a staged curriculum and an external chain-of-computation that delegates parameter-free operations to deterministic code, an explainer LLM learns to simulate the forward pass of small transformers from their weights, achieving 99% holdout accuracy on unseen targets. Phase II repurposes this infrastructure for safety auditing. We train an oracle on natural language diagnostic questions about weight anomalies using only benign pathologies as training signal, and evaluate it zero-shot on backdoors absent from training. The oracle achieves AUROC 0.93 on attention-routed backdoors and 0.81 across a diversified threat distribution including stealth and adversarially regularized variants. Hand-crafted statistical detectors are sharp on the threat models they implicitly target but collapse on threat-model shift, while the oracle remains uniformly competent across attack types. Scaling to realistic model sizes remains the principal open challenge.

</details>


### [306] [Selective Critique for Cost-Aware LLM Agents in Long-Horizon Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07335)
*Heewon Park,Somin Im,Minhae Kwon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAG (Self-improving Agent with Gated critique) is a cost-aware framework that selectively invokes critique during LLM agent decision-making by estimating the Value of Information (VoI) using action-level ambiguity signals (global entropy and local top-2 margin). It also incorporates online bootstrapped self-improvement to reduce reliance on critique over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improving reliability of LLM agents in long-horizon decision-making, where early mistakes propagate and cause cascading failures. Existing approaches using external critique/deliberation at every step are too costly (token consumption and latency), limiting practical deployment.

Method: 1) Gating mechanism: Uses action-level ambiguity signals (global entropy and local top-2 margin) to estimate utility of critique, approximating Value of Information (VoI) to decide when critique is worth the cost. 2) Online bootstrapped self-improvement: Allows the actor to internalize critic-assisted behaviors and progressively reduce reliance on critique.

Result: On ALFWorld: task success increased from 24.6% to 78.4% while maintaining token budget comparable to ReAct, yielding 3.1× improvement in normalized token efficiency. A 7B actor with 3B critic achieves performance comparable to a 14B actor without critique.

Conclusion: Selective critique invocation can recover most reliability benefits of deliberation while dramatically reducing inference cost. The framework substantially improves performance-cost trade-off compared to both no-critique and always-on critique agents across multiple benchmarks and backbone models.

Abstract: Improving the reliability of large language model (LLM) agents in long-horizon decision-making remains a key challenge. When deployed as autonomous agents interacting with complex environments, early mistakes can propagate through trajectories and cause cascading failures. Recent approaches improve reliability by incorporating external critique or deliberation, but invoking these mechanisms at every step substantially increases token consumption and latency, limiting practical deployment. We propose SAG (Self-improving Agent with Gated critique), a cost-aware framework that formulates critique invocation as a step-wise decision problem during long-horizon interaction. SAG introduces a lightweight, training-free gating mechanism that estimates the utility of critique using action-level ambiguity signals--global entropy and local top-2 margin--computed over admissible actions. From a decision-theoretic perspective, this mechanism approximates the Value of Information (VoI) of critique, enabling the agent to selectively allocate expensive feedback only when its expected benefit justifies the cost. SAG further incorporates online bootstrapped self-improvement, allowing the actor to internalize critic-assisted behaviors and progressively reduce reliance on critique. Across three long-horizon interactive benchmarks and multiple backbone models, SAG substantially improves the performance-cost trade-off compared with both no-critique and always-on critique agents. On ALFWorld, SAG increases task success from 24.6% to 78.4% while maintaining a token budget comparable to ReAct, yielding a $3.1\times$ improvement in normalized token efficiency. Moreover, a 7B actor with a lightweight 3B critic achieves performance comparable to a 14B actor without critique, showing that selective critique can recover most of the reliability benefits of deliberation while dramatically reducing inference cost.

</details>


### [307] [CausalBind: Causal Modeling and Learning for Protein-Molecule Virtual Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07340)
*Loka Li,Jin Tian,Kun Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes CausalBind, a novel approach for protein-molecule virtual screening that leverages sparse interaction patterns through causal modeling. The method addresses limitations of existing dense holistic alignment approaches by identifying and utilizing sparse cross-modality interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, salt bridges) that govern binding, rather than relying on global protein and molecule structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing protein-molecule virtual screening methods rely on dense holistic alignment, which entangles invariant binding determinants with nuisance correlations and limits transfer to new targets. The authors hypothesize that uncovering and leveraging sparse interaction patterns (small contact interfaces and decisive local interactions) is critical for generalization beyond training data.

Method: The authors formalize the problem using a V-structure causal model under Heckman-style selection, establishing three theoretical results: (i) latent concepts of interacting proteins and molecules are not identifiable without sparsity constraints; (ii) these concepts and their sparse interactions are component-wise identifiable under structural sparsity conditions; (iii) low-rank relaxation yields subspace identifiability. Based on these principles, they propose CausalBind with three implementation variants.

Result: Extensive experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks show that all variants consistently outperform strong retrieval baselines, with the largest gains on LIT-PCBA early enrichment. The method further generalizes to target- and scaffold-level out-of-distribution splits.

Conclusion: The hypothesis is verified: leveraging sparse interaction patterns is indeed critical for generalization beyond training data. The causal modeling approach with sparsity constraints provides theoretical justification and practical improvements for protein-molecule virtual screening, demonstrating superior performance across various benchmarks and out-of-distribution scenarios.

Abstract: Protein-molecule virtual screening is increasingly cast as a problem of representation learning in a shared embedding space. Existing methods rely on dense holistic alignment, entangling invariant binding determinants with nuisance correlations and limiting transfer to new targets. It has been noted that binding in protein-molecule systems involves sparse cross-modality interactions: binding is governed by a small contact interface and a few decisive local interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and salt bridges) rather than the global structures of the protein and molecule. We hypothesize that uncovering and leveraging sparse interaction patterns is critical for generalization beyond the training data, as these patterns are reusable and expected to improve performance across different scenarios. In this paper, we aim to identify and leverage sparse interaction patterns, and verify our hypothesis. Since the training data contain only observed binding pairs, we formalize this prior via a V-structure causal model under Heckman-style selection, and establish three theoretical results: (i) the latent concepts of interacting proteins and molecules are not identifiable without appropriate sparsity constraints; (ii) these concepts and their sparse interactions are component-wise identifiable under structural sparsity conditions; and (iii) a low-rank relaxation of these conditions yields subspace identifiability of the concepts and interactions. Inspired by these principles, we propose CausalBind with three implementation variants. Extensive experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks show that all variants consistently outperform strong retrieval baselines, with the largest gains on LIT-PCBA early enrichment, and further generalize to target- and scaffold-level out-of-distribution splits. Code is available at https://github.com/lokali/CausalBind.

</details>


### [308] [Stepped MoE: Segment-Level Routing with Configurable Inference Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07348)
*Arnav Kundu,Zhaoyang Xu,Bairu Hou,Chang Gao,Reed Li,Tao Lei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified framework that combines elastic architectures with sparsely gated models to enable LLMs to adapt to both deployment constraints (memory, compute) and task requirements simultaneously. A single model can flexibly use 1-4 billion parameters while outperforming dense counterparts by 2-5% on knowledge-intensive benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training large language models is resource-intensive, and existing approaches treat elastic architectures (flexible deployment) and sparsely activated models (input-adaptive computation) independently. Additionally, on-device edge inference needs to conform to memory and compute limitations of serving devices.

Method: The approach uses a model backbone that conditions on both context and target efficiency specifications, enabling fine-grained control over accuracy-efficiency trade-off at inference time. The model learns to activate task-relevant parameters within elastically-nested sub-networks, allowing a single model to span multiple capacity points while maintaining input-adaptive routing.

Result: The model allows flexibility to use 1,2,3,4 billion parameters while being more accurate than dense counterparts (2-5% improvement on knowledge-intensive benchmarks) and at par with static versions while delivering similar latency metrics as dense models.

Conclusion: The framework saves device disk space through parameter sharing, allows flexibility of serving based on DRAM and compute available, and delivers more accurate results than comparable dense models.

Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) is resource-intensive, and adapting them for diverse deployment scenarios with varying computational constraints remains challenging. While elastic architectures enable flexible model deployment and sparsely activated models allow input-adaptive computation, existing approaches treat these dimensions independently. Moreover, models catered towards on-device edge inference need to conform to the memory and compute limitations of the serving devices. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework that combines elastic structures with sparsely gated architectures to create models that adapt simultaneously to both deployment constraints and task requirements. Our approach employs a model backbone that conditions on both the context and target efficiency specifications, enabling fine-grained control over the accuracy-efficiency trade-off at inference time. The model learns to activate task-relevant parameters within elastically-nested sub-networks, allowing a single model to span multiple capacity points while maintaining input-adaptive routing. Through experiments we demonstrate that we can create a model that allows the flexibility to use 1,2,3,4 billion parameters while being more accurate than their dense counter-parts (2-5\% on knowledge-intensive benchmarks) and at par with their static versions while delivering similar latency metrics as dense models. Overall, we save on device disk space by sharing the model parameters, allow flexibility of serving based on DRAM and compute available while delivering more accurate results.

</details>


### [309] [RELACE: retrospective likelihood-based action credit estimation for long-horizon language agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07349)
*Sayak Chakrabarti,Sathish Reddy Indurthi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RELACE is a critic-free framework for training multi-turn agents that combines retrospective action assessment with state-conditioned advantage estimation. It evaluates actions through likelihood scoring under original and outcome-augmented contexts, using the resulting factor to reweight discounted returns and construct local advantages. Achieves 96.35% on ALFWorld and 79.43% on WebShop with 1.5B model, outperforming GRPO, GiGPO, and HCAPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GRPO's trajectory-level supervision provides coarse, noisy credit assignment for multi-turn agents - terminal rewards cannot locate errors and penalize useful actions alongside mistakes. Existing methods like GiGPO still suffer from credit estimates sensitive to downstream outcomes. Fine-grained, outcome-aware credit assignment without critics is needed.

Method: RELACE evaluates executed actions through teacher-forced likelihood scoring under both original contexts and outcome-augmented contexts. Comparing these likelihoods yields a trajectory-normalized retrospective factor capturing outcome-dependent changes in action plausibility. This factor reweights discounted task returns; local advantages are constructed by comparing weighted returns among actions from equivalent states within a task. Temporal smoothing and success-protecting masking stabilize the signal. No auxiliary value models, reward models, or additional autoregressive rollouts required.

Result: With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: 96.35% success on ALFWorld (+5.47pp over GiGPO), 79.43% on WebShop (+5.60pp over GiGPO). Also tested with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Substantial improvements over GRPO, GiGPO, and HCAPO.

Conclusion: RELACE successfully addresses credit assignment in multi-turn agents through retrospective likelihood-based action assessment. It provides fine-grained credit that couples retrospective relevance with observed reward, achieving state-of-the-art results without requiring critics, reward models, or additional rollouts.

Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) avoids a separate critic by estimating advantages from rollout groups. For multi-turn agents, however, trajectory-level supervision provides coarse, noisy credit: terminal rewards do not locate errors and can penalize useful actions alongside mistakes. Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO) and subsequent methods refine supervision through state-conditioned comparisons, but their credit estimates remain sensitive to downstream decisions and outcomes. We introduce RELACE, Retrospective Likelihood-based Action, a critic-free framework that integrates retrospective action assessment with state-conditioned advantage estimation. RELACE evaluates executed actions through teacher-forced likelihood scoring under both their original contexts and outcome-augmented contexts. Comparing these likelihoods yields a trajectory-normalized retrospective factor that captures outcome-dependent changes in action plausibility, rather than hindsight plausibility alone. We use this factor to reweight discounted task returns and construct local advantages by comparing weighted returns among actions from equivalent states within a task. This couples retrospective relevance with observed reward, producing fine-grained credit that complements trajectory-level GRPO supervision. Temporal smoothing and success-protecting masking further stabilize the local signal. RELACE requires neither auxiliary value nor reward models nor additional autoregressive rollouts for credit estimation. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate substantial improvements over GRPO, GiGPO, and HCAPO. With the 1.5B model, RELACE achieves $96.35\%$ success on ALFWorld and $79.43\%$ on WebShop, surpassing GiGPO by $5.47$ and $5.60$ percentage points, respectively.

</details>


### [310] [Towards Explainable Benchmarking for Data-driven Post-Wildfire Debris Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07358)
*Zhisheng Qi,Li Zhu,Utkarsh Sahu,Douglas Tommey,Josh Roering,Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified benchmark for data-driven post-wildfire debris flow (PFDF) prediction and a reinforcement learning-based feature selection framework to identify key triggering factors across different regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current data-driven PFDF prediction research is fragmented with inconsistent feature spaces, model architectures, and evaluation protocols, making rigorous comparison impossible. Additionally, there's a lack of systematic investigation into the relative importance of heterogeneous factors (meteorological, terrain, soil, burn severity) in triggering PFDFs.

Method: The authors develop: (1) a unified benchmark enabling fair and comprehensive evaluation across diverse models and feature configurations; (2) a reinforcement learning-based feature selection framework that identifies factors whose perturbations make positive and negative events indistinguishable, revealing regional mechanisms of PFDF occurrence.

Result: The paper provides a standardized evaluation platform and discovers regional underlying mechanisms of PFDF occurrence through intelligent feature analysis.

Conclusion: The proposed benchmark and feature selection framework address critical gaps in PFDF prediction research, enabling better understanding of triggering factors and facilitating more accurate predictions across different regions.

Abstract: Post-wildfire debris flows (PFDFs) are destructive sediment-laden hazards triggered when intense rainfall strikes recently burned terrain, destabilizing hillslopes and threatening infrastructure, local economies, and community safety. Data-driven methods have been proposed to learn predictive patterns directly from historical PFDF observations. However, the current research landscape of data-driven PFDF prediction remains highly fragmented across feature spaces, model architectures, and evaluation protocols, making rigorous comparison and the derivation of scientific insights difficult. Moreover, existing studies lack a systematic investigation into the relative importance of heterogeneous factors (e.g., meteorological conditions, terrain characteristics, soil properties, and burn severity) in triggering PFDF. To address these limitations, we present a unified benchmark for data-driven PFDF prediction, enabling fair and comprehensive evaluation across diverse models and feature configurations. Furthermore, to better understand the underlying drivers of PFDF formation, we propose a reinforcement learning-based feature selection framework that identifies factors whose perturbations render positive and negative events indistinguishable, thereby discovering the regional underlying mechanisms of PFDF occurrence across regions. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/KINDLab-Fly/PFDF-Benchmark.

</details>


### [311] [Dynamic Budget Allocation for LLM Evaluation under Hard Resource Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07362)
*Shai Feldman,Yaniv Romano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARP is a budget allocation method for evaluating LLMs in multi-turn interactions that satisfies hard resource constraints and adaptively reallocates unused budget. It constructs lower predictive bounds on time-to-event (e.g., jailbreak success) and provides unbiased metric estimates with finite-sample coverage guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing budget allocation methods for calibrating time-to-event bounds in LLM evaluation only satisfy budget in expectation and can exceed available budget on particular runs. Enforcing hard budget constraints is challenging because trajectory costs are initially unknown in multi-turn interactions where events like jailbreaks or task completion may occur at varying steps.

Method: HARP (Hard-budget Allocation with Reflow for Predictive calibration) uses adaptive budget reallocation to handle censored event times. It satisfies hard resource constraints by tracking and reallocating unused budget across trajectories. The method constructs Lower Predictive Bounds (LPBs) on time-to-event and estimates evaluation metrics like jailbreak rates with theoretical guarantees.

Result: HARP was evaluated on four domains: agentic task success, LLM jailbreaks, toxic content generation, and RAG hallucinations. The method achieves coverage close to the nominal level with low variance while never exceeding the given budget. Theoretical guarantees include: (1) never exceeding target budget, (2) finite-sample coverage for LPBs, and (3) unbiased metric estimates.

Conclusion: HARP provides a practical solution for budget-constrained LLM evaluation in multi-turn settings, enabling reliable estimation of time-to-event metrics and evaluation metrics (e.g., jailbreak rates) under hard budget constraints with theoretical guarantees. This addresses a critical gap in LLM benchmarking methodology.

Abstract: We evaluate large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn interactions through their time-to-event: the number of interaction steps required to produce an event of interest, such as a successful jailbreak or agentic task completion. Under limited compute, interactions may be terminated before the event occurs, so that event times are only partially observed (censored). Existing allocation methods for calibrating time-to-event bounds satisfy the budget only in expectation and can exceed the available budget on a particular evaluation run. Enforcing a hard constraint is particularly challenging as the cost of a trajectory is initially unknown. We introduce Hard-budget Allocation with Reflow for Predictive calibration (HARP), a budget allocation that satisfies hard resource constraints and adaptively reallocates unused budget. We show how to use HARP to construct lower predictive bounds (LPBs) on the time-to-event and to estimate evaluation metrics such as the jailbreak rate on a fixed benchmark. Although HARP induces dependence in acquisition decisions across different trajectories, we prove that HARP never exceeds the target budget, that its LPBs have finite-sample coverage guarantees, and that its metric estimates are unbiased. Experiments on agentic task success, LLM jailbreaks, toxic content generation, and RAG hallucinations show that HARP achieves coverage close to the nominal level with low variance, while never exceeding the given budget.

</details>


### [312] [Multigroup Fairness and Omniprediction: Separations and Equivalences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07374)
*Sílvia Casacuberta,Parikshit Gopalan,Varun Kanade,Omer Reingold,Konstantinos Stavropoulos,Pranay Tankala*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves whether omniprediction requires multigroup fairness notions. The authors show that plain omniprediction does NOT require such fairness conditions (counterexample: omniprediction for proper losses doesn't imply accuracy in expectation), but the stronger notion of Loss OI IS equivalent to calibrated multiaccuracy, meaning loss OI does require multigroup fairness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether omniprediction (a strong learning guarantee) necessarily requires some form of multigroup fairness notions (like multicalibration or multiaccuracy). This question arises because most known omniprediction algorithms rely on these fairness notions, but it was unclear if this dependence is fundamental.

Method: The authors use two main approaches: (1) Constructing counterexamples to show that omniprediction does not imply weaker fairness notions, and (2) Establishing equivalence proofs between loss OI and calibrated multiaccuracy through theoretical analysis.

Result: The paper establishes two key results: (1) Omniprediction for proper losses does not imply accuracy in expectation, ruling out even weak converses to previous implications. (2) Loss OI is equivalent to a form of calibrated multiaccuracy, showing that loss OI (which implies omniprediction) does require multigroup fairness notions.

Conclusion: The answer to the question "Does omniprediction require multigroup fairness?" is nuanced: NO for plain omniprediction, but YES for the stronger notion of loss OI. This clarifies the relationship between these learning guarantees and provides a clear boundary for when fairness notions are necessary.

Abstract: Omniprediction is a learning guarantee which requires a single predictor to be competitive relative to the best hypothesis from a benchmark class for any loss chosen from a family of loss functions. Loss Outcome Indistinguishability (loss OI for short) is a stronger notion that implies omniprediction. It requires the predicted distribution on labels to be indistinguishable from the true distribution to tests that depend on the loss functions and the benchmark class. Multiaccuracy and multicalibration are multigroup fairness notions that generalize classical notions of calibration and accuracy in expectation. Most known learning algorithms for omniprediction (both for the standard notion and for strengthenings like loss OI) rely on some version of these multigroup fairness notions, or on an intermediate notion called calibrated multiaccuracy. We ask if this is necessary: Does omniprediction require some form of multigroup fairness?
  We show that the answer is no for (plain) omniprediction, and yes for loss OI. First, a sequence of works shows that multicalibration or calibrated multiaccuracy imply omniprediction. We rule out even a weak converse, by showing that omniprediction for proper losses does not imply even accuracy in expectation, a much weaker notion than any of calibration, multiaccuracy, or multicalibration. Second, prior work showed how to achieve loss OI from a combination of calibration and multiaccuracy. We show a converse: loss OI is equivalent to a form of calibrated multiaccuracy.

</details>


### [313] [Inference and learning in sparse autoencoders as natural gradient flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07389)
*Hadi Vafaii,Tejas Rao,David Chanin,Thomas Fel,Jacob L. Yates,Bruno Olshausen,David Klindt,Dileep George,Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BeFOND unifies inference and dictionary learning in sparse autoencoders using natural-gradient flows on variational free energy, improving recovery of overlapping and rare features in neural network representations compared to amortized baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse autoencoders struggle with reliable feature recovery when features overlap (superposition) or activate infrequently (rare features). Existing methods treat inference and dictionary learning separately, leading to interference between overlapping features and slow learning of rare features.

Method: BeFOND is an encoder-free sparse coding model with closed-form inference and learning dynamics, using natural-gradient flows on a shared variational free energy. It incorporates recurrent explaining away to reduce interference between overlapping features and Fisher preconditioning to compensate for slow learning of rare features.

Result: On synthetic data, BeFOND improves dictionary recovery and rare-feature detection, with growing advantage over amortized baselines as superposition increases. On language-model activations, it improves single-feature concept detection and selective intervention, outperforming pretrained reference SAEs with substantially less training data. Feature quality continues to improve with dictionary width while baselines plateau.

Conclusion: Unifying inference and learning within a probabilistic framework enables better data utilization and dictionary capacity for interpreting and intervening on neural representations, particularly for overcoming superposition and rare-feature challenges.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders are widely used to uncover interpretable features in neural networks, yet reliable recovery remains difficult when features overlap or activate infrequently. These challenges involve both inferring which features explain an input and learning the dictionary that represents them. Here, we unify inference and dictionary learning as natural-gradient flows on a shared variational free energy. We instantiate this framework as BeFOND, an encoder-free sparse coding model with closed-form inference and learning dynamics. We show how recurrent explaining away reduces interference between overlapping features, while Fisher preconditioning can compensate for the slow learning of rare features. On synthetic data, BeFOND improves dictionary recovery and rare-feature detection, with a growing advantage over amortized baselines as superposition increases. On language-model activations, it improves single-feature concept detection and selective intervention, outperforming pretrained reference SAEs with substantially less training data. Its feature quality continues to improve with dictionary width, whereas the evaluated baselines largely plateau. Together, these results show how improving inference and learning within a unified probabilistic framework can make better use of data and dictionary capacity to interpret and intervene on neural representations.

</details>


### [314] [Fed-BRDECS: Privacy-Preserving and Heterogeneity-Aware Federated Deep Embedded Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07399)
*Haemin Park,Diego Klabjan,Martin W. Braun,Xiuqi Li,Balakrishnan Ananthanarayanan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fed-BRDECS is a privacy-preserving federated deep embedded clustering framework that addresses the privacy leakage issue in DEC-style objectives by replacing global soft-assignment statistics with a locally computable sample-stability loss. It also tackles non-IID data distribution through prediction-balanced sampling and centroid-level restarting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC)-style objectives rely on global soft-assignment statistics that require clients to transmit sensitive local information, compromising privacy. Additionally, non-IID data distributions across clients pose significant challenges in federated learning.

Method: Fed-BRDECS introduces three key innovations: (1) sample-stability loss replacing global clustering objectives to enable local computation without transmitting soft-assignment distributions; (2) prediction-balanced sampling that oversamples locally rare predicted clusters without ground-truth labels; and (3) centroid-level restarting to refresh biased or inactive centroids.

Result: Experiments on image and text clustering benchmarks show consistent performance improvements over federated clustering and deep clustering baselines under both IID and non-IID partitions. The method also improves reconstruction-based detectors in federated time-series anomaly detection without adding inference-time cost.

Conclusion: Fed-BRDECS successfully achieves privacy-preserving federated deep clustering while handling heterogeneous data distributions, demonstrating practical applicability beyond clustering to time-series anomaly detection.

Abstract: Federated deep clustering seeks to learn clustering-friendly representations from decentralized unlabeled data while preserving client privacy. However, Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC)-style objectives depend on global soft-assignment statistics that require clients to reveal their sensitive information. We propose Fed-BRDECS, a privacy-preserving and heterogeneity-aware federated deep embedded clustering framework. Fed-BRDECS replaces the globally normalized clustering objective with a locally computable sample-stability loss, avoiding the transmission of local soft-assignment distributions. To tackle non-IID client distributions, we introduce prediction-balanced sampling, which oversamples locally rare predicted clusters without requiring ground-truth labels, and centroid-level restarting, which periodically refreshes biased or inactive centroids. Experiments on image and text clustering benchmarks show that Fed-BRDECS consistently outperforms representative federated clustering and deep clustering baselines under both IID and non-IID partitions. We further demonstrate its applicability to federated time-series anomaly detection, where it improves reconstruction-based detectors without adding inference-time cost.

</details>


### [315] [What pass@k Cannot Measure: Evaluating Diversity and Capability Retention after Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07405)
*Subham Rath,Raj Dandekar,Rajat Dandekar,Sreedath Panat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that pass@k, the standard evaluation metric for RL post-training, fails to capture output diversity - a critical property it is used to certify. Training Qwen2.5-1.5B with GRPO and RFT on grade-school math shows diversity measures move in opposite directions while pass@k shows no consistent winner.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field uses pass@k (fraction of problems solved within k attempts) as the default metric for evaluating RL post-training improvements, but this metric depends only on problem probability of correct samples with no term for how correctness is distributed across outputs. The authors investigate whether this gap is merely academic or has practical consequences.

Method: Training Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on grade-school math using two methods: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT, training on shortest verifier-passed rollouts). They measure three diversity measures (token-level entropy, answer-level entropy, unique answers per prompt) across three seeds per arm, and test pass@8 and pass@32 on GSM8K and a hard MATH-500 subset.

Result: Diversity measures move in opposite directions with zero overlap across three seeds. This persists even when restricting to verifier-correct completions (lexical diversity among correct solutions is 15% lower for GRPO after controlling for length) and when isolating diversity among incorrect answers. pass@8 and pass@32 show no consistent winner on GSM8K; the hard MATH-500 subset shows separation only at low k. Compared to the starting checkpoint, no trained arm significantly improves hard-problem coverage (RFT is significantly worse, GRPO is statistically indistinguishable). Only pass@1 separates the arms, rewarding the arm whose correct solutions are least diverse.

Conclusion: pass@k misses detecting output diversity - a property it is routinely used to certify. GRPO's pass@1 edge over RFT reflects smaller loss relative to the base model, not a capability gain. This is a missing-control issue in standard evaluation protocols, not a failure of pass@k itself.

Abstract: pass@$k$, the fraction of problems a model solves within $k$ sampled attempts, is the field's default protocol for deciding whether reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training on verifiable rewards improved a model. At the population level, pass@$k$ depends only on a problem's probability of a correct sample, with no term for how it is distributed across outputs. We show this gap is not academic. Training Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on grade-school math with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and with rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT, training on the model's own shortest verifier-passed rollout) moves three complementary diversity measures (token-level entropy, answer-level entropy, unique answers per prompt) in opposite directions, with zero overlap across three seeds per arm. The gap survives restricting to verifier-correct completions only (lexical diversity among correct solutions is 15% lower for GRPO, after controlling for length) and a count-controlled check isolating diversity among incorrect answers alone, ruling out that GRPO's higher accuracy alone explains it. Yet pass@8 and pass@32 show no consistent winner on GSM8K, and a hard MATH-500 subset shows the same pattern: separation only at low $k$. Compared against the starting checkpoint, no trained arm significantly improves hard-problem coverage: RFT is significantly worse, while GRPO is statistically indistinguishable from it - so GRPO's pass@1 edge over RFT reflects a smaller loss relative to Base, not a capability gain, a missing-control issue, not a failure of pass@$k$. On GSM8K, only pass@1, with no role in detecting diversity by construction, separates the arms cleanly, rewarding the arm whose correct solutions are least diverse. We argue this is a concrete instance of a standard evaluation protocol missing a property it is routinely used to certify.

</details>


### [316] [Evaluation of Active Feature Acquisition Policies with Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07406)
*Yuta Kobayashi,Divyam Madaan,Shalmali Joshi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses active feature acquisition in offline settings using PFNs. The key contribution is identifying and correcting a bias in total predictive entropy that conflates epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, leading to suboptimal feature acquisition policies. The proposed solution targets posterior expected entropy instead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Active feature acquisition learns policies to sequentially acquire features. However, evaluating these policies from finite offline data is challenging. The authors discovered that using total predictive entropy as a reward creates an epistemic bias that unfairly penalizes sparsely observed features, because it conflates two distinct types of uncertainty: epistemic (data scarcity) and aleatoric (inherent feature uninformiveness).

Method: The authors use Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), which are off-the-shelf models that output posterior predictive distributions without task-specific training. Instead of using total predictive entropy (which includes epistemic uncertainty), they propose targeting the posterior expected (aleatoric) entropy for evaluating feature acquisitions.

Result: Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed approach: 1) consistently reduces value estimation bias, 2) yields credible intervals with strong empirical coverage, 3) translates to improved downstream policy selection.

Conclusion: By separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty in the reward signal, the method enables more accurate evaluation and selection of active feature acquisition policies from offline data, addressing a fundamental limitation in applying active learning to offline settings.

Abstract: Active feature acquisition learns policies that sequentially acquire features to maximize information about a target variable. We study how to learn and evaluate such policies from finite offline data using prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), which are off-the-shelf models that output posterior predictive distributions without task-specific training. We show that under the imbalanced coverage of offline data, using total predictive entropy as a reward creates an epistemic bias that penalizes acquiring sparsely observed features. Specifically, this reward conflates epistemic uncertainty (arising from lack of offline data) with aleatoric uncertainty (arising from uninformative features). To address this, we target the posterior expected (aleatoric) entropy instead of the total predictive entropy output by a PFN for evaluating feature acquisitions. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently reduces value estimation bias and yields credible intervals with strong empirical coverage, which can translate to improved downstream policy selection.

</details>


### [317] [Learnable Spectral Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07419)
*Tamir Shor,Or Litany,Alex Bronstein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Learnable spectral activations (LSA) replace fixed neuron nonlinearities with learnable truncated Fourier series, enabling separate optimization of feature selection (linear weights) and spectral shaping (activation coefficients), improving INR performance across various domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current INR methods improve fitting by modifying frequency access via coordinate encodings or periodic nonlinearities, but overlook a key bottleneck: networks struggle to efficiently compose frequencies into multi-harmonic internal responses, especially for signals with localized or spatially varying structure.

Method: LSA replaces fixed activation functions with a residual truncated Fourier series where harmonic amplitudes are learned during training. This creates a factorization where linear weights control feature selection while activation coefficients control spectral shaping, with separate gradient updates. The activation output is affine in coefficients given fixed pre-activations.

Result: Empirically, LSA concentrates more target-signal energy in the leading eigenmodes of the neural tangent kernel, consistent with improved optimization behavior. Across audio, image, neural radiance field (NeRF), and neural acoustic field tasks, LSA improves reconstruction quality.

Conclusion: LSA provides a new dimension of improvement for INRs beyond frequency access—by factoring spectral tuning from feature selection, it enables more direct optimization of the network's spectral response, leading to better reconstruction across multiple signal domains.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) are shaped by the spectral structure induced by their input encodings and activation functions. Existing methods improve fitting primarily by modifying which frequencies are available to the network, through coordinate encodings or periodic nonlinearities. However, frequency access is not the only bottleneck: signals with localized or spatially varying structure require the network to efficiently compose frequencies into multi-harmonic internal responses. We introduce learnable spectral activations (LSA), which replace fixed neuron-level nonlinearities with a residual truncated Fourier series whose harmonic amplitudes are learned during training. LSA does not expand the asymptotic function class. Instead, it changes the factorization of the representation: linear weights select features while activation coefficients control spectral shaping, and the two are updated by separate gradients. Because the activation output is affine in the coefficients given fixed pre-activations, spectral tuning becomes a more direct subproblem compared to architectures where it is entangled with feature selection. Empirically, this factorization concentrates more target-signal energy in the leading eigenmodes of the neural tangent kernel, consistent with improved optimization behavior. Across audio, image, neural radiance field, and neural acoustic field tasks, LSA also improves reconstruction quality.

</details>


### [318] [Benchmarking Label-Revealed Online Updates for EEG BCI Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07420)
*Bogdan Kozyrskiy,Artem Grachev,Abraham I. Camelo Guerrero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses EEG signal drift in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) by presenting a benchmark for online adaptation. It compares Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) and Riemannian covariance-based methods under time-ordered prequential evaluation, examining which pipelines benefit from label-revealed updates, whether controlled forgetting improves robustness, and how cold start compares with pretrained models. Across four datasets, online updates improved 13 of 14 model/dataset pairs with up to 18% accuracy gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG signals drift over time, causing static BCI models to degrade in practical applications. This temporal drift is a fundamental challenge for real-world BCI deployment, requiring models to adapt continuously to maintain performance.

Method: The researchers conducted a benchmark comparison using two widely-used pipeline families: Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) and Riemannian covariance-based methods. They employed time-ordered prequential (test-then-train) evaluation across four datasets (three motor-imagery datasets and one movement-decoding dataset). They investigated three key aspects: (1) which pipelines benefit most from label-revealed updates, (2) whether controlled forgetting of older data improves robustness, and (3) how minimal-calibration cold start compares with pretrained model initialization. They also used Shapley-based data-valuation analysis over temporal blocks.

Result: Label-revealed online updates improved 13 of 14 model/dataset pairs on the two largest streams, with relative accuracy gains of up to approximately 18% over a frozen model. The Shapley-based analysis assigned the largest mean value to the most recent data block in each of the three analyzed datasets, while older blocks retained positive value.

Conclusion: Online adaptation through label-revealed updates is highly effective for BCI models, with most pipeline/dataset combinations showing significant improvement. The most recent data carries the highest value for model adaptation, but older data still contributes positively, suggesting that a balanced approach to data retention is beneficial rather than aggressive forgetting.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals drift over time, which can cause static brain-computer interface (BCI) models to degrade in practice. We present a benchmark for online adaptation and compare two widely used pipeline families, Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) and Riemannian covariance-based methods, under time-ordered prequential (test-then-train) evaluation. We examine (i) which pipelines benefit most from label-revealed updates, (ii) whether controlled forgetting of older data improves robustness, and (iii) how a minimal-calibration cold start compares with starting from a pretrained model. Across four datasets (three motor-imagery datasets and one movement-decoding dataset), label-revealed online updates improve 13 of 14 model/dataset pairs on the two largest streams, with relative accuracy gains of up to about 18% over a frozen model. A Shapley-based data-valuation analysis over temporal blocks assigns the largest mean value to the most recent block in each of the three analyzed datasets, while older blocks retain positive value.

</details>


### [319] [StaFIR: Convex Learning of Stationarity-Aware Causal Filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07430)
*Lorena Egger,Mathis Linger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes StaFIR, a causal FIR filter with learned nonnegative mixture of exponential lag profiles to reduce nonstationarity in persistent time series (particularly financial data). It balances empirical stationarity with input similarity through a convex objective, outperforming traditional ADF-tuned fractional differencing in preserving input signal while maintaining comparable forecasting accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address limitations in existing fractional differencing methods for reducing nonstationarity in financial time series. Current approaches use the ADF test to tune differencing, which limits the search to a one-parameter family of lag profiles and only indirectly addresses input preservation. The authors seek a more flexible approach that can directly balance stationarity with similarity to the original input signal.

Method: The proposed method StaFIR is a causal finite-impulse-response (FIR) filter with a learned nonnegative mixture of exponential lag profiles. It uses a convex learning objective that balances empirical stationarity with similarity to the input. The method was evaluated on ARFIMA-GARCH controlled settings and rolling financial series, including a realized-volatility forecasting task.
